Very disapointing release for this epic franchise game.
I purchased and downloaded this game through Steam (naturally) and had some issues trying to get the game to run.  In the end I had to download an update patch directly from Ubisoft and bypass Steam in order to play.
Like M&M VI, you have to play this game online using Ubisoft's portal, even though the main campaign is single player only. VII has a similar look and feel to VI when you start out but once you get into the game you realize how poorly this game is designed (at least in my opinion.)
Here are some examples:
- Skill wheel from earlier versions is back! But none of the skills actually cross-link nor is there an "uber" skill available if you choose to learn all the skills in the 3 special catagories for any hero.
- Former games allowed you to bond with heroes by building them up from scratch at level 1 through 30 through multiple campaign maps.  Most maps in the campaign scenarios don't continue with the same hero you built up from the last one and the new one they provide you for the 2nd or 3rd map in the scenario is already pre-built and leveled.
- AI is pathetic!  Strong AI heroes will bypass your weak castles, forts, etc.. on their way to their target.
- Combat AI is no better.  At first AI creatures would always move forward automatically right into range of your creatures.  All you had to do was tell your creatures to wait till AI creatures have moved first.  After a recent patch, AI creatures now wait as well, but unfortunately this also includes all ranged AI creatures allowing you always to get your ranged shots off first.
- Battles are ridiculously slow, especialy if you have healing or war units, even when fastest battle options are chosen.
- There does not seem to be any option to make AI heroes aggressive.  All you can do is alter starting resources, weekly resource gain, or neutral creature growth in order to try to make the game difficult.

To be fair to this game, it doesn't exactly warrant as much negativity as it's getting. The game was very unstable prior to the hotfix (10/07/15) but is since far more stable and I personally haven't experienced any crashes. The optimisation is class; everything maxed out at 1440p and I never drop below 60fps whilst driving (4790k, GTX 970), though I have heard that Crossfire and SLi don't work.
It is a fun game, but the simulation element when it comes to car handling and feel is absolutely minimal, even more 'arcade' feeling than the previous games. I've tried multiple settings with my wheel (Thrustmaster Ferrari F430) and with my Xbox 360 gamepad but I just don't get the feeling that the tyres and track are connected, it actually takes a lot of effort to put the car into a spin, on purpose without dropping down into first and purposefully doing a donut, the car generally feels like it's floating around the track; I play with all assists off.
The AI are hit and miss, it seems to vary between practise and qualifying and the actual race; in the actual race, the AI will follow blue flag rules if you're passing some backmarkers, whereas they won't in practise and qualifying. The aggression of the AI has been turned up a notch and it's both good and bad, good because they provide a bit more of a challenge, bad because they'll often just charge straight into you like you're invisible.
Some options are missing, such as career and co-op career. The classic career mode I would have liked to see, moving your way up (or sideways) through different teams as you progress through a career for me, added to the all important immersion. It has instead been replaced with 'Championship season' where you take over a real driver and can't change teams, and 'Pro season' where you're locked into a full race weekend with no assists, parch ferme rules, legend AI, full damage etc...
The engine sounds are absolutely spot on, the engines sound authentic, but the engineer random babble (he never shuts up!) and the menu music can get annoying.
The graphics in my opinion are a backwards step overall, the game looks decent, but not as good as previous iterations in this franchise in certain areas, for instance, I haven't experienced any blocky graphics or texture pop-in, but the cars themselves don't look as good, the mirrors have this strange slideshow thing going on, the AO isn't that strong even when set to X16 and it all has this strange blur effect.
As for multiplayer, I can't comment on it as I'm not interested in it for this particular game.
So do I reccommend it? Yes and no; it is a fun game, but it is not worth the Steam retail price of £39.99. It would be a fun little pastime to snap up on sale though.

The driving physics itself isn't bad at all, its a massive improvement from other titles, and the AI is very competitive and fun (I simrace, and it was awesome to see that when I drove as Massa in the Williams on legendary AI I slotted a realistic 5th behind the Ferraris and Mercedes, even though I gave it my best). Where they dropped the ball though was the TONS of little annoying bugs which really give this game an unfinished feeling (early access-ish), and the biggest problem for me: The blurry graphics. God knows who decided it would be a good idea to blur everything, and making the player think he needs glasses.

The campaign: Fun if you are into futuristic settings. Good story line. Difficulty settings are what you'd expect from a COD title. Decent plot, especially since they included an alternate campaign with zombies in it.
Zombies mode: The map it comes with is a little overly complicated and tight, but you can get the hang of it. Some of the DLC options like Chronicles really save this title and provide fun maps, especially if you enjoyed them in previous titles. Easy to connect with friends or randoms online. The split screen function is a godsend in zombies because none of my friends are PC gamers.
Multiplayer: Here is where I really get to tear it apart. This game's multiplayer is much more fast paced than many previous titles I have played.  If you spawn and dont move to safety within 15 seconds, you will probably die. If you stray from your team, you will die. This game encourages people to run circles around the map and just speed play the matches. If you want to be any sort of tactical without rushing, you will die. As with previous COD games, there is a lag between what happens on your screen and what happens in game. You may shoot and enemy 4 times and get killed by them only to see that 2 of your shots actually happened in game. Very frustrating in  such a fast-paced game. However, when things go right, the game is rather addictcing and can be rather fun if you look past its short comings. A very diverse set of weapons and abilities to play with.
Supply drops: Supply drops are utter BS, especially if you pay for them. I bought a 100 rare supply drop pack and got ZERO guns, 4 melee weapons (useless to me), and dozens of emblems, gun camos, specialist outdits, and calling cards. These things are the worst. Activision advertises all these new weapons they add to the supply drops but your chances of getting them are EXTREMELY low. Spending money on them will only slightly raise your chances of getting a new gun quicker. DO NOT waste money on them. The guns will come eventually. You may get lucky but don't count on it.
Overall: Campaign and zombies are great with only small problems. Multiplayer is not for the faint of heart and will be great for very competitive players. Not so good for those that get frustrated easily.

I wanted this game to be so much better than it was.
I'm no stranger to JRPGs, and I picked this one up on a whim after seeing a lot of good reviews.  And they're mostly right; the things this game does well, it does EXTREMELY well.  The sound and art design are excellent.  Unfortunately, it doesn't have it where it counts: the gameplay.
Battles occur on a tiled field with you at one end and enemies at the other, and you converge to do battle over each individual unit's turn, which can be irregularly spaced depending on the number of units and their relative stats.  That's all well and good, but the game also insists on implementing a randomized bonus system, where on certain turns, whoever is currently acting gets a free boost, be it bonus damage or free healing.  The problem is, there's only one way for the player to influence who gets these bonuses, and it's situational at best.  On Normal difficulty, this is probably permissible, but I went straight to Hard (and there's another one above that) and the game balance just wasn't there.
On top of that, there are certain enemies who can just straight up kill you on their own -- and these are random encounter enemies.  Healing items are too expensive to rely on and healing spells take too long to use (this can be mitigated later, but it's still a significant problem).  Couple that with a clunky upgrade system, always having too few party members to handle a situation, and an obtuse mission system, and I find that I don't have any compelling reason to play it anymore.  I forced myself to pick this game up again after putting it down multiple times, but ultimately, I can't finish it, and it's one of a handful of purchases I actually regret.  I bailed for Dragon Age.

Abe's Oddysee continually pits you against insurmountable odds – or they would be insurmountable without infinite attempts – and still the greatest challenge of the game is Abe himself. I can't count the amount of times I was killed because Abe stopped one step too short to grab a ledge or needed to jump a little too soon after a screen transition. The game's controls suggest it was intended to be more of a point-and-click, where unrefined control isn't an issue. Then the level designer got a hold of it. Now its platforming requires so much precision (precision these loose controls just cannot support) that this game shows more of its age than it really should.
The visuals aren't exactly to today's standards either. More than once I missed a pathway or an obstacle due to how difficult it can be to make out your surroundings. But the superb art direction more than makes up for it. Everything's so grotesquely interesting to look at that it's worth the eye strain.
Similarly, the challenges Abe faces are worth putting in the effort to solve. Their difficulty is made up of how many moving parts each puzzle has, so by the time you understand it, you feel like you've built your own Rube Goldberg machine. It can take several deaths to even figure out a part of what you should be doing and several more to actually do it. This can lead to a lot of repetition as you perform the same sequence you've already memorized over and over again to only catch a glimpse of the next challenge.
For this reason, the most frustrating part of Abe's Oddysee – second only to the controls which certainly exacerbate the issue – is the placement of checkpoints. Sure, their spread out nature does ensure you've truly mastered the full sequence before you move on, but the road to that mastery can become so very dull, and the game drags because of it.
The lack of proper pacing surprisingly doesn't do much damage to the story being told here. On the contrary, the level of challenge only helps to emphasize how small Abe is and how enormous what he's up against is. It also provides a little narrative complexity when it comes to rescuing your fellow captive Mudokons. It's one thing to undertake an extra challenge in order to do what's right, it's another thing entirely to make that decision when you're already exhausted by the overwhelming trials behind and still in front of you. I found myself asking if these innocent Mudokons – no different than Abe/me – were worth saving, and that's not a question I ask myself often.
My experience with this game may have been mostly frustrating and unpleasant, but I'm still left wondering if I should try the 'New and Tasty' remake. I have no nostalgia for Oddworld as this was my first time through this game or any other in this series. But the world set up in Abe's Oddysee really gripped me. With tighter controls and a few more checkpoints, this might be a game I would come back to fairly regularly. But as it is, unless you're looking to relive an old experience, I can't recommend this version. It's not that it's a poor game at all, it's just that parts of it have aged so poorly that it's hard to see that sometimes.

Face It "A game to fight inner demons" is an Indie 3D Platforming game developed by Tlön Studios.
The strange and long title is due to the content and form of the game.
We take control of a character that makes a journey through life, represented in these dark and dangerous levels filled with obstacles.
While exploring the levels, texts/quotes (Aleister Crowley, Oscar Wilde, Carl Sagan) will show up introducing the player to the essence of the level itself, and how to approach them in order to succeed.
Of course to succeed we will have to face hordes of ghosts, spikes, and a deadly enviroment suspended in the void with the help of a flashlight, our jump skills and the "Sigils".
These "Sigils" are the core of the game, each one will grant the player an abbility, from double jump to invincibility, with them we will have to face the puzzles/fears.
Will will have to find collectables well hidden in each level in order to unlock its harder version, for the extra challenge.
Thats 59 levels divided in 4 Worlds.
Quite fun game, and brutally cheap!
8/11 but worth buying Good story

+ The gameplay never gets boring, I can compare it only to the Just Cause 3 in this regard (not a fan of GTA series though).
+ Nice dynamic atmosphere compared to the always-on-noire of the original WatchDogs.
+ Great skill tree progression mechanics, no more mission-locked skills and progression pushes you towards exploration.
+ Runs much smoother than the first WatchDogs (no more stutter while racing) and much much more optimized in terms of the HDD throughput.
+ Really nasty police, making you to play more civil and less GTA-style.
+ I like playing as a trickster (neutralizing the guards using the environment while sitting somewhere safe, sometimes with a rifle-and-scope) and this game really shines at that.
Cons:
- There could be more hotkeys for the smartphone features.
- Annoying multiplayer (the gameplay is fine, but the events frequency is overwhelming).
- Fast travel makes some missions too easy.
- Police/gangsters NPCs, called to the scene, are sometimes hilariously dumb and often struggle to find their way back from the buildings with no success.
ps/

Multiplayer: Here is where I really get to tear it apart. This game's multiplayer is much more fast paced than many previous titles I have played.  If you spawn and dont move to safety within 15 seconds, you will probably die. If you stray from your team, you will die. This game encourages people to run circles around the map and just speed play the matches. If you want to be any sort of tactical without rushing, you will die. As with previous COD games, there is a lag between what happens on your screen and what happens in game. You may shoot and enemy 4 times and get killed by them only to see that 2 of your shots actually happened in game. Very frustrating in  such a fast-paced game. However, when things go right, the game is rather addictcing and can be rather fun if you look past its short comings. A very diverse set of weapons and abilities to play with.
Supply drops: Supply drops are utter BS, especially if you pay for them. I bought a 100 rare supply drop pack and got ZERO guns, 4 melee weapons (useless to me), and dozens of emblems, gun camos, specialist outdits, and calling cards. These things are the worst. Activision advertises all these new weapons they add to the supply drops but your chances of getting them are EXTREMELY low. Spending money on them will only slightly raise your chances of getting a new gun quicker. DO NOT waste money on them. The guns will come eventually. You may get lucky but don't count on it.
Overall: Campaign and zombies are great with only small problems. Multiplayer is not for the faint of heart and will be great for very competitive players. Not so good for those that get frustrated easily.

This game has probably the best plot/story development of any game that I've played in the last 10 years.  It's as if DOMO Studio invested 90% of their budget into developing the story, voice acting, and music.  The atmosphere of the game, the interactions of the different characters, the personal growth that each character experiences and presents, all come together to bring the player a unique perspective into Chinese mythology.
With that said this game is not without its flaws, which I will point to, and
.
(XYS) game series are like the Final Fantasy games in China/Taiwan (though Final Fantasy is also quite popular in Asia).  The parallel game series to XYS is called Chinese Paladin (or Legend of Sword and Fairy, LSF; the names are interchangeable, just translation differences).  XYS is heavy on mythology/history, the main character is usually inserted into previously established mythology/history, and DOMO developed storylines/supernatural events are added.  LSF is generally original story lines with much less emphasis on history.
The XYS games have a "core" series, titled XYS 1, 2, etc..., and a spinoff series, titled XYS 外傳 (wai zhuan).  Some of the spinoffs are sequels to the core series, and some are completely independent games that are unrelated to the rest of the XYS series entirely.
falls into the latter category (for the most part).  You don't need to play the others to understand this game.
This game is about the things that happened to Earth when the
Heavenly (thanks Mew) Emperor decided to open the gates of heaven for all mortals to obtain divine power.  The reason why he opened the gates was so they could find his "dear missing daughter".  This led to tons of chaos since now you've basically got a supervillain fountain.  To stop this from happening, a tribe/civilization with divine power along with some other tribes + gods decide to seal off the gate, which leads to the story in the game.  All of this is rendered in the prologue's intro video.
The game is built on the Unity engine, so stuff looks pretty dated, however the game came out in 2015 so that's sort of expected (for a Chinese game). The characters are a bit stiff, since there aren't that many facial expressions that can be modeled; however some things are animated such as: eyebrow furrowing, sadness/tears, joy/smiling/laughing, agreement/disagreement, and "sighing".
Though the character models are so-so. the environment is great, you can just google for background images of the game and they look pretty amazing. It's unfortunate that some of the backgrounds are only used a few times in the game, but they truly look amazing in the 3D world. A significant portion of the game is also done with hand-drawn art (a XYS tradition), such as the UI portrait photos, loading screens, some of the Steam card backgrounds etc.
The game runs at 60FPS for the most part, turning down AA + shadows should fix FPS drops.
Beautiful music, that's why they have a separate soundtrack for you to purchase. It's also part of the XYS tradition to have a great soundtrack, sometimes performed at concerts (like Nobuo Uematsu concerts). You can probably scope out the music on YouTube for more info.
Voice acting is fantastic, I have no complaints here. Originally people were really frustrated because of the awkward pauses between conversations, since the engine would load the 2nd person's response a few seconds slower than expected. A patch was introduced so you could just press "confirm" and end the first person's pauses, this (though requiring a bit of manual labor) sped up the pace of the conversations to feel more natural.
Sound effects are "not bad", I say this because as per XYS tradition, some of the sound effects are reused (from as far back as games in the early 90s). But that's not all bad, they've all been re-done to sound "modern", and if you haven't played the old games you wouldn't notice.
The game is a mix of Tales style and Final Fantasy ATB. You walk around a 3D environment map, and there are monsters that randomly spawn. If you walk into them or are detected by them, a fight occurs. You can initiate the fight early with your map ability which causes specific effects.
Once in combat, it's an ATB style system (however your bar is a cooldown timer that doesn't really change unless you're slowed). Your physical attack/supportive attack is hotkeyed, health/mana pot is hotkeyed, and you can shift to 4 different spells. At the start of the game, you can only hit enemies once (no combo'ing), as you level up, additional attacks are added.
There is no "limit break" like in other XYS games (or Final Fantasy style games), though at level 20 and 30 you do get different combo finishers.
For most of the game it's just button mashing, because there's a ton of trash mobs, so I completed 70% of the game just button mashing my AOE nuke.
Towards the end of the game you have to do some micro management since the AI isn't very smart.
Example: Switch to defense hero, cast buffs, switch to healer, cast debuffs/buffs, switch to physical, cast buffs, switch to each character to attack, switch to healer, etc. Some people describe this as FF13 style (since you constantly switch characters to change spells/buffs).
For that matter, the AI is TERRIBLE. If you skill spells on your non-main, the AI will constantly spam them, and eventually consume all your mana potions (called powders in this game). However this can be worked around by the weird money glitch (which is listed in the Steam guide section).
I don't want to spoil anything, so I'll just say that the story is fantastic. However you're gonna need some patience as this game is nearly 70% cutscenes/voice acting conversations/FMVs, 30% combat. Some of the cutscenes/FMVs are nearly 20 minutes, so treat it more like a long movie/TV series/soap opera. It took some getting used to in the beginning, but towards the end, I felt it really was necessary to set up appropriate ambiance.

It's not very good, a lot of the clever puns and alliterative conversations are lost in translation. I could do a better translation, but at the number of lines per character, that might take quite a while. I'm fluent in English/Chinese, so I played the game with English subs to see what the translations were like. Often times they misrepresented the reason/emotion of what a character was expressing. Even so, I feel you can still understand the story and challenges faced by each character; (some of the best character-character sequences were non-vocal).
This game has a lot of flaws, but the plot alone is worth a playthrough.  For the last sale price ($4.49!!!) it is 100% worth it to give it a shot.  I bought it on release for $15 (which is still worth it!).  Expect around 25 hours of main story (without skipping cutscenes).  Probably 40 hours to do all the sidequests + side bosses.  A 2nd playthrough is required to 100% cheevo the game.

When thinking about Asian-styled RPGs, most people will only think of Japanese-made JRPGs. But there still exists Asian style RPGs made from other Asian countries, as seen in this Chinese style RPG by Taiwanese Studio Softstar and Domo Studio. Xuan-Yuan sword series has been a long running series starting back from the DOS days, but overtime its popularity overseas has been overshadowed by much more polished JRPGs.
The Gate of Firmament is a pretty decent entry in the Asian-styled RPGs market, even with fierce competition from other JRPG titles. The fighting and story structure is pretty similar to a Tales of game, but featuring ancient Chinese mythologies.
In general:
Fighting is decent.
Story is great.
Graphics are pretty nice.
Music is great.
The performance is a bit wonky as the framerate drops frequently on my PC even though it doesn't look like a graphically-intensive game.
I played the game on Chinese so I cannot comment on the quality of subs for the English version.
Personally I would say it compares to a mid-range JRPG, so temper your expectations a bit :)
Overall I would rate this game 7/10 and would recommend to anyone looking to try out a non-Japanese RPG.

I have held off on getting The Gate of Firmament for awhile now, mainly because of complaints I heard about the quality of translation and the overabundance of cutscenes. While the translation now is not necessarily top quality stuff, I've found it to be very coherent, with few spelling errors or typos, and good punctuation. In comparison to the other few Chinese RPGs translated to English at our disposal in this day and age, this is probably one of the finest efforts around. For this Softstar and DOMO studio are to be applauded.
As for the amount of cutscenes: yes, there are a lot, particularly in the first 3 hours or so. While the amount in these first few hours was a little too much, I've found them to even out as the story goes on. This might also be because I've become heavily invested in the storyline by now, so I don't mind them in the least. I love the setting and the mythological tone of the main scenario.
Something I found myself concerned about in the first few hours was the lack of difficulty, even on hard mode. It quickly became apparent, however, that this concern was unfounded. As long as you are not grinding like crazy, the difficulty pleasantly increases as you move into the 6~7 hour mark. I've been really surprised by the challenge the Bosses present, usually with a unique approach being key to a seemingly unsurmountable battle. This not only includes using in-battle skills, but considering the equipment you have, the demon you have bound to your fighting style, what level that demon might be, and what character(s) you are controlling in that battle. It's not the deepest system around, but I've been discovering more and more depth as I go on. I am very pleased about that.
Aesthetically, the game has a lot going for it. All the concept and character art is extremely good and a joy to look at. You can see this translated very well into a rather aging engine. Some environments are truly stunning despite the limitations inherent in a fairly dated game. The music is simply beautiful.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone looking to explore a mythological Chinese world, with great characters and an involved story. The game begins at a slow pace, both narratively and in terms of gameplay, but if you stick with it you'll be rewarded in the end.

Purchased on a whim for $40 during the Steam Winter sale, despite the less than stellar word of mouth on the first Watch Dogs 1.
I'm not a PvP kinda guy, but the random matchmaking and invasion events are an absolute blast and lead to some absolutely insane car chases through the city.  You can stand on the roof of a Nudle (Google) corporate bus and tazer NPCs while a complete stranger drives you both through traffic.  Or you could end up as roadkill when the game decides you've caused enough havoc and drops a pair of players in sports cars into your police chase and they roadkill you in the middle of some city park.
Great variety of music. Got some new favorite songs out of this.  "Drink all the Beer, Hack all the Things."  and "74 is the New 24".
Good acting and character design. Hard not to fall in love with everyone on your team. Except Ray. He probably has crabs.
Decent story. Kept me engaged till the end and I usually muddle around in a game for the immediate novelty and then dump it.
Gameplay wise, it's a mix of stealth mechanics, 3rd person shooting, droping care packages (boom boom baby) on people from drones, driving RC cars through vents, basic wiring puzzles. Powering up is a very open-ended tech tree with points earned from quest completion and pickups on the open world map.  Good game rolling in a Boing-Boing style crypto-punk/maker culture asthetic.
No technical problems but I have a fairly new rig (i5-6600k, 32GB ram, SSD) with a GTX 1070. Don't let the Nvidia GeForce experience overtune your settings though. Some minor glitches -- once got stuck in a wall exiting a RC car during a multiplayer mission, but nothing game breaking.

Having just finished beating the final mission i felt it was due a review from myself. I did enjoy the game and if on sale would highly recommend and as they are promising to put out better dlc then Watch Dogs 1 i hope they do. I was disappointed with how the game ran and the requirement for UPLay but expected this. They've tried to help the community by putting out suggestions but those don't always work. I seem to jump between playable at high quality to playable at medium quality, to unplayable at medium quality. I will address three different parts of the game being STORY, this will address cliches and will contain minor spoilers, GAMEPLAY, this will address shooting, hacking, driving, and controls, and lastly IMPROVEMENTS OVER WD1, this will be a strict what was better and what could be improved.
Gameplay i felt was rather well done, hacking options became more abundent but i did not like having the hackwheel be part of the mousewheel i don't enjoy that. The hacking options were enjoyable and made the hacking side much more viable which sadly weakened stealth and guns blazing. Enemies seemed to have ton of health. A sniper rifle couldn't even gutshot kill a regular guard most of the time with even headshots not being instant kills. Immediately being targeted after being spotted made getting melee kills silly and weapons were not needed. I would constantly use the gang warfare hack option to kill people and just sit back and let them kill each other. There was a lack of different vehicles from the beginning with you having to buy them all which was a good idea but getting money became much harder as even the old system of hacking civilians only netted a few hundred dollars per hack and were usually uncommon. Money bag drops around the map were useful but can't be picked up by RC Copter. Only allowed to hold two guns and the stun gun which i immediately never used again after the tutorial mission. Grenades are on a timer so after a certain amount of time they replenish which isn't a bad idea but felt strange as everything else seemed so 'realistic'.I'd have prefered more options of guns with most being very bad and looking ugly. Driving was alright, i didn't mind driving in the first game and just did the same thing of only using motorcycles. You can shoot in vehicles now and if you don't have a single handed weapon you just automatically use a pistol. Still no helicopters, planes, and boating is kinda redundent.
The Improvements over WD1 is very biased as i had enjoyed the gritty atmosphere of Chicago and like Aiden Pierce as the protagonist but i didn't mind the uplifting and happy version that was presented in WD2. Very nice colors from the map and if you're one of those people that require diversity you get to experience all of the 'diversity' that WD2 have to offer such as a black protagonist, transgender supporting characters, and a multiracial hacking group with not one but two black people.  More gun options and safehouse were actually useable. It seemed to me that the map was bigger and wasn't just Rich City, Slum City, Industrial, Surburban, and whatever Pawnee was meant to be. NPC's are now much more annoying about you just driving near the sidewalk even when parking and some are quite rude.
THe story is one of the biggest points of this game. I enjoyed WD1 story with *Spoiler Alert*
Well i do still recommend but think that some problems need to be fixed and would like to see the dlc be very good first.

This game is part of the Xuan Yuan Sword series. Having never played any of the prior games I cannot say whether this is better, the same, or worse. The story is interesting but with very predictable plot twists. Each of your 4 party members meet by chance and ultimately are going in the same direction. As you go through the game, you learn why each are on their journey and why you must stop the villains before they reach the gates to the gods.
The story is extremely hard to follow in the very beginning considering all the non-connecting information presented. This is probably due to the fact that this is a Chinese game with lots of history intertwined. As you go further into the game things slowly start to make sense. Each character’s plight which in the beginning seamed more shallow starts to become more understandable. The story is good but there is very little that cannot be predicted.
The game has a good cast of voice actors that do a good job at setting the mood and pushing the story. The syncing is off at times but is nothing that is overly distracting. The subtitles for the game have been mostly converted (I played with English subs). There are several parts in the game that were missed but due to the context of the situation are easily identifiable. The games text is a mixed bag. In some scenes, you have to press a button to move the text, in others there is a super long delay while it switches text, and in other scenes with lots of text (more noticeable in directions) the text moves super-fast.
The graphics in the game are really interesting and vivid. The locations are very distinctive. A lot of time was placed in creating a good atmosphere that was not overly repetitive or generic. Even the majority of characters have their subtle looks that make most of them stand out. Main characters to the story are of course more detailed than others.
There is a huge amount of cut scenes throughout the game. Especially in the first 2 hours of gameplay. If you are not a patient person, this may not be a game for you.
The music to the game is well done and vast. It is nothing groundbreaking that you would want to take with you when you go for a walk though. In fact, the beginning sections of the game sound as if they stone old martial arts and western movie music. After a while the songs start to sound more original and not annoying to hear while traveling.
Gameplay is a mixed bag. If you have ever played Jade Empire, the controls will be easy to understand and utilize. As the game is in real-time, you will have to think quick. The AI partners you have are good at supporting you however they are HUGE resource hogs. They will quickly empty out your potions even when they are not needed. The enemy AI is not very intuitive and are quite easy to defeat. Which brings one of the biggest issues I have with the game, Boss battles! Normally a boss is supposed to be tricky, stronger, and inventive in combat. With this game, there is a large curve to fighting one. Normal enemies are easy to beat while bosses almost always feel like an epic fight at the end of a game.
There are many different systems to the game that are not really explained or quickly glossed over that are quite essential to making your play though better. If you play this game take some time to go over your main system window. This will have your character’s equipment, monsters collected, crafting section, and most importantly quest window. The second thing I did not care much for! Quests show up based on conversations but you are not really told about them. In many cases, if you are not constantly checking the quests which are broken up by character or location you can easily pass over them.
This game has some really interesting concepts that show the creators did take a lot of time trying to perfect. Treasure chests once collected can be destroyed for more items, each character needs to talk to people for different outcomes and quests, characters have their own special abilities while traveling, and many other little details.
Ultimately this is a good game that will take some time to go though. There are many faults but there are equally as many benefits. If you love long romance RPGs you are sure to enjoy this.

This game is amazing. No kidding around, I think it's one of my favourite games ever made. It's about picking a character and traversing the 20 varied levels of a dungeon to fight the big bad at the end. Sounds pretty typical for this kind of dungeon crawler, but this one has so many unique elements to it and such a great design that keeps me coming back that I just want to gush about it for a while.
-The Gameplay
The dungeon consists of 20 levels, and every 5 levels the environment changes. Each environment is distinct and varied enough that the game doesn't feel repetitive at all. Usually I'm not a fan of first person perspectives, but in this game the limited field of view really adds to the tension you'll feel as you peek around every corner, checking for traps and monsters. The Egyptian themed levels especially convey a sense of claustrophobia I've never felt before in a game. In general this game keeps me gripped like no other, knowing that every single level of the dungeon could spell the end of my run at any time if I'm not careful. Permadeath only adds to the pressure you'll be feeling in the later levels.
Combat may not be the highlight of this game, but it makes sure than every single encounter needs to be carefully planned out. There are so many ways to deal with monsters- melee weapons, ranged weapons, magic attacks, potions, traps, scrolls, throwing items, human followers. You have to not only pick your fights, but also your methods to make sure you can cling to your precious health points that are so difficult to regenerate. Making it through the levels with minimal struggle and managing to bring all your strongest resources to the final boss is the key to success.
-The Presentation
It's understandable that the blocky visuals may not be very appealing to some, but I find it quite charming. I may just be biased though, since it reminds me of the old games I used to play when I was younger. Nevertheless, all of the objects in the game all very visually distinct and I can always tell what everything is at a first glance. The music is nothing special,  but fits the mood well. Ambient sound plays when near traps and monsters, alarming the players without being too obvious. Sound effects are appropiate too, and many monsters make unique sounds making you able to distinguish them easily even if you can't see them.
-The Story
This game has a story I think. Something about an evil big bad, I'm not sure anymore. I gotta be honest, it's nice that there is a story and I've read it but it just wasn't memorable enough for me to remember much of it. It's not important and not the focus of the game at all. The writing however is rather charming, as you may find books and such through your treks which are sometimes interesting or amusing.
-The Secrets
It may seem like a minor point but I love secrets in games so much. This game makes me so curious, I feel like a little kid again. And someone in the dev team loves them too, because this game is absolutely bursting with hidden stuff. If you don't believe me, I'm like 70 hours in and I'm still finding secrets. Some of it is just fun little easter eggs, but sometimes they can lead to hidden levels that can help you on your quest. And they're just hidden enough that they're not obvious, but not cryptic either. It's seriously engaging, and I have a feeling I'm still far from finding them all.
-The Faults
Alright, the game's not perfect. As much as I love to praise it, I also need to point out what's wrong to at least try to sort of make this a fair ramble. As for gameplay issues, I dislike the follower system. You'll find some friendly NPC's along your quest and you can sometimes take them along and they'll fight for you. In my experience however, they're nothing but a hindrance as they like to get in the way of your movement and projectiles, and even steal items without any way to get them back. Luckily they're fairly dumb so if you do accidentaly get a follower, you can just lure them into a trap and kill them that way. I tend to ignore followers completely.
Some items are so overpowered that they even trivialize the final boss. Most notably the shield of magic resistance, that can block every single one of the boss' and his minions' attacks! If I'm lucky enough to have one of these items drop, I don't even feel like I've earned my victory in the end, which I think is exactly the opposite of how this kind of game should make me feel.
Alright, those are nitpicks. You can just ignore the powerful items and follower system. But what I can't ignore is the awful netplay. I'll be honest, I haven't mentioned the multiplayer because I personally prefer single player games. But I have had fun playing with friends, that is, if I can get the game to work online at all. Minor visual bugs are frequent but even worse are the times our game would suddenly crash, ending our run right there. As for saving an online game to come back to it later, forget about it. Trying to reload an online saved game would cause some players to randomly lose all their inventory, or walk through a map where collisions wouldn't align with the visuals, meaning they'd go through walls and be stopped by thin air. Sometimes this bug would get fixed if we reached the next floor, but this simply isn't viable in such a difficult game. Sometimes a player would just stop in his tracks and be unable to move at all! We once tried physically pushing him to the next level, but even then the problem persisted. (Note- I haven't tried multiplayer in a while. According to patch notes many of these issues may be fixed by now, and if so I'll change my review as soon as I've tried it a bit again)
-The Conclusion
I love this game. I love how every single monster can be a serious threat if you're unprepared. I love how I've played this game so much yet it still can make me feel so helpless and vulnerable. I love all the charming text and goofy references, it adds so much personality to this game (the talking mace has amazing taste in pastel horses). I love minotaur levels so much, they force some of the toughest decisions that I've ever had to make in videogames. I'd mention how much I love every secret I've found and all the later encounters but I wouldn't ever want to rob anyone of the pleasure of finding them on their own. Games like these are what inspire me to get into game design, seriously. I know I've mostly gushed for the sake of gushing and letting out my positive thoughts, but this game, it's like it was made for me. It appeals to everything that I love about games. And as such I can't recommend it to everyone- but if you enjoy these kinds of experimental roguelites, I wouldn't think twice about the purchase.
And as if I wasn't happy enough with this game already, the devs are still updating the bloody thing! Their passion for their game shines through and through, and for that I just have to commend them again. If anyone on the team is reading this for some reason- Then the only thing I'd ask of future updates would be to add more secrets, more hidden content. Oh, and also, I love you. Seriously. A ♥♥♥♥ing plus. Alright, this ramble is getting way out of hand so I'll stop being such a fangirl for a moment and conclude it for real.
It's a fun game with lots of replay value, play with friends though :D

--The PROS--
The gameplay is a fast, action packed romp. Once you get the hang of the controls, you'll really feel like you're in a wild west shootout. There's nothing quite like ducking for cover just in time to miss a shotgun blast, or making a sudden dive and wheeling around just in time to blow away your foe. The interactivity with the environment is great, and adds an extra layer to the action.
The aesthetic of the game is fantastic. The music has the perfect mix of compelling western flair with just enough modern spice. The characters are vibrant and evocative, as are the locales. The SFX are solid too; landing the final shot that ends a tough duel sounds as good as it feels.
--The CONS--
The game's single-player options are very limited. This is effectively an online multiplayer game only. Indeed, it feels like the multiplayer options also have a lot of room for expansion (4v4 or 5v5, more maps and modes). The game takes some getting used to, and the tutorial does a mediocre job of preparing the player (definitely will need to play a few real rounds before you really get it). Also, there are the occasional bugs in the menu and matchmaking that can be an inconvenience (though they're not really significant).
Secret Ponchos is a short shot of frenetic fun. I definitely recommend checking it out, especially now while it's on free week and on sale.

To start, I would like to say that my friend bought me the starter edition of this game. I didn't ask for it, really. I didn't play it much at first either, but one day, I said f*ck it and decided to play a few casual matches. Well, two months later, here we are: I've got 240 hours on R6, and that's just playing weekends mostly.
I reccomend this game as much as I am physically able to.
Two points I would like to make:
1. R6 is not just running around on a map and Bee-Hopping to avoid enemy fire. It's reinforcing walls, placing traps, rappelling up walls, breaking barricades, watching cameras, reviving teammates, placing breaching charges, and lying prone behind cover. And peaking corners. Lots of that. By saying this, what I'm getting at is that you're thinking, planning, trying to foresee your enemy's moves. You can't just run around and do good (for the most part), and I like that.
2. DLC is completely optional. Remember, this is coming from a guy with the starter edition of the game. I feel no need to even upgrade to the standard edition of the game, let alone invest money in elite character models and stuff. And there's plenty of other good unlockables: because of the Alpha Pack system, even I (at level 83) have several top-tier skins. I got those literally just by playing the game.
3. The excitement this game causes is sometimes rediculous. I haven't felt such a rush of adrenaline and dread in any other game I've played. If it's a 1v1 in overtime, ranked or casual, you will be feeling the rush.
Like I said, I reccomend this game as much as possible. Personally, I've experienced a minimal amount of bugs, and the majority of those were shown to me by my friends. If I've ever played with or against a hacker, I wasn't aware of it (I'm not saying this game is glitch/exploit free -it certainly isn't- I'm just saying that as far as I can tell, my experience with it basically has been)
In case you're wondering, the only difference between the Standard and Starter editions of R6 is that the Starter editions has a different system for unlocking operators: with the $15 edition you start  with a few operators in the begining (I think you choose two and then have enough renown for another two/ whatever you want to buy, though operators is the obvious choice), whereas in the Standard edition you have no operators but can unlock each of the base 20 operators for almost a fifth of the renown price of a Starter Edition player. (Operators added since release, along with all other DLC are the same price for both editions, and all playable content is the same also.) Remember, I'm playing with the Starter edition, and you have my word, that it's not a huge deal. Unless you are obsessed with having all of the operators ASAP, which is dumb anyway because it means you're not as familiar with each of them.
So there. That's my review. Now go buy Rainbow 6 Siege, you pleb!

I wanted to like Stereo Aereo. I really did. I thought the concept was interesting and it had a lot of potential. However, the bits of SA that shine are blotted out by all the painfully mediocre elements. (Full disclosure, the following breakdown is based on playtime up to level 6, as something happened there that made me unable to play any further. More details below.)
The music: The music in SA is pretty alright. Unfortunately, none of the songs I came across really stuck in my head or may me want to play levels again. True to the story of the band you play as, it sounds like it was made by a real small-time group. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but the tracks for this game sound like background music rather than the driving force, which runs really counter to the idea of a rhythm game. Speaking of which...
The rhythm elements: The rhythm elements of this game are what really let me down. You control a ship which moves between 5 different lanes on a 'music highway'. Halfway up the highway from your ship are a set of translucent lines. It is *there* that you're supposed to be looking for to hit the 'notes', but your character is at the bottom of the screen dodging whatever you don't/can't shoot down. This is a little odd, but wouldn't be a problem if the timing was correct. The timing for notes in SA is so painfully inconsistent that it's frustrating. Sometimes a 'Perfect' is actually a little bit ahead of when you'd expect, sometimes it's behind, but rarely is it ever as a note is actually being played in the song. Not only that, it feels inconsistent even when you do the exact same thing over and over. To give what I'm saying here some actually credit, I've been playing musical instruments in real life for 10 years. I play rhythm games on a near daily basis, be it Guitar Hero, Love Live, Audiosurf, Osu, Beat Hazard, Riff Racer, Chunithm.. I can go on, but the point is that I know what rhythm is. I know timing, tempo, and how beats are supposed to fall in music. So it's incredibly aggravating when I do the same thing and get different results. Not just that, but sometimes to dodge you have to make more than one movement, which is more than one key press. This means that while you're moving to dodge something, you may miss your window to get a 'Good' or a 'Perfect'. You might not even get 'OK' cuz the game thinks you made the dodge too far in advance.
Aesthetics: The game looks good; I'm a fan of the 80's pop culture look and the bright neon aesthetics. The HUD is well laid out and puts everthing toward the bottom of the screen so you don't have to take your eyes off your ship or the hit line. It's nice.
Story and Voice Acting: Man, you'd think Stereo Aereo was an established franchise with how the writers toss around names and locations like they're common knowledge (if it is, let me know and I'll take this back.) I have literally no idea who these characters are or what they even do in the band. It's not really even mentioned until around level 4, though I suppose you could guess based on the shape of their ships. Anyway, these guys talk waaay too much. Get a high combo? Character quip. Get hit? Character quip. Do basically anything? You guessed it: character quip. I'd love to be able to turn this off, but that's not an option, which means you get to hear these mediocre lines spouted over and over again.
Length & Replayablity: Looking at the arcade mode, I believe that the game has 8 levels. That's 8 songs. And.. That's it. Seriously, there is so little content here it's hilarious. Not only that, if you're an achievement hunter it won't take you long at all to ace this game. I got 32% of the achievements in this game in under an hour, about 4 of those came while I was playing the tutorial. Unless you *really* like this game, you're probably only gonna get about 3-4 hours tops. That's laughably low for a rhythm game. So if it's so easy to finish, why didn't I? While playing level 6, I ran into a graphical error that made it impossible for me to continue playing. The things I was supposed to be dodging were straight up invisible. Not even sure why that's happening; I've never had any graphical error like that occur while I was playing any other game on this computer. Suffice it to say, I'm going to be asking for a refund for that reason alone.
To make a long review short, Stereo Aereo is a really cool idea that falls short in basically every category. Honestly, I feel like if they had focused on making a solid shooter and focused the rhythm elements to boss battles, this would have turned out a lot better. The boss fights were the most fun and polished part in this game. Maybe some big updates in the future can push Stereo Aereo into a more finished state, but I have a hard time recommending this game.

The following are all the things i found wrong with this game so it is quite long. This was my person experience . If you do make it through all the way i salute you!
The items you get when you first start are nice. I started mine on a celebration weekend so it may be different for others. I was given some exp potions and a starter mount upon logging in, Nice right? Well little did i know it was for the first character you started with and that character only. So if you logged in and used the mount it was for that character only. Most mounts are character only from what i found out. So be careful which character you use that mount on.
-The community-
The community is the worst i have seen in any mmo game i have played. I met two nice people in the 136 hours i played. Yes you get those people in any game but because of the Elin character which looks like a little girl the chat is filled with people that call themselves pedo's and talk about anything sexually related to that topic. Or just sex in general.
-Dungeons-
if you dont know what your doing in dungeons forget it. No one wil help. If the group dies it will disband and you will be stuck trying to figure out how to get back in. You get teleported to the nearest town and need to buy scrolls from a speciality vendor. You wont know that if no one tells you and there expensive when you first start playing. I find having to buy scrolls to get back a horrible way to get back to the instance. I personally love going into new dungeons and trying to figure the bosses and layout of the dungeon. Well All through the game, even at higher level dungeons people do whatever they want. As a healer/tank you will have a horrible time going through these as people generally just start running the second they get into the dungeon and everyone runs different ways killing whatever they see.
-Raiding/Endgame-
If you are looking to play this game for end content or looking to raid then dont come to this game. There is no raiding or end content. You go into dungeons to get gear so you can go to other high level dungeons to get gear. That is the norm. But those higher level dungeons drop the same gear as the lower except one or two pieces. Of course you need to know the fights to get into the bigger dungeons but if you dont know them you generally will get kicked and not be given a chance. You would think you could look up the fights right? Check the next problem.
-Information about the game-
Tera also has the least amount of information i have ever seen on any game as well. Any website i go to has little to no information about fights/gear/where to get this/how to get that. You mine as well just go until you figure it out and if you cant then oh well. The chat will not help.

When someone duels you, anything you are doing, looking at the auction house or gear. It will take you out of that and ask if you want to duel. There is really no way to get Hp up in this game after a fight. You have to stand there wait. yes you can have bandages and potions but if you are say at 5% hp and use both you might get to 50% hp. Questing in this game is pretty useless. Dungeons are way faster way to level up. You also get story questlines and as long as you follow the story quests and do dungeons in between you wont have to do any other quests. Though alot of the questline is annoying to get through with mazes.

Organ Trail's pretty damn fun. It's essentially Oregon Trail with zombies and a bunch of Left 4 Dead references.
I had the iOS version before buying the Steam version, and I feel like the game's easier to control on a computer as far as shooting goes. That being said, shooting is still a ♥♥♥♥♥ as far as controls go, and it's difficult to nail on the head. Some of the in-game passersby even acknowledge the problems with the controls by stating, "These controls suck!" (They do.) But having a mouse removed the issue of my finger blocking parts of the screen.
The writing is often times humorous and references things from the original game to Castlevania. It gives Organ Trail a certain charm and unusual atmosphere. Some of the locations throughout the game are rather humorous as well (one of these being--I kid you not--a strip club), and it gives me the impressions that the developers made this purely for fun, which I find admirable. It's always nice to find a game that convinces players that the people who made it definitely had a kickass time doing so.
I've noticed that, while the overall gameplay is generally difficult (even on normal), it gets progressively harder as you move further down the map, which I found reasonable, in my opinion. That being said, it's very good at screwing you over, as nothing's worse than wasting half your food and all your time stuck on the side of the road trading away for enough scrap so that you can attempt a repair on the car that ultimately fails, causing you to waste all your scrap. That actually happened to me. It's not fun. However, to an extent, the game is as difficult as your are good at strategizing and planning a course of action. You will blame yourself many times for the mistake you've made. Many times, crises can be avoided or worked around if you're prepared enough. Yet, given this, random events still occur, and if the odds aren't in your favor, you could end up doing well to being dead in a few miles. It's always important to be cautious in this game as a result.
The music is also spot-on as well. Amidst all of the humor and gags, it gives Organ Trail a more solemn tone. Also, it's generally interesting to listen you and combines an 8-bit feel with a more "advanced" (if that's the word) sound to it. I don't quite know how to explain it. But it's really well done, in my opinion.
The graphics are also very charming and reminiscent of the original games. They work really well. Not sure what else to say here. I like them a lot.
Also, the Clement's Quest minigame is hilarious. It's essentially a TL;DR Organ Trail where you control the car and run over zombies as quickly as you possibly can. I discovered it on accident and couldn't have been happier that I did.
Basically, to put it bluntly, despite the game's difficulty, I really enjoy this game and always have a good time while playing it. It was worth purchasing it the second time, and I'd recommend it to anyone who wants a challenge and a nostalgic, yet new take on a classic.

I've never played Oregon Trail in my life and didn't expect much from this title, but I found Organ Trail to be some of the most entertaining 4+ hours I've spent in a game. I recommend you choose Hard difficulty if you're familiar with games that include resource management, as I was able to beat the game with hoards of food and ammo, and even a decent amount of gas on my Normal playthrough.

No TrackIR support
No SLI support
Barely looks better than last year (and I'm playing on the max settings)
It's Formula One. If you've played the others, you know what to expect - fast cars go around a track. It hasn't really changed all that much, even with the new engine.
For me, it runs decently (i7 4790k@4.5/16GB RAM/SLI 980). Hangs around 80fps, though did drop to 50 at one point. Many people have severe framerate issues though. For what it is, it's not that well optimised if it requires a 970.
What really gets me is the lack of TrackIR support. TrackIR is a headtracking tool that allows you to look around by moving your head in real life. In these racing games, it's really quite useful. Dirt Rally has it. The older F1 titles have it. F1 2015? Nope. If you go into proper first person mode with the camera, you lose half of your mirrors. You can use a button to look left or look right, but this removes the front view. With TrackIR I could just move my head slightly, still be able to see out the front and see the entire mirror.
Handling I found was pretty decent, really light on the Force Feedback though, can be changed in the settings at least.
The AI is not all that great. I'm pretty sure they should avoid crashes whereever possible, but they instead like to just ram me out of the way. Even on the starting grid, I was messing about looking for the look left button and wasn't moving, but a car decided to just drive straight on into me instead. Maybe he should have gone to Specsavers.
They've fixed some crashes, but I still had a crash in the menu.
Sound is poorly mixed. The pit crew is barely audible. From what I can hear, it's some poor voice acting.
Also, it might interest you to know that the console users can communicate with their pit crew via commands over the microphone. Codemasters decided to leave it out of the PC version.
Conclusion: Buy the older titles, this is yet another rubbish port of the console version.

One of my favourite games of all time. I replay this game and its sequel every year or so.

Pony Island is a game that kinda doles out its best gimmicks in the first 15-20 minutes, then repeats them for a bit, then gradually makes them less and less engaging or more complicated than they need to be.
The "meta" concept of a game-inside-a-game that you're trapped in is neat, but it doesn't ever feel like it does enough to personify itself beyond those first moments.  There's no real "hook" to the "runner" portion of the pony running minigame, and by the time you get close to the end of the game, the idea is tedious and burdened with gimmicks that make it far more frustrating to play than it should be.
The only portion of the game that feels like it could have been fleshed out and had more done with is the programming puzzle challenges. There are a lot of ideas that get explored here and a lot of ways that keep you thinking, but they never feel like they grow as much as they should, or change in ways that could feel more directly tied to the other facets of the game.
Pony Island just feels incredibly disconnected from itself and maybe not be quite as clever as it thinks it is for some.  It's a great idea that really could have used more time in the oven.

Chances are, you're here reading these reviews because you at least somewhat enjoy JRPGs.
Well, there you go. You already meet all the requirements to love this game.
Still not convinced? Need details? Fine, fine. Here we go:
Graphics:
Alright, lets start with the bad stuff. Yes, this is pretty much a PSP game. No, it doesn't look great and the loading screens are kind of long. I guarantee after playing it long enough you'll get used to it, and the second game runs much better and looks much nicer. Still, if you really want da sweet graphucs, this game won't really deliver all that well. Fortunately, the walking speed is very nicely swift and maps are just simple enough that you don't have to spend too long looking around if you really don't want to.
Story:
Starts out looking like it'll be pretty typical/tropey, and it is in some ways. However, the story really picks up after a bit and the expertly written and translated dialog will have your heart before long, I promise. The characters each develop nicely and by the end you will be begging for more. Luckily, the second game is on steam now so you don't have to wait like the old fans did.
Gameplay:
Surprisngly intricate, actually. Like the story, its pretty simple at a glance, but you'll quickly figure out there's a whole lot of really smart game design that went into these systems. The orbment system, for example, I find much smarter than any skill tree. Basically, you fill your characters up with special items called orbments that give passive effects, and the colors/attributes of the orbments decides what magic they can use. EX: If you equip Joshua with Action, a time-attribute orbment that raises his speed, he'll get some time points. These time points will allow him to cast Soul Blur, a damaging time spell. On top of the EP (mana) you use to cast these, you also have a CP system that lets you use the crafts, or character unique skills. CP goes up when you get hit or hit something, and EP is replenished with potions or inns like in most games. In other words, you have one kind of resource that becomes more available as combat continues, and one that becomes less available. Balancing them feels good and makes combat very satisfying.
There's also just a lot of other nice little things about the way the game is set up, like how side quests are usually like little stories instead of simple fetch quests, or how party members constantly switch in and out as the story calls for it, giving you a great deal of time to try each character and see their strength and weaknesses before you need to pick your team.
A lot of passion went into making this series, and it really payed off. Most people who've played this game enjoy it thuroughly. Although, fair warning, the beginning is a little slow. Please stick with it and you'll see that the hype is very much warranted!

Cookie cutter characters, poor characterization, a plot that doesn't develop until the last hour of gameplay, a slow combat system, poor enemy designs, and generic locations. These are just a few of the complaints I noted while playing The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky.
The game feels like a B anime show, with mountains of unnecessary dialogue and attempts at humor that never really hit the mark. Character development feels very forced, and usually devolves to one character listing off their personality traits in a conversation.
Most of your time with the game will be spent moving from town to town, solving problems that have only a passing link to the primary conflict. The storyline quests that the characters pursue have little to no bearing on the actual plot. In short, the game is mostly filler material, with plot development only occuring in the first and last few hours.
The combat system isn't bad, but does drag on in certain fights. Animations can't be skipped in any way, so when battling groups of enemies the fights tend to drag on. The monsters you will encounter have no coherency with the locales of the world, and aren't threatening in the slightest. Most of the game is spent fighting squirrels, sheep, and bugs. The game's inhabitants are terrified of these creatures.
If you're a big fan of JRPG tropes, stereotypes, and story beats, this might be what you're looking for. It was all just a little too predictable for me.

Absolutely fantastic, grade-A PvP game. Secret Ponchos is an isometric, third-person top-down PvP shooter, with a Wild West setting, containing (at time of writing) 10 unique outlaws. These are: Kid Red, Killer, Matador, Deserter, Gordo, Wolf, Gunman, Warmonger, Phantom Poncho, and Mad Trapper. Each has unique abilities and weapons, and using them to full effect is always a challenge - but one to be welcomed. The game is difficult, and yes, at times buggy (Warmonger's weapons are known to hit in a far wider radius than they first seem to), but fantastically fun. You also gain bounty as you play in "ranked" matches (there is no penalty for losing besides gaining less bounty in the match), which raise your rank and matches you against more highly-skilled opponents.
1v1 and 3v3 matches are the only available match sizes right now, with Deathmatch (a no-respawn, best 2 out of 3 last man standing fight) being the only available gamemode for 1v1. 3v3 has Domination (get a 5-kill lead over the enemy team to win, or be in the lead when time runs out), Deathmatch, and Posse (one player is designated the leader for each round, and has enhanced health - allies' kills enhance your damage, win by killing enemy leader). There's also offline practice play against bots (who are dumb as bricks...) or Arcade, 1v1 vs bots which is a good way to check out the playstyles of each character before delving into multiplayer.
All in all, the game's fantastic musical score, high-skill, high-difficulty combat, will keep most people who play this coming back for more. I know it will for me.

I got this game quite a long time ago, it seems, as part of some sort of bundle with another game. Forgot about it until it updated just recently. So, I decided to give it a go!
Face it is a puzzle (loosely?)/platformer that seems to revolve around facing your fears inside of your own mind. You control a little man with a big head, a flashlight, and the slowest run and jump combo you'll ever see in your life. Being this little big-head man, you will slowly plod around the areas to jump on platforms, avoid spikes and fires, and use your flashlight to dispel the sperm-looking ghosts that wriggle and whisper toward you.
The platforming in this game is the worst part about it, I feel. It's slow. It's unbearably slow. And, when you miss your jump and have to plod all the way back to the same spot to try again... It makes you very unlikely to want to give it another shot. You do have a sprint, but it's not that much faster than the normal walk, in my opinion. The jumping is floaty and unhelpful. The game doesn't make it clear, in some areas (as it does give the occasional 'try sprint and jump' in others), when the jump or the sprint and jump would work best. Sometimes, you just hold sprint while you're jumping and hope that you'll stick the landing.
The enemies are usually just mere annoyances that come when you're either in an easy place to dispel them or trying to attempt platforming. I really like the idea of being able to use the light to dispel enemies and it has a twin-stick shooter kind of feel, but once again... it's too slow and there's nothing dynamic about it. You hold the flashlight over the enemies and cast them back until they die. And, that's about it.
It's a shame, because the idea of this is solid! Exploring a persons inner demons and fears, spooky surroundings and music, and having a light system to keep them away? It sounds awesome! But, the slow platforming really holds it back, I feel. Speed it up a bit and let it get frantic. Make the enemies something to fear instead of something you just wait to be over so you can continue.
At it's current build, I can't really recommend it to someone unless you're willing to overlook all this stuff and play farther than I have. I'm sure it has something for someone, but I can't really play it. I wish the developer luck, however, and will continue to see what it has in store down the line.

Do NOT, under any circumstances, buy this.
It's not because it's a port of a mobile game.
It's because it's a $9.99 port of a mobile game that is easily available for FREE on both Android an iOS. They do this because they KNOW, of course, that we'll reject any PC game with mobile-style microtransactions, paid ad removal, etc., but that's the issue here. See, with mobile, one would opt-in to paying; there's a psychological war going on between the player and developers, of course, but one still has the option of playing the game for free and never paying a thing, just dealing with the ads and sometimes ridiculous gameplay mechanics. That isn't the case with a PC game, and the style of game changes DRASTICALLY from mobile to PC, which is something that developers don't seem to understand. It's not a simple matter of converting touch controls to mouse controls; often, the mechanics themselves simply won't fit on PC, and  you end up with this.
Ironhide Games did this rather well with Kingdom Rush. I'd urge Devils & Demons' developers to check out Kingdom Rush--it's porting done right (in addition to initially being a PC game--kinda).

An interesting title, that is quite broken when played as the developer intended, and very enjoyable when played with Cheat Engine active.
I'm no stranger to roguelikes, like Eldritch, Darkest Dungeon, Rogue Shooter, ADOM, Ancients Deathwatch, Dungeons of the Unforgiven, Demon Souls/Dark Souls, and a lot more. I know they are very RNG prone, where one playthrough will be possible and others impossible, depending on how the RNG favors you and success is often determined by player skill that can often mitigate some of that RNG. However, with that said, this game will generally favor bad RNG and the player will have no way of mitigating it. In most roguelikes I've played, as the game's difficulty ramps up, the player progresses (in terms of attributes, loot, skills, spells, etc) fairly in line with it, provided you are playing the game right. Now it is entirely possible I'm not playing the game right, but I honestly don't think I would have beaten the game if I hadn't cheated (which btw leaves a sour taste in my mouth). I beat one of the bosses, Baphomet, with a level 50ish barbarian, with 300 something hp and 280 to 290 mana and I honestly don't think I would have been able to legimately kill the boss with that character if I didn't have cheats one. Now, you may be asking, why is that? Well I'll explain:
1. All scrolls randomly choose a target for their effect, and can only be an equipped item. So a scroll of repair, cannot repair a broken item, as the moment it breaks, you auto-unequip it. And as far as I can tell, items don't have a durability stat and thus they will only break in certain circumstances... like attacking a minotaur... or a cloak being burned to a crisp.  Similarly, scrolls of enchant armor, randomly chooses an equipped item to apply the effect. True, you could unequip all but one item to ensure it enchants the right item, but that is a huge irritant.
2. The blocking system is broken. Unlike a game like Dark Souls, (of which I really enjoyed and have beaten three times now) blocking in this game is more a liability than a benefit. Enemies lack stamina and can keep attacking forever and when they hit your shield, they do not recoil. Thus, if there is a window of opportunity to strike the opponent before they attack again, you have like 50-100 milliseconds tops... and I've never gotten the timing right in this game and thus I always get hit the moment I drop my guard. Also, while blocking you move at 33% of maximum speed and as carried items slow you down already, you cannot manuever around a target while blocking. Well, except for my cheated character who ran like the wind, and could go from one end of the level to the other in 2-3 seconds. So more often than not, its better to not bother with shields and use a torch instead in your offhand. As a result, melee combat feels very unfair and you constantly feel completely outclassed.
3. Healing is few and far between and enemies can easily do 1/3 to 1/2 your maximum health in a single hit. This results in a lot of frustrating deaths. Oh and that is from being attacked from a basic skeleton mind you. A cave troll will one-shot most characters; I'd know, I had a party of 4 recruited humans and we did a last stand in a room against a troll (troll, not minotaur; those are worse) and the troll killed myself, and all the allies while taking barely a scratch. Also those allies aren't levelled and thus encountering them later on in the game with tougher enemies means that an enemy merely has to tickle them and they die.
4. Item progression is basically nonexistent. Unlike in something like ADOM, where at later levels you start finding mithril or adamantine items, with much higher stats, most items that you initially find that give 1 or 2 armor, is fairly common until the very end of the game. My cheated character, had items with 3 armor, and some with 4 armor and one with 5 armor. My weapons were of course better because I had the artifact bow, artifact spear and artifact mace, but not that much better; the spear was 10 damage, the mace 7, and the bow 12 (in theory; it seemed that a spear jab always did more damage). As a result, enemies scale in HP and damage far faster than you do and you can't really catch up. The only effective way that I found to kill enemies was using spells like Magic Missile, as that did reliable damage even against the minotaur.
5. Minotaurs are nearly invulnerable and are very cheaty. Melee attacks will often deal no damage and may even cause your weapons to break. The thing destroys doors and ceilings and it even hovers over pits. Nothing can slow it down, and it does about 40 damage per hit, and thus will most likely one-shot most characters. The only way to escape it is to enter the next floor. Now it may be argued that you shouldn't try to fight the minotaur or might be argued that you can always disable the mechanic, but the mechanic in general feels out of place here as there is already enough things that can easily destroy your characters.
6. If all that wasn't bad enough, you also have 1-shot kills from boulder traps, infinite depth pits, spellcasters that can easily kill you from afar, and its permadeath of course.
7. The last point I'll raise is the tradesmen/merchants. Each item you pickup has a gold value. However, in order to sell it you need to find the right salesman/merchant. As these are randomly generated as well, you only find a merchant once every 3-4 floors. So, that means you have to lug around all that loot for a long time, until you find someone to sell it to... and theres no guarantee that the merchant you find will accept the items you are carrying around. This leads to a problem, where you don't know what item is actually valuable as if you can't find a gem merchant for your 2500 gold gem, then that gem is actually worthless and takes up a valuable inventory slot. And as all items add weight and slow your movement speed down, it makes it harder and harder to avoid traps, avoid combat damage and escape from the minotaur.
If the above problems were fixed, I would likely recommend the game, as it is clear the developer(s) put a lot of effort into the game (as I did enjoy the level designs, puzzles, and encounters). But until they are addressed, I cannot see myself legimately completing the game without cheats.
tl;dr:
Combat is broken, itemization is broken, monsters are overpowered, healing is basically nonexistent, and the only class that would likely win the game without cheating is the Wizard, as spells like fireball or force bolt or magic missile are the only reliable "sources of damage" in the entire game.
