This MMO is one of the best out there, both in terms of free MMOs and paid MMOs. Like other reviews have said, it's definitely
pay to win. Combat feels smooth and satisfying, interface is organized (and if it isn't, you can highly customize it to your liking,) and overall gameplay is really fun. Solo players like myself will find little difficulty in playing, and the community is very friendly if you ever do need help. If you are easily bothered by over-sexualization of characters, then this game will bug you to some extent (because obviously less armor means more defense!) I don't pay much attention to story, so unfortunately I can't give much insight on that.
The game makes me feel like I'm drinking an iced frappe. It's smooth, refreshing, and just damn good. Everything is highly customizable so that you can bind anything anywhere, place any GUI windows anywhere, and and more. I myself am used to playing LoL where the status bars are at the bottom center, and sure enough I can not only move that down there, but also set the transparency of the map so it's not in the way. You can flow through everything you need quite well, which is good for people like me who don't bother reading quest texts. Everything simply feels good to use. Characters are also heavily customizable, I will spend half an hour or more fine-tuning characters and it's very satisfying. The learning curve for some of the enemies in the game can be a bit steep, however. I've gotten to points where I simply can't beat enemies and have to go elsewhere and grind a bit. This doesn't happen too often, and varies depending on what class you choose.
When I am carrying a sword that is twice the size of my body, I think it should feel pretty friggin' heavy. In this game, it does. It's that healthy mix of Eastern-style MMO combat with realistic power. Magic feels magical and truely awesome as well. I can just imagine the pain I inflict with the spells I am throwing out. Combos feel especially fantastic, as the game will notify you of the next skill that you can chain which allows for some quick and powerful punches. Enemy attacks feel slightly less hurtful, but I suppose that makes sense considering you're meant to take on one after another and survive. Beware that it is very easy to miss skills, and it's screwed up combos before. I advise against playing one-handed, boys and girls. While the amount of skills you get is not on the level of WoW, there's still a lot to keep track of. I would say this game to be on the border of casual and mid-core.
On max settings, this game is truely beautiful. I actually feel immersed in the TERA universe. Again, it's a perfect mix of realism and fantasy. Ambient lighting, crisp breezes, and swaying plants makes a flawless atmostphere that I can feel comfortable in. In contrast, being in enemy lands where the grass is rotting, the sky is red, and rumbling from all directions makes me want to get my quests done soon or else I might get eaten in a non-sexy way. NPCs don't feel too unique, though, as many of them share the same quotes and voices. Also the fact that the females insist on exploiting their jiggle physics constantly tends to ruin a serious atmosphere. This is where the sexualization comes in. I question how some armor even stays on when I'm just running. However, the males show quite a bit as well in some armor. Shirtless men is no comlaint of mine.

This is probably one of the best city builders I've ever played (out of 2, but that still counts, right?). This game is kind of relaxing when you have a fully functioning city and you're just adding some new parks, or landscaping it to look nice, but still quite challenging when actually expanding on the city, and dealing with all the problems popping up everywhere. So, I am going to list several pros and cons to this game to simplify the review.
Pros:
- Large amount of land, don't have to make grids
- Great traffic simulation; every citizen has a designated home and job, and go the most
route there and back.
- Lots of details you can micromanage, but don't have to.
- Lots of customization, allowing you to change the name of pretty much anything (City, people, buildings, roads, animals)
- Challenging, there's always something that can go wrong, so be careful.
- Good graphics (in my opinion)
- Steam Workshop isn't just supported, the game actually
you to use it.
- Tons of mods
- Several free DLC
- A free update comes with every expansion to add some things from the expansion (but only small things, like nighttime from after dark or scenarios from Natural Disasters).
Cons:
- Can be VERY frustrating at times.
- Really hard if it's your first time with city builders.
- Sometimes really annoying problems appear, like all the stores and factories complaining about not enough workers while having a 27% unemployment rate, or stores wanting more customers while being surrounded by residential zoning.
- Graphic-heavy, if you have a bad computer (like me) you have to lower the graphics settings to minimum to play without (much) lag.
- Services often don't use their full capacity of vehicles (like my incineration plants which only use 1/34 of their garbage trucks even though tons of buildings are complaining about garbage piling up)
- Sometimes fire stations don't go to a fire right beside them just because a fire station on the other side of the city is sending fire trucks there.

These are my updated F1 2015 impressions. Codemasters have tossed out every part of their old games and built a new one from scratch. It doesn’t look, feel or sound like the previous titles. It lacks features from the older titles, but the core game is much better than it ever was.
Like the other Codemasters F1 games, F1 2015 requires concentration and finesse. I’m playing with a gamepad, and you just can’t mash full throttle and steering and hope to get to the other side of a corner pointing the right direction. The game uses the full possible range of analogue control available to create a remarkably deep and rewarding driving game. It’s the only racing game where I’m happy to drive around the same circuit for 20+ laps, as every moment is unique depending on the tire type, their temperature, the weather, the car damage, and whether I’m starting to feel fatigue. It strikes the perfect balance between accessibility and hardcore simulation, which I feel most simulators don’t hit. Compared to the earlier titles there’s a whole new level of realism, where the aerodynamics and skidding feel just right. When you’re driving on a rainy track and you lose traction, the sensation of sliding on the track is immediately understandable. You can feel how you could have prevented it, and encourages you to do better in the next corner. The way the game communicates what the car is doing to you, even through the imperfect medium of a gamepad, is better than any other racing game I’ve played.
Visually it’s easily one of the best games I’ve ever seen, though this opinions appears controversial from what I’ve seen from other players. Like Alien Isolation the game uses several camera tricks that don’t show up in videos because of compression. Thanks to heavy post-process antialiasing and advanced motion blur there are almost no visible jaggies whatsoever. This makes the game look more like a CG movie than a videogame. There’s a remarkable sense of coherence to the visual style. The cars and the tracks appear to be part of a larger world, and objects far off in the distance have a sense of presence that is unusual in games. It feels huge and convincing. This coherence was clearly a goal of the developers, as they’ve made improvements in pit animations. The transition animations between menus, and when you drive out to the track are all much more polished than before. There’s just a couple jerky movements here and there for the sake of speeding up the pace. I prefer how this looks to Project Cars, and any other racing game out now for that matter. The only comparable game is Driveclub. It makes me feel like I’m there, like it’s a real place, like it’s a part of a bigger world like nothing else I’ve played.
Other details like the audio has been overhauled. Engine sounds aren’t as in-your face as before, as they now sound as if they travel through the air before hitting you. Same with other sounds like the audience, reflections against walls, and tire noises. They’re all filtered differently based on where the camera is placed, none sounding like simplistic game sounds of the past. A new addition is the wind noise which changes based on car aerodynamics. If you damage the front wing, the air audibly travels differently across the car, making quite alarming sounds if it’s heavily damaged. You can hear the role it plays in keeping you on the track, even if you might not understand it on an intellectual level. This is easily the most advanced racing game sound engine I’ve heard, packed with subtleties that help make the long races more interesting.
If you played any of the other F1 games, and have been waiting that next-gen upgrade before jumping in again, this is it. It doesn’t have as extensive career options as before, but the Championship mode will still take you ~20 hours to run a single season, so it’s mostly a loss for those who are in it for the long haul. I’m fine with how this game turned out. In fact it’s better than I dared hope. The depth of the core game mechanics, the coherence to the visual design, the rich audio design, makes this a no-brainer recommendation. I’ve had no technical issues, and most of the crash bugs other people have reported have already been fixed.

I wrote a negative review which as of Patch 1.6 I have since retracted, if you want to know what was wrong prior to patch 1.6 read the many many reviews on it already here many of which won't be retracted or re-written and such is the legacy you leave if you release a game before it is tested and completed and ask people's cash.  I doubt Ubi will learn a lesson from it as they have a history of doing this but one can hope.  The amount of money this game could have made overall as a finished product released with positive reviews will now sadly never be realized.
As for the game, this game is the best Heroes iteration since Heroes IV, though as any review it is up to opinion and discussion I will try to keep it on topic and based on things at least measurable.
Graphics are very good, I did not like Heroes V or VI graphics, V graphics very much reminded me of early WoW graphics they were bulky, fat, and simplistic with tons of bright colors.  VI trimmed it up a bit, but VII is full rendered fantasy with great designs from an artist with some great concepts, the green dragons in this one look amazing for example (they look like they themselves were grown out of the forest) and many other creature designs are very well rendered, if still a bit bulky and ill defined for my tastes it is miles past V or VI.  IV had actual scans of 3d models as sprites, and III any way you look at it, the graphics are severely dated.   But I am happy with the graphics on this game, the maps are also amazing, and the towns are beautifully rendered.  In V you had 3d animated town screens with dramatic sweeping cameras but I find I don't miss them, and prefer the solid functional and pretty town screens they implemented in every other hereos game, and so I can say with confidence this is my favorite when it comes to graphics in all areas but two: 1) the animations for some creatures are a bit odd on fast combat speed, and while somewhat to be expected even on slow speeds animation starts and stops can be awkward.  2) some of running animation of hero mounts also seem off on the map.  Overall, 9/10 for graphics, I'd give more if it had the animations better sync'd with the game.
Sound is very good in this game, I love all the sounds in combat, and the music is stunning and very pleasant and there is different music for every town screen.  This seems lovingly done and very much puts me into the mood to play and does a ton for the atmosphere of the game.  10/10
Gameplay is addicting, I just had my brother and neighbor over and we played from 6pm at night to 4am in the morning hotseating and visiting.  We intently helped each other play even though we are techinically against each other, and it was a walk down memory lane and enjoyable in new exciting ways that pleased us very much.  Since the gameplay bugs were fixed we had no reservations about digging in and very much loved it.  It is all it promises to be a heroes game playing homage to its roots, and past, and community wishes.  The skill system is somewhat revamped, but I consider it an improvement, the same things that were always there, are there but it shows you everything and what you're getting into making better strategy.  Many of the broken mechanics and annoying things any long time heroes fan would know about were addressed.  Some juicy examples: you can quick combat and if you don't like the results you can play manually.  This makes for quicker turns and less gambling on how good the AI will play on your behalf (which you couldn't expect much from the AI in any heroes game but we'll get to that more in the next section).  Town building screens are very informative now, right clicking on most things lets the window stay open so you can examine abilities, AI turns are quick (heroes V had they had longer turns than players often times AI was still bad),  there is a compendium of information for heroes and units, medusas no longer guarantee kill things, minotaurs no longer have a chance to block all damage, there's more slots for artifacts, having the wrong school of magic doesn't totally screw your hero on a map when a powerful spell is found because you can still learn it just not as strong as if you were in that school... the list really goes on and on and I'm still finding large improvements on gameplay.  There are a few minor things I'd like to see changed but I can't bring myself to even mention them at the moment.  10/10 for gameplay this is the direction heroes should go.
The AI is pretty bad in any heroes game, but it is really missing decision making in this one and hopefully that is patched in.  I still prefer it to the release date heroes V AI because it would take about 5 minutes every time you ended turn and it was still stupid.  This is lightning quick, as IV, and III were and has yet to achieve their intelligence but on a normal game at least they can still come into your territory with a sizable army and make a fun diversion.  When it gets to the meat of strategy though, no Heroes AI was ever good and there's lots of ways you can beat them having bigger armies than you but that is part of the formula for heroes imo.  You kill bigger stronger foes by being smarter,it's a strategy game after all.  Sometimes it will fail in this though and you are up against an AI that managed to kill itself.  That happened in V though and even IV a few times, but it was something to laugh at rather than get mad, usually with friends.  There is definite room for improvement of the AI however.  AI is 5/10. If they start picking up ALL resources they come across and don't always buy a ton of heroes could boost that a lot.  This would let them build bigger armies and punish players who take too long to explore or wait longer in base to build up bigger armies to use weaker strategy/take less losses in capturing objectives and collecting treasure.
The worst part of this game in my opinion is the comments on the official website, while some were deserved for releasing a game that should've stayed in beta testing for 7 months, the level of irrational hatred there and raw negativity makes me ashamed to associate myself as a fan.  I really liked the idea of the shadow council, and silencing negative opinions can seem draconian, but moderation, tone and a code of conduct are still very important factors for making a game and atmosphere built on constructive feedback.  I honestly wish they'd just remove comments on their official website as it leaves a bitter taste in my mouth every time I go there.
In conclusion, the game was released too early and paid a heavy price for it, and will now always live in that shadow.  It is however through patching, now the best heroes iteration since Heroes IV.  It has improved gameplay, great graphics, been based on community desires and feedback, great music and sound, and fixed and improved upon many broken mechanics and annoyances from past iterations learning from the past in a good way and taking the Heroes franchise in a direction that I very much want to see, on the strong stipulation that Ubisoft will stop releasing games that aren't finished ruining not only their company reputation but the games that had a lot of potential to become market breakers.

The game is really fun and is incredibly unique. It has a LOT of things going for it, so much so that I would seriously consider it a gold mine if the developer(s) would just listen to some feedback. That being said, it has its problems..
Cons
-----
- The UI is alright. It could be cleaned up a lot. Item names are a bit confusing, item stats are misleading / uninformative, weight and hunger aren't explained well, and character stats should be explained (even if only briefly to keep the book that explains them in depth more useful).
- The game needs a brief tutorial. 5 hours in, and I don't even know what 80% of the items do, or what interactable things in the environments do. The devs have managed to make feeling left in the dark about what things do enjoyable, but it's a TINY bit excessive as is.
- Monsters deal a bit too much damage. When the game's basically designed so that monsters in melee range of you are almost inescapable, that blocking is clunky and that you and your opponent EXCHANGE hits (when in melee), and that monsters have long reach so walking around them in medium sized rooms is difficult, it's not all that fair that one mistake will get you insta-killed.
- Boulder traps are NOT fun. The game is too dark, too fast paced, too unforgiving, too combat heavy, and too focused on exploration to have these just abruptly killing you 40 minutes in to a run solely because you aren't staring up at the ceiling the entire time. They're unfitting. More floor traps and wall traps that are disarmable and could unlock rooms if successful would be great.
- Items that can kill you are too common. They're fun, charming, and funny, and I do like that they're in the game. They're just too common RNG-wise right now.
(EDIT) - Minotaurs are frustrating. Luckily Sheridan replied below so I now know NOT to fight them (unless prepared), but the in-game queues for them spawning are still a bit tough to follow.
- More enemies would be nice. Not too many from what I can see, but it doesn't bother you in game.
- More level layouts would be nice (you do notice sometimes that some are the same).
- More companions / pets? I love how that system works right now, so PLEASE introduce pets that you can find/keep, choose at the start of the game, and/or find in the dungeon!

К сожалению, в игре нет меню насторек, поэтому я не мог изменить разрешение, из-за чего на моём слабом ультрабуке частота кадров в секунду была довольно низкой. Также я не мог выключить музыку, но при этом оставить звуковые эффекты, потому как она стала немного надоедать своей однообразностью. Меню для выбора уровня было неудобным, потому как для того чтобы добраться до нужного уровня, приходилось пролистывать все уровни между тем, на котором я находился и тем, на который я хотел попасть. ТЕМ НЕ МЕНЕЕ, процесс моей игры дошёл до того, что я настроился на правильную медитативную волну и осознал, что мне этот процесс нравится. Он был построен подобающе, так как начальные уровни были очень лёгкими, но в процессе становились сложнее уровень за уровнем, добавляя больше разнообразия в механику игры и в эти моменты игра становилась снова лёгкой, таким образом прослеживалась прятная волна уровня сложности, которая не позволяла мне почувствовать себя глупым и фрустрированным даже учитывая насколько я плох с головоломками, но при этом игра оставалась приятно сложной на всём протяжении. Также картинки, которые Вы создаёте, и музыка отлично дополняют так называемую волнообразность и медитативность игры. Достижения в игре подобраны идеально. Мне понравилось. Но для опытных энтузиастов головоломов игра может показаться черезмерно лёгкой.

I didnt like how the combat goes. Everything seems too "slow" or short ranged. Melee chars are overwhelmed by their ranged counterparts as every shot you recieve (or almost) knocks you back so whats the point of even trying. For every attacks you make, be it range or melee, you have to actually use your "aim" button first which starts a lil "aiming" animation of .5 sec which in turn makes your quick melee dash useless since you cant just dash forward, slash, dash back for a quickie. By the time you reach your target for a melee strike, he prolly just aimed at you with his revolver/shotgun/whatever, waited for you to try your roll in and shooted his thing, knocking you back or even worse, knocking you down.
Most weapons have a very short range though I admit some have a secondary that makes them become more of a medium range. Problem is, it takes yet another 1 sec for the animation to complete and by the time you can actually get your shot off, your target rolls back out of range anyways and you have to waste your shot.
You can crouch behind cover but what for? Weapon range are way too short to even bother trying to shoot from cover and if you try to simply take cover to evade a shot, well good luck because again it takes a second for the game to animate your char behind the spot.
For those who wonder, 1 second isnt long, but in a game where reflexes counts for everything, it -is- a friggen long while. In games like CoD, that one sec is the diff between you having the headshot or your target.
The way I see it, the combat mecanics would work for matches of more than 1 vs 1 or 3 vs 3 ...Meleers could navigate more easily behind and get their attacks off.

I have to start by saying that it's been a
since I last enjoyed a game THIS much. Perhaps I've become jaded or disillusioned with video games in the past 10 or so years. There have been gems here and there, but nothing really gripping or amazing in my opinion. Nothing like the classics of my youth, at least. Until Trails in the Sky.
A little context may be in order. I've always loved story-rich games, and as such was a big fan of JRPGs in my pre- and early teens. I was a staunch follower of the Final Fantasy series from VII onwards, but their last four or five games have been quite lackluster in my opinion. Final Fantasy VII, Final Fantasy Tactics and Super Mario RPG were my favorites, along with Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, though it's not really the same style. I played Chrono Trigger, Xenogears, Secret of Mana and others -- such great games. But it felt like the "glory days" of JRPGs ended with the turn of the millenium. Maybe I was just focused on other game genres and missed some good JRPG releases, I don't know. I recently gave Hyperdimension Neptunia a try and it was fun, but a bit too silly and light-hearted for my tastes.
Enter The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky. It had been on my wishlist for awhile and it was in the Halloween Sale so I thought, "what the hell, I'll give it a shot." It had some pretty impressive reviews, after all, and I loved the classic look of the game in the screenshots. I wasn't expecting anything great...
I was hooked on the story from the very beginning, though I can see how some people might call it "slow." Personally I love a good buildup so I didn't mind a bit. The characters really interested me and I was genuinely eager to continue the storyline and find out more. The gameplay was just about perfect -- I haven't had so much fun with a magic system since Materia in Final Fantasy VII, and the battles were fun but not too difficult; I hate it when difficulty gets in the way of progressing the story! The graphics were great -- oldschool, yet beautiful. I absolutely love the sprites, and they contrast well with the gorgeously-illustrated character portraits that accompany most of the extensive text. The music is very well-done, too; I really enjoyed all of the tracks. The game world is so big and believable, and it really came alive throughout the game. And it actually took me a LONG time to finish this game -- no 2-hour playthroughs here, thank goodness! It seems like games made these days are way too short, so I loved the 50-hour timeline of this one. I just... had so much fun, I couldn't stop playing! And that's rare for me these days -- I frequently skip from game to game because not much can hold my interest the way this one did.
I haven't been more satisfied with a game in many years. I'm just sad it's over, though I really cannot wait to continue with the Second Chapter. To any fans of story-rich gameplay or classic JRPGs, I very strongly recommend giving Trails in the Sky a try. IMHO it deserves a place of honor next to the best of the classics.

This is the FPS-roguelike  I always wanted! Most FPS-roguelikes focus on gun handling, level layout, and the overall flow of the FPS mechanics. But FANCY SKULLS is the only FPS-roguelike that I know that focuses more on the roguelike aspects of that genre-combo. And that's the thing! Sure TOWER OF GUNS HEAVY BULLETS and ZIGGURAT all great FPS-roguelikes, but they forget that you can do much more with the roguelike genre. They are missing out on: secrets, a variety of items that give you buffs, a wide range of enemies and simple but intriguing combat.
To sum it all up: FANCY SKULLS doesn't try to be a randomly generated DOOM, it tries more to be a FPS- Isaac/SPELUNKY type of game.
And that ladies and gentleman is why I love this game so much! The best roguelike-FPS out there!

Alright, having finally beaten the final boss of the game I feel proper writing this review. So short answer, if you like challenging games with a good bit of RNG, humor, and permadeath, get this game. Long answer will be found below.
Pros
-Game is hard yo, like really hard
-Art is pretty good if you like the voxel style
-Music is banging, and the sound effects are pretty good, the sound of a minotaur stomping its way towards you in the darkness is mortifying
-Most item names tell you exactly what they do if you are familiar with RPG terminology
-You can disable the more tedious features of the game if, for example, you get tired of starving to death 9/10 runs and boulder smashed the last 1/10
-There is cheese to be had
Cons
-Game is really hard, it took me almost 12 hours of playing to even see the final boss, and another almost 5 to finally kill him
-The final boss is little more that a fat sack of HP with rapid fire high damage spells, he has no melee attack, instead he crams between 1 and 8 lightning bolts down your throat killing most melee characters instantly without very specific random items
-The Minotaur will almost guaranteed 1 hit kill you if he shows up before you are halfway through the game and guess what, he's faster than you most of the time, but he can be disabled from randomly showing up Dark Souls invasion style
Er, both?
-Rats are really small and sometimes very hard to notice when they are close enough to hit you, this can lead to a lot of spinning around trying to find the rat nibbling your bum and, inevitably, your friends in co-op laughing hysterically as you are murdered by a 5 pound rodent
-Blindfolds are an item in the game that you can equip, it does exactly what you think it does, I've had games in multiplayer where one person throws on a blindfold and everybody else has to try to navigate him and keep him alive while he is blindly waving around a sharp pointy spear
Tl;Dr, Fun dungeon crawler that is better with friends and has a lot of funny moments of random boulders from nowhere and amulets that murder you when you equip them.

Never been a PS man myself, making this playthrough of Oddworld my first. Judging from what I've read, I think our situation here is a terrible port of an excellent game.
The positives:
-Interesting and thought-provoking puzzles
-While meager, a fun world, sense of humor and plot
-Cool art design, yo
The negatives:
-Abysmal controls. Controlling Abe as he runs, jumps, walks slowly, rolls, mounts creatures and communicates with other characters is so blocky and obtuse to the point of aggravation. I know exactly what I want Abe to do. Translating that to the mechanics of the controls was excrutiating.
-Frame rate in the cut scenes (excellent for the 90's!) is bested by old Gumby claymation. I can hardly tell what's going on in cutscenes with all the tearing.
-Saving system is unclear. I can save at any point, but there's no telling where I will end up when I load a file. I may end up seven zones back from where I left off. I can lose up to half an hour of progress thanks to inaccurate saving.
-Several times I loaded save files without Abe. I was stuck on a screen with no playable character. Rebooting the game fixed this but geez.
-For the love of God why isn't there any controller support for Oddworld? This is killer on my hands trying to play this on my laptop keyboard! Why would a game designed for a controller not receive controller functionality during its port?
-This game caused one of my laptops to crash whenever I tried loading it.
I don't recommend this particular port. That is, assuming that your experience on your machine will be anything like mine. I wish I could play this game as it was originally designed. I can just imagine how excellent a playable Oddworld would be.
FULL DISCLOSURE: I received this product for free during a special free download day a while ago.

To start, the story behind the game is clear and simple and is explained well enough in the intro cinematic. Oddworld is a world where corporations run by a race of aliens known as Glukkons, seek to gain huge profits through the exploitation of the environment, native wildlife and most importantly, the subjugation of other species as slaves.
What I liked in the game:
- Story: The reason why I like the story behind this game so much is because its engaging. As a player you immediately see that what the corporations are doing is immoral and has to be stopped. The other side to the game is its crude humour aspect, where if the player decides they have no interest in the problems of Oddworld, they can still enjoy the game either through the simple challenge of the puzzles or mindless violence, usually involving meat grinders.
- Challenging: This game is hard, not impossible, but hard. The game has received many criticisms because of this aspect but in this review I see the difficulty as a good thing. It challenges the player to try different strategies. Sometimes patience is the best way to complete a puzzle, others its easier just to run through and hope for the best. Either way, the game rewards the player for completing challenging areas with… another, harder area. This pushes the player to get better and better or else they won't be able to complete the game, this gives the player incredible satisfaction when the complete an area and gives them a boost of confidence in the face of the next.
- Excellent Art Style: Yes, this is an old game and the graphics are not by any means HD but, still the game remains an inspiration for me. One of the most notable features is how the game plays with both the foreground and background adding another level of depth to the game.
- Soundtrack: The soundtrack is simple and engaging. Alarms sound, intense music plays and enemies chase you through halls and jungles and when you make a mistake and lose the chase, there's the music again to remind you of your failure.
What I didn't like in the game:
- Save points: This is a big problem with this game. You can only save your game at certain save points and these can be fairly far apart from each other. There is no quicksave feature and no autosave leading to the occasion repetitive experience of failing to complete an area over and over again.
- PC Version: This is a review of the PC version and not for either the original PSX/PS1 game or New and Tasty (The HD remaster). I want to start by saying I do not enjoy this game as much on the PC. The controller took a little while to map to the original controls and after that I was still having problems with using the analog sticks of my xbox 360 controller instead of the dpad. This lead to me moving one too many tiles forward or back resulting in a fast death either from falling or from electric fence. The keyboard controls aren't as bad as I thought however, as you progress through the levels they get faster and faster. I found myself fumbling around the keyboard pressing the wrong buttons. This is probably not a huge problem for gamers who use their keyboards frequently.
Overall, I love this game. It has its problems yes but you learn to adapt to those making the game even more unique. I give Oddworld: Abe's Odysee a clear 9/10.

If you have a nostalgia itch for the old Oregon Trail game, it's an okay way to kill an hour or two. That said...
I didn't have a good experience. Some of the mini-games upon leaving settlements are fun (e.g. biker attack, etc.), and the scavenging is interesting for the first handful of times. After that, everything just felt pointless.
Resources: While scavenging, you only ever find 3 of the 8 or so resources you need. It quickly became quite boring to always find the same 3 things over and over again. I ended up with uselessly huge stockpiles of these resources to the point that they became irrelevant, and spent days waiting for traders to come by and offer to trade for anything else. This may be better on harder difficulties, but it was my first time through, so "normal" seemed like the logical choice.
Party: As far as I can tell, there's no point to keeping your party alive other than just for the sake of keeping them alive. This is easier said than done, not because it's actually hard to care for them, but because they randomly wander off, and there's nothing you can do about it. Maybe I just had bad luck, but by 2/3 of the way through the trip all but one of my party had died this way. Maybe there's something that happens at the end if you have more survivors, but I never made it there because...
With just a few stops left, my party saw "something interesting" happening off the highway. I chose to invesitage, and the game locked up. Just a black screen with the music playing and a little decorative pattern at the top. Apparently this is a common problem.
Other reviewers here seem to like it. I found it repetitive, and all the progress I made was too easily wiped out by completely random mechanics and technical problems, making the game more frustrating than fun.
TL;DR: Repeatedly scavenged for the same 3 items in order to feed a party that wandered off and died anyway. Then the game crashed. There are better games available for $5. If you can get it for a buck or two on sale, it might be worth it.

I backed this game on Kickstarter as it looked like a very exciting project. Unfortunately it was riddled with bugs upon release and did not live up to what I expected of a "Rock Opera" video game.
Thankfully the development team has been good at fixing reported issues quickly, so they get some points there.
But unfortunately the game itself is just not that good. Judjing from the way it's marketed, you would expect music to play a big part in the game, but little attempt has been made to merge the gameplay side of things with the music side.
I shouldn't have to play the first level of a rock opera game in silence!
But the entire game is like that. Gameplay is accompanied by ambient noise/music and you will only hear actual songs during cutscenes and boss battles. And these are generally too short and broken up by gameplay to be enjoyable as a whole.
The concept of a Rock Opera in video game format is intriguing, but I really can't say that's what this is. The music itself is fine and and the visuals are very enjoyable to look at, but at its heart this is a mediocre platformer with glimpses here and there into what could have been if the developers had attempted to merge the gameplay with music in a more innovative way.

As a game, yes, there are certain things that are wrong with it in the version I've played. But as a first game from an indie dev I don't really see a problem with that. The problems aren't huge and as long as these problems are being fixed in a timely manner, the end result will be a very enjoyable game for gamers and symphonic metal fans alike.
This first act should be finishable in about 3 hours. Add an act 2 of the same size to that and I think you'll be getting your moneys worth in the end. The puzzles and platforming are pretty well done, albeit not all that hard most of the time. But the musical storytelling and atmosphere make up for that in my opinion. This game is an excercise in something new and fresh in the way the story is told and and the way the gameplay is represented in its setting. The gameplay occasionally reminded me of games like Darksiders or Zelda, albeit simpler, but which is still a good thing!
Yes, the controls are a bit clunky sometimes, the menus look pretty bland and are weird to navigate with a controller, the performance drops sometimes in certain scenes, but none of these things have been gamebreaking to me. Also I presume these problems will be patched out ASAP. There are some genuine lovable moments in this game and I'm very curious to see where Act 2 is going to take the game in April.
The devs have been active in support, which is a good thing too!
All in all I'd recommend this game to anyone who is in for an original adventure with a nice story and great music!

Karmaflow is a masterful blend of music, art, and gameplay. It's had a bit of a bumpy launch, but team Karmaflow rallied together and patched most of the issues by the end of Day 1. Very rarely have I seen a team work that fast at fixing bugs. This is even more impressive when you consider this is a new studio who crowdfunded the game on Indiegogo (they didn't reach their full goal) and are new to the game development world.
Seeing all the complaints of bugs on Steam, I waited until the first wave of patches before playing the game. I am happy to report that I ran into ZERO game breaking bugs and I really enjoyed my time with the game (played with a controller). NOTE: There are still some minor bugs being worked on, but what game doesn't have those?
This game is all about the music. If you don't like symphonic metal then you're probably not going to like the game, but what did you expect out of a game calling itself a Rock Opera? If you do like the genre, then you are in for a real treat. The orchestral performances of some of Metal's most recognized icons (seriously, look at the cast for this game) was spot-on and combined with the game's unique visual style, created a deep atmosphere that really drew me in.
Without going into too many details, the story follows the Karma Keeper as it travels from world to world restoring balance after the mysterious "Dissonance" has wreaked havoc. It is presented, as you would expect, in rock opera fashion by having the characters sing/scream their parts to tell their tales. There are shards scattered around the worlds that present Karmaflow's backstory, and really solidify the atmosphere of the game. The addition of subtitles (see! They were listening to the community and added this in the first string of patches!) really helped me keep track of Karmaflow's story.
While the designers are new, they did a fantastic job of using subtle visual cues to keep players on the right path. There are no direct hints to solving the puzzles, meaning if you get stuck, you will have to look around the environment and experiment with different approaches to find your way out. I love this approach because it keeps you in the game instead of constantly waiting for a hint.
The ambient sounds in the game could be better. Like when a boulder hits the ground, it would be nice to hear a solid crash instead of an odd crunching sound. I wasn't too fond of the thudding sound the Karma Keeper made when it landed after jumping, but that's just personal preference. There lots of little instances like these where I wished the ambient sounds were a bit better, but hey, this was a crowdfunded game from Indiegogo with a killer soundtrack and vocal cast, I'm not complaining too much.
Lastly, while I really enjoyed the puzzles within the game, there were no consequences for failing or dying. If the Karma Keeper dies in the game, you respawn close by and continue where you left off. There's no reset or anything. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it does remove any sense of urgency or fear from the boss "fights"/"puzzles" (I'm honestly not sure what to call them). But again, this game is all about delivering a killer Rock Opera experience, and it does that with gusto.
Overall, I would give Karmaflow a 4 out of 5 as I sit and wait for Act 2 to be released later this year!
Pros:
- Soundtrack
- Music
- Epic musical solos (noticing a trend)
- Solid puzzle mechanics
- Atmosphere
- Solid Rock Opera style story and presentation
- Game includes soundtrack (To be released with Act 2 later this year)
Cons:
- Ambient sounds could be improved
- No consequences for failing
- Act 1 is very short (roughly 3 - 3.5 hours)

Before I will share my view on this game I'm inclined to state where I got my information from. All you will read below has been gathered from the Karmaflow website, Facebook, Twitter, contact with the developer, bugtesting sessions and the game itself.
I am quite puzzled to see some people denounce this game in the way they do. Let's be real here: Basecamp Games is a studio that started out as a student graduation project, they are new to all this. Anyone expecting a fledgling studio selling a 15 euro game to deliver a flawless experience should get their heads out of their pretentious asses.
Had the game cost 4 times the amount, or if the developer created a plethora of games before this, then I might have reconsidered as well. It surprises me how dedicated Basecamp is as a studio, as they have patched some major problems out already and are (probably) doing so as we speak.
Now then, onto the game. What is Karmaflow?
In short, Karmaflow is a 3d platformer that let's you play as the Karmakeeper, a little guy who travels across the lands to try and fix an imbalance that is tearing these lands apart. There's more to it but I don't want to spoil anything for you.  Much of the narrative is brought to you in song and acted out in cutscenes. The gameplay itself is fairly straightforward, and should not be too challenging for too many.
This game stands on it's graphical style and stellar music. It's not hard to find a list of all the talented musicians that helped to compose this beautiful soundtrack, and it can be seen that the creative director is in fact a composer. During the game itself, you can find instruments that will add their sounds to the ambiant music, enahncing your experience.
Now, I do have some smallgripes with this game. The camera can be a bit weird at times, which is detrimental to your jumping & gliding abilities. The camera moves when it wishes to show you something, but it can really mess up your jumps or your sense of direction. I did not yet encounter a problem with checkpoints, but I see others have. Karmaflow runs fine on my average PC, but it stutters for a slight second every time you reach a checkpoint (as a statue of you is suddenly spawned from various shards) this game also does not tell you where to go at every point, so make sure to get your bearings when you can. I tend to get lost at times, poor me.
If you see other reviews stating there are no subtitles and the music goes out of sync if you pause during cutscenes, that has all been taken care of. Basecamp is a developer that evidently listens and strives to give you the best.
The game is rather short at this time of writing, but anyone who purchases Act 1 will receive Act 2 later free of charge as an update to the game.
Bottom line:
Buy This --> If you like games that are more about the experience and easthetic than actual gameplay, and you like the style (both music and on-screen)
Don't buy this --> If you only want gameplay, or a game that just tells you what to do at every turn, and you get easily annoyed if some things work less than perfect sometimes. If you have a MAC, wait until you are sure it works (watch the updates)
I am enjoying this experience very much, I hope you will too!

Update to my day 1 review below:
The game sure had quite a few bugs in its early stage, but now they are mostly fixed. No more gamebreaking bugs, scenes can't be aborted anymore, autosave and loading don't create stuttering anymore, sounds are played correctly and achievements finally work.
I already recommended the game before, but I have to recommend it again, now that most flaws are gone! If you are unsure though, wait for it to be either bundled again (was already bundled once) or be on sale. The price will sure drop for quite a little.
Day 1 review:
Well as one of the very first funders of this small project I sort of watched the developers through their journey developing this game.
First thing - the project leader on this game is a music composer. He gathered a sort of young team around him to produce this game, with a budget that was smaller than intended since they didn't reach their goal with their campaign.
Since the project leader is clearly a professional in music expect that the most stunning part will be the soundtrack. Also consider watching the pretty big list of artist featured in the soundtrack - which is a major selling point of this game.
Now back to the game:
Pro:
+Great design
+Beautiful world
+Sort of a different approach in the jump and run genre
+Choices in cutscenes (not sure yet how they affect the story or music)
+Incredibly good soundtrack (given you like rock and metal mixed with orchestra)
+It's like a playable musical
+controller support
Cons:
-Day 1 bugs including(which will be most likely fixed soon):
laggy menu
short freezes when reaching a checkpoint
cutscene music keeps playing on pause which makes cutscenes out of sync
couldn't start second level due to a bug where i kept dying at the respawn point (doesnt affect everyone)
soundeffect controls didn't seem to work (soundeffects where a bit harsh and loud compared to the music)
problems with collission detection (sometimes can walk through objects, sometimes must jump over a small edge on the ground)
-Menu could use a slight redesign since it's quite plain looking compared to the rest of the game.
Well and that's it for me with the cons. Be really prepared that the soundtrack will in fact be the major selling point and the best thing about this game.
BUT: I think this game might become really good once the day 1 bugs (which make most cons) are corrected.

The game's name is klocki, and it remind me of Chinese Klotski, a sliding block puzzle game that I played when I was very young. And I played that single sliding lock puzzle again and again, I played it faster and faster.
As a klocki fun, it’s easy to imagine how excited I am when I see so many puzzles, some of which are hard to realize as physical. The difficulty of this game is getting higher as you go through the checkpoints, and it tells players the basic rules gradually. Some levels have its unique rule or knack, it’s still not difficult to be learned. The difficulty of this game is not high, you will walk through this game for about two hours. From lines to patterns, form plan to three dimension, it’s really an ingenious design, each level is so different. In this puzzle game, your brain is fully mobilized, and successfully solving these puzzles is a very interesting job. The background music also makes you relaxed. I’m surprised how the developers successfully add a stereo algorithm to the game.
I bought it in a game bundle, the quality is excellent for the price.
9/10 according to me.

Klocki is a great of example of silently guiding functionality of mechanics through geometry and the player’s own intuition and exploration.
Despite being a short game, it all feels well-paced. New types of tiles and spaces come up very often and really make the hour fly by. You never feel like you didn’t get enough time with any ideas either.
Every time a new piece was placed, it feels great to move it around for the first time, discovering its simple function. From here you begin to see how a piece moves with other groups of itself and what patterns emerge from there. Klocki then progressively becomes more and more rewarding as you see your skills with each type of piece combine until you’ve created rules and patterns that you apply on a final gauntlet of bigger puzzles
Meanwhile, an ambient soundtrack keeps your mind clear and the occasion lower tone played after finishing a puzzle provides a nice boost of endorphin.
Klocki is inexpensive and a great brief yet complete game worth picking up for an hour of meditative tinkering. It’s also got trading cards and an easy 100% if you’re into gridding up your steam profile.

It's...okay. The big twist of Pony Island is that it's not about ponies or an island at all, and it's instead something else entirely. It's very good about building on the bits of knowledge it's already given you in order to tutorialize throughout the whole experience without shoving any abrupt explanations in your face about some new game element, so you feel clever when you solve a problem, like you figured it out entirely on your own even though your thought process was probably exactly what the developer wanted you to go through. Presentation-wise, it's kind of clever, a little bit irreverant about its subject matter at times, which comes across as odd when a lot of the hints at the "lore" seem to suggest it's meant to be taken more seriously. It's one of those games that works far better if you play it yourself rather than watch someone else play it, and there are several points where the narrative/game design tricks they pull honestly made me laugh. But overal, I disagree with the overwhelmingly positive rating the title is being given right now, and I don't think I'd recommend it. It's not awful, it's just that your money is just better spent elsewhere.

Game review (honest)
The tactical, tough team-based shooter Rainbow Six Siege has picked up a lot of traction in the past six months. That’s been possible thanks to the release of new maps, new character releases, updates and bug fixes, turning one of Ubisoft’s more low-key releases of the past year into one of the best shooters out there. The game’s old-school gameplay has also attracted a terrific community of people with whom to play.
Initial critic response labeled the game as a rather average shooter. At the time, the game only had one PVP mode, no dedicated campaign, and a only a handful of maps. Calling it average was actually being nice. To top it off, Ubisoft’s “updates” weren’t always stable either. Anyone remember the infamous T-Shadows? Characters would appear to have eight-foot shadows growing out of their bodies. This made identifying enemies and even staying in cover nearly impossible. It left the game nearly unplayable for an entire month before Ubi fixed it. Add in the presence of underage “team killers” and you have yourself the recipe for a pretty disastrous opening quarter to a well known franchise.
Rainbow Six Siege’s success is not in its ability to be fresh, but rather in its ability to be, well, old.
However, even with its rocky start RB6 Siege now thrives and actually has a lot of people playing it and singing its praises. What’s causing this buzz? I think it is one simple fact that I discovered the moment I turned it on: RB6 Siege provides some of the most heart-pounding and gut wrenching gameplay available on the market. Combined with its rather mature community, its emphasis on strategy and team play, and its unpredictable and unforgiving difficulty, Rainbow Six Siege sets itself apart as one of the boldest FPS’s in decades. Not only does the game stand out among the rest of shooters in this era, it pummels them in terms of sheer gameplay and replayability.
Rainbow Six Siege’s success is not in its ability to be fresh, but rather in its ability to be, well, old. From the moment I turned on the game back in December, I was immediately taken back to the ‘90s. I was back to sitting cross-legged on the floor in front of my mom’s tube TV with the original Rainbow Six cartridge plugged into my N64. I played that game religiously. My childhood friend and I would try to beat the game, playing co-op on the harder difficulties. And when I say it was difficult, I mean it was painful. The game was rated T for Teen back then, but, trust me when I say it was meant for adults.
The only thing easy about that original Rainbow Six was getting killed. That was something I loved about it. It was the challenge. The computer was unbeatable. I saw grown men struggle through it. That alone gave me hope as a young 7-8 year-old trying to master a game technically only made for people two to three times my age. And now that I am two to three times that age, I can say that RB6 Siege picks up amazingly right where its older predecessors left off.
Today’s shooters like Call of Duty and Battlefield are more concerned with theatrics and run-and-gun gameplay. Granted, I think this is beneficial for the younger gamers of this generation. Let’s face it, this is the era of Facebook, Snapchat, self-driving cars, and short attention spans. But what about us old schoolers who like a slow, chess styled challenge? This is where RB6 Siege shines. The game is made for thinkers and strategist, for guys and girls my age who want to move slow and calculate, guys and girls who know that death could be waiting around that next corner.
Siege’s more strategic style of play has attracted more mature players to the game. I have never been surrounded by more mature gamers. I’ve played with cops, ex-military, firemen, postmen, and even some colleagues from a newspaper I worked for. Everyone is so mellow and calm on RB6 Siege, although you will have your cheaters and team killers. Ubisoft has done an amazing job in regulating them since the release of the game last year. For the most part, everyone acts with a level of class and respect. I have made many friends online playing this game. Most players I run with are older (late 20's- mid 30's). The fact of the matter is the game feels like it’s made for adults. Unlike COD, this is the game where instead of getting cursed out after death, you actually learn something and can apply it to the next round, or even help your teammates survive the ongoing round by giving critical information. This is largely due to RB6 Siege’s emphasis on strategy and team play.
Teams who coordinate their every move with one another usually obliterate teams with no communication. It’s such a stark difference that you can actually feel it when you are against teams that have no strategy.
Success in RB6 Siege is ultimately chalked up to the three C’s, Communication, Communication, and Communication. I have never played a game that relied on the comms as much as RB6 Siege does. Teams must plan and calculate their moves to be successful. I have spent many hours playing with and without my fireteam, and RB6 Siege is a completely different experience without communicating with others. If you think you can get in there with no mic and lonewolf it all day, you will get your feelings hurt rather quickly. Updated information is critical to your own survival. So being a quiet, “I will kill em all” kind of guy won’t get you or your team very far. Teams who coordinate their every move with one another usually obliterate teams with no communication. It’s such a stark difference that you can actually feel it when you are against teams that have no strategy. Players get a chance to think outside of the box–whether it’s by blasting through walls for entry, opening up floor hatches as escape routes, or even sniping from across the map.
The way the game pans out is ultimately up to you and how you and your team want to assault or defend. I love this aspect of the game. It let’s the players choose how to interact in these environments. There have been many times when I was the Marksman on our fireteam. I would follow closely to whoever wanted to be my shield (Usually Blitz). They would enter a room and absorb any fire with their shield and then drop down so I could pick off targets while shooting over their shoulder. While it didn’t work every time we did it, this strategy was a bread a butter for my team for a long time. This is just small example of the endless tactical strategy of RB6 Siege. There are no prompts or tutorials to give you this type of knowledge, either. My friends and I came up with ideas like these in the planning room or on the fly via comms. Yes there are other games like the Battlefield franchise which rely on communication and strategy as well. However, it’s RB6 Siege’s unrelenting and unforgiving no-respawn system that truly sets it above the rest.

I'll try to be as fair as possible with this game. I've played both campaigns on difficult setting with 100% gold, though I had sometimes the urge to just quit the game. First of all, the game looks neat, especially by 2002 standards, the basics of gameplay are pretty easy to learn, the AI is ok and the soundtrack is really atmospheric. So much for the positive aspects of the game.
The story is rather lame, run-of-the-mill fantasy with some steampunk elements. But the cutscenes and the presentation of the story make up a little for the weak story.
The biggest problem with the game are the messed up hitboxes. And that's a big issue in a hack 'n slash game. Arrows going right through enemies, melee fighters can't hit enemies on stairways if they are below them and missiles going right through massive obstacles. That seems to be intended for magic missiles, but I have noticed some examples where enemy bowmen attacked me through a solid wall while I couldn't hit them, which is pretty frustrating. Also, the 1st person view is rather glitchy, especially in narrow spaces.
The balancing is a mess. Sorcerers spam homing missiles at you which drain 1/4 of your life AND do damage over time while most melee fighters are push overs. Since the overall difficulty isn't very high (except for level 13 in the light campaign, that one was really tough), you can rush through most of the levels. You can beat this game with difficult setting and a 100% score in less than 15 hours.
I've never even read a single word about bugs referring to this game, but it has its fair share of them. Enemies dropping of cliffs who were supposed to drop gold => 100% no achievable. Traps not triggering. Even important NPCs tend to get stuck in the environment, so you have to start all over again. To be fair, most of the levels are pretty short (sometimes even ridiculously tiny), so that's not a big problem.
In summary this game could have used a lot of testing, it feels a little unfinished in some places. But for 5 € you can't go wrong, and as a hack n slash fan you should definitely try this one out.

I'm in two minds about whether I should review this as a curiosity, or whether I should review it purely as a game experience.
If it's the former, I think it's worth checking out - And as the latter it's not worth the time and money.
So far there's about 40 minutes of content, and the gameplay never really becomes challenging in any real way. There's issues with the controls not being responsive enough for a platformer, the environments are a little confusing to navigate in this first episode. There's no major faults with the game outside of it not having incredible gameplay design and execution. But then I don't entirely expect it either. It's very difficult to get that in a 3D game from an indie studio.
As for the music side of things - I wasn't blown away, but thought it was a very fun way to conduct the game narrative. Subtitles are something sorely missing, however - And with growled vocals some players would have difficulty understanding the plot - And this is assuming they can hear the vocals clearly through the sound levels.
I'm yet to see music form an integral part of the gameplay itself, which is something I was really hoping for. While it's still possible that the game could get better in the future, the gameplay and musical elements are two very disparate parts.
In all - I want to recommend this game sorely for the lovely idea, the pretty settings, and for it being interesting. As I say, I can't recommend you play it as a game - It's more a curiosity. Check out some videos before you make a purchase, 'cause it's surely not for everyone.

Before making this review, I kept a few things in consideration:
1. It's a completely crowdfunded game. They did NOT make full fuding, yet they DID finish working on the game.
2. It's not a big company with 100 people working on one game. This means that if there are bugs, I don't expect them to be patched out twenty times a week.
PRO:
- Artstyle
- Music
- Story seems interesting
- Native controller support
- Rather unique game in the whole "music based" games
- No "go here now" kind of hints! Look around, jump. Maybe you CAN make that jump. Maybe you CAN'T make that jump. Maybe you shouldn't even go that way in the first place. Where am I? Am I supposed to be here?
You play the game, rather than the game plays you (quicktime events, aarg)
CON:
- Bugs. It's day one, what do you expect? Even bigger games come out completely bugged nowadays (skyrim or asscreed anyone?)
- *** PATCHED *** (Subtitles would be nice, as some of the grunting lines were unclear to me, making me feel less involved in what's going on in the game)
- Pausing during a "cutscene" (characters are singing the story to you), pauses the game but not the audio. Hence, after unpausing, lipsync is off.
Who should buy this game:
- People who like metal music
- People who like platform puzzle games, like Papo & Yo, Ico, Fez, The Swapper, Giani Sisters, etc.
- People who visited the karmaflow rock opera in Den Bosch
- Parents who want their children to play something without shooting, violence, etc.
Who should not buy this game:
- People expecting a finished game
- People who are looking for a game to put 50+ hours in & replay the same game over & over.
Recommended: YES, taking all things said above in consideration.
It's a small studio, it's day one, they decided to release without having all the funds, give them some time :)

I'll just start with the bad things to get it out of the way. The first release of this game was clearly rushed. Music tends to get out of sync when you pause the game, the menus are very bland and when you use the controller in the menus it works as a mouse pointer.
To top it off, I had to use "continue" to start the game instead of "New Game" which would take me right back to the menu. This is made even stranger when I finished the first part of Act 1, because after a long loading time I was put back into the main menu and had to choose "Continue".
Collision detection in the game is a bit shabby now and then as well. As a last minor point it would've been nice if the game had subtitles for the vocals, eventhough they are pretty clear. So far none of it has been gamebreaking though.
So much for the bad stuff, onwards to the good stuff!
The game looks great! The art design is beautiful and the choice of colours is perfect, giving the areas either a very 'warm' or 'cold' look. The music is pretty awesome as well, but since there is a lot of metal it has to be your kind of thing to enjoy. Especially when you've got some growling vocals.
Every once in a while you'll have a scene where people sing, making it feel like you're playing a Disney movie. And it is great.
The gameplay is pretty simple and intuitive. You get a few pointers on what to do and then you'll figure out most of it yourself. So far the puzzles haven't been too hard, but then again I don't play it for the challenge, I play it for the great music and superb visuals.
Bottomline; the game needs some more polishing up, but since none of it was gamebreaking I really enjoyed playing through the interesting world. It looks great and it sounds great and movement is pretty fun.

It's...okay. The big twist of Pony Island is that it's not about ponies or an island at all, and it's instead something else entirely. It's very good about building on the bits of knowledge it's already given you in order to tutorialize throughout the whole experience without shoving any abrupt explanations in your face about some new game element, so you feel clever when you solve a problem, like you figured it out entirely on your own even though your thought process was probably exactly what the developer wanted you to go through. Presentation-wise, it's kind of clever, a little bit irreverant about its subject matter at times, which comes across as odd when a lot of the hints at the "lore" seem to suggest it's meant to be taken more seriously. It's one of those games that works far better if you play it yourself rather than watch someone else play it, and there are several points where the narrative/game design tricks they pull honestly made me laugh. But overal, I disagree with the overwhelmingly positive rating the title is being given right now, and I don't think I'd recommend it. It's not awful, it's just that your money is just better spent elsewhere.

If you've played Oregon Trail, then you know what you're getting with the original Organ Trail; a pure parody of Oregon Trail set in a zombie infested post-apocalypic wasteland. Its gameplay is similar, its ideas are similar, and it's a lot of fun, just like the original source material.
Here's the thing though, Organ Trail: Director's Cut is everything the original Organ Trail is, and much much more. Rather than just a parody - and I agree fully with what the creators say they intended the game to be - it is a game that stands above and beyond its own source material as a game in its own right.
It's fun, it's dark, it's darkly funny, and it's honestly quite creepy in several places. The soundtrack is incredible and Ben Crossbones' musical talent lends itself perfectly, creating a wonderous, lonesome, tense and tragic air to the whole game. Rolling into a settlement (or the remains of a city), buying supplies and fixing/upgrading your Station Wagon, or learning new combat skills, trading and scavenging and talking with strangers was great before, but with the soundtrack it turns it into both wonderous relief and soul-crushing despair as you realise these are the few survivors left, and you should take what levity you can on your perilous road to a CHANCE at salvation.
Be warned however. Easy difficulty may not be as rewarding but it is fun. If you want the extra points bonuses, rack up the difficulty, but be prepared for ungodly amounts of pain, because the jump from Easy to Normal is IMMEDIATELY visible. You will suffer at the hands of the game for your greed, so be sure you're REALLY good at aiming for a start.
Total recommendation, totally worth every penny in sale or not. Get it, play it, love it. Just uh... don't play it late at night before you go to bed. You may have interesting dreams. o_o;

I... really can't recommend this game, even for the low, low price for which I got it. I can be told that I'm "missing the point," but frankly... I really recommend just playing Oregon Trail. It's a similar experience, but slightly more enjoyable.
The problem is that most of the time, this just felt unfair to me, in ways that a game should not be. Allow me to elaborate: I was playing on EASY, because I KNEW this game would be hard. And NONE of the minigames felt like a DECENT challenge. They were either so easy as to be pointless, or difficult to the point of frustration (like the shootouts with bandits who never miss and barely ever pop out of cover... Time Crisis felt more fair to me, and that's a game that's designed to EAT QUARTERS.) Every now and then, an interesting event would happen, but more often something would just be taken from me for no reason, and I had to accept it. No strategy, no rhyme or reason. I literally once picked up 3 cans of fuel as a raandom event and IMMEDIATELY had 4 stolen from me by bandits.
And these bandits are the scourge of the gods. They are always teeming, always a threat, no matter how many you strike down, and are seemingly unaffected by zombies and hold no valuables, even bullets, that do not disintegrate once slain. They can steal fuel from the tank of a moving vehicle. They can kidnap a party member (again, from a moving vehicle) and hold him at gunpoint to force a single shot rescue with no grace on the aim; you LITERALLY have to be PERFECT.
The game just makes it feel like you have no control over... anything. And not in the realistic way. Shops and jobs rarely offer what you need, ammo and fuel are insanely overpriced, your party members are mentally deficient enough to break spare parts for the car on a regular basis... and unless you have an $80 perk, you can only find food, scrap, and (I believe, rarely) ammo while scavenging. And I was only ever able to learn the perk that allowed me to find medkits.
In short... I found this game just frutrating and disappointing. Maybe if you're a ridiculously huge zombie fanatic, it'll be more fun. Otherwise, I think Oregon Trail is just better-designed, and all the little "jokes" and references can be read for just as much effect. The game has potential, but it just feels like it doesn't offer enough. Nothing bad that happened to me (okay, save one gunshot wound that I quickly patched with my dozens of medkits) seemed like it happened as a result of my input... that much lack of control, where you can (seemingly easily) lose through no fault of your own, just doesn't appeal to me.
This game is a whole lot of fun for the price. The game seems simple, but if you screw up like I did the first time, you be stranded out in the middle of nowhere with no way to fix your car.

This game has wonderful graphics and a nice soundtrack. On the first zones, the puzzles are well designed and make for a challenging, yet somehow relaxing experience. I bought this for my son, but found it very enjoyable myself - until we reached the later levels, that is.
By adding extra zones which add little to the story, with increasingly longer and more difficult levels, the author continuingly denies us the satisfaction of finishing the game. What's more, while the first zones seem to have been carefully crafted, the later zones seem to have taken much less thought, with things like difficult control and poor camera angles getting in your way.
It is kind of sad when you consider that this game seems to be made for children, but ends up being so frustrating that they can't finish it without help from adults. My son ended up giving up on playing, and eventually so have i.
Still, because the game's strong points outweigh its flaws, i still recommend this game to anyone who likes the 2D Puzzle Platformer genre.

Deep down, I really, really love this game.
It's adorable, the morphing blob concept is great, and some parts are really fun. But man... does it have some of the most annoying platforming I have ever experienced. If your position is off by a fraction of a pixel or your timing is a milisecond off, you will plunge into spike pits and get eaten by evil blobs over... and over.. and over. It does not help that the controls are not particularly responsive (at least, I do not find them to be). To say nothing of the boss battles, which are even more awful.
It gets really frustrating. If you like cute things and have lots of patience, it can be fun. Or you might just give up after having to repeat the same section ten times in a row.
It's one of those games that I hesitate to give either a thumbs-up or a thumbs-down because the first half is really fun, but as the game progresses... but I feel like the frustration outweighs the fun.

I'll start off with the single player campaign. The first half of it was mostly boring with forgettable levels and story. These levels were somewhat emersive but I could tell that they were rushed mainly because when the level became boring, the game would put in what felt a forced COD cliche like a helicopter crash or a slowmotion break-in into the room with either a hostage or an enemy boss inside. Back in the day, these were really cool concepts, but now, we are looking for a new concept other then an up your sleeve COD stereotypical game element. These cliche's didn't fit into the gameplay that well as I was left confused or irritated by these. The second half was actually pretty emersive for the most part with levels that seemed pretty well designed and executed. The cliche's in this half, unlike the first half, fitted in well with the game and added to the experience. The characters were excellent as their intentions and actions were clear and understandable. One of the main enemy bosses in this half was an Asian women. I was so excited at this point where I could break in and have a nice boss fight. But no, once you break into her room, she fights you in a cutscene, then you put her head in the fire where she dies. This left me disappointed as the game hyped up this moment so much but failed to deliver. When you are in the dream world at the end of the game, you go through a lot of sequences until you get to the end and save the day. When you feel like you've just saved the world, you black out. I found out that nothing in the game was real except the start and it was all just a dream and the ending is you dying from your injuries from the start of the game. This made the single player campaign go from average all the way to down right disappointing.
Now for the Multiplayer. The multiplayer was fundimentally the same as your standard annual Call of Duty game. There was nothing really new that I'm aware of except for some new guns, abilities and a whole different theme. As usual it became very addictive for a while.
Overall, Call of Duty: Black Ops 3 was an disappointing game. It was fun, but it was lacking the well orchestrated design that made the Modern Warfare trilogy so popular and loved.

I have a strange suspision that Enclave might not be a very good game. On the other hand, I enjoyed this third person hack 'n' slash enough to finish both of its campaigns (the Light one and the Dark), so maybe it's not all that bad either.
I wish I knew what the story in this game was about, but it was delivered in the most boring way, so my mind began to wander everytime I was exposed to it, making me unable to take notice. Basically, what you get is something that I like to call "a talking book" - cutscenes showing nothing but an old looking book with a voiceover put on top of it. I guess, all you really need to know is that the good guys fight the bad guys, right? What really matters, is the gameplay...
...And the gameplay is quite engaging. You play through different levels unlocking new characters that you can choose between at the beginning of each stage. All the playable characters are essentially split between three classes - a fighter for melee combat (sword, axe, hammer + shield), a ranger for ranged combat (bow, crossbow + different types of ammo) and a mage for... ranged combat also, but with MAGIC (various staves that shoot magic missiles). As you go along, you are also provided with better equipement, that you can chose from based on the collective amount of gold you aquired on your adventures. Good stuff.
Graphics are quite nice too. Must have been really nice when the game came out. Not much else to say. Overall, I had fun with Enclave. Might recommend.

You don't typically level so much as each stage you complete has gold hidden in it, as well as a set reward at the end of each stage. You get that gold, and can use it on items at the start of missions. You don't buy it permanently, just for that character for that mission, although you keep the gold if that makes sense. I would like to say, when I first bought this game, I had doubts like any other people who played Watch Dogs 1. But in the end, the game itself has shined through the darkness of its' old-self.
Design wise, the game itself was made to resemble the world we are living in, and that it has this unique colorful world that  appeals more to the millennials generations. Why? Because Watch Dogs 2 based on the internet in this current state which riddled with memes, propaganda, false informations, news, social medias, etc. and the developer succeeded in replicating that Internet in the game. Kudos to the developer for that.
Gameplay wise, the parkour and combat system is little bit more interesting than Watch Dogs 1, and with the ability to engage the surrounding even more makes the game much more fun, although most of the engaging the enemy type of deal can be skipped now with the ability to hack using drones and mini robots (which is cool) but it creates some sort of "exploit" that you can abuse to get through the level without experiencing all the shooting. I'd recommend mixing a playstyle of gun and run with hack and crack to fully experience the game.
Story wise, well, from my perspective, it follows the mold of man versus world kind of deal, but it feels like being made before, it's just under the hat of a hacker I guess. I have no problem with it, so 5/7 would story again.
Last but not least, the Character development. I'd say, Ubisoft did a great job in giving everyone a different personality and they are all fun to interact with, but there is one person I'd love to have more development: Horatio. Throughout the whole game, I felt like Horatio didn't get much screen time, and I think he only has like 1 mission. Also for the fact that, in many cutscenes (most of them) I don't see Horatio at all, like where did he go? I mean after the cutscene you can literally sees that he's sitting there in his desk doing some hacking and stuff. Overall, I'm only upset for Horatio, which has like no screen time at all, and I would love to have more side missions with Horatio and get to know him better.
To conclude this review, I'll give the game a 8.5/10. Love the gameplay, love the memes, give Horatio more times, love the hacking, and above all, it was worth it. Go buy the game.
Edit: I only play to enjoy the single player mode, not the multiplayer mode, so I don't have a specific review for it ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
