Very good RPG. If you're big on story and are looking for an JRPG with extremely well developed characters, exceptionally well written dialogue and one of the best endings in a game look no further. Trails in the Sky has one of the best and most robust casts of characters I've ever seen in a JRPG. Each character is great by being interesting, having multiple sides to their personalities and backstories loaded with depth. I can only think of maybe three or so at most JRPG's I've played in my entire life that can stand up to this game's story, characters, writing and plot twists. The gameplay of Trails in the Sky is turn based and the game has no random encounters. Trails in the Sky's gameplay is good, but not absolutely amazing. If you're looking for a revolutionary combat system or something way different from the norm the combat system may let you down a little. However, the battles are still fun and the game is fun to play. An annoyance can be though that sidequests are easily missable and dungeons are tough to navigate due to not having maps in them. Turn based JRPG fans such as myself though will like the combat system a lot, but won't find it anything mindblowing. Last, the music of the game is very good. Trails's soundtrack is a great game soundtrack and I greatly enjoyed the vast majority of the songs in the game. If you're a fan of JRPG's especially ones with good stories and you liked games like Lunar, Grandia etc then Trails in the Sky is a must play. I could very well say even despite this game's flaws it just might be one of the best JRPG's of all time.

A Boy And His Blob is an adorable reimagining of an old NES game. While it's not a perfect game, I really enjoyed this game and find it easy to recommend to people who'd like a casual puzzle platformer.
I'd like to also add that my listed playtime time does not reflect the amount of time I put in this game; I'm most familar with the Wii version which I have played through a couple times but I've played the Steam version enough to know the differences between the two. (which is almost nothing but control choices)
The art style is refreshingly vibrant and colorful and along with the solid sountrack (though I don't think it'll be blowing anyone away) I think it does a great job just building this almost fairy tale-like atmosphere. Puzzles, especially solutions to the various boss fights in the games felt rewarding and were just fun on the whole. I didn't find anything in this game too difficult and it was easy to just sit back and play through this, it's a pretty relaxing little game. I personally had no problem with the controls at all and used the keyboard without remapping any of my buttons but it might take a minute or two to get used to cycling beans and controlling your character fluidly.
If I had anything negative to say about the game the first would be that I actually found the game too easy at times, and things kind of became a slog. Blobs AI can be finicky at times too where he gets stuck in places he shouldn't. Just a tip though, if it ever gets stuck in a spot and he won't come to you, spam the button that calls him repeatedly and it'll force him into a balloon where he'll float right over to you. It's not a perfect solution, but I'm glad the function is there so when this does happen it only takes a few seconds to get back on track.
All in all while I don't think this game is for everyone due to it's simple nature that can bore some, if you're looking for a comfy puzzle platformer this is a great game in my book and is an easy thumbs up on that alone. I did a video on a more in-depth review of the game if you're interested and while it's based off the Wii version, the two versions are identical.
This game could be great if they didn't cheap out on the graphics, I mean, comeo on, you have a great Idea and a great game mechanicm don't cheap out on the visuals.

Let's get this out of the way: This is a straight port of the 2009 Wii game. Apart from the new button prompts, the sprites and background are meant for a 480p display and are not redone in HD. This bothered me at first and I didn't want to buy it as a result, however I got it for cheap in a bundle a while back and decided to give it a shot last night.
As someone who's never played the original, I'm only going to judge this game on its own merits. All I can say is that it's very calming and cute. If you want to unwind after a long day, then it's a pretty great game for doing so. Although the art is low-res, the beauty of it still shines through, and I didn't have any qualms about putting it in full screen on a 27-inch QHD monitor. The game isn't very difficult, with even the unlockable "challenge" levels being fairly trivial, so if you're looking for difficulty then you're not gonna find much. The protagonist is a mostly-silent 6-year old boy (whose age is confirmed in the game's unlockable concept art) and a cute, lovingly-animated white blob he meets in a forest. There's even a dedicated "hug blob" button!
My few complaints are that the controls are a bit imprecise (tapping the arrow key/d-pad made me blow right past ladders and off platform edges multiple times) and the game does feel a bit dated compared to newer 2D platformers, since it originally released in 2009. Despite that, it's a very calm, cute game with great art direction.

I remember playing the original game on a friend's NES and also playing the Game Boy part but only finished both games
once after
play session. Most of the frustration came from only having a certain number of
each jelly bean which resulted in getting stuck and being forced to restart if you wasted some beans - which happened quite often
due to not being able to target precisely.
Fortunately, both issues are gone in this instance of the game, i.e. you can target your throws properly and have infinite
beans. The environments are beautifully drawn and you can practically feel the love that's been put in this game... though you get "artifacts" when scrolling and the camera is extremely annoying, especially in later game parts
.
There are 4 big areas in the game with several levels and a boss fight. Every level has a predefined selection of usable jelly beans and contains 3 hidden treasure chests which unlock challenge levels when collected and when you finish those you unlock concept art, etc. Nothing special but surely nice to have.

Ok... i've been following this game since it was announced but didn't buy it because i'm a cheap person.
Well... this game is great...
Pros:
Fun combat. And that's something strange for me to say. Normally i get bored in a few minutes... This, i really like, when i saw the game i thought: ohh it's another smash the keyboard isometric game. Well, nope. It requieres for you to think about what to do. You have 2 weapons or a main weapon and an accessory that changes depending of the character you're using (dynamite, a medkit, a critical enhancing badge (yes.. weird), a knife, a lasso, molotvs, etc). You also have at least 2 styles of using your main weapon that can inflict status (like wonded, reducing movement speed, or blindness. You also have a stamina bar that allows you to dash and make melee attacks (if you choose a melee oriented class). Aiming is quite difficult in the good way, gamepads respond perfectly but you really have to aim or you won't hit... So it's all about timing and resourcces, running out of stamina, bad timing, not looking at the map. It's a really good game that mixes skill, strategy and knowing your opponents... To me, fun factor is 9/10. Every character feels different, so you can play in various styles.
Characters: there are about 10 right now. Everyone is different in playing styles. And i found everyone (but the tipical obese/nasty one, for now) being really fun. Normally i go one character and i'm done... here i'm playing with everyone online . I like that they stayed in stereotypes but they didn't at the same time. You have the characters you thought you would... but their designs are interesting. There's not the lawful sheriff or the big bad guy, they're all... normal... excentric characters... I love them all... But again, since i like them all, i would like to have more so...8/10 (skins are too expensive).
Music: Great, i didn't mute it... that's saying a lot. I normally play while watching something on the other monitor... Well, nope, i like it, but to be honest you eventually can get tired. Also, i don't remember any song but the title screen one.. so 7/10
Art style: i LOVE it, 10/10. it's that simple. I'd like more creativity in some characters (again, big ugly guy again)
Balance: Well, here's something odd. I was playing a match thinking: ITS IMPOSSIBLE, THE SNIPER IS TOO STRONG... then i played with it and i found that the trap-ster kicks it's♥♥♥♥♥.. But the rogue-speed guy defeats him (well, in a rocks paper scissor style, it doesnt mean you will win with him, you'll have more chances). So, there's balance issues in 1 vs 1... 2 vs 2 thing changes. Example, we were playing 2 vs 2 and we were two ghost ponchos (low range+dashes) against a bowgirl and a trickster (2 with the most range of the game) Impossible to attack them before being shot in the face. Eventually we found openings and made a strategy, without talking, without ... nothing, just by playing and syncing, and that happened lot of times... strategy becomes that intuitive. It really REALLY becomes a team game where you can work as a team, it's not about a guy sniping and killing everyone, it's about aiding each other. So... balance wise, it's balanced yet it's not... 2 vs 2 yes, 1 vs 1 ... not a lot...... 7/10
Matchmaking: I'm from south america... I had it for a few days, i managed to find about 10 people online (i think it's regional matchmaking). I wouldn't say the game is dead, but it could use a boost. Also, it kicks you from matchmaking if you've been waiting for too long... so if you're 3 waiting for the 4th player the room could dissolve. BUT, matchmaking, when there's people works like a charm. IT's -> click -> you're in the game. No waiting at all. Also, i'm from south... again... my ping isn't the best with ANYONE, and i can feel lag sometimes, still when i'm hit i cant curse a lot because i knew i was going to be hit. I have to lower the score because im from a third world country and no one buys games here so i'm alone like every valentine's day 6/10
Overall... i love this game... It's great. It would be awesome if the matchmaking worked a little better for me...

Mysteries of the Past has almost everything a good hidden object game needs: great hidden object scenes, a variety of scenery, and a storyline that serves as an actual driving force for the game.
Blue Brained Games has an ambitious motto on their home page, but their debut game, Mysteries of the Past: Shadow of the Daemon, can warrant some self-confidence.
On the surface, Mysteries of the Past is a generic HOG: we play as a paranormal investigator hired to find a missing family in a wood resort, only to find the trails of a mystical conspiracy orchestrated by a demon worshipper. Contrary to most HOGs though, our heroine narrates a lot, which is a surprisingly good trick to keep the player interested in the otherwise fairly standard plot.
Another good choice was to mix in several hidden object scene types; they aren’t difficult, but their variety adds a lot to the fun factor. This stands in a sad contrast with every other gameplay elements, which are mediocre at best. Luckily, their blandness isn’t too distracting, so the end result is still an enjoyable HOG.

In
, you play a paranormal detective who has been summoned to a hotel to investigate some spooky occurrences. However, a bad situation takes a turn for the worse when you find out
and dark magic is at play! It’s your job to rescue the pair and also defeat the evil entity once and for all using keen detective skills as you play through puzzles and a plethora of hidden object scenes.
The story starts off simply: You’ve been asked to look around the hotel but then discover two of the guests are missing, leading you into a world of magic. There aren’t many twists to the story, though -it’s rather predictable. The dialogue is not the best and there are some translation errors, however it’s all passable. I was left with a few questions, like why were you even summoned to the hotel? All you did was get in the way and ruin the villain's plan. What happened to your car, did it stop working or something? Why didn’t the villain just kill you? They had multiple chances to do so. I know we must suspend disbelief at times when dealing with fiction but
In terms of gameplay the game runs well, it’s point and click so you have to use your mouse to perform actions. You click on an object to interact with it, add it to your inventory or whatever needs to be done. The game has plenty of mini games of different styles, some easy and some hard, so I did like the mix there.
, the game offers a bit of variety where this is concerned. There is the classic list of items you have to find in a scene, there are also some where you have to collect scatter objects and arrange them in a room. However some are different but not as needed, like one where you’re given four different colored locks and have to find the not-very well-hidden keys for them. I did enjoy the attempt at re-imagining hidden object scenes.
The art in this game is lovely, the hidden object scenes are well done and most items aren’t too hard to find if you have bad eyes. The character models are good, the scenery is well-done and thematically appropriate. The game is also fully voice-acted, for better or worse. I didn’t mind the main character’s voice or acting much, it would never win an Oscar but it worked here. The other characters, however, are all
The way most lines were read felt stiff. There was even a grammatical error in the text and the main character read the sentence word for word, highlighting the error even more. I won’t even start on how stereotypical the Shaman’s character and voice acting was. Music in the game is good, helps keep you in the game’s atmosphere.
Over all,
is a middle-of-the-road hidden object game. It functions well and accomplishes its purpose as a game, however it’s not really a must-have. It’s often the little things that stick out and make you ask “Why?”, like having to find a chisel three separate times when I could have just kept the first one. This is a hard review, one of those situations where I wish there was a "meh" option rather than yes or no.
If you're a fan of the HO genre and, like me, you run low on this type of game to play when you're in the mood, it's certainly not terrible and worth a shot.  However, I would exhaust the other options in your library first, and i would HIGHLY suggest waiting for a big sale as $9.99 seems far too much for what you get here.
The plot is pretty standard, nothing unique.  The dialogue is horrid and the voice acting is even worse.  It's simply not well written (or possibly not well translated, in this case).  For instance, the dialogue from the little boy in the story sounds like nothing that a kid that age would say in a real conversation; for me, it was a little jarring.
Puzzles are your basic minigames that you find in this sort of games, nothing that stands out overly much.
Hidden object scenes are not bad and some have multiple parts which I enjoyed; for instance, picking up objects in the first stage and then placing them back into the scene during the next stage (essentially "cleaning up" the scene).  My only complaint would be that some of the situations weren't intuitive where you had to complete a series of steps to get the items.  That premise isn't unique, but some of the sequencing didn't make sense, as in "why would I ever even think to do that?" situations.  Other than that, and some oddly named objects as another reviewer mentioned (likely translation issues), the HO scenes are pretty well done.
TL;DR:  worth it if you can get it on sale and have exhausted the rest of your library, just don't expect anything above-and-beyond the ordinary.

JRPGs have a reasonable following in the world at large, but it’s only in the last few years that they’ve become readily available on Steam. What was once a barren wasteland for JRPG fans has slowly blossomed, and gamers now find themselves with a decent catalogue to choose from whenever popping online. So now we found ourselves, over a year after Trails in the Sky’s Steam release date, investigating to see how it holds up to the competition.
In many ways, Trails in the Sky is standard fare for JRPGs. You have a coming of age story for the two protagonist siblings, Estelle and Joshua, a budding romance, and a seemingly small quest that expands to world-saving proportions as the game progresses. You could even fairly say that the story of the game isn’t particularly exciting, and doesn’t begin to move until you’re about thirty hours of the game. Instead, Trails in the Sky leans more heavily on the character interactions throughout the game to keep players interested. Of major note is the way your party changes as the game progresses. Unlike many JRPG titles, most party members in Trails of the Sky are not permanent additions. As a result, you have a rolling party roster instead of one that slowly grows throughout the game. Players get to know a new character throughout each chapter of the story. It’s a neat way to give players a chance to constantly get to know characters, but it’s not always for the best.
A distinct pattern sets in as the game progresses, with each chapter’s progress marked pretty similarly. You meet a new character. A small incident occurs requiring your attention, and you help them out. The trouble grows, and more about the new character is woven into the adventure. It’s not a bad way to write a story, but seeing it four times in the same game? It’s a little much. Thankfully, all these meetings do culminate into one impressive final chapter, but it’s a shame that the story takes so long to get off the ground as a result.
Luckily, Trails in the Sky’s combat is much less formulaic. The standard turn-based system players might expect is quite a bit different, and instead you’ll find yourself battling enemies on a small map. Characters can freely move around the map on their turns, and you must rely on your position and turn order to take advantage of your opponents. In fact, turn order might be the most crucial part of the battle. As the battle progresses, you can see bonuses that certains will acquire on their turns. If you time your magic spells correctly or insert yourself into one of those turns using a special attack, you can grab bonuses from your enemies for yourself. As a result, carefully managing your craft points (CP), which increase every time you deal or receive damage, is vital, as you need at least 100/200 to launch one of your “Special Breaks.” A large, screen-dominating attack that can be used any time during the battle at the cost of all your character’s CP points. As a result, battles rarely feel stale, even if some of them can drag on a little long.
Longer boss battles can be a lot of fun, but against your everyday grunts it starts to feel like a chore later in the game. This isn’t helped by cheery, yet repetitive battle music throughout the adventure. The same music persists outside of battle as well, and until the final chapter, you can expect to hear the same town, city, overworld, and dungeon themes no matter where you go. Thankfully, the themes we do have are quite well done. I only wish we could’ve had a few more of them. It’s to the composer’s credit that I didn’t ever dislike the music, but spend fifty hours with any song, and you’ll start to get bored.
For all my complaints though, I enjoyed Trails in the Sky. It’s a slow starter, but the ending was strong and left me anticipating the second chapter’s release on Steam. If you’re not a patient gamer, then Trails in the Sky might not be for you. If you enjoy getting to know a large cast, starting an epic, 3-game saga, and interesting combat, give it a shot!

Really fun game so far in my 17 hours of playing, so here's some thoughts on the game thus far.
▪ Quirky,humerous and well written dialogue. Some had me lol'ing quite a few times, especially the banter between Estelle and Joshua.
▪ Nice graphics. The backgrounds are well done and the monster design is interesting.
▪ The story gets off to a bit of a slow start but it picks up a little once you reach the second town.(Bose)
▪ The gameplay is pretty cool, you can customize different abilities into slots that you can unlock as you play.
▪ The challenge feels pretty good, it's not too hard or too easy and the turn based battle system is implemented well and      is fun if not entirely innovative.
▪ In 17 hours I only had one technical issue and that was loading a battle, it took about 30 seconds to load so I actually didn't have to close the game down.
▪ Things I miss from this game that other RPG games have are items hidden in barrels, drawers, crates etc....there just aren't any, so don't expect to find a potion in Granny's panty drawer. (Not sure if you'd want to though to be honest)
However there are some sparsely scattered chests throughout the maps and dungeons you travel.
Also there's not a lot of interactivity with background objects either, some kind of history or little nuance when you click certain items would have been a nice touch. (Although ... if you try and loot a chest you've already opened....) .. but overall this is a small gripe.
All in all It's a solid JRPG worthy of your collection.

Cities: Skylines is a very in depth, complex, and well-made city building game. As if you couldn't have guessed that already. It allows you, in its basic state (that being without DLC or mods), to create a city from a fair variety of maps, each with different things going for them such as water quantity, oil reserves, building area etc. Your task is, simply, to get as many people to live in your city, keep them happy, make it as good as you can, and make a load of money. The same as the government’s job, really. Except the "keeping people happy bit"...yeah...
The game allows you to design and expand a city with the use of many tools such as zoning, district planning and other features that let you change the smaller, more intricate details of your city. You can set different laws within your districts to make them work more efficiently at what you want them to do. I feel like this is all done really well. I have not got any DLC's, and only recently did I get a few mods, but I don't feel like the game ever really needed them.
Over the course of your cities expansion, you will face challenges. You must supply water, electric and road access to people, and zone your areas well to create a nice amount of residential, commercial and industrial areas. As the demand for them increases, it is expected that you appease them. You will also have to work around the formation of the land that you are on to make your city as functional and as sustainable as it can be, otherwise it will lack in efficiency, and perhaps upset the people. If they don’t like your city, they will first stop paying taxes, making it much harder for you to amend your previous errors. After that, they will leave, and you will be very lonely in that ghost town of yours. And probably quite angry as you’ll have to start a new game again. One problem that is hard to manage is the flow of traffic. You must make reliable and efficient road networks throughout your city, otherwise it will become stagnant. Public services such as busses will be rendered useless, nobody will be able to get to work, and emergency services will be crippled if your roads are congested all the time.
As your city progresses in size, the feature is available to you to buy more land, thus enabling you to continue your expansion. Eventually, if you are good enough at this game, you will fill the maximum amount of land you can buy, at which point, you’ll probably be feeling quite proud of yourself. Well done.
Overall, I would rate this game a well-earned 10/10. I can’t really fault it on anything. Out of all the city building games out there, this is the most detailed and intricate, while remaining fun to play, and enjoyably challenging. Graphically, it looks great, and the gameplay feels smooth. It has to be the best game of its type.

Despite being a greatly-executed game, there are a lot of holes that only someone who spent hundreds, if not likely thousands of hours in other decent city building/management games, especially SimCity series. As an add-on, I spent over 2000 hours over the years between SimCity 3000 and SimCity 4, hundreds in other city/economic building games (like Anno), had to learn from scratch how to properly, but properly design cities and districts, because back then not only there were barely any communities, but there was no YouTube to look at tutorials to at least get an idea of what other people are doing right. This review is going to be a handful to read, hence why this is more directed to the ones more familiar to this sort of game.
To start it off, point 1:
Traffic. Prepare to pull your hair out due to traffic management in this game. Leaving aside the fact that, since this was a new game for me, I messed up a couple of times, not even now I managed to put down traffic to levels that I can tolerate. The bigger the city gets, this problem will increase exponentially, and you don't have the financial luxury to pre-set the roads, because they cost significantly to plop and maintain. This could have been done, but this topic will be revisited later in this review.
Now, leaving aside the human factor, the issue with traffic is also a part where the developers messed up. I have not had time to purchase and play Mass Transit, but from other people I've talked with only now they fixed a pathing issue as old as the game. The one I'm talking about is, on a 3-lane road, for some reason the 1st lane is used for going straight in an intersection, but ONLY to go to the right. Same story about the 3rd lane applies. Repeat this several times on a grid format city like I build most of the time, and you're in for trouble with traffic starting from early on. Here let's say that you can somewhat fix car traffic with mass transit (the basic one you get without DLC), but in industrial areas, NOPE. In SimCity 4 you could have designed complex interchanges and highway systems if you wanted to, but here you are forced to at some point.
Same story applies to cargo trains as well, I personally did not see a significant difference, but with train traffic, if you plan on having both cargo and passenger rail, that becomes again a complete clusterf*ck that needs to be addressed with building a lot of dedicated lines that cost a lot.
Point 2:
The expansion model. Buying grid after grid outwards, rather than have each grid be it's own separate "region" like SimCity 4 had but still be able to jump from one into another fast (like in SimCity 2013), involves a lot of headache with design and planning, part of which I addressed in the previous point: if you want to pre-set the roads for something, in Skylines you'll not only go into the red but also pay a lot in maintenance fees for unused roads, meaning that you have to improvise on the way how you build the city. This means roads, districts, mass transit lines...if you messed up, you got to roll back significantly. By comparison in SimCity 4, you plopped the roads in a grid region where your CBD would be, so to say, with avenues, side roads, metro stations, then you left it like that and went to address residential in one region and industrial in another. If you remember, each of these grid regions was treated as a new city, meaning each had it's own budget. Of course your CBD region would lose a tonne of money until you zone commercial, when the entire map is full of avenues and kilometers of metro lines, but that was ok because once you satisfied R and I in other regions, your C would skyrocket and, in the moment you loaded the CBD map, immediately the zones would develop; you were not losing money in the other regions you were working on, because the other region was not part of what you were currently doing.
Let's say in C:S that you need power, and you go plop a coal power plant in a corner of the map to keep the pollution away from R and C, at one point when you expand you got to demolish it, build a new one and completely somewhere else because where it sits you plan on expanding residential there, or you want to get offices/high tech industry but the pollution that is pumping out is not helping. Such issues due to grid region separation were non-existent in SimCity 4.
Point 3:
DLCs. There are a few issues here.
Snowfall does not simulate snow as a weather phenomenon, but you play maps which are permanently stuck in this sort of weather; might as well call it Edmonton Simulator with Trams.
Natural Disasters is a one-hit trick DLC worth $15. You used it once, that was it. Optimisation was bad for it.
Mass Transit should have been already in the game, not as a DLC appearing 2 years after the game's release.

Watch Dogs 2 (stylized as WATCH_DOGS 2) is an action-adventure video game developed by Ubisoft Montreal and published by Ubisoft. It is the sequel to 2014's Watch Dogs and was released worldwide for PlayStation 4, Xbox One and Microsoft Windows in November 2016.
Set within a fictionalized version of the San Francisco Bay Area, the game is played from a third-person perspective and its open world is navigated on-foot or by vehicle. Players control Marcus Holloway, a hacker who works with the hacking group DedSec to take down the city's advanced surveillance system known as ctOS. There are multiple ways to complete missions, and each successful assignment increases the follower count of DedSec. Cooperative multiplayer allows for competitive one-on-one combat and connecting with other players in order to neutralize a player who is causing havoc.
Ubisoft Montreal, the game's developer, studied player feedback from the first game to assess what could be improved in Watch Dogs 2 and the setting was researched by making frequent trips to California. Ubisoft Reflections was responsible for overhauling the driving mechanic. Real hackers were consulted to validate scripts and game mechanics for authenticity and references to real life hacktivism were fictionalized, like the Project Chanology protest. The original soundtrack for Watch Dogs 2 was composed by Hudson Mohawke.
The game was released to generally favorable reception and praised for improving upon the original Watch Dogs in areas like the hacking, setting, characters and driving. However, character inconsistencies, firearms and frequent technical issues – later patched – were cited as imperfections.
Similar to its predecessor, Watch Dogs 2 is an action-adventure game with stealth elements and played from a third-person perspective as protagonist Marcus Holloway, a young hacker, the game features an open world environment set in a fictionalized version of the San Francisco Bay Area, an area more than twice as large as the Chicago setting from Watch Dogs. The Bay Area consists of four different areas: San Francisco, Oakland, Marin, and Silicon Valley, all of which have different characteristics and aesthetics. Players can navigate the game's world on-foot or by the various vehicles featured in the game, such as cars, trucks, buses, cable cars, motorcycles, quad bikes and boats. The driving mechanic was overhauled and designed to be more accessible. The players can shoot their weapons while driving. Marcus also has improved acrobatic skills, and the ability to parkour around the city. Players can use different methods to approach the game's missions, choosing between the aggressive approach, in which they defeat enemies with guns which are made with a 3D printer; explosives, like mines; or Marcus' own melee weapon, a billiard ball attached to a bungee cord. Alternatively, players can use the stealth approach, in which they can evade enemies or paralyze them temporarily with Marcus' taser. Players can also complete the game through hacking alone. When players commit too many crimes, the police officers will become alerted and will attempt to arrest the player. The game upgrades system is a returning feature, with items being divided into three categories: Ghost, Aggressor, and Trickster. Players can choose their upgrades in accordance with their own playstyle.
Marcus can hack into various electronic devices connected to the ctOS system with his in-game smartphone. For example, Marcus can modify the personal information of non-player characters to have them arrested, hack and manipulate every mobile phone featured in the game, disrupt traffic by hacking cars and traffic lights, hack into monitoring cameras, and carry out "mass hacking", which hacks the electrical equipment of a large group of people. Players also gain multiple options while hacking the same object. For instance, if the player attempts to hack a car, they can gain direct control over them, or have the car lose control and crash in a random direction. If the player hacks a junction box, they can choose whether they should deactivate it or turn it into a proximity mine. Unlike Aiden, the protagonist of the first game, Marcus has an arsenal of advanced equipment, including a quadcopter and a remote-controlled car, both of which can be used for remote hacking and scouting. Marcus' apparel can be customized with over 700 articles of clothing, available for purchase in stores that maintain fashion styles unique to what is worn by the denizens in each area. The game features several main story missions, and side-missions known as "operations". Once completed, Marcus' follower count will increase, which is an important part of the narrative
Multiplayer returns in Watch Dogs 2. The game introduces a seamless cooperative multiplayer mode, in which players can meet and interact with other random players. They can explore the open world and complete missions together, which will also help players to gain followers. The game features an emote system, which allows players' characters to communicate with each other through basic gestures. The game can be played completely online or offline. It also features three competitive multiplayer modes:
Hacking Invasion: A one-versus-one competitive multiplayer mode, originally featured in the first game, in which a player covertly joins another player's single-player session and steals virtual data from them. The invading player must stay hidden while stealing the data, and escape once successful, while the defending player must identify and kill the invading player.
Bounty Hunter: A new mode introduced in the game. If an online player creates too much chaos in the world, the mode will be initiated. Police, alongside one to three other players, will join the player's game with the hope of killing the hunted and claiming the bounty, which gives them experience points. The hunted could either strike back at the hunters by killing them, which gives them greater rewards, or escape from them until the bounty expires. The hunted, meanwhile, also can be assisted by another player if that player chooses to join the hunted. Players can manually place a bounty on themselves using the in-game smartphone.
Showdown: A mode added in a later update. In this mode, 2 teams of 2 players battle each other in short missions. Missions vary from the first team to steal 3 hard drives to the offensive team having to hack the servers the defensive team is protecting in a limited amount of time.
Following the events of Chicago, San Francisco becomes the next city to install the ctOS (central Operating System), which connects everyone with everything. Hacker Marcus Holloway (Ruffin Prentiss) is punished for a crime he did not commit by the upgraded ctOS – ctOS 2.0 – which categorizes him as the suspect. Realizing the system covertly brings harm to the innocent citizens of San Francisco, he decides to work with the hacking group DedSec to take down the ctOS 2.0, and Blume, the company behind it. Marcus joins DedSec and works with fellow hackers Sitara (Tasya Teles), Wrench (Shawn Baichoo), Horatio (Michael Xavier) and Josh (Jonathan Dubsky), and they begin using their skills to expose corrupt organizations and corporations that are secretly using stolen personal ctOS data for their own ends. The game begins with Marcus – known also by his hacker alias Retr0 – having an initiation test: deleting his own ctOS profile. Accepted into DedSec, he is alerted to a Church called New Dawn that serves as a criminal organization, after which, Marcus mainly serves to bring about awareness of the hackers' goals through both social media and hacks to help get enough computers to bring down Blume, the 'figurehead' of ctOS. Eventually, they stumble upon the existence of a subliminal message and Bellwether, a data manipulation program being fed ctOS data by Dušan Nemec (Christopher Jacot), Blume's CTO, to manipulate world finance and politics.

The short and sweet of this review is that if you like more tactical RTS games this is a really good one and would recomend in a heart beat. The game functions well and the setting and the way the setting is used gives it that edge over other games of this type.
Now for the long winded version.
The game plays like a mix between Company of Heroes, Men of War and a splash of Theater of War.
In most battles you control a company sized unit, with some missions having less and some more. With maps being large enough to encompass a small city, two towns or two districts. Maps are varied enough, taking advantage of the diversity of terrain in Syria as well as of combat situation. Some missions might have you fight over in a fully urban sectors, others in open desert and others in mountainous villages.
Infantry units have a combined ammo pool but health is separate for each individual solider with a relatively low time to kill. And if a solider in a unit dies he can not be replaced until the battle is done.
Vehicles have a semi realistic damage system, with the generality of unless you are dealing with the top tier units if you can penetrate the armor you can kill it in one hit.
There is a fully fledged logistics system, with vehicles and infantry requiring ammo for their weapons. Infantry being able to get ammo from troop transports while vehicles require a logistics truck for it and vehicles using fuel as they travel and being able to refuel from a fuel truck. These logistics unit have limited supply pools and if you need more you will need to scavenge or call some as reinforcements.
There is a scavenge system. There are often assets spread across the map(these assets are often hidden achievements) and many a times you will disable an enemy vehicle without destroying them, these vehicles you can capture and repair and rearm (each unit has a supply pool of spare parts, so there is a possibility of not having enough to bring back a vehicle), also enemy infantry units carry specialist weapons like MG's, Mortars, RPG's and you can pick these of the ground.
The game also has a off map unit management system. You are given Command Points for winning missions and can use it to buy new units, and can also sell your own units to get CP back. All the vehicles you capture and are manned after the battle is done are sent to this off map unit. So one can get CP by capturing vehicles and selling them. This off map unit is your reinforcement pool. In most missions you start off with a few free units and a limit of units you can bring to the field. At designated points during a mission you can bring more troops from the pool (also you can buy units if you have the CP and order them as reinforcements during these instances)
The Mechanics are tight, my only real complaint is that auto save only kicks in at the start and end of missions so you have to constantly save. I have already 200 save points with just 20 hours of play. The game is really hard and missions take a long time, would not recommend Iron Man mode.
Though the game play is really good the biggest selling point is the setting. And they do it so well, not just as a backdrop to the gameplay but fitting it within. You start off the game as a Syrian "police"(the reason for the quotes is because this police force acts as more of a militia/gendarmes force and I wonder if that's a translation error which there are quite a few) unit brought into the conflict, with the first 3 missions being you just pressed into service and making do with little. And you make do with little, you get very few free units or CP and you are required to scavenge, but it's not just the lack of manpower the first two objectives have been the hardest I have encountered in the game. One requires you to capture and defend a mountain pass and the other has you assault 6 enemy positions in an urban area. Also the game has many story side objectives littered throughout that will have an effect on your game if you chose to do them or not, some will grant you free units in a battle others CP some might even have long lasting effects.
And I will describe the urban mission as it exemplifies the game. You start off the mission with the posibility of 1 Tracked Vehicle(if you can afford one or scavange one). 2 motorised vehicles, 4 infantry squads, 2 free sapper units and 1 free truck.
You then have to assault two heavily defended compounds protected by land mines. When you get to the 2nd compound the enemy will start a mass counter attack of both infantry and armored vehicles against you puny force.
This is where the game setting shines because Two Mi-18 Helicopter Gunships come around and bring hellfire upon the enemy. A force that would cost you so many casualties and take you so much time to defeat on your own get obliterated in a few seconds, for those few seconds those Mi-18, those big, fat, battered, outdated flying cows feel like angels coming down to smite your foes. And the game is not done with just a display of Deus Ex Machina as those Mi-18 land and drop of 6 squads of properly trained and equipped regulars that make your police troopers which by now would be veterans seem like amateurs. And soon after you have to fight a counter attack on your own this time, the game not letting up one bit.
This is what makes the game shine. CAS, Reinforcements, Elite Units are not something you take for granted. They are few and far between but when you get them they feel as powerful as they should, not just a fireworks show but a true game changer. And when ever the enemy get their own Elite Units it's a scary sight and one that will put the hurt on your troops if you don't deal with it. And what makes it even better is when you can find, scavenge or recover something really powerful.
The Graphics are not something to write home about, it's in my opinion the games weak point. They are not bad, they just feel dated, the game looks as if it's 4 years older than it is. In my opinion this is not an issue as the gameplay and make up for it but for you it might be a bit of a let down.
Sound effects are really good, no gun or vehicle ever feels wimpy and it works as a way to draw you unit.
The in battle voice lines of your unit also add to the game, is just that there isn't as much variety as I would like and would not mind if they added something like a DLC for more voice lines or voices for your units.
The "Story" voice acting is okay, it's biggest hindrance is that it feels like a game voiced and written in Russian and translated later (because it is).
The Soundtrack is amazing. And perfect for the game, the sound track feels like a mix of the Battlefield 2 Theme and Command and Conquer. In fact I would recommend listening to it outside of the game.
In my opinion Syrian Warfare is a great Tactical RTS, in my opinion up there with stuff like Codename Panzers. And it's so great not just because of gameplay but because the gameplay fits with the setting. It actually makes you feel that you control a rag tag unit making do among the chaos of a civil war. It's not too cheesy and not too dramatic. Just a good hard game that represents it's setting well.

I want to like this game, but I can't and requested a refund.
Positives:
+Good graphics

+Fantastic performance/high framrate

Negatives:
-Camera controls are TERRIBLE (Home/End area keys) and are IMPOSSIBLE to rebind; even through the game files

-Forced Right-hand mouse buttons even if specified as reversed in Windows.  Makes it impossible to play if left-handed.
-Tutorials are awful, you basically have to read through a huge manual just to understand the UI
-The campaign is story driven yet the voice acting and writing is atrocious (not a big deal)
-There is only a single campaign. No skirmish or free play, no multiplayer/co-op, and you can't even select a campaign mission to play individually.  This kills the replay value.

Side note:
I have Avast anti-virus and this game keeps getting flagged and put into the virus chest. I had to uninstall, manually disable my anti-virus, add exclusions for the game files, reinstall, and it finally worked.

Surprisingly amazing RTS. The story is full of low-key(And sometimes less than low-key) memeing and humor, and the gameplay is a nice middleground between games like Company of Heroes and Men of War packed into a very playable package for even beginners to RTS while still having enough depth for veterans and enthusiasts. Combat is grounded and fairly realistic with a few concessions made for the sake of playability, and it strikes a very satisfying balance without going as plodding and autismal as games like Combat Mission. In many ways, it seems somewhat inspired by games of old like JTF, Blitzkreig, and Sudden Strike.
The only real downside, though it is a glaring and large one, is the complete absence of multiplayer. I don't know what the developers were smoking(Or, given that they are Russian, drinking.), but somehow they got together at a table while discussing the development for this game, and decided that the most crucial, core part of an RTS was totally unnecessary, and ought not exist. This is the kiss of death on replayability, unfortunately. Once you beat the campaign, that's it. No skirmish, no playing against people, no testing your tactics and strategies in a dynamic arena against others in a way no AI could replicate. The price, thankfully, reflects this...but it still leaves a bad taste in the mouth. This has massive potential to be a cult classic that could compete with the likes of Wargame, Men of War, Steel Division, and Company of Heroes...But unfortunately we'll never get to know. Such a massive waste of potential, for such a great game.
All in all, it's recommend, though, especially on sale. Just know that you're basically paying for a one-shot experience.

I decided to update my post to add more clarification.
'Barony' seems to be inspired by 1992's 'Wolfenstein 3D' (which is a classic shooter; but a terrible melee game)  and someone decided to convert it into a rogue-like dungeon crawl.

Pros:
The game shines in the ability to choose your character class (warrior types, rogue types, mage types), a means of appraising the items you find, multi-player, and a procedurally generated dungeon.
Cons:
Imagine you were playing Wolfenstein 3D, and you were expected to use the knife consistantly.  That's pretty much how melee combat works in 'Barony'.
Conclusion:
Like most dungeon crawls, it's insanely difficult, but sometimes for the wrong reasons.  I don't think it's a bad game, I think it's a game that is really designed for ranged combat and was meant to be played with friends. If the devs can improve the melee experience, I think then it would be worth a buy.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A response to those saying this game is pay to win:
No it is not. Sure you can pay to unlock operators faster but all of the operators are unlockable through standard play. On top of this, the operators are situational and balanced. Also, this is not a game where you can simply pay to be good. If you don't develop your skill then you are screwed. If you don't believe me, buy the complete edition, play for a bit and see for yourself. You will suck until you develop your skill even with all the operators unlocked.
A response to those complaining about microtransactions and lootboxes:
All microtransactions and items found in lootboxes are cosmetic only. The only exception to this are boosters which temporarily increase the rate that you earn in game currency. R6 credits are the in game paid currency and renown is the standard in game currency. Lootboxes cannot be bought with real money or with R6 credits. They must be bought with renown or earned by winning matches and you cannot buy renown with real money directly or with R6 credits. Most cosmetic items can also be bought directly (meaning not through lootboxes) with either R6 credits or renown. Some cosmetic items can only be purchased with R6 credits or directly with real money.
Now that I explained how microtransactions and lootboxes work in the game you should understand how this is not an example of intrusive microtransactions or harmful lootbox gambling. You could argue that I'm wrong about harmful lootbox gambling because technically you can pay for boosters that earn you lootboxes faster but that's a stretch since they still have to be earned.

Cities: Skylines is a very in depth, complex, and well-made city building game. As if you couldn't have guessed that already. It allows you, in its basic state (that being without DLC or mods), to create a city from a fair variety of maps, each with different things going for them such as water quantity, oil reserves, building area etc. Your task is, simply, to get as many people to live in your city, keep them happy, make it as good as you can, and make a load of money. The same as the government’s job, really. Except the "keeping people happy bit"...yeah...
The game allows you to design and expand a city with the use of many tools such as zoning, district planning and other features that let you change the smaller, more intricate details of your city. You can set different laws within your districts to make them work more efficiently at what you want them to do. I feel like this is all done really well. I have not got any DLC's, and only recently did I get a few mods, but I don't feel like the game ever really needed them.
Over the course of your cities expansion, you will face challenges. You must supply water, electric and road access to people, and zone your areas well to create a nice amount of residential, commercial and industrial areas. As the demand for them increases, it is expected that you appease them. You will also have to work around the formation of the land that you are on to make your city as functional and as sustainable as it can be, otherwise it will lack in efficiency, and perhaps upset the people. If they don’t like your city, they will first stop paying taxes, making it much harder for you to amend your previous errors. After that, they will leave, and you will be very lonely in that ghost town of yours. And probably quite angry as you’ll have to start a new game again. One problem that is hard to manage is the flow of traffic. You must make reliable and efficient road networks throughout your city, otherwise it will become stagnant. Public services such as busses will be rendered useless, nobody will be able to get to work, and emergency services will be crippled if your roads are congested all the time.
As your city progresses in size, the feature is available to you to buy more land, thus enabling you to continue your expansion. Eventually, if you are good enough at this game, you will fill the maximum amount of land you can buy, at which point, you’ll probably be feeling quite proud of yourself. Well done.
Overall, I would rate this game a well-earned 10/10. I can’t really fault it on anything. Out of all the city building games out there, this is the most detailed and intricate, while remaining fun to play, and enjoyably challenging. Graphically, it looks great, and the gameplay feels smooth. It has to be the best game of its type.

Despite being a greatly-executed game, there are a lot of holes that only someone who spent hundreds, if not likely thousands of hours in other decent city building/management games, especially SimCity series. As an add-on, I spent over 2000 hours over the years between SimCity 3000 and SimCity 4, hundreds in other city/economic building games (like Anno), had to learn from scratch how to properly, but properly design cities and districts, because back then not only there were barely any communities, but there was no YouTube to look at tutorials to at least get an idea of what other people are doing right. This review is going to be a handful to read, hence why this is more directed to the ones more familiar to this sort of game.
To start it off, point 1:
Traffic. Prepare to pull your hair out due to traffic management in this game. Leaving aside the fact that, since this was a new game for me, I messed up a couple of times, not even now I managed to put down traffic to levels that I can tolerate. The bigger the city gets, this problem will increase exponentially, and you don't have the financial luxury to pre-set the roads, because they cost significantly to plop and maintain. This could have been done, but this topic will be revisited later in this review.
Now, leaving aside the human factor, the issue with traffic is also a part where the developers messed up. I have not had time to purchase and play Mass Transit, but from other people I've talked with only now they fixed a pathing issue as old as the game. The one I'm talking about is, on a 3-lane road, for some reason the 1st lane is used for going straight in an intersection, but ONLY to go to the right. Same story about the 3rd lane applies. Repeat this several times on a grid format city like I build most of the time, and you're in for trouble with traffic starting from early on. Here let's say that you can somewhat fix car traffic with mass transit (the basic one you get without DLC), but in industrial areas, NOPE. In SimCity 4 you could have designed complex interchanges and highway systems if you wanted to, but here you are forced to at some point.
Same story applies to cargo trains as well, I personally did not see a significant difference, but with train traffic, if you plan on having both cargo and passenger rail, that becomes again a complete clusterf*ck that needs to be addressed with building a lot of dedicated lines that cost a lot.
Point 2:
The expansion model. Buying grid after grid outwards, rather than have each grid be it's own separate "region" like SimCity 4 had but still be able to jump from one into another fast (like in SimCity 2013), involves a lot of headache with design and planning, part of which I addressed in the previous point: if you want to pre-set the roads for something, in Skylines you'll not only go into the red but also pay a lot in maintenance fees for unused roads, meaning that you have to improvise on the way how you build the city. This means roads, districts, mass transit lines...if you messed up, you got to roll back significantly. By comparison in SimCity 4, you plopped the roads in a grid region where your CBD would be, so to say, with avenues, side roads, metro stations, then you left it like that and went to address residential in one region and industrial in another. If you remember, each of these grid regions was treated as a new city, meaning each had it's own budget. Of course your CBD region would lose a tonne of money until you zone commercial, when the entire map is full of avenues and kilometers of metro lines, but that was ok because once you satisfied R and I in other regions, your C would skyrocket and, in the moment you loaded the CBD map, immediately the zones would develop; you were not losing money in the other regions you were working on, because the other region was not part of what you were currently doing.
Let's say in C:S that you need power, and you go plop a coal power plant in a corner of the map to keep the pollution away from R and C, at one point when you expand you got to demolish it, build a new one and completely somewhere else because where it sits you plan on expanding residential there, or you want to get offices/high tech industry but the pollution that is pumping out is not helping. Such issues due to grid region separation were non-existent in SimCity 4.
Point 3:
DLCs. There are a few issues here.
Snowfall does not simulate snow as a weather phenomenon, but you play maps which are permanently stuck in this sort of weather; might as well call it Edmonton Simulator with Trams.
Natural Disasters is a one-hit trick DLC worth $15. You used it once, that was it. Optimisation was bad for it.
Mass Transit should have been already in the game, not as a DLC appearing 2 years after the game's release.

This is a pretty awesome game for those who have made memories with Oregon Trail, those who are looking for retro graphics, those who like zombies, and those who enjoy satire towards any of those things.
-Great Humor: (If you are a zombie fanatic, and have watched every zombie movie, played every zombie game, and read every zombie comic book, then you will pick up on all of the excellent humor sprinkled throughout this game. On top of that, there are a ton of nods to just older games in general, which is always awesome.)
-Retro Graphics: (A plus if you like them)
-Replayable: (If you only play through this once, you will only see about 10% of the humor, challenges, etc. Each playthrough yields different things, such as events, and you can take a different approach everytime. You can stock up on different items, strive to do different things, and changing your sense of morality at anytime. The only really linear thing in this game is the path. You go from Point A, then Point B, all the way to Point Z, which is the safe haven you are trying to get to. It is what happens on your way to each point that makes this game interesting.)
-Soundtrack: (This game has a really good sense of approach towards the situations you may be in, and one of the big reasons I say that is the soundtrack. The game always has fitting music, and good music at that.)
-Gameplay: (This is a subjective con. The gameplay is interesting in that it really is true to how an older game like this would play. But that doesn't mean it is easy. My only complaint on this is the aiming. Considering you must fight off the undead with a ranged weapon, you HAVE to be good at aiming it. On top of that, you can't waste ammo, as it could be out of reach due to price, or the shear lack of it in the zombie wastelands you explore. The aiming is...weird. I suggest looking up a video of gameplay so you can see if you can cope with it. I've gotten used to it, but at the same time I shouldn't have to. Gameplay should be fluid and creative, yet natural. Honestly, I would like just one of those, but aside from this one con, if you can overcome this one annoyance, then this game is definitely worth it.)
Everything about this game is near-perfect, aside from one thing. Gameplay. While everything else is so good, this is a big thing to do deal with since without gameplay, it wouldn't be a game. At the same time, you have to see if it would bother you so I suggest looking at a video of the gameplay to decide. If, afterwards, you decide that isn't too bad, then nothing else should be stopping you from getting this game aside from lacking the funds to do so. Everything aligns almost perfectly for this game but one thing, so decide from all of this if you would truely like it.
P.S. There is also a mobile edition available for Android and iOS, so if you want to try this game but feel playing it with a mouse is a deal breaker, then that is the next best thing. The one thing both editions have over the free, Facebook alternative is that they are much more complete, and have A TON of addition content that adds to the experience of this game. The developer did fairly well on this title, so I trusted the mobile edition would live up to the PC edition here. Long story short, there is no game that really keeps itself consistent across all the platforms it's available on so well like this one!

I tried with this one, I really did. The original on the NES was always fascinating to me, with its bizarre mix of open levels, tricky partner mechanics, and inexplicable economy of jellybeans. I only got halfway through it the one time I rented it but the experience has stuck with me for decades. The remake, in stark contrast, is having trouble staying fresh in my mind for more than a week. And when I do manage to remember what I was doing, it isn't with any sort of fondness.
A young boy goes investigating a meteor impact in the woods at night, as any possible forest-dwelling orphan might, and ends up making a new best friend. The blob tags along with him wherever he goes like an elastic puppy, accepting hugs and summons and harboring a hunger for jellybeans. Feeding the alien a jellybean will cause him to shapeshift into something useful, like a ladder or parachute or hole in the ground somehow, all depending on the flavor of bean. Together they embark on a quest to do something I didn't get to see for reasons I will explain shortly.
In the original ABaHB, you and the blob used his elasticky powers to search for loot in the vast caverns beneath maybe New York, use the cash to by vitamins, and then blast off for a candy planet to save blob's friends from a saccharine tyrant averse to pills. It was insane and impossible and like nothing else on the system, which is what earned it its cult following. In this ABaHB, you use the blob and a limited assortment of jellybeans to puzzle through short levels. There are collectibles to score in each level but the main goal is to reach the end, as with virtually every other puzzle platformer in existence.
Look, I appreciate WayForward's effort to bring ABaHB into the modern era, and in a limited sense they succeeded. The controls are solid and familiar to most players, as opposed to the touchy and slippery ones of the original. The graphics are charming as hell and incredibly well-animated. And the levels present simple challenges to overcome with the tools provided. The problem is that none of the things that made the original worthwhile have survived the revival process. Gone are the open maps, the diverse challenges, the unique threats, the odd jellybean strategies, and the 80s fever-dream atmosphere. The formula has been boiled down to the faintest resemblance, draped over a game you've seen a hundred times before in the indie platformer scene.
And then, once you dig into what's left, you find even that lacking. Despite the quality of the graphics and animation, nothing that happens in the world has any impact. All of your movements are floaty and disconnected and enemies don't even bother to attack, they just touch you and you crumple. Outside of the obvious tutorial applications it can be hard to tell where and how you can use powers like holes and ladders, and the trampoline is a deathtrap with the harsh falling damage to be found here (though this was certainly true in the original, as well). There are collectibles to find but they're generic chests you don't even get to open, they just make doodads appear in your treehouse and unlock short, boring challenge levels if you find enough.
I really did want to work my way through this title to see the full spread of what it had to offer, but I reached a point near the end of the first world where the puzzles stopped being any fun at all. It was in a dreary swamp, there was a big charging enemy I had to finagle my way around, and flubbing any part of the process made me do the whole thing over. I kept trying and getting frustrated and losing interest, and I felt bad because surely I was just missing something. But then I checked the achievements and less than 10% of players had gotten past where I was stuck. And this is the first world! Maybe there are closer ties to the original deeper into the game, but I'll never see them. Honestly, I wouldn't suggest you go hunting for them either.

A Boy and His Blob is an cute adventure game where you play as a boy and his friend alien Blob which goal is unknown to you.
The graphics are well done, it's not amazing, but that's not a bad thing. Usually, the levels are colorful, but some levels has a darker tone, depending of the world.
You control the boy with the directional buttons and he can also jump (really low, but he can) and throw a seed to his friend Blob, which follow him all the time. The boy is really fragile, because only one hit of any enemy will kill him and you'll need to start over the level again. But the Blob is the true hero here, because you feed him seeds which will make him transform at some different objects that the boy can use to overcome his obstacles and pass the level. Some of them even allow him to hit enemies, like the ball transmation, where the blob surrounds the boy and they become a large ball which run fast and kill some enemies and protect him from other enemies.
The seeds you can use are different for each stage and you need to think hard at later levels how to use them right. The boss battles are nice to fight, but its concept is kind of lame, because the boss isn't very smart and do uncecessary moves, probably so the main character has a chance to defeat it. This is not a thing which affects this game is a bad way, but it's worth mentioning.
The musics are usually calm and good, without big hits. There are some darker tunes, but nothing really scary. The boy has some audios, but only a few, when he is calling the Blob back, for example.
The story is kind of lame, like most of the platform games: this boy lives alone in a forest and finds a alien blob, which helps him in exchange of seeds. He go through many worlds overcoming obstacles and that's all. I didn't finished the game yet, so I can't say if the story explains itself at the end. But this is not a issue which affects gameplay. Sometimes, you just need to go right to the action!
It's a nice and simple platform game, with a interestinfg feature through the different transformations of the blob following you. You need to be strategic to overcome the challenges, it's not only jump and move here. Nice for any platform fan or even non-platform gamers.
Graphics: 8/10
Audio: 7/10
Gameplay: 9/10
Overall: 8/10

A charming little puzzle-platformer based on the rather obscure NES game of the same name, A Boy and his Blob not only offers a diverse array of item-based challenges, but constantly shuffles what items the player is allowed to use, forcing the player to always think differently while maintaining a pleasant level of difficulty that only occasionally dips into "frustrating". Puzzles can often be solved in multiple ways, usually made possible by an impressive amount of object interactions and in-game physics for a 2D platformer.  80 stages (40 required, 40 optional) range in length from two minutes to twenty, for a satisfying 10-15 hours of gameplay that never wears out its welcome.  All this is bundled together with adorable hand-drawn sprites, gorgeous environments, and a rich orchestral soundtrack for an overall very enjoyable experience.

Trails in the Sky has possibly been one of the most solid JRPG's I've played since Final Fantasy and Grandia 2. While combat isn't necessarily quite on par with the two games I've mentioned, it certainly takes steps into innovation. While there are still turns, you play on a grid with the ability to move your characters around. Although this doesn't seem like much, there are abilities and magic that requires positioning. Sometimes a character's ability will require them to walk to specific areas of the battle map, and sometimes the characters will find themselves out of range for attacking. It's a unique addition along with the dynamic turn system which decides who moves first, second, or last, mixing up battles and making them unique.
The second innovation involves "Orbaments" in which the characters all use a mineral called "Quartz" in order to obtain certain and unique spells. The Orbament system allows you to specifically create your character for a certain role, as the Quartz combinations not only get you spells, but also certain stat buffs. How the system works sounds simple but it can be incredibly hard to 'build' a character accordingly. The Orbament system acts a bit like a minipuzzle, with each Quartz having different properties of certain elements (water, earth, wind, fire, space, time etc.). Not only do you require a certain combination for certain spells, but each character can also have 1-5 different 'lines.' This pretty much separates how your elements 'stack' and you have to think about where you place your quartz. A very cool way to implement a customization system, and it allows each and every character to adapt to specific situations (however some party members will have a unique 'slot' that only allows a specific element of quartz).
While many might complain about 'grinding' I found out that you actually don't have to grind that much at all. As long as you don't sell your Sepith, you can get the higher tier quartz, and open up slots for all your characters. The reality is, you don't necessarily need the slots but if you want them then you'll have to search out specific monsters to grab them. Once you do the quests and explore the surrounding areas, the game doesn't become too 'grindy' or hard. But if you want to make it harder on yourself, you can completely ignore the Orbament system, and areas.
As for the story, Trails in the Sky gets quite detailed. Some say that the plot doesn't pick up until chapter 3, but I found chapter 1 and 2 to be equally great. The only downside to Trails in the Sky is the fact that it is possibly "too detailed." For some players, they might not find reading text bubbles to be all that engaging, and in fact I found myself trying to skip the dialogue at some points. The game does drag itself, but it is a fairly minor issue.
The next downside of this game is that... even though it has "Trails in the Sky" you don't actually use an airship. I was hoping more or less, that our crew would end up on an airship going around different towns and places. However, it becomes a bit misleading, and I was disappointed.

I went into this hearing from a bunch of people, "Go into this blind, don't read anything, it's great."
Well, I went into it blind, didn't read anything or watch anything, and...it's disappointing.
I can see what the devs were going for. I can see why a lot of people liked it, even. But I honestly didn't enjoy my time with the game.
Pony Island initially presents itself as a game where you...play as a pony jumping over fences. But then things start breaking down, you start hacking the game with some help from a stranger, and it's at this point that practically all of the games' cards are dropped onto the table. 30 minutes in to a hour and a half to two hour game, and you already know all the twists. (This, of course, is unless you read anything at all about the game...
.) The game is programmed by the devil to keep you trapped in limbo, and you're trying to break free.
So, what else is there besides a boring/unpleasant autorunner? Well, there's a desktop involved with some amusing things going on there. The rest of the game alternates between the autorunner and some relatively simple puzzles.
Yes, there is more to it than this, including one sequence of fourth wall breaks that works relatively well. But having spent about two hours playing it, having about fifteen minutes of genuinely amusing/interesting gameplay doesn't make up for the other two hours of monotony.
So you finally get to the end, defeat Satan, set yourself free...and the helper from earlier
, which at this point I did so very willingly.
And then you look it up and HEY THERE'S AN ALTERNATE ENDING WHAT A SURPRISE. Lots of hidden details requiring multiple playthroughs...involving those same autorunning levels and puzzles. Oh, and you can figure out how you died and all that...if you play through it multiple times. No thanks.
So...yeah. I mean, there are interesting ideas here. The alternate ending sounded neat. But I'm not putting myself through another two hours of this game to get to the story. I wouldn't recommend anyone else to do it, either.
I don't know, maybe? Depends on how much a decently interesting meta-narrative can carry bad gameplay for you.

Most of my experience with Enclave has been via the DotEmu and original Xbox releases. So don't let my Steam stats fool you.
Enclave was released at a time when third person action games were really gaining an edge: the 6th generation (early 2000s). What sets Enclave apart is its RPG-like character unlocking, character swapping, upgrades, and back stories. During the 5th generation (PS1/N64/Sega Saturn) we had the likes of Tenchu and Syphon Filter, but nothing quite like Enclave. While the likes of Blood Rayne and Prince of Persia were backed by bigger budgets and better marketing, it was games like Enclave and MDK 2 that injected the third person action genre with this thing called "replay value".
Whether you're a fan of the steam-punk aesthetic or third person action games or just want a fun (and very cheap) boredom killer, Enclave is a worthy addition to your PC gaming library.

A Boy and His Blob is a 2D side-scrolling puzzle platformer, a spiritual successor to the NES game A Boy and His Blob: Trouble on Blobolonia, and a port of the Wii Virtual Console version of this game. The premise is that you are a boy, with a Blob, and the Blob transforms into different objects based on the type of jellybean you feed him. You use these objects to navigate the world and solve puzzles. As someone who spent many childhood hours playing the original, I can tell you right now that this is no Trouble on Blobolonia.
First of all, the original game was very unforgiving. Even getting past the second screen of the game could be difficult. In comparison, I have played through the first three levels of A Boy and His Blob, and every "puzzle" has had a billboard telling me the solution. If you have so little confidence in my ability, why don't you just play the game for me?
There are "challenge" levels which do not tell you what to do, but you are only provided with the jelly beans required to complete the level, and the most I have been provided with is 3 jelly beans. This means there is always a clear, obvious solution to every problem.
Another way the successor differs from its predecessor is exploration. A Boy and His Blob: Trouble on Blobolonia was remarkably open-ended for such an early video game, and encouraged you to explore (and die trying.) A Boy and his Blob on the other hand features short, almost entirely linear levels unlocked in a predetermined order.
The only settings available to you are fullscreen or windowed, screen resolution, and music and sound effects can be either on or off; no volume controls. There is also no option to disable vertical sync, which may cause problems as the game aggressively locks frame rates to either 30 or 60 FPS, and some area feature inexplicable frame rate drops. These drops cause the game to feel like it's being played on the moon, in slow motion.
This is a game pretty clearly aimed at young children, but it's also kind of an insult to their intelligence. I loved the challenge of the original game as a child, and the "puzzles" in this game are pitiful even before you are directly told the solution, whether you wanted that information or not. I honestly can only recommend this to very young children, and even then some of the deaths (yes, you can die) might be too scary for them.
I don't recommend this to fans of the original game. While it shares some very basic gameplay similarities, it has none of the challenge, charm, or rewarding exploration found in A Boy and His Blob: Trouble on Blobolonia.

I'm still in the process of finishing this for a perfect game, but I feel I've played enough to give an accurate review.
A boy and his blob is a remake of the classic NES game of the same title. Having grown up playing the original, I loved how charming it was, and it had unique mechanics that were never really duplicated in any game I can call to mind.
This remake accurately takes the charm of the orginal and turns the dial up to 10. This game oozes charm, from the enemies, to the various forms your blob can assume, the artwork is gorgeous. Gameplay is decent, though somewhat monotonous, but the game isn't very challanging, and when it is challanging, its usually due to being unfair. What I mean is that some animations take so long (and there are ZERO invunerability frames) that a boss will kill you, or an enemy will kill you because your timing is off. The second boss in the game is exceptionally frustrating due to this. As well, the controls are very wonky for some of your blobs moves, not to mention you have to bash the call button a bajillion times to get him to come to you.
So the breakdown:
Pros
-----
* Gorgeous game
* Accurately remakes an NES classic
* OK puzzle/platforming gameplay
* Charm out the wazoo
* pretty long if you 100%
Cons
-----
* Sometimes frustrating gameplay due to slow animations and wonky controls
* Really easy when its not overly frustrating
* Wish there was a true tutorial level...
* 90% of the trophies are given on the last world, which is really weird
Overall I'd give this a 6/10. Not a must play by any means, but definitely one to pick up on sale if your a fan of the original, or just want some platforming action.
