I cannot reccommend this game enough. It's kind of like an old friend who you can always come back to. I'll go and play other games for a while but it is this one that I always finding myself coming back to. Here are a couple quick reasons why I love this game.
+ Difficulty- Whether you are playing with infinite money to flex your creativity or with a limited amount, I think this game is fair. It may be easy to buget and maintain the finances of your city or keep it safe from crime, but the difficulty in traffic makess up for that. Mass Transit (the latest expansion as of when I'm writing this) has created more options to help alleviate traffic, but the main way to clear it has always been to be creative; to sometimes restructure the whole city so that everything can be as efficient as possible. An epidemic can break out because the abulances cannot reach the houses, so you have to plan accordingly. It's creative difficulty, and not just balancing sliders.
+ Mods- This game reminds me of Skyrim with how many mods are available for it. The workshop is fantastic for this game, and I reccommend everyone to fill their game up with assets to diversify your city. I will say that the vanilla game has too few building assets, but mods easily solve this. I can just check in every month or so, and over time have enough buildings to make my city look more realistic than ever. Mods also allow those who want to get really in depth that oppertunity, If you want to manually create a shipping yard by your docks, mods can let you do that. Most of the features that I wish were in the game have been added with mods.
+ Graphics- Coming from Sim City 4 I was hoping for anything that would be a step up. While this game does not have the most hardcore or realistic graphics. There is something inexplicably  beautiful about the way it looks. When your city is shining in the night, you'll know what I mean.
+ Gameplay options- This game really allows you to build the city you want to build. If you want to follow the traditional grid design, you can, but it also allows you to build complex interchanges and experimental cities that are sure to amaze. The game is a canvas, for you to fill.
+ Stability - I've rarely had this game crash on me, and it seems to be relatively bug-free. I've never encountered a game breaking bug even with all the mods I have installed. The game is built on solid foundation and recieves frequent updates from a company that listens to its players.
Of course, if you're not in to city builders you're not going to be in to this game. However, I believe this to be the quintessential city builder to last us for a couple decades like Sim City 4 did. The game's frequent updates and expansions always keep me coming back for more as the game keeps improving. It truly never gets old for me, and I cannot reccommend it enough to anyone who is a fan of city builders or simulation games.

Pretty fun little game, if you like dying repeatedly and making no progress. If not, here's my advice:
1) Disable the minotaur that has the ability to teleport to your location every few minutes but for some reason doesn't just kill you outright in the beginning
2) Disable hunger, which pops up more often than a diabetic's
3) Use ranged weapons whenever possible because the melee system is about as refined as Minecraft's
Also, ignore the comparisons drawn in the description. While it has a few features of Nethack (procedurally generated levels and permanent death) it is not a roguelike. While it is a dungeon crawler like Ultima Underworld, the combat isn't even that sophisticated, not to mention the utter lack of content or side stories in comparison. System Shock is also more sophisticated in terms of combat and mobility and the game has essentially nothing in common with Daggerfall other than having repetitive dungeons and character sheets.
What you are getting, for better or worse, is a first-person, real-time Nethack with co-op, that is hard in even less believable ways than Nethack. Without turning the minotaur off, just imagine playing Nethack with a Nethack minotaur that appears based on a timer instead of turns, regardless of level, and who can walk through walls. Without turning the hunger off, imagine getting hungry at about the same rate as you do in Nethack but in real time. Who gets hungry 5 minutes after eating a fist of ham? Do you?
Regardless, the game is successful in other ways. You will improve as a player with every playthrough, just like Nethack, and unlike Nethack it has multiplayer which I suspect was the point of the whole thing in the first place. The game has also been rather stable on all my Windows computers, though I can't speak for other operating systems. At its low price it's hard not to recommend.

AUTHOR NOTE.
While i have only a few Minutes on this game, i have played it and beaten it multiple times on a Non-Steam Version.
The Best Oregon Trail Zombie Simulator, Ever.
Literally, when i saw this title i was surprised by its atmosphere. The Music is a factor but so is the music. I feel like people are being eaten, things are bleak and grim in this chaotic outbreak spanning across mainland america. The game ultimately is extremely bleak and sometimes even masochistic at times, even gameplay. I mean seriously, what other game do you have where you get a choice between marrying a bride to her groom's corpse or to put her out of her misery and blow her brains out? I felt like a Devil playing this game, offing each of my members to get to my location. I felt like my Car constantly was breaking down and we had nowhere to run, even when we stopped by to examine the dead in their graves! (Which is pretty stupid, i mean why would you do that. Would make sense if it was the graves of your fellow team but its not.)
The Gunplay is literally Apple 2 esque, you "draw" the line you want to shoot with your mouse, it takes alot of getting used to but its a mechanic chosen well, otherwise this game's combat would be very easy. You also walk at a SNAILS Pace while running from zombies, and should judge the distance of the undead with which location you should go. Juking the Zombies, its been done similar in other games and remains a interesting mechanic that makes it much easier to survive the combat portions of Organ Trail.
Also the wages you get paid are ridiculous and the difficulty ratings are extremely intimidating initally, the higher ones are defintely not to be taken lightly and i'd recommend wasting a few peons on it to get used to the missions because your not getting money any other way besides taking jobs. Money is so important, i cannot unstate how much ive seen my own people die because ive been a few dollars short of a medkit or my entire car fall to pieces in a few miles. Its rage inducing but there is something in Organ Trail that i see in Risk of Rain almost, where in that i just NEED to find a way to make it all work. Its that which makes it all the more devastating or victorious when you actually Win or Lose in this game.
Its hilariously cheap, to a level that i think it personally doesn't deserve but i come back to this title every now and then for another ride on the amazing organ trail.
TL:DR?
Fun but Nigh on Masochistic. Gameplay takes learning.
Defintely a great title to get at the price. Recommended.

The game does what it sets out to do--create a version of the classic Oregon Trail game, but with zombies. There's some neat nods and references to other zombie franchises out there, and it captures the feel of the original game pretty well while still having its own identity.
That being said, it also reminded me how boring the original Oregon Trail really was. Although there's a few neat scenarios and moral conumdrums this is mostly a resource-management game with a few very basic zombie-shooting minigames involved (that have controls that are a little frustrating to deal with). If you play the game for too long it can get pretty repetative, particularly when you hear the same dialogue over and over.
Admittedly part of my disappointment might be because the version of Oregon Trail I grew up with was Oregon Trail II, which had some pretty campy FMV stuff in it but had more stuff to do overall and felt like a fuller game. I'm also getting a little bored of zombies at this point and Organ Trail doesn't attempt to do anything new. So I'm definitely coming at this game with a bias. It's not a BAD game, just one that I ultimately felt "meh" on once I finished it.
If you have a lot of nostalgia for the original or just can't get enough of zombies, there's definitely far worse games you could pick up, particularly at the price point. But don't expect anything too surprising, the game more or less plays out the way you'd expect, so if you're on the fence I'd maybe wait for a sale or get something else instead.

I bought this game because I played the original Knights Of The Pen And Paper +1 and enjoyed it immensely. The first game was a fun little time sink with a lot of content and quirky characters. I wish I could say this game is a good, but frankly it simply isn't. To start with, it is MUCH shorter than the original as well as MUCH easier. There's less quest variety as well. Most of the game felt like filler content that the dev team added to round out the length of the game. There are also way fewer characters and classes to play as. Even worse, the game sorely lacks depth in its combat and equipment compared to the first.  If I had played THIS first and moved on to the original game, it would have felt right. Almost every aspect except graphics is a downgrade.
Viewed away from the original, the game barely stands on its own merits. It is fun and quirky, but much of the humor feels forced. The game is incredibly easy even without grinding and becomes downright trivial if you complete every quest available to you. The lack of content is very noticable, with the main quest taking maybe two hours. You can cram in maybe 8 more from filler if you want with all the DLC but the DLC felt like it was simply trying to stretch out the existing experience without actually adding more content.
Overall, the game had some very solid ideas to improve the series. Adding in more ways to spend your gold and being able to craft your own gear was a nice touch. Unfortunately, all the new systems feel like they are half completed, like they were stopped halfway through development and shipped as-is. Realistically, that's how the entire game feels. It's not even a case of content being stuck behind a DLC paywall, it simply was never created.
In the end, this is probably worth picking up on a deep discout sale but I'd not suggest paying full price for it. Skip the DLC unless you REALLY enjoy the game. I'd suggest playing the first one over this if you haven't already, it is superior in every way except visually.

This game was a short, but very stimulating experience for me. I laughed, I was confused, I had to think hard about the puzzles, and in the end, I was left pondering over all the intertwined "levels" of meaning those highly gifted developers lead me through.
It becomes clear quite early, so I think I don't spoil anything by describing some of those levels: You, the player, are a real person sitting in front of your PC. You run this game. In the game, you play a protagonist using an arcade machine (coloured 3D graphics) - and you may or may not learn from flashbacks later in the game who "you" actually are. The arcade machine presents a game named "Pony Island", a 2D-scroller with a character that is called a pony all the time, but looks like a unicorn (black and white retro graphics). It turns out that this game is not here to entertain you, but to punish you - you go through the hell of maliciously amateurish game-design, game-breaking bugs and crashes - and to steal your soul. In order to escape, you have to enter and manipulate the code of the arcade game (text and symbol based puzzles)... You see how many meta-levels are built around one another here, making you wonder what you put your heart and soul into as a passionate gamer.
My point is: Don't be fooled by screenshots of the arcade game! It might look like a cheap and boring indie production at first glance, but this is actually a deliberate design choice within a very intelligent, self-aware, self-ironic, even self-deconstructive game of unique charm. What they did with the third boss (and the fourth wall) was pure genius, a moment I will not forget as long as I am active on Steam.
I will say no more, except: 8.5/10!

I really like the genre, with all the bad puns everywhere, but there is big room for improvement here, mostly in dungeons:
- Dungeon traps. Everywhere. Unavoidable. Fixed damage. I died in a level 5 dungeon with my level 40 team because I kept running into traps.
- Too few different dungeon events. If I'm going to cross dozens of rooms, I'd expect to have somewhat different runs (I mean, there could at least be a few location-related ones). If I'm going to fight mobs, I'd like to see something other than a portal or monster coming from behind curtains everytime. Not to mention that more than half are traps, so it's both boring and frustrating.
- Events have different outcomes, but since there are so few of them you quickly know the outcomes. And often, the best choice is to do nothing.
- Expanding on that. Dungeon event reward.... nothing. The same event happen in the first dungeon just like the last. Whoa, so happy to find two +5HP trinkets when I'm level 30+. Man 15 gold? I'm so rich now, I have 6015 gold ! Can't wait to get that sweet 300XP book, that's a big help towards the 30k I need. But you know what? These garbage rewards are only one outcome of an event... the other being most of the time a trap. Unless you're at the first dungeon, pass your way it's not worth the risk.
- Random drops. Come on, I just killed a level 45 dragon, and all I got was a 5g weapon you can buy at level 1 in the shop.
- Crafting is very limited. Shop included, there is exactly one weapon and one armor for casters (unless you have the trait to ignore penalties on armor, and even then it's just a regular armor).
Other than that, the game is pretty fun, with references and horrible puns everywhere. Dungeons are bad but you're mostly playing for the dialogues, and they're pretty good.

I love games that mess with games as a medium, and this game gives me ever reason to.
While the gameplay can be dull at moments, its creativity exceeds in its other aspects, such as its self-awareness and tricking the player. There are moments when I was yelling at my monitor as the game tricked me into something so obvious that I shouldt've fallen for it. (That sounds really vague, I know. But I musn't spoil anything. Describing around the game is the best I can do.) Not to mention as the game gets much more interesting as it preogresses as you learn about the purgatory you're trapped in. You'll need to play it many times over to capture all of the secrets of the story, that is if you chose to.
I'm going to compare it to Undertale, as both games mess with a lot of aspects of video games, but both are actually vastly different in how they present thier story. Though, saying that, I do feel Undertale does its job better than Pony Island in the way of character development and player engagement. This is not to say Pony Island is mediocre, it is actually very much not so, but Undertale was a much more meaty game that had me thinking about it for weeks after finishing it. Pony Island isn't forgettable, but I don't think I'll be thinking about it as much as Undertale.
Other, less important things, such as control handing and bugginess, I had no issue with. The game is very well polished. Not to mention the sountrack is pretty damn good.
Pony Island is a brilliant game about games that tricks the player and tells a story not only about the devil, but games as a medium.

It sounds simple, but there are increasingly complex permutations (multiple cubes, shifting of tile directions and positions, black tiles that can't be next to other black tiles, or a combination of all of the above in one puzzle).  There are no time limits or move limits, it's just you exploring the minimalistic puzzles until everything works out.  It's a serene, calming experience, even as the puzzles become real brain teasers. There aren't a huge number of levels - it took me 90 minutes to complete the game, and I was doing other things at the time. But for a $1.00 game, it's a very nice casual experience.

"Trails in the Sky" is a truly special Japanese RPG from Falcom, with all of the classic turn based goodness and none of the bloat that can at times make the genre tedious.  You play as a pair of young adventures who set out across a vast continent to explore and help those in need.  Things slowly escalate into a story of friendship, love, betrayal, espionage with of course lots of monsters.  This is the first game of "The Legend of Heroes trilogy".  The other two are still being localized for English audiences (due out 2015/2016).  It’s taken a while to translate due to the incredibly vast amount of text in each game.  This is great if you love a good story, but you will have to be willing to read a lot, there is no voice acting to be found.  However if you stick with it you will be rewarded with a memorable yarn.
Graphically the game is dated (2004) but still very enjoyable, very bright and vivid, and the lovely sound track really compliments the visuals.  Game play is a refined and polished turn based affair with attacks, magic, special moves and a fair sized casts of unique characters to try out in battle.  There is also a gem system that allows you to customize your characters magic as you see fit.  All foes are present on screen (no random battles) and you can save at any time (not just at check points).  Plenty of side quests to complete and special loot to find make “Legend of Heroes" very addicting for the JRPG crowd.  Overall "Trails in the Sky" is one of the crown jewels of the JRPG genre this century, a must play for JRPG fans and worth a play for anyone who likes to dabble in the genre on occasion, and it plays great with a gamepad.

This game was surprisingly easier compared to The Testament of Sherlock Holmes. I still enjoyed it nevertheless.
For me, there were fewer puzzles to complete and a lot of the information was given to you basically on a silver platter. It was very rare that I had to remember an important details or event, as they were always wrote down in your journal and I was always told what to do next, which I didn't enjoy (as I prefer to figure it out for myself).
On the flip side, I thoroughly enjoyed the fact that you have to make your own conclusions, and you could even make the wrong decision if you don't have enough clues or missed some dialogue (specifically the silver vs ice dagger dilemma I had). However as mentioned above, the game basically tells you if you're missing a clue so I didn't really have the problem of not having enough evidence. The characters were interesting and unique, and the cases kept me enthralled (although I found myself losing interest in the second case in which a train goes missing, much prefer the brutal murders and autopsies).
I did enjoy this game, however it did not leave me feeling angry, frustrated, or wondering how to solve something, which is what I really wanted. There were no "Eureka" moments, or basically impossible puzzles to drain my brainpower. I can understand not everyone wants that, but I would have loved a puzzle in which I feel the strong urge to smash my head against my desk instead of an armwrestling game...

Glad I've found this game!
Pros:
- It is not an easy game. It's challenging in a good way.
- It runs stable on my system. Not a single crash while actually in the game (yet a few while loading but that's not a big deal at all)
- The balancing of units is well performed and certainly based on real battlefield experiences.
- The physics of this game are also well performed. There are no real flaws that I noticed in the game mechanics which is something that made me happy and kept my immersion alive.
- It tells the story of the Syrian Civil War from a perspective of the Syrian government and the Russian Federation which by itself is something your should have heard about. The conflict is not easily explained yet western media tends to only give easy explanations on difficult topics especially about Syria. Assad = bad. Rebels = Fighting for freedom. And it's not that easy. By looking at the details you'll notice that at least from our perspective measured by our moral values rebels in Syria are not the poor suppressed victims who are just struggling for survival and freedom but they are actually pretty bad too. Not saying that Assad and Russians are the moral winners. But I'd at least like to point out that in Syria in the last few years there were no moral winners anymore. There is no hand without blood on it anymore. There is noone who could be supported by us Westeners anymore without taking our part of the guilt of the suffering of innocents. I find it important to point that out and it's a big plus for this game because it's pointing its fingers in a direction where not enough fingers are pointing: Rebels in Syria aren't the good guys.
Cons:
- This game is utterly difficult sometimes which is a good thing in general but also kind of frustrating for a few moments.
- You have limited ammo. Your enemies have infinite ammo. Not cool!
- The biggest Con for me: The game is way too short. There are not enough missions. The actual playtime is a bit too little. Maybe it's okay for the price you pay, arguably. All in all I had 7 hours fun with this game which just wasn't enough.
- The narration tends to feel a little propagandistic. The game might be and certainly is right about a few things that are important but that doesn't mean it's right about everything, from a political point of view. It's just "too much" at some points.
All in all I loved this game. Game-wise there sadly is very little coverage of the Syrian Civil War. So I really enjoyed this experience and I'm looking forward for more content from this studio. Good job!

TLDR: Bought the game for $40, definitely worth the 60 when the sale ends, IMO.  Campaign/side stuff is great fun.  Online could use some work.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I never played the original Watch_Dogs.  I heard a lot of hype about this sequel and that it didn't tie in with the original story so I kept Watch_Dogs 2 on my watch list.  I was reluctant to pay $60 for it and was very happy to see the winter sale price of $40.  I bought the game 3 days ago and have almost 34 hours on record now.
The story was well written, while there was one particular character that didn't seem to play much of a role.  I heard the humor and culture was cringey, but I disagree.  I think it's just the right amount of geeky/gamer humor and wasn't overdone.  Story wasn't too long or too short.  I do wish it was slightly longer because I really want more of this game!
I really really enjoy the fact that you can play through the story with whatever form of action you prefer (aggressor, trickster, ghost).  I completed the campaign without killing a single enemy (aside from some times when it was required).  The amount of skills you get for your RC jumper and quadcopter make them very resourceful.
The online interaction has been a bit weak.  I don't have any friends that play on PC with me, but I frequently check "LFG" websites to group with people looking to accomplish the same stuff as me.  There is NO TEXT CHAT at all in this game, and you can only directly invite friends you have on UPlay.  There are tons of co-op missions to do online, but it's really aggravating that you can't communicate with your teammate unless you have a headset on.
The online CONTENT has been fun.  With improvements on what I said above it would be great.  Short co-op missions with straightforward objectives, bounty hunter/fugitive pvp (very short encounters...not all that much fun IMO), hacking other players (fun, but happens a lot in free roam single player when you don't want it to...I recommend disabling in settings if you don't want online interruptions while playing)...With some tweaking, Watch_Dogs 2 multiplayer could be longer lived.
I'm a bit disappointed at how easy it is to gain every achievement.  Mentioned above, I've had the game for 3 days and only have 2 achievements left to unlock.
The one major complaint I have about this game is the controls with driving.  I play a good amount of GTAV and it isn't nearly as fluid.  It took a lot of getting used to.
Compared to other reviewers, I didn't have any issues with the game running.  I'm running a GTX 960 and i7 2600.  Wasn't monitoring my frame rate, but felt pretty close to 60.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game to anyone looking for an open world, sandbox game that has a different feel than the other AAA titles out right now like GTAV.

I decided to spend the remainder of my Steam Wallet on this game. It seemed interesting, with enough of a challenge to keep me entertained. However, I was very disappointed with my purchase. Here are some problems with Barony:
The UI needs work. Even though Hunger is an effect, there is no meter to show how hungry you are. Only an icon that pops up on occasion. You become hungry at the worst possible times. And when you try to sell an item, it isn't straightforward. Half the fun of loot is selling it, and you can't. When items are damaged, you can't tell. There is no durability meter on items. They seem to break at random.
The game is lacking even a simplistic tutorial. It's irritating to have to figure out controls from online guides and the Settings menu.
Why is there a guy selling things in the dungeon? It makes no sense.
Combat sucks. Enemy swings can barely be seen, so you can't time enemy strikes. And shields don't provide as much protection as they should. Shields in Minecraft, for example, were implemented very well, providing players a great deal of protection from enemy strikes. But the shields in Barony feel like they're full of holes. With weapons, swings feel sloppy; like I have little control of how far my swing goes. I have the modify the FOV heavily to find the right distance. In Daggerfall, the FOV was fine, since the weapon is seen swinging at a distance, rather than the hacking motion from Minecraft. The FOV isn't a problem in Minecraft, because enemies aren't swinging weapons at you. They just cause damage or shoot projectiles. Combat feels chaotic and sloppy; this could be remedied with faster movement, allowing for fast-paced dodging. This is how it worked in Daggerfall. Also, Daggerfall used a random damage system. Players could only determine if they are close enough to strike with their weapon. Blocks and damage were generated at random. This worked well. However, your character feels slow, and enemy strikes can rarely be avoided. In a game as difficult as Barony, a strong melee system is very much needed.
The system of appraising items sucks. Only the Merchant can reliably appraise items. It makes sense if the other classes appraise slowly. But if you have to wait an entire minute to appraise an item, only for the appraisal to fail, it wastes time, puts characters in danger, and takes the fun out of looting (My favorite part of RPGs, btw). Appraise skill should simply increase the speed of appraisals instead of increase reliability. It hurts people early in the game. Also, more items should be general items, without need for appraisal. In Diablo, for example, most loot weapons don't need to be identified. However, the only items that do need identification are magic items. This made identification VERY satisfying, since it was always a pleasant surprise to see what powers a magic weapon had. But in Barony, players are often left disappointed with their new items once they are appraised. Also, you should not need to appraise food. That's ridiculous. Food just needs a sniff and a once over, not an appraisal of value.
It makes sense that the game is a difficult roguelike, and that all loot and level progress is lost upon death. However, you should be able to save characters, so experience isn't lost. The fact that you lose absolutely ALL progress if you die is extremely frustrating. The game stops being enjoyably hard and start being frustrating when you gain XP, only to die easily later on. At least in DARK SOULS, you keep your level when you die.
Mana and Health recharge VERY slowly. This was okay in Daggerfall, since the designers were fresh D&D players who didn't know better. When Daggerfall was made, it was based on D&D combat. D&D combat lasted far longer per enemy, so high mana and health costs were okay. But in a Videogame, you need that health and mana back very quickly. In Daggerfall, the player could rest in order to regain lost health. However, you have no way other than random potions to rapidly regain health in Barony. And note that those potions might be poisonous. Therefore, it is VERY easy to die. Or you have to wait several minutes to regain health and mana. This slows the game's pace immensely.
Items become cursed very easily, for no apparent reason. Loot becomes unusable. I cannot stress enough how much I LOOOOVE Looting in RPGs. So when all the loot I find becomes useless for no good reason, the game stops being fun.
For some reason, the mouse buttons cannot be rebound. The game feels strange to me, since I'm used to "E" to interact, RMB to block, and Space to Jump. But I can't rebind the mouse buttons to my liking. Not that jumping is in Barony, of course.
Traps are very difficult to see until it is too late. There should be a visible tripwire or something hidden in the ground, but there isn't. Not even a subtle clue of any sort. So all your progress might be lost at any time from any trap.
Multiplayer servers are barren. Probably due to several of the reasons I listed. Really, I see what this game was going for. I do. It has the foundation of a great, addictive Videogame. In playing this, I couldn't help but explore and loot the dungeon. I have been bored with RPGs lately, so for Barony to pique my interest, it is an astonishing feat. The description of Barony states that it is inspired by games like Daggerfall. But in reality, it poorly executes what games like Daggerfall did well. The heart of those classic games like Daggerfall is there; but it is executed poorly. I hate to give a low rating to this game, since there is an online community that still loves this. And the designers clearly cared about the project. But I think my money could have been better spent. Hopefully, the designers will pay attention to these reviews (As well as mine) and patch the game so it can become the indie classic it was meant to be.  The game is only a year old; it could still become great.

This is one of the games where Steam would need a "meh" option. The original game is pretty old and the Remaster doesn't help very much. The story and characters are badly written. It contains time travel and falls into every trap that stories about time travel will open. The voice actiong is sometimes laughably bad. The hidden object scenes vary very strongly in quality. The minigames are never explained but they do have a skip button in case you can't figure out what they want.
HOWEVER, it is very interesting to play for people who are either interested in game development, or in the evolution of the genre HOG. Playing from this game, where I skipped a lot to the last game of the trilogy where I got all achievements because I was so engaged was a really interesting experience. It is amazing to see how bit by bit the developer evolved, How much they learned in every iteration and grew by actively trying to make their games better. This game really made me appreciate how much work Artifex Mundi puts into their games and how serious they take their work as artists! So even if I gave a thumbs down, because most people coming here will not appreciate that perspective and will prefer the later entries in the series, it was definitely a learning experience for me.

I swore I'd never buy another Paradox game. But it was only $2, so I went ahead and bought it. I really shouldn't have bothered. Knights of Pen and Paper 2 suffers from the same problem all Paradox games suffer from: they prioritize paid DLC over putting out a high-quality base game. At least Knights of Pen and Paper 2 isn't as buggy as most of Paradox's other products.
But it could have been great if they'd made a few simple improvements. Why oh why can't I speed up the animations? If you enjoy watching a computer roll dice, do I have a game for you. Hundreds of dice. Thousands of dice. Rolling slowly.
Then there's the inventory management headache. You have a lovely vault, but can't access it from the crafting screen. So you wind up spending time on three different screens dragging junk around. Fun. You also can't see all your characters' items at once. Finding a particular item can take 5 clicks or more.
I might have let all that ride, but then they started me on a quest line that ends--I kid you not--in a "quest" to buy their DLC for $4.99. So I wasted time a bunch of time watching dice roll only to be told I can't finish the quest line without paying for it.
Honestly, Paradox, this shouldn't be hard. Put out a great base game, and I'll happily buy your DLC. Or better yet, take a page from Thea and make the DLC free, and give us the option to donate if we enjoy it. There's a company that truly values its customers, rather than just trying to milk us for another buck.

Many people in the steam forums argue about the way the story is written. It's basically an argument between people who get their information from two very oppsite sides. Both have certain merits, and biases obviously.
This game is russian made, and is set in the reality of the conflict plaguing Syria today. Should it be considered insensitive ? I don't think so. When Modern Warfare came out, it was clearly set in middle eastern envirronment, with americans battling the local army. While america was in the midst of the Iraqi occupation. Should this game have been set in a fictional war ? It could have for sure, but it would lose the main plot which makes it an interesting campaign to go through. So at this point, it's up to you to ask yourself, do you feel like playing on Assad's side ? Against the terrorist groups who took over the country, and eventually became ISIS. It's definitly not, a genocide simulator. It's mainly about about protecting people actually. If you can't fathom that might have happened in real life. Then you might not want to buy it. If you subscribe, or want to try and understand the point of view this game provides. It's definitly a good story. the dialogues are rather well written.
Put aside the politics, and focusing on the gameplay. This is a medium scale, micro managment based tactical game. It is mostly based on positioning your footmen who come in various classes, to give them the advantage over the enemy, and keep them alive as long as possible. It's mostly urban envirronment so you will spend a lot of time setting yourself up in buildings, moving up streets one block at a time. You also have trucks, IFV, Tanks, and even choppers. If you had an unlimited reserve of bombs and tank shells, you could technically bring down the whole map. Buildings can come down and your garrisoned units will lose protection if they stay inside.
Suicide bombers in trucks or cars can bring it down in a single blow and severely impact your mission.
It's a very hard game, and requires to be quite conservative with your units,  picking the right units each time you have the possibility to deploy reinforcements is essential. Which might require you to restart missions or roll back as you can't predict what might come at you the first time.
2 small RPG squads can make the difference between ending the mission with a final tank blowing up, or being stuck in front of it with the remain of your army stuck in a building, and the mission failing.
The handling of units is nothing really different from what you might have seen in other games. Footmen can enter buildings, throw smokes or seek cover on demand, and also have different behaviors and formations possible, which you might not always use but they're there. Each units has ammo that goes down and replenishes using trucks. Same for vehicles, which can be repaired to some extent, and take damage depending on the hits. There are no health bars, they might get blown in a single hit from behind, or take several hits, it's up to you to position them properly. The AI can be a bit silly though.
It's graphically a bit outdated, but still good looking. For the price tag it is sold for, i wouldn't ask for more.
Overall, considering it's price, it's definitly worth it.

TLDR: Bought the game for $40, definitely worth the 60 when the sale ends, IMO.  Campaign/side stuff is great fun.  Online could use some work.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I never played the original Watch_Dogs.  I heard a lot of hype about this sequel and that it didn't tie in with the original story so I kept Watch_Dogs 2 on my watch list.  I was reluctant to pay $60 for it and was very happy to see the winter sale price of $40.  I bought the game 3 days ago and have almost 34 hours on record now.
The story was well written, while there was one particular character that didn't seem to play much of a role.  I heard the humor and culture was cringey, but I disagree.  I think it's just the right amount of geeky/gamer humor and wasn't overdone.  Story wasn't too long or too short.  I do wish it was slightly longer because I really want more of this game!
I really really enjoy the fact that you can play through the story with whatever form of action you prefer (aggressor, trickster, ghost).  I completed the campaign without killing a single enemy (aside from some times when it was required).  The amount of skills you get for your RC jumper and quadcopter make them very resourceful.
The online interaction has been a bit weak.  I don't have any friends that play on PC with me, but I frequently check "LFG" websites to group with people looking to accomplish the same stuff as me.  There is NO TEXT CHAT at all in this game, and you can only directly invite friends you have on UPlay.  There are tons of co-op missions to do online, but it's really aggravating that you can't communicate with your teammate unless you have a headset on.
The online CONTENT has been fun.  With improvements on what I said above it would be great.  Short co-op missions with straightforward objectives, bounty hunter/fugitive pvp (very short encounters...not all that much fun IMO), hacking other players (fun, but happens a lot in free roam single player when you don't want it to...I recommend disabling in settings if you don't want online interruptions while playing)...With some tweaking, Watch_Dogs 2 multiplayer could be longer lived.
I'm a bit disappointed at how easy it is to gain every achievement.  Mentioned above, I've had the game for 3 days and only have 2 achievements left to unlock.
The one major complaint I have about this game is the controls with driving.  I play a good amount of GTAV and it isn't nearly as fluid.  It took a lot of getting used to.
Compared to other reviewers, I didn't have any issues with the game running.  I'm running a GTX 960 and i7 2600.  Wasn't monitoring my frame rate, but felt pretty close to 60.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game to anyone looking for an open world, sandbox game that has a different feel than the other AAA titles out right now like GTAV.
Fun to play and has a good story line with fun missions. But it requiers a powerful PC.

A generally competent and enjoyable hidden object game that has a few flaws, also the first installment in currently a trilogy of games all in the same vein.
So overall the gameplay is fine - the point and click sections are all fairly decently done, the puzzles are fairly varied but easy and not really challenging (for example we do a 4x4 knight move puzzle, except you can reuse the same squares over and over to cover all 16 squares, so you can't get lose), the hidden object scenes are mostly decent and playable with the exception mainly of the history archive which has this weird glow that fades in and out and made it difficult for me to look at the screen for long (kind of a problem for a hidden object game!)
In terms of the story it is fairly standard stuff, you are some amazingly special person that has to save the world using your time traveling abilities, everywhere in time you go everyone lavishing praise on you as one of the smartest people of all time, which you prove by solving one or two very simple puzzles. The structure also makes it a bit repetitive as you do exactly the same series of actions seven times as you recover each of the rings you drop at the start.
Other flaws for me include being British the protaganists accent was very annoying, but probably works fine for American audiences. Another being the weird non-animation of speaking characters where static images of their head kind of bulges and warps when they are speaking.
But overall this is perfectly playable and decent enough, although later entries in the series are somewhat better from what I remember, the main reservation I would have is the glow effect in the archive which did nearly get me to quit the game half finished a couple of times (and note you go to the archive seven or eight times in all)

I came to this version of Knights of Pen & Paper before finding the original.  I'm not going to bother comparing the two as I've barely touched the first game.  I'll also add the caveat that I haven't finished the KoP&P2 main campaign yet.
This is a solid, humorous and quite engaging game that portrays tabletop gaming in a surprisingly accurate light, from the party diversity to the edition loyalty to the gaming magazines.  Experienced tabletop gamers will recognise the majority of the references, both positive and negative, while those new to tabletop gaming may get some idea of the elements that make it such a rewarding - and at times frustrating - hobby.  Having done my share of GMing over the years, something I find very familiar are those moments when the GM in this game seems to shrug and roll with some ridiculous thing one of the party has just suggested.
There is no main protagonist in the game per se, and instead the player takes on the role of a whole party of aspiring adventurers.  The GM takes the party through a whirlwind series of adventures in a broad gaming world that will challenge, amuse and annoy at various times.  It is a love note to the hobby which preceded (and eventually gave rise to) computer RPGs and should be taken with several grains of salt.  Sprinkled with more than its share of absurdist humour, this is not a game that you're supposed to be taking seriously.  The world's called Paperos.  If that doesn't give you enough of a hint as to the game's intended ambience, I doubt anything will.
The player options are stereotypes which, I feel, manage to be entertaining without belittling or insulting the hobby's fans.  From the Jock to the Goth to the Cheerleader, everyone has some unique talent to bring to the table, all of which are useful.  The class types are varied and yet familiar.
I heartily recommend this game, but only to players who can enjoy the absurd.  If you can't help but approach tabletop gaming with your 100% Absolute SRS BSNS Face on, you probably won't enjoy KoP&P2.  The game is laden with culture references (just like plenty of real tabletop games I've been involved with), some of which are groan-worthy and others quite clever, so if that isn't your poison I suggest you look elsewhere.  Likewise, if you're a misogynistic♥♥♥♥♥♥who can't stand women in gaming, best leave this alone.
The only real complaint that I have regarding this game is the complete lack of a campaign creation tool.  This would be an ideal game for allowing users to create and share their own campaign scripts, whether set in Paperos or in user-created worlds.  Particularly on Steam, this would add a dimension to the game which would fit the genre perfectly.  If the developers ever expand Knights of Pen & Paper 2, or ever happen to make Knights of Pen & Paper 3, I would suggest strongly that user-made campaigns would be a shining gem in this somewhat pixellated crown.

Real Boxing is a solid game marred by a few problems. The announcer is hilariously obnoxious. I really wish there was more and better boxer customization. There is no real variation in frame or facial structure. I can't play a slick, wiry bantamweight that looks like Rigondeaux - I have to look like competition-fit Kai Greene, with my choice of gear, facial features, and skin colour. You'd think that with how much variation there is in the build, height, and reach of boxers, it would at least be addressed in the game. But nope, every boxer uses the same re-skinned model.
Graphical gripes aside, when I actually play it as I believe it was intended, Real Boxing is such a fun game. There are many elements to the strategy of boxing that they successfully incorporated game mechanics for. If you choose, every fight can be a chess match, with specific punches chosen to counter whatever they throw, fun and rewarding micro with timing headslips, and a range system that ends up modeling boxing footwork fairly well.
Unfortunately, aspects of the game are broken -the stamina system and the stun / combo mechanic. These mechanics are supposed to reward skilled play; ideally you go in to trade 3 or 4 accurate and carefully chosen punches, then cover up and get back out of range. Unfortunately it is vastly more efficient to select the right perks and run forward while repeatedly jabbing your opponent to unconsciousness. Run at them, jab the guard until it breaks, jab them while they're stunned. Rinse, repeat. Boring.
There is multiplayer and I have not yet dared. Who knows though, maybe amist all the cheese and jab spam, something resembling Real Boxing might happen.

This is no Super Meat Boy, but probably a good introduction to the genre.
This game is a precision platformer, and a decent one at that, but it falls into the common pitfalls of the genre.
It is all built on a 2D tiled grid map structure, which allows for easy map building.
Overall the visuals are good, the narrator is quite charming, but overall the gameplay is a bit forgettable.
Falling on the tactics from most of the free versions of these games, rather than focusing on a small set of mechanics and progressively making harder and harder challenges, this game presents more and more mechanics as the story progresses, making more and more complicated runs.
What this then means is the game tends towards complicated messy mazes of multiple different mechanical triggers and alleyways, all of which you must explore before getting to the exit.
This often left me lost in the higher levels, and rather gets in the way of making a 'clean' fast run on the first attempt.
Also the earlier levels are not difficult, read first half of the story missions, but rather introduce said many varied mechanics, and were easily completed.
Similarly, the higher difficulty setting does not affect the difficulty of the challenges, but rather turns off the game's mid-run checkpoint system. Which, isn't increasing the difficulty, as to get an A+ ranking you also need to complete each level within a time limit, and dying/respawning using the checkpoint system often sacrifices this ranking.
So I would suggest only playing in Normal mode and going for A+ rankings, as then you can quickly see the level on the first attempt, albiet dying a couple of times, affording a clean run shortly after.
There were also some mechanical issues.
Namely same mechanics do not behave in a set fashion.
Most notably there is some bouncy terrain that will shoot the player in a different direction based on the angle that the player hits it.
However when said terrain makes up a flat surface, hitting the terrain along the edge of the adjacent terrain pieces (2D grid map remember) will cause the character to jump in a different manner than if they hit in the center of a single terrain piece.
This causes complications when moving through rooms entirely built of this terrain whilst trying to avoid other obstacles.
There are other minor grievances here in that other obstacles also don't behave identically each time the same obstacle.
Lazers have random on/off periods.
Enemies don't behave consistently.
And so on.
But that largely doesn't matter as the stages are not usually built for difficulty in the first place. So adapting to these minor random elements rarely causes frustration.
Of course, this game also has player made content (due to the grid etc making it easy).
And these levels -do- attempt to be difficult, and so the random elements -do- screw you over in these circumstances.
The game also has multiplayer arena battles and local play.
This is probably where the game becomes far better than a decent platformer.
However, at the time of writing, I could not find any online play to experiment with, and nor have I tried local co-op play.
In all, this is an easy platformer which has charm and personality.
I'm sure kids would have fun with it, especially when blowing each other up in local co-op.
But for me, the only hard section in the story was in the level immediately prior to finishing the game.
As a result, I was quickly bored and rushed through the story missions, whist avoiding all encore missions, just to let the narrator finish.

Enclave is one of those old-school games from back in the day, from times that are now forever gone. It won't come up as a surprise for you, that this title has no DLC microtransactions or an insane amount of senseless grinding, instead being a true type of an adventure RPG with solid, fun gameplay. In the most accurate sense, Enclave is more of a hack-and-slash action rather than a RPG, although roleplaying elements are definetely present in this game. Despite being released way back in 2002, Enclave still manages to thrill and entertain even today, in large part thanks to its graphical quality and a relatively well created atmosphere.
In terms of the plotline, Enclave is your typical dark fantasy, where the ever encroaching darkness is about to swarm the last remains of hope... literally. Long ago, a great demon waged war against all that is good in order to destroy it, but in the process of doing so, he got slain. This event shattered the face of the planet, and the last hope of victorious men is now but a single stranded kingdom, known as the Enclave. After many years, those who were once loyal to the demon yet again are now ready to kill and destroy, and it seems that the demon himself is about to reincarnate back into the grim of world of Enclave. Without going too far into the details of the story, it can be noted, that even though the storyline  is kind of average, it still gets the job done and keeps the player hooked. Every single mission in the game has a very unique environment, ranging from trap filled tombs and lava sizzling valleys to strange places of mystical power. There are two campaings in Enclave, allowing you to try yourself out in both the roles of a hero in a not so shining armor, or an ugly looking baddie with an amusing, albeit not a quite threatening appearance. Old timers that played such games as Heretic II or Arx Fatalis will love Enclave, although the two mentioned titles are still ofcourse different in many ways.
Throughout the game, your arsenal will include alot of melee and ranged weapons. Melee arms consist of various swords, clubs and axes, ranged weaponry consists of bows and magical staves. In terms of protection, your heroes will have three types of armor and alot of shields. Usually, as one would guess, the most expensive type of protection and weaponry is the most effective one, and as the game progressesess, you will be able to equip your heroes with the best type of gear, if ofcourse you collect gold and valuable gems that are scattered throughtout missions. Otherwise, you will have to play as a raggedy orc or a cloth-clad gnome. Battles are usually straightforward, especially when it comes to melee. Most of the time, you will try to deal a blow to the enemy while protecting yourself with a shield. Ranged duels with bows are more thrilling, and so are the fights between mages. In terms of combat and gameplay in general, Enclave is an entertaining game, just the kind of a game to relax with after work or study. The missions are challening, but at the same time are not annoying. From time to time, cinematics with explanation to the background lore will keep the players entertained and focused, and the music that is present in the game is pretty good and atmospheric.
In a summary, it can be written, that Enclave is a game worth to be recommended. Without a doubt, time has taken its toll on the game, and some younger, more demanding players might not like it, but if you are not too critical when it comes to older titles, and if you enjoy a good action game, Enclave is for you.

This game is absolutely wonderful, and I'll enumerate why it's great, but there are several really good reasons to not buy it if they apply to you.
Don't buy the game if:
>You don't like to read a lot of dialogue
>You expect to 100% the game without a guide
>You want a plot that's exciting and stuffed full of action throughout
>You don't want to wait for "the summer of 2013" for XSEED to localize the Second Chapter (sequel)
Getting past all of that (which is easy if you have any manner of patience), you've got a really nice, quaint JRPG with SRPG elements like battle placement. The plot is simple, engaging, and well-crafted, but it really hooks you in because of its characters. If you take a few seconds to open yourself up to the characters, you'll find that they're really quite extensively shaped through the game's dialogue. The two protagonists are both fleshed out nicely and work very believably together. The combat systems are fairly robust, and the orbal system (by which you gain the ability to use spells and get some passive buffs) is done well, even though these systems really start to shine in the game's sequel/second chapter.
The PC port of this game (it was originally a PSP game, as I recall) is extremely efficient. Toasters and microwaves could run this game easily. Many standard options for PC versions of games that you'd expect are there, and the controls for the game give you enough control to play the game with no trouble at all; most of the time you could play the game with one hand if you rebind all your keys for use near WASD (or you can control the game entirely with your mouse).
If you're one of those weenies that cares about your JRPGs being too tropey or whatever, you don't really have to worry about that. There's nothing that's gonna ruffle your delicate feathers in this game, and it's really not anything you'd see in a cheap anime. There are a few elements borrowed from culture at large and some clever extrapolation can get you figuring out some of the twists before they happen, but you're mostly going to be in the dark.
Expect a cliffhanger ending, since the game is and always has been part of a planned trilogy. Completing the game, however, is still quite satisfying, and I really do think that most fans of the JRPG and SRPG genres will quite like this game. I CERTAINLY did.

I remember buying this game back when it was released for the PlayStation 1. As far as I remember, it was a popular release and it received many positive reviews by the major publications of the time. I was excited to buy it but as soon as I began playing it, I remember being disappointed. I can't remember whether or not I beat it back then but chances are high that I got bored and quit playing just as I did now.
Despite what the multitude of nostalgic, rabid and headstrong fans say, Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee  didn't age well at all from what was already a mediocre effort to begin with. While the character design is interesting and charming, everything else is quite flawed. The background graphics and animations are average to below average, the music is nearly non-existent, the sound effects can get borderline annoying at times, and worst of all, the controls are extremely unresponsive, sluggish and awkward. Getting Abe to perform the most basic of platforming moves such as seamlessly running, stopping, climbing on a ledge and then sneaking is painful and inadequate. Controlling Abe feels very much delayed and as if the movements were restricted in some way. The puzzles and rooms are designed competently for the most part but when you have to deal with the game's awful controls, solving each screen is too aggravating and devoid of any fun whatsoever. The gameplay revolves around traversing the game world one screen at a time. Even though not every screen presents the player with a puzzle or a situation that needs his or her attention, there is still the need to advance through each screen individually and with a slight pause between each transition. Deaths come often and the player will be forced to repeatedly wait through a lengthy death and restart animation that takes about five seconds to complete. The save system is based on checkpoints, so if the player dies several screens beyond the last checkpoint, every screen from the checkpoint to the point of death will need to be redone as many times as it takes until you reach the next checkpoint. Without mentioning any spoilers, it is encouraged that there is at least one additional playthrough after you beat the game once. In relation to this, one of the worst design choices in the game presents itself. The goal is to rescue slaves. Unfortunately for the player, many of the slaves are hidden away in secret areas that are absolutely not easy to find. Thanks to this design decision, this means the player will fail at the goal the game has set to be accomplished.
It's surprising to me how much love Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee has garnered through the years. It has far too many flaws to be enjoyed and it's way too annoying to be played to completion. This game could easily have been so much better than it actually is.

Well that's weird, I have to write the review for Abe's Exoddus here because the time I spent playing that has been applied to Oddysee for some reason not known to man nor beast.
This release of Exoddus is broken due to port-induced bugs. Glukkons are totally immobile once possessed, which breaks the game and makes it unfinishable due to the need to use them to finish certain puzzles. I got this as part of the Oddbox and along with the utter disgrace that was Stranger's Wrath, i'm sadly forced to slam the No button when it comes to recommending a series I used to adore wholeheartedly.

While the game's remake is already available on Steam (under the title New 'N' Tasty) you can still pick up the original Oddworld game which was released back in 1997 - almost 20 years ago! This was what started the Oddworld franchise that since that year has seen several sequels.
These games are all about Abe, the titular character, who is a Mudokon slave being captive in a factory. Initially just a worker, but later labelled as "meat to be processed", Abe sets out to escape from his captors and also to free his fellow Mudokons in the process. The game's first cutscene (which is pretty long considering it is an old game) summarises the story very well and we can quickly understand what's ahead of us.
This is a 2D platformer, so we go from screen to screen and every new "room" represents a new challenge. We have patrolling enemies as well as traps and of course members of the Mudokon race who we need to rescue. We can issue some basic commands to them to make sure they follow us - this part where you communicate with the others can be hilarious.
Do note that this is one of those games where one mistake can lead to certain death. Checkpoints are regularly placed, though, so at least the game is not punishing you for being a little careless from time to time. One particularly interesting thing is how you can make other Mudokons die if you are not careful - the game does not take you back to the last checkpoint so you may think this is not a problem. Truth is, the number of saved Mudokons determines the ending of the game - you can either get the Good or the Bad ending.
The gameplay is really good - Abe can do a lot of things in terms of movement and activating various mechanisms throughout the factory. Sections tend to get more and more difficult but Oddworld offers an acceptable learning curve here. I haven't tried the remake so I do not know how good a job they did - still, if you like old games or you are, just like myself, someone having played this back in the '90s do give it a try once more!

The game doesn't break far from what the typical Ubisoft open world game is but man is it entertaining. This game oozes personally. Now for a few bad stuff. I've had some horrendous framerate problems, mostly when driving. It's dropped down to 1 fps at times. I mean hell I set the game to the lowest possible resolution I can 1024x768 on LOW graphical settings and I still get frame rates drops while driving. THORNYWAY- The Game (REVIEW) (By Paradox29 from Chicken Tikka Gaming)
To start off, a huge thanks to developer x0maze for sending us this copy of this game for review.
Due to technical reasons, we couldn't record a gameplay session of this game, so it's just going to be a written review. (OBS and Shadowplay screwed us over and we have no idea why)
We at Chicken Tikka Gaming heard of this game introducing a new concept of conveying the story through the music of a band named, Thornyway, and we absolutely loved this idea. And as expected, the music in this game was just marvelous.
The piano scores immediately resonated with us, as we are fellow musicians as well. We could very well have just sat there and be immersed in the masterpieces that Ian Kmit, Roman Chernitsky and Pavel Dyshlevich along with the vocalists and composers have produced. Kudos to you amazing people!
Unfortunately, the rest of the game doesn't fall into place quite as well as the music did.
From constant frame drops that manufactured migraines, to buggy controls - the "jump" wouldn't work sometimes, even while you are running - to completely non-intuitive gameplay, made this game a chore to play rather than a pleasant experience as this game wouldn't fit into the "Casual" tag that we see on steam.
The starting location had a ton of glitches with random wall flickering as well as stuttering and for a game that requires very low hardware requirements for it to run, this is completely unacceptable considering that this is a finished product and not one that is in Early Access. The frame rate would abruptly drop to about 15 to 20 fps and then shoot back to 60 fps in an instant - which simply induced headaches for us while playing, dissecting us from the immersive and soothing music in the background.
The controls are just a huge mess. There is no indication of a sense of direction and objective, which makes this game the antonym of a "Casual" game. The sounds cues (which we believe are there for guidance)  only led to a dead-end with no where else to go.
Overall, this game - with the amazing concept expected of an indie developer - will definitely appeal to fans of the band, but not gamers in general. If you're in for just the music, we'd suggest you to buy the music album from stores, when it goes on sale.

Absolutely amazing game. I am a big fan of Sherlock Holmes, even though I don't know much about the mytho. However, with what I know, I can see this game is very true to the source material. I deeply believe this is the best Sherlock game ever made.

Intriguing, amazing textures -- some of the best I've seen! -- a variety of investigative gameplay that bears some resemblance to L.A. Noire, and a variety of clothing and disguises to select, with the humor of Holmes and Watson, of course, present.
However, the result of your investigations feels almost unrewarding, considering you can opt to retry your decision of who you convict, see each outcome, and who was actually the culprit, leaving your long endured, pain-staking decision meaningless; though, you can ignore the option to retry!
Having been immersed with the first investigation, I had spent several hours during my day struggling to decide who to convict, and to my despair, I was presented with a disappointing short cutscene and an option to retry my decision. This had ultimately led me to lose immersion with the game, and my eager anticipation to later replay the investigation, discover anything I had missed, and see what impact these decisions -- and decisions from future investigations -- would have on the game. Albeit, the option to retry those outcomes is NOT mandatory and can be ignored, thankfully, should you desire to ignore them; immersion doesn't have to be totally broken.
Overall, it's an interesting gander into the world of Sherlock Holmes; finally being able to explore his home on Baker Street, and investigating with Watson in the original time period, as though you were visually interacting with the books themselves. Fans of interesting story games, and Holmes fans, especially, will enjoy this title!
Is it worth a buy? That's up to you, but, in my opinion, for a good deal, why not.

Excellent third person adventure. Great dialogue and character interactions. Great stories/cases, both from the books as well as the ones written for this game. The puzzles are enough of a challenge to make them fun, though they are a bit of a step down from the previous testament title in my opinion. For people who get stuck or annoyed by aparticular puzzle, or just want to be engrossed by the progression of the cases and the Holmes and Watson banter, the puzzles are completely skippable. These are my favourite Holmes and Watson depictions from any movie, game, or tv series; the game is worth it for the writing and acting alone.

I've always been a fan of the "vibe" that Frogwares has created with their Sherlock Holmes games. This game continues the trend of mentally transporting you back into the late 19th century but has taken another step in the beautification of the graphics. I also appreciate that the game is broken up into multiple "stories", some of which reference the original stories by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle. If you're a fan of Sherlock Holmes I feel like you'll approve of the way he and Watson have been represented in this game.

Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments was unexpectedly good. I've heard pretty poor things about the series as a whole, but also heard that this one stood out. The production values are much higher than you'd expect with really strong voice acting and character models and it's refreshing that the stories and crimes you're solving are relatively small in scale compared to most games.
Doesn't quite scratch that Ace Attorney itch, but it's damned close.

This is no Super Meat Boy, but probably a good introduction to the genre.
This game is a precision platformer, and a decent one at that, but it falls into the common pitfalls of the genre.
It is all built on a 2D tiled grid map structure, which allows for easy map building.
Overall the visuals are good, the narrator is quite charming, but overall the gameplay is a bit forgettable.
Falling on the tactics from most of the free versions of these games, rather than focusing on a small set of mechanics and progressively making harder and harder challenges, this game presents more and more mechanics as the story progresses, making more and more complicated runs.
What this then means is the game tends towards complicated messy mazes of multiple different mechanical triggers and alleyways, all of which you must explore before getting to the exit.
This often left me lost in the higher levels, and rather gets in the way of making a 'clean' fast run on the first attempt.
Also the earlier levels are not difficult, read first half of the story missions, but rather introduce said many varied mechanics, and were easily completed.
Similarly, the higher difficulty setting does not affect the difficulty of the challenges, but rather turns off the game's mid-run checkpoint system. Which, isn't increasing the difficulty, as to get an A+ ranking you also need to complete each level within a time limit, and dying/respawning using the checkpoint system often sacrifices this ranking.
So I would suggest only playing in Normal mode and going for A+ rankings, as then you can quickly see the level on the first attempt, albiet dying a couple of times, affording a clean run shortly after.
There were also some mechanical issues.
Namely same mechanics do not behave in a set fashion.
Most notably there is some bouncy terrain that will shoot the player in a different direction based on the angle that the player hits it.
However when said terrain makes up a flat surface, hitting the terrain along the edge of the adjacent terrain pieces (2D grid map remember) will cause the character to jump in a different manner than if they hit in the center of a single terrain piece.
This causes complications when moving through rooms entirely built of this terrain whilst trying to avoid other obstacles.
There are other minor grievances here in that other obstacles also don't behave identically each time the same obstacle.
Lazers have random on/off periods.
Enemies don't behave consistently.
And so on.
But that largely doesn't matter as the stages are not usually built for difficulty in the first place. So adapting to these minor random elements rarely causes frustration.
Of course, this game also has player made content (due to the grid etc making it easy).
And these levels -do- attempt to be difficult, and so the random elements -do- screw you over in these circumstances.
The game also has multiplayer arena battles and local play.
This is probably where the game becomes far better than a decent platformer.
However, at the time of writing, I could not find any online play to experiment with, and nor have I tried local co-op play.
In all, this is an easy platformer which has charm and personality.
I'm sure kids would have fun with it, especially when blowing each other up in local co-op.
But for me, the only hard section in the story was in the level immediately prior to finishing the game.
As a result, I was quickly bored and rushed through the story missions, whist avoiding all encore missions, just to let the narrator finish.

Straight forward roguelike with nothing interesting or new to experience. I didn't have any fun with this one mostly due to a shallow and tedious combat system (mash the attack button while trading blows since walking backwards is made too slow to allow for dodging), extremely dark levels that require a torch at all times which renders shields useless, and finally instant unpredictable deaths that ruin the exploration. I died several times from traps that I couldn't even see such as boulders that just appear at deadends or clicking on an object to have an enemy spawn right next to me that kills me in one hit. This is a perfect example of unfair difficulty. Combat in itself is cheap as you must trade blows, your equipment and stats are the only thing that determines success which is very traditional of very old school RPGs but has never felt right to me. I can accept defeat when I am outskilled but I cannot accept it when I lose simply due to RNG affecting which equipment I find or enemies are spawned.
It's a shame though because there's a lot of cool assets here and the overall ascetic is nice even if generic. The shallow ceilings are a bit of an eyesore but the voxel graphics are neat. Overall a solid roguelike held back by archaic game design and lack of originality.
Recommended only for roguelike fanatics.

If klocki were priced much higher than it is, I'd have to give this a thumbs down. But the fact of the matter is, the game is very good for its price.
klocki is a simple game: Make all the tiles activate by swapping, rotating, sliding, etc. Some tiles are 'wires' that need to be connected with no loose ends. Some tiles are black boxes that will turn into white circles when they're isolated from other tiles of their kind. Some tiles are circular and rotate on their axis; later levels will have you rotate entire chunks of the level to connect the lines.
It's a short game, so don't expect to spent a whole day playing klocki. And it's not massively challenging, either. All the levels can be solved with a little critical thinking and a solid thought process. But for a dollar it's a pleasant little experience and more than worth the money if you like simple puzzles and have nothing else to use that spare buck on.

Usually with puzzle games, I find myself having a fun time, a soothing and/or challenging experience, for the first ten or twenty minutes before some actually difficult mechanics are introduced. Normally I'll try to brute force my way past this point or simply give up out of frustration. This game, klocki, resulted in the same experience, and while that mechanic introduced is one I have particular trouble with (slide puzzles), I stuck around because of what came before it. The first twenty-ish minutes of this game were a delight, very relaxing while remaining engaging, likewise surprising and impressing me with new mechanics and elements that were rewarding when overcome. So, looking for more of that, I kept trying and trying to get past the bits that stopped me, and after a good ten or twelve minutes, I was able to do so, learning from the experience, and the rest of the game flew by, not quite as hard as the initial roadblock but not quite as rewarding as the first stretch either.
And that's what this game was, really. There's not a ton to write about. The graphics are fine for this sort of thing. The music is pretty good, reminding me a lot of A Winged Victory for the Sullen. Moving around various knobs and levers looks, sounds, and feels great. It's short enough that it doesn't feel daunting while also giving you a good chunk of game to get through (apparently I spent nearly two hours with this game, though it felt like quite a bit less). So what you're left with, after all that, is a game that is mentally and emotionally rewarding, which is what puzzle games should be. I'm no expert in the field, but I've played my fair share of puzzle games, and I can't remember one that delighted me quite like this one. Come to think of it, I cant think of one in a long while that I was able to beat before giving up out of frustration, which might be a big part of it. I was a bit let down by the final puzzle, though the ones that came before it sure were a challenge, so I suppose I should think of it more as a soothing epilogue than the final climax.
In any case, this is a hell of a cheap game and it packs more of a punch than you'd think for that price. Buy it and put it on when you need to come down from a long day of work or just need a break from something. It's certainly worth that much.

TL;DR
I recommend you to try it, just for the sake of playing an almost forgotten genre, but it will bore you quickly.
Longer version.
The game is gorgeous looking (for an indie) and decent sfx, you do have some nice details on the face (blood, cuts etc) and you even start hearing noises when you get hit hard, some blood splatter in the screen.
The boxing itself isnt really that bad. Not that strategic, but fun semi arcade boxing.
Combat its simple, 6 different buttons to hit (jab, hook, uppercut) x 2 hands, thats for the headshots, you have to press an aditional button to land it on the body. One tap of a button to dodge an incoming hit, keep pressing for a block.
If you dodge a punch succesfully, you regain some stamina and the game gets into slowmo, allowing you to counter attack, but the AI can also dodge and counter, so you can get some really nice chains in slowmo.
You do not block specific parts of your body, its automagical, and not so strategic.
And thats about it about the combat, not that complicated to start trowing some punches at the IA. Its decent enough, when you start, but then income the problems.
When you start, you have about the same stats than your opponents. Your punches look and seem powerful, they do damage, though you can only hit 2-3 times since you will drain all your stamina, you have to wait to fill it again (few seconds without receiving hits or dodging a punch). After a couple fights, you will get some quick wins.
But the scaling is terribly. You cannot train whenever you want or have cash for it, this only happens every few fights
and you can only train once per stat. If you have leftover money, you can pay for the increase of each stat (what?).
Once you finish your first tournament, the stat difference becomes abysmal. You do virtually no damage, while your opponent hits a jab and does like 5 times the damage you did with a perfectly timed uppercut. Stamina wise is about the same, you can throw 4-5 punches now, but they can throw a flurry of punches. And unlike you, when you are hitting your opponent with a combination, they do regen stamina.
So at this point you practically are negated a KO fight (seriously, your opponent ends 100% hp every single fight) you do have to box and win by desition, so it gets boring real quick.
Training itself its boring as well. you just have to press a button at the right time, each training its about the same as the other one, the only difference its the pace at you have to press the buttons.
If you are a fan of boxing, well, you have like 1hr gameplay on this one. If you have tolerance for boring fights, then prepare yourself, you will hit with wet noodles and have to win most fights by desition (unless you want to make some grinding in already won tournaments).
