Barony is a dungeon crawler which is heavily inspired by oldschool RPGs, such as Rogue or Hack. A lot of mechanics, items and interactions are translated from the ASCII based world of classic turn based Roguelikes into a blocky 3D real time environment à la Delver. While the esthetics and first impression reminds a lot of Delver, this dungeon goes a lot deeper in many different ways.
The first person controls feel tight and responsive. Nothing is too complicated and after a few rounds I learned how everything works just fine. But even with the good controls, some things feel clunky. The combat in particular feels unfair at times. You can tell that the developers tried to capture every bit of classic roguelike and put it into 3D, but when it comes to combat, this gets rather complicated. The enemies are just as powerful as in for example Nethack, but in Barony you miss out on the 'luxury' of turn based combat. When you encounter an enemy in Nethack, you can think about the situation, look at your equipment and prepare your next step. In Barony it's do or die! Some classes can die in just a few hits from the very first enemies, which is sure to be a major turn off for a lot of players. In ordinary roguelikes the combat often isn't the main focus, but in a real time 3D dungeon crawler, at least to me, it is.
There aren't that much different items to discover, but the RNG gives the available ones a lot of variety. Every item can be cursed, blessed or have a special power. Food can be rotten or fresh and equipment broken or brand new. It's always a little thrill to identify a new found item.
Speaking of identification: to identify an item you can go the nowadays established way and use a scroll/spell of identification or in Barony you have the option to appraise an item. To appraise an item you have to right click it and hold the mouse button. Then hover over the now visible appraise button and let go. Depending on the characters appraise skill, the length and success rate of the identification differs. For example a merchant can appraise nearly every item very quick, right from the start. A warrior on the other hand appraises really slow and often fails. The appraise mechanic almost feels like the balancing for the unforgiving combat, so you don't always have to rely solely on your luck when it comes to loot.
The dungeon of Barony is great. Even with the 'Minecrafty' esthetic of the game, the environment feels dark, mysterious and dangerous! Every floor is randomly generated and is filled with monsters, items, special locations and traps. You can find a variety of things, from your generic treasure chest to giant falling boulders and succubus summoning fountains. Every part of the dungeon has it's own theme. After about 5 levels the scenery changes and also the general layout of the floors. The first floors look like an abandoned mine, but sooner or later you find yourself inside a dark forest or an ancient labyrinth. Additionally there are secret areas to find, which are tricky to find/survive, but can hold great rewards and that should make every adventurer happy :)
Last but not least, a probably very important aspect for a lot of interested players: the multiplayer. Currently the only inbuilt way to play co-op is in a local network, but appearently the developers are already working on online multiplayer and a lot of other features. There is a way to play online, which is via Hamachi. There are guides on the Barony Community Hub on how to set everything up for online play. I tried it with a friend of mine and in my opinion the multiplayer fits great into the overall experience. It doesn't ruin the atmosphere and even with two players, the game is still really challenging. At some points it may even be more difficult, because you have to split up loot, but that always  depends on how much you can find anyway. Some things are a little bothersome, such as no fast restart option when the whole party dies and no server browser, but if you have ever played some older multiplayer games, you know what's coming. We played for about 3 hours and really had a great time.
Barony is by no means a perfect game, but even with it's flaws, especially in combat, it still got me hooked! Where the mechanics can't deliver, the sense of adventure, the atmosphere and the constant drive to delve deeper into the forgotten mines does. Every run teaches you something else, shows you a new creature or an mysterious item. And with a little practice and the right bit of luck, you will advance even further into the depths of Barony with every try you take. Should you feel like this is too much to handle on your own, you can always bring a friend or two. Of course it can and will be frustrating, but there is a lot to find in Barony and if you are a friend of classic roguelikes and would like to experience them from another perspective, this is the game for you.

Wheew, what a ride. Definitely my personal surprise RTS of 2017 so far!
is a classic Real Time Strategy game brought to you by tiny Russian developer
. Since some members of the team also worked at GFI before, you could say the game is an unofficial sequel or spin-off to the 2008 RTS
. Judging from videos or screenshots (and even the title font) the similarity is evident.
Now if you already enjoyed pseudo-realistic military RTS or TBS games from Russia like
,
,
,
or
, then look no further. You'll
this game. It has great combat gameplay mechanics, almost completely destructible environment (which you can use to your advantage), simple micro-management and definitely an interesting, modern military setting.
Speaking of that, you play as Syrian Police Officer
who first commands a small unit of Syrian Police Forces and later in the game changes to the regular Syrian Arab Army. To those who still don't know at this point - that's the Assad Forces of the
Syrian Civil War. Over the duration of the whole game you first fight against
militants while later the focus shifts on destroying professional
forces.
At this point some words of clarification - if you've got personal issues with the Russian / non-western point of view of the events of the Syrian Civil War, then better look for another game. Let me explain it like this: It doesn't exactly portray the events in the likes of CNN, BBC, NATO, the SOHR or the White Helmets. The game deals uncompromisingly with the military struggle against (moderate) terrorism in Syria. It even goes as far to settle with political correctness by showing the player ironic messages from fictional social media pages that hint at the ongoing information war about Syria. In the current age of
or
I found this a refreshing point of view... Political incorrectness at its best! :) It's kinda like the ending of
, if you remember that one. Another cool game from Russia.
But make no mistake - this game is tough as nails. If you mindlessly let your tanks and APCs charge into open fields and streets, you're already doomed to be the target of countless ATGMs. In just a blink of a second all your mechanized units may evaporate in a storm of steel and fire. Enemy snipers hiding in apartment blocks will ruin any of your infantry attacks. Many fields, country roads and streets are covered with anti-tank and anti-personnel mines, which can only be detected by sappers and special forces. Hidden forward observers will see you from miles ahead and mercilessly call mortar, howitzer or MLRS strikes on you. To make things worse, they will even send VBIEDs - suicide bombers - against you.
To survive through all that mess you'll have to clinch to every unit and resources available to you. Ammo and Fuel are limited and have to be re-supplied with trucks. To blind enemy observers you can use smoke screens to cross streets and buildings. To avoid being hit by ATGMs you must hide your tanks between buildings and structures and let them only briefly come forward to shoot and get back to cover again (remember those T72 GoPro videos from
?). At some points in the game you'll receive support from Russian Special Forces and the Russian Airforce, which due to the very limited resources you'll have to use wisely. Enemy tanks with strong front armor you have to take out from behind with fast and versatile ATGM technicals. You may use snipers or RPO rockets to take out forward observers in buildings and to clear the way for your assault squads - and the list goes on. Thankfully there's also a «Pause Mode» in which you can freeze the game and coordinate your commands. This makes things considerably less difficult.
Individual units can gain experience in battle and can be used again in later missions. You will definitely love that glorious moment when you lead your favorite tank crew in a brand-new T90 to the final battle of Palmyra - just some missions before they were absolute rookies handling a rusty T55.
At some points it's a bit too much of a «Trial-and-Error». Your troops may bite the dust pretty often and you'll get accustomed to the loading screen flashing on your monitor. Even on «Realistic», the medium difficulty next to «Normal» and «Ironman», the game is
forgiving at all. Normally I don't start playing video games on the easiest difficulty mode, but in this case I rather recommend to do so.
Due to the tough level of difficulty you'll have to spend about 20 hours to complete all 7 missions of the campaign. For the current price and the prospect of possible DLCs or sequels I find that absolutely OK. Another forte I must praise is the mission design. Some of these missions, like the rescue of the Russian pilot shot down by an Turkish F-16 in 2015, are based on real events of the Syrian Civil War. The developers, even if they may dramatize to some degree, made a good job of recreating an authentic experience. If you closely followed the events of this conflict or watched reports by
you'll definitely notice so on many details.
Now despite all the praise, are there any downsides? Yes indeed. The pathfinding can be frustrating at some points and you may occasionally yell at the stupidity of your own troops («WHAAAA..! WHY ARE YOU EFFIN' EXPOSIN' YOURSELF TO THAT ENEMY ATGM AGAIN FOR THE EFFIN' THOUSANDTH TIME!!»
). Some minor bugs like delayed mission scripts also leave a bittersweet aftertaste. The voice acting may annoy some linguistic purists, but I found them actually really OK.
+ Highly interesting yet controversial setting
+ Awesome combat gameplay mechanics
+ Huge tactical depth, but still simple gameplay mechanics
+ Destructible and interactive environment and buildings
+ High level of detail in terms of military equipment and events
+ Political incorrectness ;)
+ Simple micro-management of units
+ Individual units gain experience for further missions
+ OK graphics engine with some gorgeous effects
+ Great price for the value
+ Good music and sound effects (incl. Arabic voices)

A fun turned-based JRPG. You are the players of a Dungeons & Dragons-type tabletop roleplaying game, run by a dungeon master. Your characters have a race, a class, and some inherent stats from themselves that help you whether you choose classes like thief, warrior, paladin, mage, etc. There are some unlockable classes as you go along and two expansions (only one--Here There Be Dragons or whatever--is available on Steam. The other can be bought in-game). If you've played the first Knights of Pen and Paper, not a ton has changed. They've slightly changed the way stats are generated, how saves against conditions like confusion or rage are done, and the graphics are better (now more of a 16-bit feel instead of an 8-bit feel). There are also "rare items" available as drops that are super powerful, providing resistance to conditions, or making your attacks better, or making your character more resilent. If you enjoyed the first one, you'll enjoy this one. You definitely don't need to have played the first one in order to enjoy this one. This is an entirely new campaign. There's tons of pop-culture goodness in there (both in the background art and dialogue), so it's fun. As for skills, there aren't a ton of them, but like with any RPG you can level up your skills how you choose to fit your play style. Likewise, there are a bunch of different locations with interesting art, but after you unlock all of them you'll be going back to the same places over and over, so it can get a bit repetitive. Likewise, I did a LOT more grinding in this version than the original to be able to beat some of the bosses, so that was frustrating, but there is a "Bestiary" function that unlocks more information about enemies (including bonus damage if you collect enough kills of a certain beast), which made the grinding at least have some use.
Altogether, I played about 30 hours (Steam said 37, but a lot of that was idling and some grinding I did voluntarily), but that included the Here Be Dragons expansion pack, which added three new areas, some new items and a ton of killer dragons.
Overall 8/10. I prefer the original, but this one has a lot more depth and a much longer playtime. Still, I wouldn't mind starting from the beginning with the new classes I've unlocked. A lot of them I unlocked so late they would die in every combat so they never got a chance to get awesome enough to use in combat to their full potential.

They just took him. Grabbed him from the back seat of the car and took him. Sure, he was annoying at times. He lost more cash than he ever earned, and somehow got himself shot by a stray bullet, but Sketch was one of us y'know? Us survivors have to stick together.
So I picked up my rifle and stepped out of the car. I didn't have much choice. I wasn't going to leave him behind. Ottah hadn't looked good for some time since the first Z he saw took a chunk of him. Sleepy got bitten soon after. As for Rabid, I'm pretty sure she was high the whole time. She never got ill, never caused a problem. I forgot she was there most of the time.
So, there I was. It was an old fashioned stand-off. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ was hiding behind Sketchy, holding a pistol to his head. I didn't need to think. I just shot.
From that moment on, there was no turning back. Anyone who stood between my guys and Safe Haven, dead or alive, I took them out.
It was tough, but we made it. All of us made it. Hopefully Ottah and Sleepy will be able to live with the bites. As for me, there are more survivors out there and someone needs to help them ...
That was the story of my first adventure in Organ Trail. I foolishly played on Easy, which I wont be doing again, as once I learned my way around the game it wasn't very challenging. I guess I'm too used to recent roguelikes murdering me on my first turn! (I'm looking at you FTL)
I always get an extra kick out of games where I can name multiple members of a party. Naming the characters after my buddies helped me grow attached to them. Or hate them for constantly being ill (Ottah!) or a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥(Sketch!). The shooting took a little to get used to, but it was okay once I got the hang of it.
As for replayability, Endless Mode offers up unique starting scenarios and there are a fair few of them. I'll be making a start on those real soon!
The sound style matches the graphics, but I'll happily play this on mute and listen to my own music. It's not a problem with the style of the music, I just find it to be quite bad. Also, I'm sure I heard a dodgy distorted version of the 'Happy Birthday' tune at some point.
The most important thing I have to say about Organ Trail, is that I want to play more. As soon as I finished the game, I wanted to play again. That's the sign of good gameplay. Organ Trail doesn't have fancy graphics to fall back on. All it's can offer is its solid gameplay. If you're a fan of survival games, and don't mind the design this is something that you should pick up.
Bottom Line: Organ Trail is fun and leaves you wanting more.

Many people, including the game's creator, prefer the EGA version to this VGA version.
If you've purchased this and would like to run the EGA version through Steam, it is possible.
1 - Download and install LOOM through Steam
2 - Download ScummVM 1.8.1 from
and install (or copy) into C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\LOOM\ (ScummVM 2.0 doesn't work for this)
3 - Download "Loom (Floppy DOS EGA)" from
or another trusted abandonware site and unzip to C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\LOOM\loom-ega\
(You already own the game, so you are not doing anything illegal)
4 - Run ScummVM.exe and click "Add Game.."
5 - Highlight the loom-ega directory and click "Choose.."
6 - Enter "loom-ega" into the ID field and click OK.
7 - Exit ScummVM
8 - Delete (or rename) Loom.exe from C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\LOOM\
9 - Rename ScummVM.exe to Loom.exe in C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\LOOM\
10 - Right click Loom in your Steam Library and choose Properties
11 - Click on Set Launch Options
12 - Enter the following: -f -p "C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\loom\loom-ega" loom-ega
13 - Click OK.
You should now be able to seemlessly run the EGA version of Loom through Steam, just as you would the VGA version.
To revert to the VGA version:
1 - Right click on Loom in your Steam library.
2 - Click on "Properties"
3 - Go to the Local Files tab
4 - Click on "Verify integrity of game files"

To put it simply, this version of the game is missing a lot of what the full package should have been. I haven't even played any other version prior to trying this one, and I was wondering why it had absolutely 0 music except for a couple of cutscenes. It seemed totally odd, most games even of this era always had music in the background. It seems this version removed a lot of content (text dialogue and music) to fit full voice acting audio on CD back in the day. That's no good, and for this reason I'd recommend looking elsewhere for the original version of this game unless you want to play it with absolute silence.
The storyline is pretty interesting, and gameplay is a bit different from normal point and clicks since instead of collecting items you memorize tunes to play that activate incantations, sort of like ocarina songs in Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. It's a cool mechanic, and what makes the game unique. I can see why it was well received in the past.
Regardless of the game's quality, the experience of this version is damaged due to removed dialogue and music to allow space for complete voice acting. Not really worth it, I'd say, look for the original version and play that.

A very good Picross-style game.  There are A LOT of puzzles, which is definitely a good thing.  I don't love that many of the puzzles have dimensions that are not multiples of 5 (ie, 8 x 16), but the flexibility in dimensions also allows for a great variety of puzzles.  Another difference that Picross fans might find unsettling is that the game doesn't penalize you for making a wrong move.  This makes it possible to screw up a puzzle to the point where you have to start over.  I kind of like this because the game doesn't give you any clues, so to speak, but it also can be frustrating when you have to restart a puzzle that you've spent 20 minutes on already.  There might be an option to change this, but I didn't look real hard for it.
This game does have a nice set of options and modes, which make it much more robust than your typical Picross-clone.  I haven't messed with much of that stuff, but it just goes to show you that these developers really tried.  If you like Picross, this is probably your best option on Steam.

This game leaves you with some interesting things to think about - often, the "hacks" that you put into use to complete the game and "escape" can be seen as criticisms of game design in general. At one point, the "developer" seems to expect you to grind through 100 levels for 1 xp a piece to unlock an upgrade. The player decides that this is a bit much to ask. Another time, the player is asked to wait for the developer to "create additional content," an obvious reference to DLC needed to actually complete a story. The player finds a way to skip to the already-created ending. The game is hilarious. It's quite a power trip to be able to circumvent some of gaming's most irritating Skinner Boxes.

Well, i kind of bought this game after some recommendations from Steam users, but i simply
I was in the process of ending a FF game, and i can only say this... The moment i started this game out of curiosity, i stoped playing everything else. The game hooks you, both in the history and the battle system, which i find it to be refreshing, even though i've seen dozens of similar turn based RPG's. The history is rich, the game is funny, and it's very easy to like and relate to both main characters.
The leveling system is somewhat different from the usual, making it a little better, with less gruesome grinding, and there are some really interesting bosses. As far as the story goes, even though i wasn't surprised with most plot developments, the last "boss" is truly surprising, and the "ending" (1 of 3 chapters) leaves a lot to discover after.
With the second chapter already translated and with the port to Steam to be announced soon, i guarantee that will be bought on day one. If you are considering a JRPG game, go for it.

Let me tell you a story about some unlucky adventurers;
It began, as you might expect, in the land of wherever-this-is-land; Lord Flix, mighty warrior and dashing gentleman, with a thirst for glory and adventure ventured unto yon dungeon.
“Well, alright, I’ve got a table, wonder if I can bash with my spear” Whack whack whack, “yes I can can. Ah! that’ll learn you stupid table”. He walked right to the gate, pulled the lever and climbed down the ladder. “Well then, this is a fine dungeon indeed ! A bit dark mind, but overall fine looking. Uh what’s this then ?” Lord Flix picked up a queer looking stone off the ground and looked deeply into it, like way more than a sane person would. I mean it’s just a rock. “Hum, a rock. Wonder if I can throw it” fwooooop thunk. “Why yes I can”. But Flix’s untimely and rash rock throwing catched the gaze of a vile skeleton. They both looked into each other’s eyes, bloodlust was in the air. He knew that this ungodly abomination would have ill intent towards him. They would have to fight. “Roight, have at thee vile undead !” whack whack whack “Wait, how do I use my shield ? Gaaarrffffh” Alas ! If only Lord Flix knew how to parry the many swords strike that fell on him he might live today. But it was not so….
Thus begat the adventure of Lord Flix II.
“Right ! Better do some shield trainning then, I don’t wanna die again” and he did, a lot, a lot. With renewed inspiration and courage he went down the ladder just like his predecessor. “Hum a rat, I guess I can take on a rat” whack whack “WOOO I killed my first thing ! I am mighty indeed !” For a long time Lord Flix II simply wandered aimlessly, never encountering another soul. But his resolve was put to the test; he could not see any monsters, but he could hear them. The queer, unnerving sound that only a vile beast of the underworld could make. “Screw me ! Where you at monsters ? Came at me bra!” Still no sign of life, yet the eldritch sound was there, always there. “Uh what’s this then ? A hole in the celling ? Why that looks interes…” BLAAM. A giant boulder fell of the hole and squashed mighty Lord Flix II to death.
Thus begat the adventure of Lord Flix III
“Mmmkay, in retrospect that was fairly predictable”. For Lord Flix III knew of the dire end of both his predecessors, somehow, because of magic maybe ? Yeah let’s go with magic. Anyhoo you know the drill, down the ladder we go ! “ He wandered thither and hither, slayed a bunch of rats and skeleton along the way. He felt mighty, powerful, and emboldened by the knowledge he gathered from they who dwelt here afore him. “Well would you look at that, a fountain ! Why that’s not suspicious in any way, nooooooope” With that in mind our handsome hero drank deep from the fountain, assured that he would receive some boom for a kindly spirit or something. Alas ! It was not so, to nobody’s surprise. We never said that the Flix bloodline was particuarly smart y’know. He felt quite dizzy from the water, perhaps some foul wizard had cast a vile spell on it ? Suddenly he realized he wasn’t alone, sharing the room with him was a naked blue lady. Because that’s not weird or anything. “You wot ? Where’d you came from ? Why are you laughing ? Hold on there keep your distance I don’t thrust you” Slaaaaaaap ! “Did you just slapped me ? Oh hell no, Imma thrust my spear right into your face you dumb blue lady !” he paused for a second and thought about what he said “Wait, that came out wrong, meh, scew it” But Lord Flix III did not know that this blue lady was in fact a dreaded Succubus, the vile seductress from beyond the veil of reality ! A mighty opponent indeed ! Anyway you probably know where this is going.
Thus begat the adventure of Lord Flix IV
And down the ladder we go ! But this time to our fiercely awesome hero’s surprise the first door was locked ! “Whatever shall I do ! “ He tried and tried and tried to open it to no success. “Wait, damnit I’m such an idiot ! I can just bash the damn thing”. And he did, and he also felt really dumb, ‘cause you know, the solution was obvious. Anyway after a bit of exploring he ended up in a dark maze-like part of the dungeon. He didn’t want to sacrifice his shield for a torch even though he had collected like, an ungodly amount of the damned thing. He slowed down wary and looking everywhere for any sign of ambush. He might have been carefull but two skeletons did ambushed him anyway. “GAAARRGGDFDFJH  ARE YOU KIDDING ME YOU SUNAVA….” whack whack.
Thus Ended the life of Lord Flix IV, and also this “review”
That’s a good game, that ! Well if you like 3D maze-like dungeon, and rogue-like elements, and permadeath. Also for the love of god, stock up on light sources, mind the celling and watch out for blue ladies in fountains.

It is like a combination of Wargame and CoH. The combination of strategy, urban warfare and survival is what makes this game so unique and enjoyble. however, it is not lacking in propaganda.

The good:
* Destructible terreain - you can destroy almost any part of a building down to the balcony level.
* Logistics - every unit has limited ammount of ammo (for each type). keeping a logistics route to the frontline avilable is crucial.
* Units - wide varaiety of land units. you can't just send the heavy tanks, you must cover each unit's weaknes.
* Units ownership - if you capture a unit during the battle, it will be yours to keep until the end of the game or until it is destroyed.
* Voice acting - for the main story you get several  VA with british accent while the units themsels speak arabic / russian. helps a lot getting connected.
The meh:
Air  units - are just not fun, airplanes are hard to the point of being almost totaly useless.
Performance - loading times can be incredebly slow at large maps. at several points I expirenced very low framerate.
Bugs - not many of these, but at some mission I had to save and re load to fix the mission progression.
The bad:
* Propaganda - the story is one giant propaganda machine, with lots of points about the being bad and such. feels like it was weritten by RT.
* The minimap - ♥♥♥♥ the minimap, just ignore it until they rewrite this awful thing.

From developer ebi-hime and publisher Sekai Project comes The Sad Story of Emmeline Burns, the anime visual novel. Released in 2016, this is a yuri casual adventure game, that's been rated very positive since it's release to Steam. Seeing it, I decided to give it a go and see what it was like.
Toma Andrews, aged 14, has always felt like an outsider. She enjoys spending time in graveyards, and feels more comfortable among the dead than the living.
That is, until Toma meets a strange girl in her local graveyard who might be a real ghost.
The girl asks Toma if she will stay for a while and listen to a story. A story about a girl called Emmeline Burns, who died a tragic death back in 1851.
Toma is compelled to listen, but at the same time, she feels uneasy. After all, what can she do? How could she ever hope to help somebody who has already died?
After reading this summary on Steam, I was really intrigued after downloading it, even more so than I already was, and had to jump in.
I admit, I was a little bit disappointed. There wasn't much to this game other than a story. The story itself got a little boring at times, and it was a struggle to get through. However, the artwork was absolutely beautiful. I was shaken by just how much obvious work had gone into character and background designs. The artists did so much work on this short game and it has definitely paid off. I was expecting some choices in the game, but came across none, which was part of my disappointment, but the rest of the game definitely made up for it.
The achievements are all story related and are extremely easy to get, so it's definitely a good one for achievement hunters to pick up an extra 83 TSA points. It's a quick game, 0-1 hours for completion, and I think it's definitely an hour well spent.
I love this so much, and I cannot wait to see what else ebi-hime develop. I recommend this to anyone who enjoy anime and/or visual novels, and people with an interest in artwork in games.

Abe's Oddysee, a beloved game from the past and a "gorgeous bit of crumpet" [Caddicarus, 2013] set in an abstract world seemingly run by a corporate overworld called 'the glukkens'.
Here's the thing, as some people might find nostalgia and enjoyment out of a game they loved so much, I went in completely blind and had to learn everything and experience everything from a modern perspective. At first I didn't mind the old look about it, Abe was adorable and charming, the story was sinister and the enemies had reason to be enemies.
I began playing, runnin away from soldiers, saving mudokens and having a jolly good time...until I escaped. After a silly cutscene of Abe escaping the farm, I'm tossed into a pit with more escaping to do. This is where the absolute BULL**** started to seep in. The 'puzzles' began to lean into the side of "get to the other side before the creatures get you/soldiers shoot you" and that's when my thumb went from up to down. Don't worry I gave this game a fair go, I escaped the pit, made it through mudoken city and through the desert of pointy faced f***ers, only to finally stop at the next trial. It was this place I finally learned that this game is dated, the controls are kind of like a pokemon game in which Abe is only in one specific spot at a time which can lead to extremely pinpoint interactions of having to be in one specific square on the grid that is this game's exploration.
The puzzles themselves start to get horrendous, sometimes with no visible solution and the only plausible way of getting around it takes 20 tries to get right, each try sending you an unfair distance back due to a lack of quicksaving or well placed checkpoints.
There is a completionist goal however, there are 99 mudokens to liberate and they can be either well hidden, out in the open or in a place where they'll be killed if you don't act or do the wrong thing. The fact that they're so well hidden gives this game plenty of replayability if you want that sweet completionist rating, however the puzzles are too bloody difficult that I'm going to have to dissapoint Mr. Jirard Dragonrider Khalil and never complete (let alone finish) this frustrating mess.
Overall 2/10, for all the praise this game gets, it sure does give me a ton of broken furniture.

It is medieval fantasy TPP hack-n-slash with bits of platforming actions.
Looks decent and level design lets you have some fun looking for hidden treasures. But fighting is boring. Like really boring. It just doesnt work at all. And as for h-n-s it is major issue so nothing can save this game.
On the bright side game has two nice 'twists' that could interest somebody.
First is multiple of characters to play as. During missions you can meet some NPCs in trouble and if you manage to save them they will join you and act as playable characters for the rest of the game. On the other hand this undefined main character causes story to be unrelated to characters. So dont expect any story from this game. Just almost random stages, enemies and your character of choice. It could be arena-type game and it wouldnt be any different.
Next 'twist' is that you can outfit your hero before every mission. Equipping your character is based on limited budget mechanic. Every piece of gold you collected adds to the pool of gold which limits gear you can wear. Every piece of equipment substracts from this pool so you have to pick if you prefer balanced setup with average elements or maybe you will sacrifice armor in favor of better weapon. You cant pick your playstyle and enjoy the game your way without being forced to play some fixed archetype.
Mentioned gold you receive for completing every mission and even more you can find during the mission as extra hidden treasures that require from you taking extra risk. And risk here is high - death equals restart of the level. But thats fine, levels are short and fun part is mastering every level.
To sum it up: game is quite interesting and as such curiosity you could grab it to have a look, but i was unable to finish it - simplistic fighting mechanics are boring and no amount of customisation of character can change that.

After falling into a coma you are seemingly lost in some kind of limbo, lost and confused you start exploring your surroundings to find a way out.
Coma:Mortuary is a short walking simulator that sadly can't either provide an interesting story or some decent gameplay thus quickly turning into a dull experience.
-some areas look nice enough
-parts of the soundtrack are decent
-story is too vague and cryptic, ending is unsatisfactory
-lacks atmosphere
-bland graphics, horrible screen tearing, some instances of completely blurred screen while moving
-parts of the soundtrack, like the heavy metal during chase scenes, feel way out of place
-bad voice acting, the line delivery often sounds robotic
-extremely dull gameplay, you slowly walk through maze-like areas trying to activate levers in the correct order
-a couple of chase scenes try to mix things up a bit but just end up becoming a frustrating experience where you have to memorize the correct path
-some levers are slightly buggy
-cutscenes are somewhat low-res and feature unconvincing camera movements
-laughable attempts at jump scares also suddendly take control of the camera away from the player
-extremely short at around 45mins
Having played and enjoyed other games in the genre I found Coma:Mortuary mind-numbingly boring...walking simulators require great story and atmosphere to make up for the general lack of gameplay and Coma simply fails here. The characters and cutscenes will blurt out information about the place and what it means to be dead in there but they never bother explaining what they are rambling about: I can appreciate a cryptic plot that leaves things open for you to interpret but when you explain nothing and keep throwing vague bit and piaces at the player then there's no way for me to understand it and care about it. There's also no atmosphere whatsoever since most of the corridors and rooms look the same and have few interesting things to see in them: the few attempts at making you feel threatened by suddendly making the camera move due to a noise are also so clumsy to just elicit a chuckle.
The gameplay isn't any better, the atrociously slow walking speed makes navigating the cut and paste environments a painfully dull proposition and the only thing for you to do is look for levers and randomly try to pull them until you get the right order: some of said levers are also buggy and will require a few tries or some repositioning before they work. The two chase scenes are also dull, you simply run away trying to figure the right way to follow and, if you fail, you get an instadeath and have to retry.
If you decide to play through the game don't expect much by the ending, you'll simply get some more vague exposition and a slow cutscene paving the place for a second game, said cutscene also bugged for me since it kept repeating all over until I had to quit the game.
Coma:Mortuary is simply not good enough to warrant a purchase, not even at the 1$ sale price: the lack of any interesting story or gameplay coupled by the overall vagueness and a "to be continued" ending that feels way too pretentious for what's offered means you can safely skip this one.

While I really wanted to like this game and find the gameplay overall fun I simply cant recommend it beacause of the 3 really dumb problems that treyarch and Activision have ignored or refused to fix.
1. Servers and connections.
This has been a problem since MW3 some of it is down to the engine but mostly its down to the poor servers that is used by the game. Im pretty sure most players have experienced the issue of inconsistency in connections such as poor hit detection, rubberbanding and 1 frame instadeaths. Even though we got custom dedicated servers in late 2016 the options we got for them where very barebones and dont really help with the issues if at all.
2. Matchmaking and playlists.
The Problem here is trying to get in to a game other than Team Deathmatch and domination is downright impossible beacause no one is playing those gamemodes. Also even if you do manage to find a lobby you are often waiting up to five miniutes at a time just for people to join. This would have easily been fixable by filling the remaining slots with bots after about 2 minutes and could have bots be added during matches to replace leavers, While not a perfect soulution it would at least have kept the game playable.
3. MICROTRANSATIONS!!!
I will never understand why a $60 game with a $40 seasson pass needs to have microtransations that affect gameplay.
Adding new weapons would have been great if they were not locked behind rng supply drop walls. Chances are even if you pay $30 in supply drops you will likey never get all the added content because of the rng loot boxes that often give you duplicates of stuff you dont need or already have. Adding to the insult is some of the supply drop weapons are BETTER than those in the base game creating a very F2P (Fee-2-pay) enviroment that screws players that dont give out money for a small chance to get these weapons.
While I would recommend this game for its core gameplay I have to say stay away beacuase of the total insult that Activision have done to its players with F2P microtransactions and not addressing the issues with servers that had been around since MW3.

Syrian Warfare is a game set in the still ongoing, and, of course, controversial Syrian war. In the game you follow Police Lieutenant Anwar, who takes control of his hometown's police forces to defend against invading terrorists in a realistic strategical game of modern warfare. As time progresses, you will rise through command ranks and eventually will be given military units to command, as well as being allowed to call in Russian bombings on your enemy. In addition, units that survive and vehicles you take from the enemy can be carried on to the next mission, allowing you to build a preferred core of units if you don't let them die.
The first thing one may notice is the lack of a skirmish or custom battle option. There is only a campaign with pre-set missions as far as I have found. While there is plenty of content in the missions and you will almost certainly need several attempts to do everything in them, it would be nice to have a way to set up my own engagements, even just for things like testing out unit accuracy or to see how long one can hold out in defence.
Secondly would be the graphics. They look good, and I find myself wanting to look at the action as it happens.
And that leads to the next thing I want to point out, namely the difficulty. Things move quickly, and they die quickly. As can be expected from an era of warfare where there are weapons against everything, your men are not safe even inside a tank or a big building. Using vehicles or squads of soldiers properly is a large factor in whether or not you are successful. Anti-tank missiles do exist, and are very capable of taking out your armoured vehicles. At the same time, a smaller car or technical vehicle can be taken down by a machine gun, and it is often more likely to kill the driver or crew of a vehicle than it is to destroy the vehicle outright. Which in turn means that you can take over and often repair the vehicle for your own use.
Aside from that a large part of the difficulty comes from the numbers involved. With limited forces and limited reinforcements it is difficult to attack. Defending is easy enough, fortify a position and hold them off. But to attack when the enemy outnumbers you is difficult. To do so while also under time pressure for optional objectives that you will want to complete is even harder. Some missions need you to take out 500 or more hostiles, while you will not have even half of that. As you do not 'build' units like in most RTS games and instead only get a limited amount at the start and limited reinforcements this can make for a very difficult situation where I found myself often asking 'Am I missing something? Am I doing something wrong?' while I am micromanaging the one squad of infantry that hasn't been reduced to a single living squad member to clear out several buildings.
Or maybe I'm just bad at modern tactics.
Everything appears to be very detailed, from vehicles having many parts to them that can be individually disabled to buildings seeming to be fully modelled, though without furniture, to every individual soldier having their own health and carried weaponry. Buildings can have parts of them get exploded, and even fully collapse. I've found it a pleasure to watch what happens to a building and the hostiles in it as it gets shelled by a tank.
In between missions you will be able to follow the social media, giving you stories from people involved in or commenting on the Syrian war. Some serious, and some amusing. Others give background information to Syria for those who haven't paid attention to the entire conflict. At this point, I will say that this game displays some favour to the Syrian army (and Russia) and not as much to the opponents of said army, though it does so without politics getting in the way of gameplay - perhaps it simplifies the situation a bit, but complex politics would not really do much for the gameplay itself.
There are some negatives as well. Aside from there not being a custom battle option, it seems the pathfinding is a bit questionable. Often it will drive, or walk in places you really do not want it to. Infantry in a building can be given a command to face one way, but they will ignore it if fire is incoming from the other side. Such as large explosive tank shells. And then they will stand on the balcony where said tank shells are hitting. They will go onto the roof even when mortars hit, and you can't tell them to take cover in the lower floors when artillery strikes the building and takes off the top floor. Along with the tendency for a squad to get split up this makes it difficult to shield your infantry from harm.
At times it appears the AI doesn't do much - except for a few times it mostly seems like it is up to you to attack, and it does not always seem to react to being attacked. I'm not sure if this is good or bad, because if it would react then I am sure I'd be losing pretty much every time I try something.
I have also found the camera to be restrictive. At one point I managed to fly a helicopter to the side of the map where I couldn't see it anymore, at others it felt like I couldn't zoom out to take a look at the whole situation, something that often resulted in me not noticing an enemy RPG team trying to sneak up on my vehicles.
Sound and voice acting are good. With dialogue and voice acting being well done with a touch of humour at times, and the sounds being as one would expect - good quality and distinct enough to be able to tell what is happening without looking at them, though often only when you're late because that rocket flying at your troop transport means you're already too late to stop it in most cases.
In conclusion, Syrian Warfare is not a meme game or trying to sell based on controversy. It is detailed in many aspects and very good in many more. Though there are some slight issues with the pathfinding and the AI, it is very much worth playing for anyone who is into modern strategy, or if you just want to see how well you can do at it.

+ Frankly stunning level of worldbuilding. Not only is the world you're stepping into built upon the solid foundation of a rich and fleshed-out lore, but everything that you'll encounter in-game is tended to with a similarly remarkable degree of attention to detail. There's no such thing as "Villager F" in Trails; every NPC has their own name, house, family and unique dialogue, and many of them you'll encounter more than once as you go about your travels, acting out their own, more mundane story arcs independent of your own. The in-game locations feel like more than quest hubs - they feel like proper towns, living, breathing and part of a wider, bigger world that ticks on by whether or not you're in it. And quite famously, every single chest in the game has a unique phrase that appears on examining it after you've looted its contents - while it's not on its own particularly impressive, it speaks to the sheer degree of love and care that's been poured into the game.
+ Great cast of characters. Trails has a lot of strengths, but its single greatest one, the keystone without which it would all fall apart, is its cast, their relationships and their interactions; your emotional investment in them, and in their stories, is what makes the whole thing tick. And fortunately, its characters are strong enough for that to work - each is distinctive, and often even exaggerated and eccentric, yet all feel very human, sincere and believable at their core in a way that does a fantastic job of bringing them to life. From the foppish and frequently-hilarious Olivier, to the irresponsible yet ultimately warm-hearted Scherezard, to the magnificent duo of protagonists Estelle and Joshua, each is painstakingly built up and fleshed out as the game progresses, and even those who are recognisable as traditional JRPG tropes on their introduction reach the finish line as something more.
+ Stellar translation. Unlike certain other localisation outlets (whom out of courtesy I'm not going to name, although I will say that the worst offender begins with "N" and ends with "ippon Ichi Software America"), Carpe Fulgar have taken a great deal of care to preserve the spirit and character of the original dialogue, and their effort pays enormous dividends. Conversations which could easily have been cliche and tedious instead flow naturally, and are extraordinarily entertaining to read; the cast sling insults and good-natured jibes at each other with all the wit, precision and timing you'd expect from actual proper comedic writing, never mind from a translation. I'm being entirely serious when I say that this game is now the benchmark against which I judge all other localisations - it's that good.
+ Outstanding soundtrack. I don't know how much Falcom pay their composers, but it's not enough; Trails's music is incredibly versatile, swinging from warm and comforting, to austere, to joyful, to mysterious, to inspiring and back again. It's bouncy and light-hearted most of the time, but calm and serene when it needs to be, and is fully capable of being serious if the occasion calls for it. It's easily one of the game's strongest features, and while it's difficult to convey how great it is through text I can't recommend enough that you tab on over to Youtube and go give it a listen.
~ Combat is pretty laid-back. Provided you adhere to level-appropriate areas and sidequests, which is very difficult not to do because of the restrictive way that experience scales as you gain levels, you're not likely to have any significant difficulty until the final dungeon. Difficult encounters do exist, but you'll usually have to deliberately head into dungeons or take on bounty requests that you're underleveled for to find them. Additionally, every non-story encounter can be escaped from with 100% reliability, and every battle can be retried from starting conditions on loss - while again, that naturally means that you're better off looking elsewhere if you want a serious challenge, it also minimises the impact of sheer bad luck on the player, which is arguably a good thing. The combat system does have a depth well beyond what you're actually required to master, but I reiterate Trails is not the game to be playing if you want the gameplay to push you (that's what Ys is for). Although, in truth, that's really not what you play it for anyway.
~ Pacing is extremely slow. Trails in the Sky cares far more about building up its setting and cast through everyday (or at least relatively mundane) interactions, and while that's obviously its own reward it's also the death of plot momentum. It's a lazy gondola ride of a game, and while there's no question that it gains focus in the latter chapters it still takes an extremely circuitous route to get there. You'll either love what it does or hate it, you'll find yourself either enthralled or bored, and there's not much that will be able to redeem it for you if you do find yourself in the latter camp. This is by no means an inherent negative, but it points directly to the question that's really going to decide if this is the game for you: are you willing to sit through a dozen distractions from the main questline if you can better get to know the characters by doing so? If not, you're probably going to find Trails a very frustrating experience, but if so then it's definitely worth your time.
- Graphics are what you'd expect from a mid-00s JRPG on a conservative budget - that is to say, not much. Some nice backgrounds and environments stand out, but Trails always looked like it could run on a handheld, which is primarily because it originally did. It's certainly not awful, and it works well within its own limitations, but if you were expecting Final Fantasy XV you're going to be disappointed.
- Optional content can be obscure to the point of absurdity. You're not acquiring the maximum possible Bracer points, completing all the available sidequests or collecting all the chapters of Carnelia without a guide. You're just not. If you enjoy the challenge, this could count as a positive, but doing it all without help would almost certainly require multiple playthroughs, a lot of experimentation and a healthy dose of just plain good fortune. The game is still a full experience without it, but it can be frustrating to be denied 100% completion because you didn't perform some obscure set of actions that no-one would ever have a reason to do.
It has to be said that ultimately, with Trails in the Sky, you don’t get much originality for your money as far as JRPGs go. Most of what you’ll see here you’ll probably have encountered before, in some guise or another, in another game. What you do get, however, is Falcom’s magic touch that somehow elevates an experience that would probably be mundane and cliché in the hands of any other developer to something instead wholly human and believable. And in the end, that’s really what this game is, a traditional JRPG, but one that's executed really well. Its characters are mostly fairly recognisable tropes, but they’re recognisable tropes implemented with a touch of humanity that renders them far greater than the sum of their parts. Its OST isn’t particularly distinctive stylistically, but it’s a traditional OST that couldn't really have been pulled off any better. There isn’t even really anything particularly special about the world of Liberl, but what
there has been painstakingly crafted with love and care. Falcom have taken the traditional JRPG formula and maximised it, squeezing the best they can out of every single aspect. It’s most definitely not going to appeal to everyone, but if you’re in the market for a comfy-cosy JRPG that cares far more about breathing life into its vibrant cast and setting than about saving the world (although there’s just a little of that too), then you’re in for a treat with Trails in the Sky. And who knows? It might just win your heart while you're at it.

Knights of Pen and Papers 2 is the second game for the Knights of Pen and Paper series or KoPP for short. It is a turn-based RPG strategy game developed by Kyy Games and published by Paradox Interactive. It was released in October 2015 on Steam. I have played KoPP +1 before. It contains a lot of improvements to KoPP +1 as well as new mechanics, which I will explain about later.
You will start by creating two players to start off with, and later you will have five. You must choose a character, class, and race for each player. There are eight characters you can use to start with, each has their own unique bonuses. There are also six classes to choose from, each with different and unique skills. You can unlock more classes and characters as you progress throughout the game. The tip is to create a player with a good combination of character, class, and race.
You can level up your character by getting exp points. Each level up gets you one skill point that you can use to improve your skills. You can get exp points from finishing quests and battling monsters. The game doesn't have a difficulty level, so it will be harder as you progress. The body, sense, and mind point are a new addition to the series. It affects the players' stats and the chance to get status effects. In KoPP 2 is how random number generation plays a bigger role in the gameplay, whereas in KoPP +1, it only affects minor things, such as: traveling, dungeons, and fleeing.
There are also items and equipments which you can buy with gold or find. You can get gold from finishing quests, defeating monsters, and dungeons. The items and equipments will increase your players' stats if you equip it.  Another new addition to the series is the crafting feature. You can create items, equipments, and consumables from crafting. You can also enchant your equipment with charms and enchantment scrolls to further boost your stats. Also, mechanics like HP/MP steal from attacks, and HP/MP regen per round which is on the previous game is absent.
The first thing you will notice is the pixel-art which I think looks good and beautiful. It has a lot of more depth compared to the previous game. What I really like most about this game is the humor, which is filled with geeky humor that is written brilliantly in my opinion. The NPCs are also filled with pop culture references which I enjoy. The game still gets a new update every few months which I hope stays that way.
One of the new additions that I like is that you can now fully reset your player without losing your current level. In the previous game, you can only reset your player's skill points. So if you would like to change class, character, or race, you can do it now. It costs a lot more to reset though, so you must plan it wisely. The dungeon is a lot better though, but it gets repetitive sometimes.
The main story should take you several hours to finish, but there are a lot more quests after that, especially from the Here Be Dragons DLC. The story itself is great and funny in my opinion, I really enjoyed it. The soundtrack for this game is excellent and memorable as well.
However, there are a things that I don't like. The first thing you will notice is the 3d-party DRM, which is the Paradox Account. It doesn't bother you that much, but this game is not supported by Steam Cloud, however, it uses the Paradox Account as a cloud for some reason. I haven't lost my save file, but I still find Steam Cloud to be more reliable because sometimes, when I start the game, it asks me which save file should I use, the one in the cloud or the local file even though it is the same exact file. It happens a few times, which I find annoying.

Recently finished this game, have not perfect cleared it, having some issues finding all of the content. To summarise: pretty much the same as the first game, some nice added stuff, some things taken away, some improvements and some things worse. Kinda short but still worth the price for the silly fourth-wall-breaking humour.
The game is very much the same as the first game but with a few tweaks. The game is mostly improved, especially the dungeon layout and the addition of little features such as choices in quests and secrets discovered only by rolling a 20 during travel.  However, it feels shorter and not as challenging, and I miss some of the features that were taken out, such as a choice of GM, the in-house pets and being able to have a space alien as a player choice.
The general theme is that you are playing as a bunch of tabletop roleplayers and their characters at the same time. You can see your room and customise it (with the same money as you spend in the game world, for some reason) while also seeing the adventure as it happens. The monsters and NPCs break the fourth wall constantly and everyone is aware they are in a computer game, despite it meaning to be a simulation of a tabletop game.  The complete lack of fourth wall makes it very light-hearted. However, the game is sometimes very insightful about gaming ethics.

This retro tabletop RPG was a thoroughly satisfying meta-roleplaying experience. It made pop culture references both old and new, sighed wistfully about the good old days, and made many jokes. Speaking of jokes, this game deconstructs every RPG cliché in the book. No main story quest ends the way you'd expect it to, and by my count, there are three, including the "Here be dragons" expansion. There are also many sidequests to flesh out each main story by giving the NPC's some love.
Grinding is optional. If you do all the quests before moving on, you'll be strong enough to handle the dungeons and bosses. The dungeons test your endurance, but that's easily solved by crafting enough HP and MP potions. The crafting system becomes much easier if you make 1 of each item to compare them.
Character roles and classes are straightforward and easy to unlock just by playing the game to gather enough gold. As with the crafting system, knowing which role/class to use becomes much easier by trying each at least once. I recommend focusing on only 1 or 2 skills per character. Evenly spreading your skill points around all 4 skills is a bad idea for almost every class.
Certain classes complement each other very well. You can swap out classes without losing levels, redistribute skill points, or even delete characters altogether.
Try this game if you like retro RPG's!

"Crimes and Punishments" is a classic adventure that let's you solve a handful of murder cases as Sherlock Holmes. It's a highly polished game with good graphics and (mostly) excellent voice acting. And it does a good job of capturing the essence and the quirks of the Greatest Detective, making it a good buy for fans of the famous character.
But what really makes this game stand out amongst other adventures: "Crimes and Punishments" actually gives you a chance to fail without reprimanding you for it. You will form your own deductions based on the clues that you find. Evidence will be ambiguous, leading to various possible outcomes of each case. The correct solution is not always obvious. And if you accuse the wrong person of comitting a crime, the game follows through. No "You failed", no "Reload and try again". This notion of non-linearity is somewhat of a novelty for adventure games which I thoroughly enjoyed.
My only criticism would be the lack of an overarching, meaningful story to tie it all together. The game tries to get a bit of closure during the last case, but feels way too rushed and too contrived, resulting in a rather bland anticlimax.

An evolution of adventure game. Frogwares developed their game to a higher level with evolved game system. After L.A Noire, I dare say this is a new history of adventure genre.

Frogwares has been on a very long roll with their Sherlock Holmes games for a very long time. This game is no exception.
Pros:
Gameplay. Amazing, feels more explorative than a few of the earlier titles. Love being able to look for clues myself instead of being pointed to everything. Dialogue feels more choice based than previous as well.
Choices. The deductions you can make are nuts. You can get things wrong, cause people's deaths, put away the wrong suspect. It's limited, but then, these titles are smaller than other companies' and what they are doing in terms of choice is still pretty incredible.
Story. A mix of canon and new cases makes the game pretty enjoable, and not as predictable as it would have been if they'd had cases from the story at every turn.
Visuals. BEAUTIFUL. Although lacking in a few areas, so many of the enviornments were very pretty and immersive. It was great to look around at the scenary while progressing.
Voice acting. The best so far in the series, I think. Loved Holmes' actor.
Cons:
Choices. Limited. Want more hands on ability. But obviously we're getting there.
Exploration. The worlds felt very alive and very cool, and being able to miss clues makes me want to go out further to explore things. The day we get an open-world Holmes day will be amazing.
Story. The short cases were great. However, it lacked a story on the whole as the previous games had one. I missed that. Working to an end goal of a larger mystery while tying up these litttle problems would have been incredible.
Pros and cons aside, this game is defnitely worth playing if you like the title, and if you're into seeing how mystery games are progressing. Looking forward to seeing more.

Years ago, I played the EGA version of Loom. It came in a box with a book-on-tape that described the setting and the game's backstory and a lovely and creative manual that included a host of "drafts" (or spells) that weren't included in the game but which expanded its universe.  The game charmed me before I even installed it, and once I did, I was captivated by its gorgeous art, which used minimalism to make a 16-color palette more than ample, and its beautiful arrangement and rearrangement of Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake.  The gameplay was simple and approachable for a kid, with no inventory to manage, no death, scant dialogue trees to wade through, but the puzzles were clever and made me feel clever when I solved them.
In the quarter century since first playing Loom, whatever flaws it had were forgotten and its many virtues grew, as is the case when you fall in love with something as a kid. When, in interviews, I was asked about Primordia's inspirations, Loom was always among the first I mentioned, and I would always recommend it for people as an entry point to point-and-click adventure games. So, when my four year old was looking for a game to play after we did Primordia together, I naturally got us Loom.
It has not aged well, the VGA "talky" version is somewhere between the restoration of the Great Wall and the "restoration" of the Ecce Homo painting in Borja, which is to say not very pleasant. Moreover, I had forgotten (or been unable to recognize) many flaws that exist even in the EGA version.
- The additional VGA colors conceal the artistic feats of the original, and in some instances simply look worse. This video makes the case well:
- The sampling of the voice over is extremely poor, and many audio clips are mistimed and oddly cut.
- Most of the music was removed from the game.
- Certain scenes are shortened (not so badly, in my opinion) and certain parts were bowdlerized.
But even setting aside the problems with the VGA version, the game itself is ludicrously short -- we beat it in under two hours, taking time for the four year old to take her stab at the puzzles.  While the game feels open and experimental and somewhat exploratory on the initial island, it becomes increasingly linear, and the last act of the game is *entirely* linear, with every sequence an exact duplication (in gameplay terms) of the last:
Bobbin is not as endearing a character as I remembered, and neither is Hetchel -- the loss of the audiobook introduction to her, perhaps -- and Chaos is much less threatening.  While some of the puzzles remain relatively clever, others are easy and sometimes tedious (in particular, the main puzzle in the blacksmith guild, which is worsened significantly by voice over freezing you out of interactions).  I appreciate brevity in games more now than I used to, but every sequence feels two or three puzzles too short, and as a result none of the characters ever has anything more than a cameo, save for Rusty, whose ambiguous role in the story is as puzzling to me at 36 as it was at 11.
Despite these ample flaws, I still think Loom is a very special game. Its gentleness and the novelty of its spell-based puzzles are undiminished with time, and many of the scenes remain striking, even in VGA. There are many other games where you'll get more bang for your buck, but I think it is still a good entry point to the genre, and an important piece of adventure game history, one that shouldn't be forgotten.

TL;DR skip to last paragraph.
This is a linear game.  There is a story to be told, and it will guide you through with that end in mind.  For 90% of the game, I would say the story was . . . cute.  Nothing spectacular.  Nothing terribly unique, even.  Never, in my 30+ years of video gaming, have I seen an ending like that.  Not that you couldn't tell something was going on, but the big reveal was pretty epic.  It puts the whole game in a different light.  I instantly wanted to play through the whole game again, just to see it in context.
The mechanics are solid.  By the end, though, I was yearning for a bit more complexity.  The system was fine, but I wish there were more options in terms of equipment, orbments, and characters.
Equipment was mostly linear.  You buy what's in the shop, then pick up an upgrade in a dungeon.  You just rinse and repeat for each chapter.  No real choices.  The next piece of equipment is always better.  There is the option of finding the ultimate weapons, but that is little more than the final step in a relatively linear progression.
The orbment system was actually pretty complex, but they could have done much more with it.  Once you get the hang of it, though, you can spend most of a play-through just playing with orbment combinations.  Sadly, it doesn't take long to master.
As for characters, this game was pretty unique.  Many different games have you picking up team-mates as you progress through the story; but most let you keep that character from then on.  In this game, your comrades only join you for brief periods at a time.  It's a bit irritating, but it also makes them feel more like characters, rather than just extra bodies.  Each comrade has their own motivations.  They aren't going to leave everything they care about just to follow some strangers around the world.  It makes them feel more real.
The combat was excellent for a turn-based game.  The choice to move around the field of battle turns out to be more than just a gimmick.  Rather it affords a new dimension to combat (for instance it lets you position your enemies).  Status effects are worthwhile but unessential.  They managed to strike a perfect balance.  Using them makes many fights much easier, but every fight (but one. Errrr  LAWRANCE!!!!) is possible without considering status effects at all.  Skills, S-breaks, and weapon effects make combat complex enough to stay interesting.  The turn bonuses are mostly gimmicky, but play a big roll in the BIG fights.
Overall, 9/10 for first playthrough, 7/10 for subsequent playthroughs. The game is worth playing for the story alone, and the combat is sufficiently complex to stay interesting.  The game is simple enough, though, that it's only good for a couple runs and some nostalgia runs years later.

To start out with I'd like to mention that I'm a sucker for the Final Fantasy series, but have been pretty terrible at getting my act together to try out other acclaimed JRPGs. I didn't know about this game until it's Steam release was announced and people seemed to get pretty psyched about it online, so I figured I had to try this. More than half a year later I got my act together and have just now finished it. And holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ This is one of the best games I've played in years.
Is it a perfect game? No. First of all the combat system grew old and a little too repetetive on me quickly and there are pretty far between serious combat challenges. Mainly due to this, the game is fairly easy (there's a few really tough battles, but not that many).
I think my main concern with the combat is also due to the "battlegrounds". They look different, but throught the entire game they're essentially the same. It's a fixed square area where characters and enemies can move around. The nature is a little different depending on where in the game you are, but there are no obstacles or interactive objects on the battlegrounds whatsoever, which is a shame as that would have added an additional element to the combat.
That is pretty much my main gripe with the game, though. Well, that and the fact that it starts a bit slow, but I'm alright with that.
What really makes this game phenomenal is the story. It's not just good. It's really, really good. It has everything - romance, tragedy, political intrigues, humor, war, betrayal, and I could keep going. And it's not just implementing these themes - it's implementing them together very, very well. The characters are also well-written and have some pretty good interaction. They're different both in personality and in their role in the story. I never found that any of the main characters felt out of place or unnecessary, which is pretty impressive with a fairly large character roster.
There's also a ton of side stuff to do with varying difficulty. Standard monster-killing sidequests, take item from A to B-quests, escort quests, etc. Alongside all this, there's a lot of hidden stuff and collectibles, that are completely optional and a lot of it is pretty well-hidden. If you truly want a 100% completion then you have to extremely thorough and visit and revisit almost all areas - and you have to do it before progressing too far or some areas will be locked. Normally I hate this locked approach, but I actually find it works alright in this game, as there's always something new to do in whatever area you end up in next.
Completing the game took me just under 50 hours - and I tried to be thorough in finding most collectibles and items (and failed...). If you're not into all these extras I reckon the main game can be completed in less than 30 hours without rushing anything. If you're into JRPGs you should definitely not miss out on this title!
Be warned, though. Halfway through the game I learned that this is just the first of three chapters. It was originally released in 2004 and they're still not done with the localization of the second chapter, yet, so finishing the entire story is going to require some patience. Playing this game is still completely worth it, though!

Let me begin with this review that it being very cheap (only $7!) feels like I'm pirating the game, when you compare the quality to the price. I would pay $20 for this game and still get the same out of it, though if you want to pick up copies for friends (trust me when I say you'll want to after you get a taste) or if you're simply a cheapskate, and the below text appeals to you, you would be making a mistake not to buy this game.
This is easily the best game purchase I've ever made, and I don't regret buying it for around four other people within my first few hours of playing.
Like games such as Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup, Dwarf Fortress, and other roguelikes, though especially NetHack (which is renowned as the grandfather of every roguelike and video game RPG that exist), this game will eat you, chew you, spit you out, set you on fire, and then stomp on you; and that's on a good day, and usually only if you're playing with friends.
But like games such as Quake, DOOM, and other classic first person shooters, the controls are easy enough to get used to, while not compromising complexity or challenge.
Roguelikes tend to be represented by tileset based graphics like a board game, or letters/numbers/other characters to represent things in the game world. They're also turn based, and typically never multiplayer due to the turn based gameplay.
Barony violates these 'rules of the roguelike' with the following:
-
(extremely important)
- a three-dimensional voxel graphic system (3D pixel-ish, but is still very aesthetically pleasing, and actually feels nostalgic with a 90s feel unlike your average game that uses pixel art graphics for no good reason)
- a first person perspective (as opposed to a board game look where you see everything from above)
- real time gameplay (roguelikes are usually always turn based)
There are probably other important roguelike rules I'm missing, yet, despite these changes, this game is the purest example (besides NetHack itself) of what a roguelike is, and is largely directly inspired by NetHack (not the same story, but definitely the same spiritually).
(in fact, these changes make the game easier for people to pick up and get into, but that's just my opinion)
In terms of what a classic dungeon crawling roguelike should have, Barony excels in such:
-
- extremely hard and unforgiving
- extremely fun overall (in terms of actual fun, and Dwarf Fortress 'Losing is Fun!' fun)
- cryptic and doesn't make anything obvious (while every bottle of swirly orange liquid will do the same thing, it won't tell you what it does unless the effect itself is obvious, like invisibility -- only if you identified it through appraisal or a scroll of identify will it tell you what it does before you drink it)
- many levels, with randomized layouts that change every time
- is NOT simple, even though it looks like it is (you normally wouldn't expect eating too much to be a problem, until your character vomits and suddenly you're starving to death because your stomach is empty)
- lets you learn from your dying experiences so you know not to make the same mistakes -- this is very important, as death is a learning experience as opposed to you simply not being good enough or bad luck
- also is likely to make your death hilarious as opposed to frustrating
- near death experiences are also very fun (don't believe me? you will after you escape a minotaur)
- many different ways to play
- many secrets
- a lot more that i'm forgetting
In addition, Barony's co-op play is not only extremely fun, but somehow turns the death of every party member except you from horribly frustrating to uncontrollable laughter at the circumstances through which your friends died. It somewhat violates the permadeath rule in that the party heading to the next level respawns who died, but this is offset by the fact that you may not be able to carry all of the equipment that your friends had to return it, and that your chance of surviving long enough to get to the next level to revive them is as low as their chance not to die first was.
My only complaint is that even though I haven't beaten it as of the time of writing this review, and probably won't for a very long time, there doesn't seem to be that much content in comparison to NetHack as far as levels go (from my understanding of the game's insides, the shortest a game can be is 20 levels), and there could be more tiers of equipment beyond wooden/bronze/iron/steel (correct me if i'm wrong).
Condensed, here's what I think of the various aspects:
Graphics - 8/10 (this is probably because i'm biased toward old school voxel graphics, but if Minecraft is pleasing to your eye, Barony will be something your eyes will savor)
Sound - 7/10 (could be more realistic, but the sound effects do easily match the graphics, which are old school)
Music - 9/10 (very fitting, and very nostalgic)
Gameplay - 10/10 (see everything I wrote above)
As far as suggestions go, if the developers or anyone influential on the game's direction can read this, I would suggest more equipment, more enemies and maybe more bosses (skeletons are cool and all, but i'd love to see more), more levels, pretty much more everything if there's no plans to already. NetHack had an absolutely overwhelming number of enemies, items such as wands, weapons, potions (which were randomly generated in every playthrough! I would recommend having a system such as that, akin to Binding of Isaac's randomly generated pill effects), etc. Of all those, my main request would be more enemies. As a nice addition, perhaps sliders or difficulty/'complication' levels would be a good idea to either new or hardcore players, as too much can easily overwhelm a person (which NetHack does with no problem) and spoil their experience -- though balanced in such a way that it still remains true to it's roguelike roots.
If you like everything I wrote above, are tired of more casual games being too easy, want some more challenge, love NetHack and want something similar, love NetHack and want to play it with friends, or are just looking for the next RPG to sink your time into, get this game.
Or get this game anyway and see how many times you die in your first two hours. (My count: 43)
(also add me on Steam if you want someone to play this with!)

Okay, here's a no nonsense review of the game itself, leaving all the political controversy aside.
Syrian Warfare is a tough-as-nails, challenging but surprisingly fun tactical RTS game that does wonders plunging you headfirst into tactical urban warfare.
The player is tasked with a seemingly impossible mission at first: with his little team of a few infantry squads and an APC or two you are expected to fight and win a battle against overwhelming odds.
Hell, even on the normal difficulty your forces can be easily wiped out in the blink of an eye by a sudden suicide truck attack followed by a tremendously powerful explosion, that even shatters buildings.
Speaking of buildings, while they provide great cover from small arms fire for your infantry, you'll be shocked to see how well the game engine handles partial, or even full destrucion of a building. All of that can change the tactical flow of the battle, so keep an eye out and switch the positions of your units accordingly.
After an intense mission like that—filled to the brim with artillery barrages and enemy suicide truck explosions—you will be treated to a picture of an absolutely destroyed city block with husks of buildings smashed to pieces.
All in all Syrian Warfare provides a challenging and fun experience for fans of a tactial engagements in urban warfare scenarios, especially for such a low price.
