Developer Frogwares alongside publisher Focus Home Interactive have pushed out the latest game in the Adventures Of Sherlock Holmes series. This latest entry, titled Sherlock Holmes: Crimes & Punishments, has launched on almost all non-Nintendo platforms including PC, PS3, PS4, Xbox 360 and Xbox One. Crimes & Punishments is Sherlock’s first appearance on our new current gen systems, and what an awesome experience it is.
Crimes & Punishments plays out over the course of six different cases. Each case will take roughly two to three hours to complete and are each unique in their own way. The cases can range from solving murders to uncovering thefts to investigating burglaries. You are Sherlock Holmes: the greatest detective around. Crimes & Punishments places you in charge of uncovering all of the clues, using the clues to create deductions, and eventually using the deductions to solve your case. The gameplay is played out in a way very similar to that of L.A. Noire. Though Crimes & Punishments isn’t quite as open world as L.A. Noire was, it’s still open, enabling you to freely roam any of the available locations for that case. You’re free to look around for clues, talk with people and interact with items scattered about all to help uncover new information. This formula is one that really succeeds. In Crimes & Punishments all locations are well designed and fun to explore, and while most clues are in plain sight, it’s still quite nice running through such different locations on the hunt to finding some clues. Occasionally you will even get to switch out from playing as Holmes and get to enjoy playing as Dr. Watson, and even their dog, Toby. Dr. Watson may not have actually changed gameplay much, but it was always nice to find clues while following scent trails as a dog.
Crimes & Punishments is also filled with plenty of mini games and puzzles. From cracking into a safe, or lock picking a door, to building molds, to doing chemistry there are mini games all over. Most are relatively simple to solve, though I did often encounter an issue. When connecting lines, in uncovering an image or picking a door lock, the lines would need to line up perfectly. If the lines weren’t perfectly straight the game would not set through as completed. This can get very frustrating at times, but the developers had a fix right there. If you’re stuck on a puzzle or simply don’t want to bother doing it you can press a skip button which will automatically do the puzzle for you. This feature was a life saver because when a puzzle got too frustrating I’d have the ability to just say “screw it” and move on with the case.
Crimes & Punishments is also an incredibly beautiful game, and one that really feels like it belongs on the current gen platforms. All characters look incredible and are given amazing little details like light bruising, scratches and other unique traits. Obviously these are helpful in learning about people in the actual case, but in a sense the differentiations and great design of each character is a real accomplishment. They not only look amazing but they truly feel different. The characters are not alone in their beauty though. The environments are all very well designed and are absolutely gorgeous. The vast detailing that went into each location stands out and the environments cannot help but feel like real life locations, either currently lived in or abandoned.
It seems to be the small things that really make the game work. From small details on the skin of the character to smaller more unknown features. Crimes & Punishments gives the user the ability to switch between first and third person modes whenever they want to. Additionally, a user can use a sixth sense type mode in which certain locations, or during certain events, should the player activate it they can play out what happened, helping to put clues together. At the end of a case, once you’ve uncover the truth, you are also given the ability to make a moral choice of how to handle the situation. Turn someone in to the police, knowing they will be hanged, or was their crime not that bad and let them off the hook? The choice is yours and it actually adds a lot to the experience.
Overall, I went in to Sherlock Holmes: Crimes & Punishments with very low expectations, and I was extremely surprised. Crimes & Punishments is a very good looking game, and a very fun playing game. It’s really a case of all the care and small details its developer put in working together to create an amazing experience that players will enjoy and will end up finishing the game only to want more.
9/10
PROS
• Beautiful Graphics
• Fun and rewarding game play
• Various types of cases
• Entertaining mini games give an option to skip them should you not be able to complete
CONS
• Police and Dr. Watson often come across unreasonably stupid or get in the way

A quest for japanese videogames is always an adventure, that’s for sure.
Since they‘re masterpieces as often as not, you constantly search for unexplored brilliant, beauty of which emotionally tears you apart from the inside, and... you fail every time. This is their main component, so to speak: they appear in front of you suddenly, when your soul isn’t ready for waterfall of feelings and when you’re most vulnerable.
But there are exceptions even among ideal pieces of work: they are just too perfect. Sora no Kiseki is most vivid example. You had dreamt about such kind of game, you didn’t know about its existence, but there it is — you watch first cutscene (made with nipponese dedication to details) with lil’ Estelle, and in the next breath you become a part of the big journey into the ocean of all sorts of human nature.
And what I‘d dreamt about before I encountered with Trails in the Sky? What principles lie in the foundation of those dreams? First of all, it is a ginormous strategy, which creators know how minimise your agoraphobia by turning each five acts of odyssey to a completely new experience. Relying on your skill of empathy, authors engage you in «to-the-moon» family story, detective investigation with peaceful lunch on the mesmerizing shore or restoration of Eastern-like spirit on good-old hot springs.
Secondly, it has a unique art style, thanks to which you can feel battles, relationships, the theatrical production and the one adorable inventor’s diminutiveness in all their glory. Furthermore, «unique» is adjective for all aspects of videogames that made with great love and zeal: for soundtrack and characters, for design of monsters and towns, for background of sidequests and even minor events. Your heart melts every time when Joshua is playing on harmonica. You become excited as often as new inimitable person joins in your party.
And, you know, next thing isn’t third and not even tenth. The Legend of Heroes is way too big — too deep — for just citation of facts. It is only the first chapter of the trilogy and you already have immeasurable impressions and obligation to return in majestic Liberl.
What I got to say? It is a curse. When your childhood was marked by Front Mission, jRPG has become ever present part of your life. This curse is above price, and you need to say thanks for it.

Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky is a game I bought last August right after it came out on Steam because I had some extra money and I generally like JRPGs. I didn't actually end up playing it until January 2015, and after finishing it I can't believe I didn't play it sooner.
As has been stated in other reviews, the world building in this game is great. I was sucked in pretty quickly and was fully invested from very early in the game until the end. The characters, while not all exactly unique, are very likeable and fleshed out. From all the supporting cast to the party members (and especially the two main characters), they're all memorable and have their own distinct personalities.
The combat system isn't groundbreaking but it's very solid and I liked it quite a bit. Think somewhere between Skies of Arcadia and Final Fantasy Tactics. You move around on a grid and your movement is limited, but your positioning very much matters, as line attacks or AoE attacks can hit multiple units on both sides. My only real complaint with the game (and it's a relatively small one at that) is that it's somewhat restrictive in where you can go. After you clear the first region for example, you move on to the next with no option to return. There's no real reason to ever go back even if you could, I just like being able to go anywhere in a game like this.
After finishing the game, I've been extremely eager to play the sequel which, barring another delay, should be out within a couple of months in English. If you like character and story focused games (and if you like JRPGs how could you not?) then you won't be disappointed with Trails in the Sky.

is a fantasy action-adventure game. The rift that separated the Enclave of Magic from the Outlands is slowly closing, and heroes emerge from both sides, either to defend or conquer the Enclave.
: The game offers two campaigns, first the light campaign where you defend the Enclave from the invaders, and then the dark campaign where you are a minion seeking the glory of conquest. As the story progresses, you find or unlock additional equipment and up to six characters (per campaign) to play as. At the start of each chapters, you get to pick your character and equipment, limited by how much gold you found in each mission. For the most part, you can backtrack as much as you want for each missions, and replay any of them at any time if you missed out on some gold and want to try to do better (allowing you to select more equipment).
: I don't know why this was tagged as an RPG on Steam, 'cause it sure isn't: you have no stats, no upgrades, no character interaction or dialog choice. You don't even really purchase and manage an inventory, gold serves as "points" that determine how much equipment you can bring in a mission, being able to swap out at full value any item in between chapters. It is a Hack & Slash in the most basic fashion, battles consisting merely of slashing in the wind, only knowing whether you hit anything if damage numbers appear, while the AI is monstrously bad (enemies just jiggle about, only occasionally chasing assuming you don't break line of sight, like passing behind a chair). Voice acting is horrible, the story is rather poor, character progression is absent, and having up-to-date resolution doesn't save the graphics that have aged so badly that most 3D Fantasy early access indie titles are doing better than this blocky 2-Gen-Old world.

The game is the standard "simple-game-turned-fourth-wall-breaking-adventure" and it's completely unremarkable in this regard.
The gameplay is terrible as a design choice, but with lengthy segments with no interesting plot it becomes a chore. The puzzle parts are fairly trivial and quickly turn into a chore as well. The rest of the game - figuring out how to "hack" around the machine - is essentially just navigating menus and clicking things, with no clever or unusual solutions involved.
The plot is fairly simple and far from mind-blowing, and the fourth wall breaking elements are cliched. There's some arguably cringy talking-with-the-programmer humour, and Satan himself feels more like a grumpy game developer this kind of game usually involves. There are some secrets and token collectibles in the game, but they don't save the plot, and they don't make the game worth replaying. The game is really short, taking a bit over an hour to beat.
The graphics are pretty good, although the retro aesthetic gets hard on the eyes after a while. I also get the impression that a handful of 3d elements and sounds are stock Unity assets, which feels a little bit out of place. Overall I don't recommend the game, unless this is the first fourth-wall-breaking indie game you've ever played.

I'm having an absolute blast with this game. You have an incredible toolbox of toys to play with, to use with stealth and hacking, and the co-op is tremendously fun, though maybe a little repetitive at times after awhile. Player invasions, which you can turn off if you want to, are pretty fun as well.
As far as ways to complete missions, there are many. Pretty much everything can be done with your bots if you want to (same rules of stealth apply), or you might find a mission that works best with a combination of bots and going in yourself. If you fail at stealth, your options depend on what you were trying to do. If only your bots got caught, you can just try again if you want. If you got caught, yourself, you probably are now in a "kill them all" situation unless you can flee and hide for a bit.
Driving is fun, but I'm using a controller for driving and mouse/keyboard for everything else. I've never been good at driving with the keyboard, so I can't really tell you if that is implemented well.
Lastly, I'm finding the upgrade system really fun. It's always giving you new tools to use.
So, yes, I do really enjoy this game, but I'm also a fan of other Ubisoft open-world games, too, so you may want to take that with a grain of salt.

I really love this game. I prefer turn based games versus the more popular real time fighting styles, which makes it rather tricky to find a game that I like for pc, as I don't have a different gaming console.
This game is much better than I thought it would be. I hadn't heard of it before, so didn't know its anime, or PSP renditions going in. The game is much more complicated than I anticipated (the prologue was a little confusing for me with the orbs, quartz, etc, when I was just reading through the explanations), but it quickly fell into place and was pretty straight forward. The heroine is a little annoying at times, but she is a sheltered, headstrong 16-year-old, and the other characters call her on it, and she is an interesting foil to Joshua, the male lead. As the game progresses, her behavior matures a bit, which is rather astonishing to have character development in a game like this.
My only complaint about this game is to do with the conversations. THere are A LOT, and you can hold down a key to try and speed through the speech bubbles, but that doesn't help much. It gets annoying very fast, and very tedious, especially since there isn't a way to exit out of a conversation, and EVERY NPC has dialogue. In its sequels, I hope this is changed. Some chapters have so much dialogue, you have to take frequent breaks to not get frustrated (at least, I did).
The game has replayability factor, is incredibly detailed, and the vernacular is great! There are allusions to sexuality, but it is not blatant, no boob armor, and the humor isn't overdone. It really is a very good game. I am tempted to get a console to play its sequels that have been released already in other mediums.

So I'm going to cut to the chase, I really love this game. If you enjoy a good story that evolves as it progresses and can handle somewhat basic battle systems, you will enjoy this game.

The biggest downside is that it pretty much relys on its elemental resistances and main attack vs magic attack and doesn't get any more challenging. They do however, use this system to create some fairly difficult battles in the later part of the game.
I apologize for this review being much smaller than my others, but I was putting off writing this and decided I would just get it out there to let the world know how awesome this game is.

NOTE: There will be spoilers for this. If you want the TL;DR, it's that you should get the game and play through it if you like JRPGs. It's the first game in a trilogy, so be aware that the story is not complete with this game.
This is a JRPG about growing up and finding your own wings while living in your parent's shadow. It also has saving the region as a secondary characteristic, but there you go.
The game was confusing to get used to for the first several hours, but it's pretty intuitive and well-designed once you have a grasp of what means what and how things work together.
The battle system isn't revolutionary or anything, but some strategy is still necessary for a lot of fights. The magic system isn't a new concept to me, but the way it's presented is unique enough to be a neat idea. It's an interesting way of allowing every character to use magic, but it really differentiates who is a strong magic-user and who is probably better just sticking to basic attacks and skills.
The story does its job and the characters are interesting enough. I can't think of anything off-hand that feels out of place, although there are a few segments that don't feel all that necessary. The pacing of characterization is in a good place, especially for the two protagonists.
The character balance in-game felt a bit wonky, though. I have only played on Normal difficulty, so take this with a grain of salt, but I've noticed that magic-heavy people are incredibly strong in the end-game and more physical-based people are much less strong. This basically makes Estelle+Joshua+Kloe+Olivier the best endgame line-up by default, since Kloe and Olivier are the two mages of the group. I also felt that Tita felt pretty much worthless past the first couple of quests that you have her in. Her AoE blind was fantastic when I first used it, but her stats are below average and she blows up when she's sneezed at, so there's not much you can do with her.
The second game hasn't come out on steam yet when I'm writing this review, so I can't really comment on the ending at this point. The plot twist, while being foreshadowed throughout the entire story, still came out of left field and shocked me. It makes sense on a surface level for it to be possible, but the fact that it ended on a huge cliffhanger makes it difficult to take it seriously until I see it come up again in the second game. The verdict's out on that one.
All in all, this is a solid game that will give any JRPG fan a good time.

If you ever wanted to be a Sherlock Holmes. You have a chance now.

If you enjoy classic Sherlock Holmes, you will enjoy this game. The meat and potatoes of this game is the deduction system where you combine relevant clues together to find inferences, which allow for 1 of 2 interpretations that ultimately lead to different conclusions for the case. Its an enjoyable mechanic that makes you think and is supplemented by the ability to do character profiles of the suspects (rather simple) and QTE counters when the suspect is lying about a point based on the evidence you have. There are also puzzles but only a few are tricky.
In terms of length, the game is fairly long for its type. Six cases, about 3-4 hours each. You get your money's worth.
Graphically-speaking, this game is a definite improvement from its predecessors. I've played the older games and Frogware has come a long way. It still has its quirks- Watson was submerged halfway into the floor in one case and there are some occassional spelling errors in Sherlock's casebook.
As a whole, a great game for what it is. The individual cases work better than perhaps one overly long story found in previous games in the series. Hopefully there are more games in the future with better polish.

Comparing Crimes & Punishment to Testament of Sherlock Holmes:
As there are enough reviews going into gameplay details I will present a short overview in comparing the two games.
Testament has the more complex and interesting puzzles and an enthralling dramatic plot. Controls are sometimes clunky and not as smooth and well impemented as in C&P. Same goes with graphics.
Deduction system: In Testament there is one way to put the clues together. In C&P some criticize that you can evaluate the hints to deduct different solutions without making it clear which solution leads to the real bad guy. You can easily arrest the wrong one. I see that as a strenght of the game as it depicts analytic thinking and its various traps. You do your job and as in every job mistakes can happen and you have to live with that.  Ok there is a problem. Everyone arrested confesses, that is a weak point in the game I can accept. The unjustified accused should say so in the end.
Crimes is a little too easy to play but has fantastic flow in gameplay and exceptional architectural  leveldesign. It depictures 19th century London just beautiful. Playing C&P is like a wonderful effortless walk in the garden. It may be the best adventure of all time in terms of gameflow. Testament is more of a gritty dungeon crawling experience and with some puzzles you really get mad at the game, can`t stop thinking about it, coming back an hour or day later solving it and go on and on. In this regard Testament is true to the classic 90`s adventure era.
In the end I`d say Crimes is the more complete  adventure where all elements form an  addictive connection that transcends into an alltime top 5 adventure. I don`t like the whole narrative with these ugly children in Testament. It kind of ruins the immersion sometimes. Without them it would be better, but even with these little brats Testament greatly succeeds in storytelling and puzzle implementation.
Both are top of the line adventures. If you just finished Crimes you will need maybe 1h to adapt to Testament because it has a very distinct feel to itself, you have to work more to enjoy it. I loved it so much that I finished a second playthrough and got all trophies just because it is that good. I normally don`t do that.  If you start with C&P, well just walk through the looking-glass and get captivated in this  unique beguiling experience . Nothing else to say. It is that good.

Organ Trail is a very simple, but very entertaining game. The premise is that you are in a zombie apocalypse, and Washington DC is going to be destroyed by a nuclear weapon in a few hours, so you and a band of your friends head out for 'Safe Haven,' a land out west said to be free from the zombie infection. along the way, you battle zombies, ram aggressive bikers off the road in your station wagon, and try to keep your friends healthy and alive.
Just by looking at the title, it's easy to see that its a parody of the game "The Oregon Trail" from the 1970's. The gameplay is incredible simplistic, and the graphics are very minimalist, similar to that of an Atari 2600. That being said, it is great fun. The game has many randomly generated events, leading no playthorugh to be the same, and there is quite a bit of strategy involved as you try to ration out your resources and keep your entire party alive all the way to Safe Haven. I don’t really know what it is, maybe the simple graphics, the eerie music, or the thought of running out of some important material halfway to the next landmark, but this game is also very atmospheric, and you can start to get attached to your companions along the way. However, the game is not incredibly difficult on lower difficulties, though I have not tried out the higher ones yet, and sometimes the events can be a bit repetitive and tedious. On normal, even the jobs with a difficulty labeled "suicidal" are fairly easy to complete.
With all that said, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who is interested. It’s a very enjoyable game with a lot of content, plenty of replayability and an eerie atmosphere around it, even though it is so simple.

I love these kinds of puzzle games for playing whilst I'm doing other things, and this game has certainly provided a good few hours of puzzle-solving distraction. It's pretty much what it looks like - a logic puzzle game where you 'create' pixel art based on number clues given to you.
+ Quirky bright graphics
+ Easy to use interface
+ Decent number of puzzles
+ Sufficient level of challenge and the player chooses which challenge level they'd like for each puzzle
+ Few additional things to aim for over and above just finishing the puzzles, if you want to earn all the achievements
- I might be wrong, but I don't think all of the 'master' level puzzles are solvable through logic alone. If true, that's not great - I don't want to be forced to play out a guess in these kinds of puzzles.
*Edit - Although I still don't agree with having puzzles in the game that are unsolvable by traditional methods, I do want to add that the developer is extremely responsive and as a result of mine and others' feedback has added a message in the game that lets you know if a puzzle requires the mark-up mode before you start it. I'm impressed by their response to constructive criticism as too often (in my opinion) devs either don't respond or respond badly it seems. Kudos to the devs on this one.
Not exactly 'cons', but... While you're solving each puzzle there's a 'painting' in the top left which paints the pixels in colours as you progress. In some cases, this made it obvious where the next squares should go - I hid the painting by using windowed mode and pushing it off the screen, but it would be nice to switch this off. (I didn't spot this option in the settings). Also, and this is really a personal preference, but my favourite logic puzzles are ones with text puzzles to help you solve the grid, so it would have been great to see a few of these thrown in to mix it up a little.
All in all, does what it says on the tin, and if you like grid-based logic puzzles, you'll like this game.

After putting in 100 hrs I feel I can finally give a pretty solid review of Seige
Overview: I really enjoy the gameplay, all the guns feel like they have weight when fired, maps are fairly large, and there is quite a bit of strategy that goes on, if your team talks. Coming back from a 1v(any amount of enemies) is probably the most stressful aspect of the game, especially if your aim replicates that of a potato. Operator abilities are varied and pretty useful for different situations, Ex: Fuze + Hostage. The game still gets plenty of fresh content: maps, operators, loot, and modes, and.....Operation Health. The lootbox system is pretty solid, but having to win to roll, and missing on like a 60% chance can be disheartening. There is a pretty big learning curve to this game, you will probably be outplayed by veterans, getting your first few kills is quite rewarding, actually any kill feels rewarding in this game. That being said, the game is by no means perfect, if you look up Seige videos on Youtube, you'll find that out pretty quick. If you buy the Starter edition, while cheap, you will be grinding a lot for new characters, unless you purchase season pass or coins. In the 100 hrs i put in, i bought 3 operators, 2 non-dlc, 1 season-1 dlc character, and a bunch of attachments. Some of your deaths may feel like bs, and some of them are. Overall, the game is great and will give you a bunch of unnessecary stress 11/10

YES YES YES FINALLY someone releases another first person "free look" dungeon crawler like Ultima Underworld and Delver. I've only played it for an hour so far but I already feel that Barony's unpredictable dungeons, simple but satisfying combat, and dark atmosphere makes for some compelling dungeon crawling.
Do you like King's Field? Ultima Underworld? Delver? The Elder Scrolls games for their first person dungeon crawling aspects?
BUY THIS GAME.
One issue I have is that it doesn't support 1366x768 fullscreen. This is a very common resolution and it should be in the list. Better still the list of resolutions in the video options should be replaced by a drop-down box to select from. It would also be nice - similar to Ultima Underworld and System Shock - to have a "mouse cursor" mode could be implemented so that the player doesn't have to be directly facing an object to interact with it, though this isn't really important.
There are so few of these kinds of dungeon crawling "action-RPG" games that have ever been made. Sure, many crawlers have the fixed grid-based movement, but for those of us brought up on UU, Hexen and the like, we want full player control! Barony brings this in a solid, atmospheric dungeon crawling environment and does it very well. I feel like I've waited YEARS for a game like this to arrive! Bravo, Turning Wheel.

Its hard to call this a game or a walking simulator.  It lacks the length and emotional dialog that one would expect from a slow pace atmospheric title like Dear Ester or Gone Home, and the moments that the player is actually making choices that have any effect are few and far between and simply come down to a small amount of trial and error -- leaving it feeling more like a short, not very scary, horror story.
The Narration is good, but it feels like the writer was trying a little to hard some times and certainly lacked the skill to drive the emotions home.  However, the ambiance of the dark and depressing catacombs that the player walks through at a grueling rate are well done.  There were a few moments that can become a little spooky, but nothing in comparison to many of the other horror games out at this time.
It was worth one... "play-through/walk-through," but there is little to no reason to ever do it again.  Its worth the time if the game can be picked up for a dollar and change; unfortunately, some people must have payed full price for this title -- not a good idea -- even though it is only $3.00.  It took just over an hour to finish, and most of that time was spent walking down dead-ends then walking back to the, otherwise, liner path.

I for one will not waste my money getting the second episode unless it is a free continuation.

Spolier Free: If you're a Horror Game type, looking for something that combines well-textured maps, planned out locations, building suspense and simple confusion... well Coma:Mortuary is a game you should give a shot. While it isn't the most terrifying game I've ever played, the suspense did have me on edge up until the moment that I died - which is what I wanted more than the fear. This isn't your average RPG Maker or Slender-Spoof horror game; this game takes a repeating scheme of locations and uses them to make you feel trapped, to lead you the wrong way and to freak you out. No jumpscares required.
All in all, I'd give this game (based on the few minutes I've played, alone) a 5/6. For maps, textures, storyline, general enviornment, creepy ambience and playability. It has its issues - what game doesn't - but it's worth at least a quick play, to see if you'll enjoy it further.

Where to start? Trails in the sky is a gem of a JRPG. The characters are great and 3 dimensional and each gets their own share of the spotlight and character development. The combat, though a little strange at first, is easy to understand but harder to fully master.

First of all, let me save you some time.  If you consider yourself a fan of JRPG's, buy this game immediately.  As a fan myself, I promise you won't be disapointed at all.  That said....very minor spoilers possible in the review (nothing big I promise)
- It's long, I'd say 35-45 hours depending on how much side missions you do.
- The music is great, if not exceptionally varied.
- The story and characters are top notch, I enjoyed using every character in the game.
- There are tons of side missions to do that reward you with dialogue and Mira (money)
- Every person you meet in this game will have different dialogue just about every time you meet them.  You could spend dozens of hours reading all of it alone.
- Combat is fun and kept me interested for almost 50 hours.
- The Orbment system allows you to customize your characters skills and stats just about in any way you want.  Figuring out how to unlock different Artes is almost as fun as using them.  (The games Bracer Book will give you all possible combinations)
- The story is light hearted and fun.  Most of this game doesn't involve you trying to stop anything evil and super powerful.  Most of the time you're just helping people out and the world reflects that.
- The story and intrique really picks up near the end of the game.
- Visually it looks nice for it's age.
- The ending is fantastic.
- The ending leads directly into a soon to be released second chapter of the game!
- You don't get to pick your team almost the entire game.  The final dungeon is the only time you will get to use all of your characters.
- Environments can be a bit stale, nothing really wow'ed me until the final dungeon.
- It's not overly difficult.  The hardest fights in the game are chests containing monsters that guard the loot.  Boss fights are moderatley difficult but if you prepare you won't be taxed.
- The game likes to use cheap "instant kills" and "misses" to make fights frustrating.  It's worse near the beginning of the game.
All in all, the game was fantastic and probably one of the best JRPG's you will find on PC.  9/10

The Legend Of Heroes: Trails In The Sky is an JRPG with a deep, rich world to explore. The protagonists, Estelle and Joshua embark on an adventure filled with lots of interesting characters with their unique personalities and abilities, It only took me 3 minutes to instantly be engaged to the story, grasping my complete attention that left me to forget there are other games to play, I wanted to experience this game exclusively until I reached the end. As you just read, the story is one of the best aspects of this title.
The amazing soundtrack of Trails In The Sky will be in your mind, from the calm tunes, to the intense sounds of battle, it is almost impossible to not like it at all, it is extremly well done. The gameplay is a classic turn based battle system that lets you strategize your movements, going in for the kill on the various monsters you will face. Patience with the tougher enemies is key to a successful win.
Is there anything bad to say? Trails In The Sky does have some cliche parts in the story, but it makes up for it with its extensive detail in character development, something you will see grow as you progress through the chapters. Depending on your taste for JRPGs, you may see a lot of good or a lot of bad, it is a title directly for the JRPG fans, but is also welcome for newcomers who want to try something different.
Without a doubt Trails In The Sky is a hidden classic that many do not know about. I myself did not know about this game either, I am glad that I did. I highly recommend anyone who LOVES RPGs, no matter if WRPG or JRPGs. For those who haven't bothered trying out JRPGs, for those who haven't tried RPGs, The Legend Of Heroes: Trails In The Sky is the game to play.

Now, Normally I do not write reviews. I can be pretty bad at this kind of thing what with lack of detail. However, Given how I enjoyed this game so much, I could not back away from this laptop.
I should start with the length of this game, I spent 60 hours, with about 12 to 15 hours a day, trying to beat this game. Not as long as skyrim mind you, but truthfully it would have been 70 had I continuosly spoke with every character in the game. Now this may be unecessary, but it was interesting(and sometimes boring) to see what other people would talk about after every main quest, sidequest or hiddenquest you have finished. Of course if you don't like reading, which is weird because you are reading right now, this game is not really for you. there are 1.8 millions texts, or so I am told, in this game. Heck I could finish moby♥♥♥♥♥♥in that time.
Texts aside, as you start to control your character in game, there is going to be quite a bit of handholding. It is a little pointless, but given how they designed the gameplay in battles and healing I think it may have been neccesary to have kept it longer. I realized at the final chapter you could use arts(Spells) outside of battle to heal yourself. To be honest I do not really like the design of how you battle out the enemy. I have no good way of explaining it, but the game automatically moves your arrow to a button. The most annoying part is that the Arts you will have to scroll down to use against an enemy. I mean Seriously! Scroll down to find a spell after every round? That is incredibly annoying. Still the battles are good enough so that you won't get bored, unless you are constantly heckled by monsters.
On to the characters of this game. I have just one complaint. There are no theme songs for any of these guys. I know it is knit picking, but there are too few songs in a game so big and a lot of times they do not match what is going on in the game. Besides that I find the characters to be quite enjoyable. Even the duke, (who is a slob, a drunkard, and possibly sexist) is a character I enjoy seeing because of his stupidity and drunkeness. My favorite character of this game would be Olivier. Olivier is an... unique person. I'd tell you more, but I would not want to spoil the fun. I can say that he has saved me from boredom from time to time as rpgs sometimes get to that in certain scenes. There are other comedic characters in this game too, and this is usually why I play anime games such as this.
My final say is that at the end of the game, you will be blasted with an incredible and shocking ending. I cried through these scenes. Heck you'll be mindblown reaching the ending, course if yer perty smart, you may have a good idea what it is. I had an idea, but boy was I off on some points.
That said, this game is great, do not buy it if you go to college and have 19 hours of school. You will not get any sleep... like ever. The game is way too addicting to close. in fact I lied about playing it 12 to 15 hours a day... yeah.... I've actually had only 3 hours of sleep until I finally finished it. So that is how addicting it is. Enjoy!

I had to look twice to see if this was a retro classic that had been re-released or ported to the steam store. But it turns out it's not, and is indeed an original/fresh game.
The graphics are authentic of what you would expect from a game during the days of the sega master system (and before). Do not be put down by the graphics however, as the gameplay is certainly there. I haven't had so much fun with a pixel based sprite game in at least a decade. There are lots of elements to the game that give you a rush of nostalgia, be it the music, the menu systems, or the animations, it certainly brought back memories of some titles on the sega mega drive; for me.
The various gameplay mechanics also work well, even though they are fairly simple. It's also quite fun to discover an old gravestone on the road-side (with a personal message that you wrote) on the next play through.
I also have to say that the soundtrack is brilliant. Most games that i enjoy for years to come have succeeded on the basis of the music and the gameplay alone, i think Organ Trail might be one of them.
I ended up with this game after the purchase of a recent humble-bundle, but having played a few hours through Organ Trail, i think it's somethin gi would've paid full price for on it's own.

2 hours, finished the game with max stats and all unlocks. Waste of $8 wish steam offered refunds for abandoned projects and 1/4 finished games.
Interaction:
Was hoping for a game like EA fight night where dodging and blocking as well as good combos would win the day (i.e. skill). Dodge is the same button as block, press to dodge (i.e. tap spam) and hold to block (i.e. wtf i pressed dodge not block... oh you gotta tap spam to dodge). Took me about 30 matches before i figured out how dodging worked. Even after I figured it out, it's not interactive. You dont dodge incoming blows, you predict them before any form of movement has ensued.
Apparently this is a mobile app port, makes sense as playing on PC you can't react to anything in real time as i explained above. Its like a dance simulator except minus the visual cue's. If you react while a punch is being thrown its too late. You need to react before the punch is being thrown, like some form of anticipatory foreplay. This made me really sad as it removed all tactical gameplay.
Gameplay:
So playing through single player, you will notice STATS MEAN EVERYTHING.
There are 3 main stats (ikr way to many to manage :P) Strength ((how much damage you do, opponents strength stat affects this) ie. 100% strength will do way more damage vs 68% strength than 92%)
Stamina ((how quickly you gas out) doesn't really affect♥♥♥♥♥♥as even with max stamina vs low stamina you can only throw 3-4 punches before being gassed, it only really affects recovery speed in a high vs low stat (like strength as above))
and speed (who hits first) this doesnt really affect much either as i will explain later. Doesnt matter who hits 1st unless its against high level bots who can dodge like it has its own button :P
For instance you can have better Stamina and speed yet be losing by 3 points of strength, the person you are fighting will hit you and do 3 to 6 times as much damage (ie. 10 vs 30 or 60 damage). even though you are hitting 1st and more times.
Punching doesn't involve any tactics either, as there is a generic high block and no real dodge function. So if you both swing both will hit (depending on punch choice), then it comes down to stamina or strength. i.e. Who can punch for longer or who hits harder. So if you have more speed and stamina you can do 1 more hit at less damage against someone who does more damage in less hits with strength i.e. as above ^
So playing through all the single player if you just level up before proceeding you can come out and 1st round KO everyone by just swinging then block recover stamina and swing (rinse and repeat)
Character development:
As stated stats progession is the main point of the game. If you try to play through the game and do the minigames every 5 matches you will have a bad time. Mainly because the minigames are horrible. You are better off just restarting the tournaments and buying all your stats with the cash winnings.
Character creation:
You can choose between about 8 premade characters and where you are from and your name. Def next level for a mobile 99 cent app port.
Multiplayer:
finished the game, decided to try multiplayer got some poor guy without 100% stats. Noticed a lot of lag and blackscreen between the knockdown screens i.e. 3-4 seconds. Also noticed a lot of delay, so im guessing matchmaking isnt done on ping.
All in All:
Wasn't impressed, the game offered no challenge and when it did (i.e. understats vs higher levels) the lack of an effective counter (i.e. dodge) really made it a pushing isht uphill problem. I actually like playing fightnight against way OP opponents as you could still dodge and outskill them, This game offers none of that depth. Its a 3d SNES port of mike tysons punchout.

This game's primary draw is in the story.  Basically, the devil has laid claim to your soul, and is forcing you to playtest his repetitive and terrible game until you surrender your soul.  The conflict revolves around trying to escape.  I don't want to talk about it too much, because spoilers are really bad in a game like this, but it's important to note that the game has clever writing that plays with the fact it is a video game.
However, the gameplay is actually quite good as well.  While I called it terrible and repetitive before, that's only for the first two minutes of the game.  There are two sides to the gameplay, puzzles used to debug/hack the "game", and the platforming sections.  The puzzles are unique and interesting, as well as creative.  The platforming is initially bad, as you jump over low hanging stationary obstacles with no control over your speed, but it gets spiced up considerably as you give yourself upgrades and level design changes to accomadate the new abilities.  It gets to a point where it is genuinely challenging and rewarding.
The only slightly negative side to this game in my opinion is that it only takes two hours to beat, and replayability is low.  The only reason to return is to reexperience the game, or to show it to one of your friends, or to collect all the collectible "tickets" hidden throughout (24 in total).  However, this minor complaint is seriously offset by the 5$ price point, especially when you can get it for even cheaper on sale.  Aside from this, I can't think of a reason to not recommend it.  Maybe if you aren't a fan of meta humor or of the idea of a platformer simple enough to be controlled entirely with your mouse, you may not like this game.

This is, without a shadow of a doubt, my favourite Sherlock Holmes game yet. The deduction system which allows for multiple conclusions gives the game great depth in comparison to the previous installations. Another interesting feature is the ability to read people by freezing time and studying details about clothing, expressions and appearance which gives unique dialogue options.
Additionally, the graphics allow for fantastic immersion and clearer view of the objects around you, which makes clue-finding more natural. This is something that always bugged me in the older Sherlock games (I still have nightmares about Mystery of the Mummy). The voice acting is a lot better this time around, but it's nothing exceptional.
The only issue I have with Crimes and Punishments is its longevity, as a full completion of the game clocks at about 15 hours if played slowly, with a total of 6 great cases of varied difficulty.
Would I like to play more? Yes. Is it still worth the money? Definitely yes.

Everything about this game is fantastic except for the arbitrary nature of the deduction system. There will typically be at least three solutions with separate suspects and different means of having committed the crime. The different clues which have been collected during the investigation must be arranged to form different deductions in order to single out the perpetrator. The system is genius except for the fact, that the developers have failed to make some deductions more correct or coherent than others. Thus you can never be sure your chosen solution - based on solid reasoning (what Sherlock Holmes is supposed to be all about!) - will be correct. Even if you have taken all things into considerations and logically chosen the most likely explanation. This have been incredibly frustrating and immersion breaking.
To further explain what I mean by the solution being arbitrary, I will provide the following observation:
Any case in  "Crimes & Punishments" will have established means, motives and opportunities for all suspects, if you diligently have found all the different clues. The problem as I see it is, that there should at least be some few things that makes one suspect more likely than the other, or deductions that stood out as far less sound, as they appeared to be in conflict with other circumstances like causality or the existence of contradictory evidence, but no. All the solutions are equal in likelihood and reasoning, and as Sherlock Holmes we are bound to make a decision on who we would most wish to see having committed the crime or who we intuitively believe did the crime based on knowledge of crime cliches.
It seams the developers have constructed the clues, deductions and solutions in order to  fit the model of "means, motives and opportunities" as conditions in order to establish guilt as found in common law legal systems. This still only provides a dissatisfying experience, as this doesn't prove the actual guilt of the suspect, which in turn today nor in Victorian era Britain were enough to lift the needed burden of prof of having committed a crime. Establishing the presence of these three elements is not, in and of itself, sufficient to provide a conviction beyond reasonable doubt; the evidence must prove that an opportunity presented was indeed taken by the suspect and for the crime with which he or she is charged. In "Crimes & Punishments" the different solutions are entirely equal in probability, and this is the prime weakness of the system: If all the suspects can be reasoned to be equally as likely the ones who committed the crime, then they are all equally as unlikely to be guilty, and in a court of law this would actually make providing a conviction impossible. The conclusion simply  cannot be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.
It frustrates and saddens me, that the deduction system have been built in such a way as the solutions are wholly arbitrary and in total disconnect with the books of sir Arthur Conan Doyle. Mainly because if you can ignore this, then the game is fantastic. The atmosphere is fantastic and the locations and voice acting is great.

Simply put, Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments is one of the finer adventure/crime solving games I've played. The writing is excellent, and each case will intrigue. The lack of a coherent overarching storyline is a tad disappointing, but that's simply not the focus of the game. It follows Sherlock Holmes doing what he does best - solving crimes and administering punishments.
The atmosphere and overall presentation are quite on point as well. Some of the animation can be stiff, but the overall attention to detail is commendable nonetheless. If someone has a limp, you can guarantee that they'll actually walk with a limp in the game. The texture and general location quality is also of note. While the game isn't taxing by any means, it looks gorgeous cranked up to maximum settings with detailed recreations of Ye Olde London. There isn't much music, but it's used to good effect when it pops up, and helps set a much darker tone and feeling than most Sherlock Holmes properties.
Finally, the detective and puzzle gameplay itself. It's quite good! The puzzles never become extraordinarily difficult, but they strike a nice balance between needing actual thought and not being so complex as to slow down the pace of the story. There's good variety here, as well, with a number of small, mini-game esque challenges to beat (though they can be skipped if that's not your thing), interrogations, autopsies, crime reconstructions and even a few notable sequences of trying to rebuild the sequence of events in Holmes' imagination. You won't need a membership in Mensa to make progress here, but it will challenge just enough to make you feel like Sherlock Holmes himself. Ultimately, given that the game has his name on it, that's probably the biggest praise I can give this.

Paint It Back is a great nonogram puzzle game with a painting theme that I am absolutely addicted to (as you can probably tell from my playtime). A nonogram is a puzzle where you are given a grid and each row and column has one or more numbers by it which tells you how many consecutive cells need to be filled in in that row or column. You will need to use logical thinking and information from other rows and columns to figure out which cells are the ones that should be filled in and complete the painting.
It's hard to explain why Paint It Back is so addicting but it is. It is definitely one of those "one more turn" type of games. You will sit down to play it for an hour to wind down and it will be past midnight before you know it. I think the main reason why it is so fun and addicting is that it is a very simple game to play but it also requires a lot of logical thinking to complete the paintings.
Paint It Back offers a lot of bang for your buck. At the time of this review, I had put in over 21 hours and I still have a lot of puzzles left to complete. I estimate that it will take me at least 25 total hours to complete all of the puzzles and that's with me focusing on mainly the normal and pro paintings (the master difficulty puzzles are very time consuming).
If you like puzzle games at all and especially if you like nonograms or similar puzzles like Sudoku you should definitely check out Paint It Back.
Note: I received a free review copy of the game but received no other compensation for this review.

Picross. That’s the thing I keep hearing whenever I see games like this come by. These sorts of games are easily spotted, because of the large squares with numbers on the sides, and a picture of what you’re creating in the corner. I remember having played one or two of them back in the day but to be honest I can’t remember what they were like. Time to find out if there may have been a reason for this…
The story is quite simple and begins with a ghost wandering around in a museum. It finally manages to scare away all of the paintings and now it’s up to you to paint them back. It’s goofy and it sets the tone immediately. It doesn’t take itself seriously and that’s exactly what it should be like. It’s a casual game at heart, as in anyone can pick it up and play. The difficulty is also targeted at a casual audience and since there’s no time limit you can take your time until you have finally figured out how to paint it properly. However, you can also choose to play a more difficult/advanced version of puzzles and these puzzles then consist of multiple blocks merged together to make it look like one big (wide) puzzle.
Gameplay wise it’s relatively simple. Easy to learn, even easy to master, but it does take some brain activity to figure out how to paint the blocks exactly. The game puts a board in front of you and that board can also be seen in the upper left corner, but on a smaller scale. If you paint a block on the big board – by just clicking on it – then you will also see that block get painted on the smaller board in the corner. By clicking a block again you can remove the paint and by right-clicking you can choose to disable a block to prevent you from accidentally painting over it. While I felt this was fairly useless at the beginning it became more important later on when the boards get bigger and more complex.
Anyway, there are numbers written on the top and left sides of the board and these tell you how to paint the blocks. By looking at the numbers you can figure out how to paint the blocks properly.
So if you have a 10x10 block and on the ninth line (horizontally) is written ‘10’ then you have paint all ten blocks horizontally. It’s not a very good example, but it’s a little hard to explain without actually drawing an example. But just take a look at the screenshots and you’ll see probably understand what I mean.
Once the painting is complete the smaller board will be enlarged to show you the end result. It’s always a pixel art painting (I always appreciate good pixel art) so don’t go and expect a DaVinci painting or anything, although they do get more complex a few hours into the game.
Also, starting from area 3 puzzles become larger and may even consist of several parts. This means that a painting can be divided into, for example, 2, 4 or 6 parts. This doesn’t influence the actual coloring of the blocks but instead of creating just one big painting you’re then painting several parts that ultimately combine into one big painting. You do get to see the entire painting in the corner, by the way, so you always have a clear idea of what the final result will or should look like.
There are multiple areas to play through, 15 in fact, each with their own theme, but I somehow missed how these paintings exactly relate to these worlds. They seem completely random, but I guess with a little thinking you can see the or some sort of relation between them. It seems farfetched, though, but I assume that’s just part of the goofy style and humor.
Overall the game feels very polished. The only thing I think needs improvement is the audio, of which there is just too little variety. With some added tracks (or at least more rotation) it’s actually pretty much perfect in my opinion.
So, thus far there doesn’t seem to be a whole lot of diversity as far the music is concerned. The first hour or so I heard the same song over and over with every painting I created. Then out of nowhere I finally heard another song. There seem to be more songs but they currently repeat a bit too often, which is an absolute shame, even though the focus is not the music per se. But more variety (as in: more tracks, or more rotation) would definitely help add to the immersion of being (or at least feeling like) a painter.
Visually it’s a beautiful game with a great looking cartoony style. The cinematics (although I wouldn’t really call them that) look fabulous in motion and the boards animate nicely whenever you complete a painting. Other than that there’s not much animation. The pixel art shown in the frames looks great, but sometimes it still looks a bit too simple. I personally thought it would’ve been cool if the pixel art would animate upon completing a puzzle. It would give it just a little more personality, but to be totally honest you can’t say that this game lacks any. It bursts with personality actually.
Anyway, the text is sharp, the use of colors is diverse and the graphics scale nicely: the game makes the screen (not the game itself) less wide or wider based on what is shown. It looks cool, but is a little inconsistent.
(Please note that I’m playing on a 21:9 monitor and this may therefore not occur on your monitor.)
There are 150 paintings to complete in total. Most of them can be completed in just a couple of minutes so if you do the math then it should take you anywhere between 10-15 hours to complete. And this is just for the normal paintings. If you choose to complete more advanced paintings then you can easily add another dozen hours to that number. Plus, there’s an Endless Mode for even MORE replay value. Oh yes, you get plenty of bang for your buck. Guaranteed!

TLDR:
Really amazing competitive 5v5 shooter with plenty of characters for you to choose from (with more coming). Amazing gameplay with a destructible environment, very much worth the money.
Basically...
There are a whole lot of characters to choose from, ones for defense and ones for offense. Offense has better scopes (Acog) for farther ranges (some defense operators have the acog). There are three gamemodes. You get paired with 4 other people (5 in a team), or you can squad up with your friends. You shoot and kill all enemies or play the objective.
Gameplay:
Bomb:
A multiplayer gamemode where defenders protect two bombs. Attackers need to plant a defuser in the same room as one of the bombs. If the defuser defuses the bomb, the attackers win, but if the defuser is disabled, the defenders win. If all attackers die, but the defuser was planted already, the game will still go on until the defenders disable the defuser or, if they run out of time to disable it, the attackers can still win.
Secure Area:
A multiplayer gamemode where defenders protect a room with a biohazard container. Attackers need to stay in the same room as the container for a certain amount of time to win, the defenders can stay in the same room and prevent the attackers from gaining any "time".
Hostage:
A multiplayer gamemode where attackers need to extract a hostage and the defenders need to prevent the attackers from taking back the hostage.
Terrorist Hunt:
A solo or Co-op gamemode (up to 5 people). They can play the same gamemodes listed above, but with bots. They can also choose the difficulty- Normal, Hard, Realistic.
Situations:
Singleplayer content. (ish) I would classify it as tutorial gameplay. There are 10 Situations where the game teaches you how to play certain characters. After playing all 10, you will unlock an 11th, a situation that you can play with friends or randoms.
In casual, the objectives and the spawn place or random for all players.
In competitive, players can choose where they spawn (attackers) or where they want the objective (for defense only).
Ranking System:
Personally one of my favorite ranking systems because you retain your rank even when you done play ranked games, unlike other games *cough cough* Overwatch *cough cough*
Bronze4 B3 B2 B1 Silver4 S3 S2 S1 Gold4 G3 G2 G1 Platinum3 P2 P1 Diamond
Lowest ---------------------------------------------------------------> Highest
You play ten placement matches at the beginning of the season and you will be placed based on how well you do, the majority of players are in Silver and Gold.
Community:
I'm not sure about others, but from my experience, competitive has nicer people than casual. When I make a good play in competitive, the enemy players will congratulate me, but when I'm in casual and make a good play, the enemy team will cuss at me. Feels bad man. *keep in mind these are my experiences*
Graphics:
Graphics are great, there are some settings that will DEFINITELY tank your pc, but they might have fixed that by now.
All maps look very beautiful at all ULTRA and you can definitely tell they took their time making it.
Controls:
Basically what you would expect with any shooter, except ctrl is lay down, alt makes your character make less noise, but makes you move slower. You can ping so that your teammates know what you want them to do.
DLC:
For me, since I love shooters with destructible environments, the DLC was very worth it. ALL PLAYERS get all the maps that Ubi comes out with, but they dont get the operators for free.
Season pass holders get more xp, more renown (in game currency), and higher chance of getting loot boxes (called Alpha packs). They also get all of the DLC operators for free, without paying any in game currency. It may feel that getting money in game is hard and takes a lot of grinding, but when you start playing more, you realize that you get a LOT of renown really fast.
Overall...
An amazing game with a lot of content. Well worth the money. Get it with a few friends, your experience will be so much better, whether you play it really competitively or just mess around.
Pros:
- Great graphics
- Great community
- Plenty of content
- A lot of variety
- Not repetitive
- Competitive
- Uplay has been fixed (at least I havent experienced any bugs with it)
Cons:
- Ubi doesnt always keep promises, they ended up not making a map they promised us
- Some glitches here and there

Without a doubt, one of the best Competitive shooters on the market at the moment. The wide range in operators bring variety on the table as you pick classes that suit your playstyle. Operators were designed to be played fast or slow paced, solo or group orientated and some were even designed to counter specific classes. The experience in multiplayer is comparable to counter strike in the sense that you work towards devising strategies and operator compositions on a mixture of maps to win 5-a-side matches. However, both games have focuses on different areas of progression. Counter-strike focuses more towards practicing reaction times, aiming and flicking (solo play), whereas Rainbow 6 is aimed at the best counter plays, strategies and map knowledge which can only work in team play. Intense moments are driven by the players ability to improvise, think fast and react to certain situations using their 400IQ brains due to the vast sea of game mechanics and small niches.
Needless to say, this game was built for the Rainbow 6 fans out there unlike other Ubisoft franchises that were made to milk. The develepors actually balance operators and revamped maps based of suggestions posted on the forums. Operation Health (Season 2, Year 2 patch) focused on network stability and connection to the servers. You can't run out of game content as every season offers new maps and operators to bring more styles of gameplay.

You're looking at a game that's unforgiving as Teleglitch, as pretty as Delver and as addictive as the old style arcade games. It's a glorious throwback to the older style of games that gave no craps about "lives" or "checkpoints" or anything of the sort. All you have with you is what you can scavenge off of enemies and buy from merchants in a procedurally generated dungeon full of creatures that would love nothing more than to eat your face. And your sword. And all of your money. A good emphasis on combat, but it also wants you to keep food, ammunition, water, and all of your basic resources in mind as well. There's meat in the caves just waiting to be sliced off rats and water to be turned from rusty faucets-which incidentally may be guarded by a really ornery skeleton mage or another plinky little rat.
Pros:
-Gorgeous style of 16x16 textures. This ain't Minecraft. This is more like Dungeons and Dragons. Memorable and well drawn.
-Really satisfying combat and animations. The slight head swing during attacks adds the perfect amount of immersion.
-The music is really fitting and enjoyable.  Somewhat scarce for variety, but that may be an early opinion. There's always just playing a YouTube playlist of other music you know ;)
-Local AND ONLINE MULTIPLAYER! Take yourself and 3 of your buddies to form that awesome adventuring party you've always wanted... until one of you is crushed by a rock and the other 3 are eaten by a minotaur. :D
Cons:
-Movement is a tad slow, especially on "slower" characters like Wizards. Best be ready to take on that skeleton firsthand or he may be up in your face before you can turn around to him.
-A lack of any sort of third person. This is a personal view, just because I'd like to see my bangin' Wizard in all of his fresh gear swing at an enemy instead of just seeing my weapon. Not a big deal, just a personal preference.
TL;DR
It's basically what NetHack would be if it wasn't text-based, not to mention a heck of a lot more accessible.
The only things I could even think of that would make it even better is perhaps an overworld or moar adventure after you beat the boss. Though the replay value of this single setup is enough to have you keep coming back for more brutal loot-grabbing for quite a while.

Though not entirely forgotten, LOOM is rarely the first game mentioned on a list of SCUMM engine masterworks. Make no mistake, however, because it is brilliant and immersive.
Unlike most SCUMM games, LOOM is rarely funny, and tries its very best to build a universe taht you can believe in. Also, its soundtrack (and various story elements) originate from the Tchaikovsky masterwork Swan Lake, serving to bolster the games lofty high brow tones and sense of believability.
Given its dirt cheap cheapness, its hard to think of a reason not to play through this once, simply to say you've experienced it.

LOOM is the work of art from Lucasarts, who back in the past were a dominant game developer. Released back in 1990, this point and click adventure game became one of the best known of Lucasarts enormous library.
You play the role of Bobbin, a wizard who is ready to see the council to become a full pledged wizard. As he gets to the council the higher elders are cast into swans so they can escape 'Chaos'.
It is up to the player to help the higher wizards return to the world and close the gates of chaos's world forever, where you must solve the hardest of puzzles, and of course master the grand instrument 'LOOM'.
This game is amazing. The music is absolutely stunning, soothing, and really captures the mood of the game. Sure, It's a hard game, and without writing down each spell you are stuck, but with that all checked, this game is definately worth It's weight in gold.
LOOM is a must buy for anyone who loves the point and click genre. It's a game which cannot be missed on Steam.

Title:
"Coma: Mortuary"
Developer(s)/producer(s):
N A GA Entertainment
Genre(s):
Adventure-Ambient, Horror
Mode(s):
Singleplayer
General info:
The introduction part of a trilogy, Coma:Mortuary is an indie-game released in May of 2014.
Gameplay:
The game is played from a first-person perspective, with the player controlling the character by looking around using the mouse and walking/running using the WASD/arrow keys.
Most exploration is done in a slow, walking pace and by using a flashlight - which can be toggled on and off - the player can light up their surroundings.
The narration of the plot is done through subtitles, which are read aloud by the character when reaching certain points and areas.
The game features a few point and click-interractions.
Story:
The story revolves around a man who has lost all meaning in his life, because of the tragic death of his girlfriend.
Drunk and depressed, he gets behind the wheel of his car, determined to commit suicide in the same spot where she died.
Somehow he miraculously survives the attempt, but falls into a deep coma.
After the violent crash, he finds himself in the world of the dead, which his soul now must wander...
My opinions:
When I first saw this game, I thought it looked promising. As a fan of horror-games in the style of "Amnesia: The Dark Descent" and "Outlast", this game seemed nice enough to buy.
However, I read a couple of reviews before purchasing it (and most of them were negative), but I decided to give it my own opinion.
First of all, this game is not very unique. It felt very familiar to play, since it features a well-used concept; exploring dark and haunting surroundings through a first-person perspective. I was almost immediately reminded of two other Indie-games that uses the same style of story-telling and progression: "Dear Esther" and - as said before - Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
However, don't expect any interesting or mind-blowing puzzles in this game. There are some "puzzles", although I wouldn't really want to call them puzzles, due to their simplicity.
The mechanics are simple and the only thing required by the player is basically walking and listening, with the occasional interraction with objects in the world.
Although I listened to everything, I didn't find the story very interesting and soon lost interest.
For being the first part in an intended trilogy, I think the developers made a mistake by not giving the story more time and focus.
To be fair, I suppose the story will flesh out and get more interesting in the following parts, but it would had been a smarter move to get the player properly introduced and not just scratch on the surface.
The developers of the game has also stated that the length of the game - I completed it in little more than an hour (including some Googling) - was due to the fact of it being an introduction, but I still think some more could have been done.
Also, for being a horror-themed game, I didn't find this game to be that much of a scare at all.
Sure, there was one jump-scare that got the best of me (+ a stressing sequence at the end), but overall this game failed to be scare me.
In the end - even though this game does have some of negative sides - I decided to give it a thumbs up.
Considering what you get as a player, the price of 0,99 Euros is completely reasonable and there is no need to wait for a sale in the case of this game (unless one is really mingy!).
I recommend this game to people who enjoy the horror-genre and who are willing to wait for the upcoming second and third installments (which are hopefully better and more enjoyable).

I don't do many reviews, but I feel that this game is getting a lot of undesvered and unwarranted hate.
Let me just go ahead and say that this is not Fight Night. If you go into the game trying to compare it to that, you'll be disapointed to say the least. But, if you go into it looking for a game where you can waste a few hours every now and then beating on peoples faces, you'll quite enjoy this. This is a mobile port, but I was surprised to see that it's not your crappy run of the mill port that you usually get. The graphics are decent, not mind blowing, the controls are very responsive, and it just feels good when you land hits on the AI. There is a career mode where you can create your own character and fight various other fighters in a bracket for a belt. Leveling up your character is quite fun. The more fights you win, the more points you get to help level up your character. You can even buy perks for your character to get more of an advantage. The fights do sometimes come down to button mashing, but there are also tactics involved in being proficient at the game.
There is also multiplayer. I've played a couple matches and it's great so far. I got my butt kicked in both, but I admit that it was a fun experience. There was hardly any lag and I connected immediately when another person was found. I was surprised that the multiplayer even worked considering how some of the big AAA titles that get ported to PC can't even get their multiplayer to function properly.
Now, are there things that this game can improve on? Yes, of course. Many. Camera animations, voice acting, more mini games to help boost your characters stats, better character customization, and just overall a lot more content can be added to the game. But, if the devs continue to improve upon this game, it can turn out to be something truly fantastic.
Edit: Yes, you can play against your friends in multiplayer. They just have to be ready to accept the invite quickly. I expect that to be fixed very soon though.

I will start off by saying this is not Fight Night. Fight Night is a 'Triple A' title from a company with a seemingly limitless budget at it's disposal. Don't be turned off by so many bad reviews that this game has to be Fight Night or it's junk. Fight Night is a full-priced title and this is a budget-priced title ($8 at the time of this writing). Some people need to set their expectations appropriately.
That said, I really enjoy this game. Part of it might be related to how long I have wanted a boxing game on PC. Part could also be due to having my expectations set so low by reading so many negative comments from others. I can say with certainty that I am glad I didn't listen to all of those comments. The game is not nearly the "button masher" that several people have made it out to be. Speaking of button mashing, you can also use the analog sticks to fight, which was a pleasant surprise to me, as I must have missed that bullet point prior to purchase.
There are already several accurate reviews already out there (look up "Courteous George"'s for example.His is spot-on in my opinion), so I won't go into great detail. I will just sum this up by saying it's not Fight Night, but it's not a button mashing half-hearted boxing game that was made in a few weekends as some sort of money grab. It is a quality budget title (yes, they can co-exist!) that I would have no problem calling Fight Night Lite, for those who cannot get past the Fight Night comparison. :-)

REAL BOXING- This may not be Fight Night but let's face it, EA Sports has all but abandoned the PC player with no sport titles except FIFA, what about Madden, NHL and Fight Night for PC, oh well.. I have this boxing game (REAL BOXING) on my iphone and I enjoy it, here on the PC version they have removed the micro transactions and given you the ability to move around the ring which is something that feels added because that part of the game just seems a little sluggish, there are no Muhammad Ali dancing masters here just flat footed Rocky Balboa type club fighters. But I have to say this is the best "PC" boxing game I have ever played and will gladly support it in hopes we get more Boxing games on PC. The graphics are good, the game supports both keyboard and controller inputs, I like that you can adjust the number of rounds and length of rounds.  There is a quick fight or a career mode, in career mode you can customize and train your fighter to improve his attributes, (although you cannot rename them* UPDATE- The Devs say you can rename the fighter when you create them, click in the box with the name and retype the one you want), there is also multiplayer which is nice and I look forward to. I do not care too much for the in game music or the lame commentator, however the punch sound effects are decent.  I would like to point out that although the Ring Card Girls do seem to have nice physics for their breasts the game really could work on Presentation and Fighter Damage. I would really like to see the DEVs work on and add various cuts, fighter fatigue, some swelling, better footwork, corner men working on fighters between rounds, camera men outside the ring, better fight commentary, a in the ring referee, and ability to change fighter name and face. I will say that I did have a great 12 round fight last night that was very close, I knew this going into the last round and was worried, I did win on points!  I am really hoping that the DEV Team continue to update this game, there is some great potential here and a wide open market for it, now if we could only get someone to make good hockey game! So if you are on the fence I would say get it, it's your best PC option for boxing right now and a decent game for the price.
