An interesting and enjoyable, if a bit rough, investigation game that actually allows you to do the investigation, rather then following the scripted sequence.
Environments and characters are beautiful and rich, while still holding quite firmly to their setting. the suspect profile mechanic is well suited to the game and shows off the obvious care that has been put into both in the polygons and in the planning. So well constructed are the models that it comes as a shock when Sherlock's pet basset hound, Toby, is added as a mechanic in later cases and is modelled somewhat inexpertly, leaving him with a model that is merely good among a cast of great.
The "deduction" system that acts as part hint system, part progress meter and part inventory system for clues is a unique addition to the genera. It's fortunately flexible enough to allow you to follow the case in your own route, revealing enough information to grease the mechanics, without washing away all the challenge.
The imagination system is a rich concept that is tragically underutilized. This unique mechanic allows Sherlock to simulate events and see how they would fit the facts. The 2 or 3 times it's used to it's fullest effect, it's dead-on in terms of tone, style and function, but it's often not utilized, utilized only minimally, or outright replaced by other, similar, less well polished mechanics.
suffers a little bit from adventure game syndrome, but a lot less than many other games; there were only 3 places where I felt a puzzle was contrived for progress reasons or arbitrarily gated, and most of those could have been easily lamp-shaded away with some dialogue exposing the in-universe explanation.  The path based lock-picking mechanic is a bit weird, but it's nice to have something other then literal bumping or rotational hotspot systems, and it works with the narrative of Sherlock "deducting" the lock open.
There are some technical issues as well. One puzzle was simply impossible to complete due to a crash to desktop, and I’ve seen reports of others seeing similar issues with other puzzles. Fortunately, these aren't game-blocking, thanks to the developers including a no-guilt skip button on nearly every puzzle, acting as a pressure valve on frustrating puzzles (and the rare crashy sequence).
the major complaint that I have is that there is clearly a "right" answer to every case, but the cases are structured so many of the different solutions fit just as tightly. the discovery of the "right" solution in some of the cases is partially trial and error, and partially jumping on the train of thought of the designer; in one case, quite literally. I often felt less like a masterful Sherlock, and more bumbling Watson, when it came to wrapping the case, comparing two or three equally explanatory, equally comprehensive, and sometimes equally incomplete, explanations for the same set of facts and clues.
of additional frustration, the punishment phase of every case includes a "moral choice" to absolve or punish the suspect. while there is no "right" answer, the choice is a false one, as which choice you make doesn't affect the ending of the case very much, but affects the epilogue substantially in non-obvious ways. the designers clearly had a "right" ending in mind and In a game all about the freedom to follow the clues and act upon the evidence, the decision to base the final ending upon unrelated choices from unrelated situations seems discordant and atonal.
In all, it's a highly polished, well built and interesting take on an area of culture that is largely absent from gaming.  At ~12 hours and ~US$30, it's well worth the little bit of frustration for the feeling of being the Great Sherlock Homes.

Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments is an absolutely beautiful strategy game where the player's choices ACTUALLY matter. It is simply a must-have for any strategy game junkie.
What I loved most about Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments (SHCP) is that
: interesting work, a bit of a challenge, a beautiful experience, and the feeling that the game isn't trying to force-feed you the right answer. The cases that you work on are distinct and memorable; there are no two cases that share similarities. As you work through the cases, SHCP offers just the right amount of hand-holding to keep the momentum and to really allow the player to feel like Sherlock Holmes. If you were to constantly be getting stuck, it would be easy to fall out of character. Finally, the true hallmark of a great deducation game was the fact that I felt compelled on multiple cases to hold off on accussing someone because I wanted to go revisit the locations, the evidence, and the documents.
what I want in a game like this an SHCP delivered.
Something SHCP uniquely provides is the opportunity for the player to make a wrong accusation and the game continues on. There's no "game going back in time" so you can't fix it, or even the game preventing you from making that decision. You are
to make mistakes and it will not penalize you for it. This really allows it to feel as close to reality as possible.
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Although I'm a huge fan of this game, there were some aspects that could have been better. Replayability for this type of game is unlikely- it's just the genre. However, I figured I would call it out for the buyers who may take this into consideration when buying. In SHCP, there is a very small story line that connects each case. It is so small that I actually forgot about it until the end. It seemed like an after-thought and could have probably been left out. Finally, there was one large missed opportunity to make the game even better. There is a mechanic to call out inconsistencies during conversation which is a real treat. However, if someone says something questionable the game makes it very obvious by slowing down time so Sherlock can speak up. I wish that wasn't the case. The small bits of information you gain from those integral parts should only be award to the people who noticed the lie (just like real life!)

Casual Labs
Casual Labs
is a picross/nonogram puzzle game developed and published by Casual Labs.
The story is basically non-existent: you are the curator of an art gallery, and, after a ghost has stolen the content of every painting, it is your job to paint them back (get it?) and re-open the exhibition. Since there are no cutscenes other than the initial one, I'm not gonna take this into account.
The game adopts a very colorful art-style that well suits both the tone of the different rooms full of paintings and the puzzles that you complete. While the paintings get bigger and more complex the more you paint them, most of them are still very simple and lack detail.
The game is essentially a digital version of nonogram:  are picture logic puzzles in which cells in a grid must be colored or left blank according to numbers at the side of the grid to reveal a hidden picture. In this puzzle type, the numbers are a form of discrete tomography that measures how many unbroken lines of filled-in squares there are in any given row or column.
I had never played this type of puzzle, and it has easily become my favourite: the constant calculation of numbers and the huge satisfaction of seeing a finished work make this game one of the most relaxing and easier to get games of the year.
The game's puzzles get increasingly difficult, but you can always choose the difficulty of each one (for example, for a 50x50 puzzle you can choose Normal to complete small 10x10 areas). They are never impossible to complete, and usually waiting a couple of minutes to clear your head up helps.
The soundtrack to the game is quirky and relaxing, making this game one to be picked up when you want to chill for 5 or 10 minutes.
The game features a total of 150 paintings to complete and 20 Steam achievements to unlock, giving you more thane enough content for its cheap price.
Overall, both fans and non-fans of puzzle games (especially nonogram/picross) will enjoy this game thanks to its simplicity, challenge, huge satisfaction and relaxing soundtrack.

I enjoyed my playthrough of Organ Trail.  As fun as it is, though, it still plays like an educational game from 20 years ago.  It's still a fun throwback, though, especially if you have fond memories of the original Oregon Trail.  If you want a more modern analog, though, try "FTL: Faster Than Light" instead.

The Men Who Wear Many Hats originally created Organ Trail as a flash game and after some fund raising they were able to release an expanded version of their original title on mobile devices and now PC. Organ Trail takes it's primary inspiration from the original Apple II iteration of The Oregon Trail and opens with your character encountering Clement, a fellow survivor who kick-starts your odyssey across a post apocalyptic United States. Much like the game it parodies, Organ Trail is about balance. You will need to ensure that your party is fed, rested and your car in tip top mechanical condition. With every mile that ticks by your parties health degrades as well as your trusty station wagon. Injury and disease are common occurrences on the road as evidenced by the many tombstones that can be encountered on your journey. These tombstones are not only reminders of the peril that face your party but also opportunities for upgrades and supplies. Party members can be bitten on your voyage and may require a euthanizing rifle blast to the head. Of course, if you are a misanthropic sociopath you could always off your healthy party members and not have to worry about keeping them fed and healthy. Dotting the trail to safety are landmarks and cities that allow your party to trade, buy and sell items, upgrade your car and purchase perks for your character. You can also take on jobs to earn some cash or supplies and chat the locals up for information.
Scavenging is often the easiest way to stay supplied on your journey. By opting to scavenge an open field pops up with random items spawning. Little green zombies home in on your character as you attempt to scoop up scrap for car repairs, food for nourishment, and cash for additional supplies. It's possible to defend yourself from the zombie onslaught while scavenging with a rifle. You must click and pull your mouse back which brings up a line of site on the screen which you can then spin while in a fixed position to dial your site in on the revolting rotting flesh heaps that converge on your position. Releasing fires and these controls take a bit of time to acclimate yourself to. A couple of seconds to reload between each round ensures a bit of tension as you scramble for goodies. Bosses are also randomly encountered on these scavenging excursions. They are more robust creatures that put up a bit more of a fight than your average walking corpse.
The jobs that are on offer use variations of these mechanics. Some require you to defend a position by taking cover and killing zombies before they reach your position, some have you locating an item in a scrolling field while zombies swarm and the last variant has you trading gun shots with others humans in fortified positions. These mini games can feel repetitive after a while since your character doesn't receive new weapons and enemy types are limited. The randomness of these events will keep you coming back however. Also, random encounters with biker gangs and hordes of zombie deer mix things up while in your station wagon. Random interactions with other travelers on the road also spice up the core game and offer a little bit of narrative. Prompts will appear that ask if you feel inclined to investigate something on the road. Doing so kicks off an old school adventure sequence that often results in a reward of some sort. This touch adds quite a bit of re-playability to Organ Trail. While the randomness of Organ Trail ensures a new experience every time it can  also lead to frustration. It's not uncommon for tragic events to occur in quick succession and take out a party member or even your party leader. It can be upsetting, perhaps off putting for some, when a well supplied and positioned expedition fails because of a bout with dysentery and broken ribs...
Ultimately Organ Trail: Director's cut is one of the best games to emerge from the zombie zeitgeist that has gripped popular culture over the past half decade.

The Organ Trail is a remake or Oregon Trail (that game everyone played in 4th grade computer class) with zombies, because everything these days must have zombies. The player manages supplies and health while rolling across America in a station wagon and making pit stops at settlements, where the player can do jobs for additional supplies. If you've played Oregon Trail, you pretty much know what to expect. It's a short game that can be completed in about two or three hours if you don't die, but you might be inclined to playthrough a few more times, though not much changes. The main difference from Oregon Trail is the zombie combat. It's simple and rather clunky, but it fits the style of the game well. The game is a fair challenge on normal mode, but should be manageable to most players as long as they are careful. For five dollars, Organ Trail is worth the money.

Who doesn't love a good zombie apocalypse? I know I do! And Organ Trail: Director's Cut delivers! The game play is reminiscent of Oregan Trail, a game where you ran a wagon across the Manifest Destiny? (been awhile since I played) to create a homestead for your family. This game is just like that except you and your family are going to a place called Safe Haven (I think, been awhile since I played this as well). Along the way you must manage resources and fight off the undead. This game can be very hard, and even though I logged several hours into this game I still haven't beat it. Gotta love the 8-bit graphics!

Organ Trail: Director's Cut is a surprisingly entertaining and fun game. It pays homage to the original Organ Trail and places it into the grime world of a zombie apocaplyse. The game consists of traveling across country and keeping yourself and your crew alive as long as possible. The plot is thus your own journey and your own interpretation of the visuals and events that take place. There are many unexpected events that can occur during a playthrough which gives this game high replayability (one playthrough can last a couple of hours).
The gameplay is good, but it does require you to learn a lot of it on your own. It's also a bit of a hard game. Shooting your gun requires you to drag and click the mouse which can be difficult. The game doesn't force you to do certain tasks and the freedom was a nice change gaming wise. The music is entertaining and fitting. Like the game, it's a mixture of humor and even a bit melancholy. The graphics are pixelated and minimal, which seemed to go well with game's theme and origin. It's really good and original for an indie game.
If you liked the original game, like zombie lore, or like games with strategy I would highly recommend.

Organ Trail is a unique throw-back parody type of the original Oregon Trail game. The idea behind the game is you are in a station wagon fleeing through the zombie apocalypse. It features everything an original Oregon Trailer game would have including trading, hunting and random events.
The game does a good job capturing the old-school vibe but at the end of the day doesn't really hold up. It's an okay playthrough the first time but there's really no reason to go back. It's a good game for a "goof" or if you really love the zombie genre but overall the game could be a lot more.
Replay value is pretty low and I wouldn't recommend the game.

Seriously that’s pretty much it and there’s no need for a fancy storyline.
If you’ve played Sudoku then the game’s pretty much self explanatory and in case you haven’t well the tutorial does one fine job explaining it.
Let’s get into it. You start of by facing a blank 5x5 field and you have to paint the right squares while leaving others blank. Later on in the game you’ll have to repaint bigger like 16x20.
The game even tells you not to guess but to think. Sure you could guess your way through the early levels and the smaller painting but good luck with that for the bigger ones.
Your only tool is a brush with black paint. You don’t have to worry about choosing the right color for the right square. All you have to do is to paint the right ones. The other
you have is the right click. If you right click a square you’ll cross it out so you know that you have it blank.
The game, just like sudoku, gives you some hints so you know where to start and which squares to paint.
On the outside of the field of your painting you see certain numbers. Let’s say the upper left row starts, vertically, with a 4. That means that you have to paint 4 squares in this row and so on.
Some fields have more than one number on the outside. The first number or in this case the outer number’s the same as before and tells you how many squares you have to paint. The second number however tells you that you have to leave some squares blank and then start painting again. Let me demonstrate on a 5x5 field.
Let’s say the upper left, vertically, row starts with a 2 and the next number is a 2 as well.
That would mean that you have to paint two squares, leave one open, and then paint again two.
So you see you get the hang of it pretty quickly.
The game does require a fair amount of brain power though. The beauty of it is that, just as the developers name implies, it’s really a casual game that you can pick up whenever you want.
You can even save your progress in your current painting and come back later to it to finish it.
The game itself has a cartoonish look to it and is quite fitting. The paintings however look great.
The pixel art in the game’s pretty fun, good looking and for me easily the best part of the game.
The early painting might not look the best but they’ll look better and better in the higher levels and way more complex.
Overall it’s a fairly nice and sweet looking game and the whole cartoonish art style was a good choice.
The music just fits and manages to stay in the background while also maintaining presence.
It’s not too subtle but at the same time not too intrusive.
I mean at the end of the day you’ll find yourself paying attention to the music and it will probably hinder you a bit but it’s not too bad.
The tracks used however are quite short which I personally actually like since the level that you’re stuck on won’t get too dull too fast.

This game is something else. Not many games start out as a buggy, glitchy mess, then approach the brink of complete destruction before being brought back out of the ditch and raised up as a truly enjoyable and popular title for years after its expected lifecycle. This game is not perfect, but it is so incredibly fun. The intense combat, with one-hit-kill headshots possible in any firefight, is absolutely gripping. The tactics possible in this game are extremely enjoyable, too. You can flank around maps, approach from virtually any angle, and use wall and hatch destruction to your advantage. It's pretty rad. The operators, while confusing at first, are all fairly balanced and equally interesting with the special gadgets and methods of attacking and defending that they bring to the team. Overall, this is a truly different and fresh FPS experience, despite not offering a lot to the table in terms of mind-blowing originality or norm-breaking when it comes to the genre.
The main criticisms I have are regarding some of the bugginess of the game still present. They have a few kinks left to iron out. The servers are also bad for how popular the game is, and even professional players with perfect connections notice bad hitreg and goofy stuff happening every once in a while. Overall, I tolerate this because most of the time, it works, and most of the time, it's great fun.
Also, having some buddies, even if they're randoms with mics, helps the experience immensely.

In a world where horror means gore, Slenderman and inappropriate jump scares, Coma:Mortuary is the scariest game that I have played in a long while.
The game uses atmosphere and sound beautifully to create a tense atmosphere, and pretty soon you feel helpless, wandering around endless corridors, enduring the terrors that appear. This is one of the few games that has appropriately used jump scares and managed to form chase scenes that go on for the perfect length of time – you don’t get away too easily, but you’re also not running for so long or regularly that you’re bored.
I have a few issues with this game, however. One of which is that you cannot run or even jog at will, which makes the game feel like it is dragging at times. Even a slightly faster walk that the player can use would help prevent this feeling of drag. Additionally, the puzzles were less “use your brain” and more “Does the hand appear when I hover over this?”. Finally, after the credits there is a sequence of rolling down a corridor, interlaced with scenes from the game (With added footsteps), so you feel like it might build up to something. Has the game ended? Is there another scene? No. It just loops. It doesn’t build up to anything and it doesn’t end, which ruined the end of the game for me when I was waiting for it to take me back to the menu screen (as most games do when they are done). So just be aware of that.
But overall I did really like this game and I would recommend it.
If you want to see a bit of game play to consider buying it for yourself, I have linked my playthrough of this below.
If you like walking very slowly through Unreal Engine levels while a narrator reads out a script with some at times awkward English then this is the game for you.

I felt that I had to write this review.
Before I get to the "This game is absolutely undefeatable by any other games in any aspect in the gaming history", I want to clarify that I'm really not an arcade fan. I've been trying so hard to get myself into arcade but it's just not my type. However, this game is able to incorporate so many different aspects of various genres of games into one simple, 2D, pixilized, and story-rich game. The thing that surprised me the most was when this game used a common steam feature to actually "play" me dead. I'm not spoiling too much here so you should find out by yourself by playing this game.
This game isn't long. It took me 3.1 hours to beat it without using any community guide(I spent 7 hours on my first undertale run). The puzzles are fun and not extremely hard.
I'm not sure if the game designer was trying to present a philosophical reminder to gamers or purely just to show how desperate he was to make a good game. I'll leave this to be answered by the designer himself.
Also, great soundtrack. No offense to anyone who loves this game, but I can actually find a lot of similarities between Pony Island, Lisa the painful, and Undertale. Since both Lisa and Undertale were earthbound-inspired, I wonder if there is a tiny bit of connection between Pony Island and Earthbound as well. However, it is just my assumption. That said, all three games have their own merits and extremely positive reviews.
So far as I know, there is at least one direct reference to an Undertale character in Pony Island(if you do the required thing).
Final reminder before you play this game: Don't judge a game based on its graphics.

Organ Trail is nothing short of a fun realization of the old classic with the tried and true zombie twist.
At first glance it's easy to scoff at this game and even write it off, but presentation shouldn't fool you. Once in the game, none of that will matter as the solid gameplay, comedy aspect, and nature of the genre take hold of you. You'll be crossing fingers as you push through the hordes hoping they don't take notice. The scavenger side missions are also gratifying, but the controls are a bit awkward, making it more of a flustering challenge than maybe it warrants.
After a few runs, things get a bit repetitive, but that's the nature of the game. It's no short haul to make it across country and there's plenty in between that'll you need to survive.
I would definitely recommend playing this if you havent, and especially if you are old enough to have enjoyed the original Oregon Trail.

Do not be put off by all the negative reviews comparing this game to Electronic Art's Fight Night series of games. Fight Night is a AAA Sports title created by a developer who has a long history of developing boxing games, and it costed 6-times as much as this game. Of course Fight night going to be better, but that does not mean Real Boxing is not an enjoyable game worth it's $10 price tag.
Real Boxing Is more arcade than simulation, and there is not a lot of depth, but the action is fast paced and the multiplayer mode should be entertaining for hardcore boxing fans, at least in short spurts.  The single player career mode is basic, and there are not all that many different characters to fight against, but the mode exists. There are options for editing the appearance of your boxer, but you do not seem to be able to edit your boxer's name, which is a little bit annoying.
Aside from that, there are also the standard training mini games that you would expect to see in a boxing game. These mini games require you to press the right-stick in a certain direction in time with the on-screen cues. As you might guess the mini games become repetitive very quickly (but so did the mini games in fight Night).
The in-ring boxing action is not very simulation-like, but it's not exactly the mindless button-masher other reviews make it out to be.  You can throw all the punches you would expect (using either an anolog stick or the buttons) but there is no option for using dirty tactics such as headbutts or low blows. You can grab and clinch your opponent, but only when your energy drops below a certain level. Blocking is done with a single button, and it automatically blocks head or body shots as needed. You can also use a perfectly timed press of the block button to slip an opponents punch, creating a slow-motion effect allowing you an extra moment to throw a counter punch. There is no bobbing/weaving. There is no way to take a knee if your getting pummled, and there is no option for switching from orthodox to southpaw stance.
Pros:
- Fast paced action with easy to pick-up controls
- Decent looking graphics and presentation for a budget title
- Online multiplayer boxing matches
- Commentary is repetitive but sounds good for an arcade boxing experience
- it's the only (somewhat realistic) boxing game on Steam
Cons:
- Boxer movement/footwork is not very smooth
- Small roster of characters - No real world boxers
- Short/uninspired single-player career mode
- No matchmaking options for the online multiplayer mode
The bottom line is that it's not exactly a great game, but it's the best boxing game I have on my PC. The game will not have much appeal for most gamers, but hardcore boxing fans will probably find it fun being able to swap leather with other players now and then. It's not Fight Night Champion, but it's actually better than I had expected it to be.

"Just Hero is Just a platform" is a sentence that describes fully enough the game. The classic platform mechanics are always there making it quite intuitive to play, you run, jump, pick up stuff, you take down enemies by jumping on them and some surfaces hurts (water, lava and stuff like that). Just Hero has a very cartoonish-pixellous look which might be fine except for the fact that the main protagonist and few characters around have some kind of sad and wrinkly look that kind of doesn't fit the supposedly happy mood of the game.

I didn't finish the game, so keep that in mind
Have you ever wanted to like a game, that looks fun and you hope it really is, but in the end you got bored and never finish it? I'm sure you have. This is the case with Enclave for me. After 6 h (around half of the game, I think) I just stop playing it. The game is not bad, but few things I don't like, contribute for my boredom.
For such an old game it have a lot of video options. Resolution, separated menus for graphics and textures, sliders for sound and music and even syncing with refresh rate. Last but not least, you can rebind keys, use a controller, on and of damage number indicator and so on. But make no mistake, the game is ugly, but not unbearably ugly. Graphics didn't age very well, textures are bad, enemies tends to jump really high, levels don't have enough details, but it's an old game, so it's expected.
The story is simple – you have to save the world and it is the worst part of the game. There somewhat interesstig backstory, but the developer didn't capitalized the fun premise. In the end, one can say it is absent. Even other reviews pointed this. It is cliché fantasy story, not develop enough.
So, next is gameplay. It is where I had some fun and there is a lot to talk about. Here you can find some interesting ideas – character classes and fighting system. Let's dive in.
The game have two campaigns – Light and Dark. As far as my knowledge, first you have to start with the Light and beat it to unlock the Dark. Enclave is hack 'n slash third-person action game with options for first-person, focusing on strategic combat for melee classes. If you enter thinking that this is similar to Devil May Cry or Dynasty Warriors, you will be killed really fast. The combat is slow and methodical. I think the best comparison is Dark Souls, but probably not that hard. Your shield is valuable as much as your weapons. The game is tough, but I can say with some patience every challenge can be overcome. The character you start is a Knight class. He is using melee weapons primarily. When you enter a battle, it's with your shield raised. You have to keep track of enemy hit patterns to find when is the best time to strike. You have to be patience. Interesting thing here is that size matters. What I mean is you may raise your shield, but your feet and head are not protected. You have to consider where to put it. In the beginning you will encounter short imp-like creatures and lowering the shield is crucial and vice versa. If your characters is short, taller enemies are easy. You can even use the terrain at your advantage, if you manage to get the enemy on higher ground. When using a melee weapon you can do a three hit combo and with every hit your damage increase, but it leaves open for attack. So, it's up to you to decide do more damage or hit once and bring up the shield. It's risk-reward situation. Depending on your movement, you make a different swing with the weapon and this add to the strategic gameplay.
Through the most of my play time, I used the Knight class. At some point I decide to see the other classes. What I found is range classes are boring. The combat with them is like any other third-person shooter and they weren't interesting as melee classes.
Every character have a melee and range weapon, but depending on the class, they are specialize in certain play style, so don't expect Knight class, for example, to get the best range weapons and vice versa. And speaking of classes, they are total of 12, but you don't get them right away, you will unlock them by playing the game. I don't like that. Why? What is the point of that? Unlock them from the beginning. But there is one interesting thing about that. You don't level up by getting XP. You just have to gatter gold for new gear. And since this is the case, the dev decide after each level, for all unlocked classes, you will get additional money, so you can swap character before entering a level and not playing the whole game again. New gear is unlocked by beating a level. This is all it required. They don't have statistic, so i assume, if it's cost more, it's better. Weapons include swords, crossbows, maces, bows, axes and so on. Some classes have can equip additional stuff like bombs, different types of arrows and so on.
One of the things I don't like is the AI. I feel enemies can walk only in a straight line and when get the chance I use this the get them to suicide or to stuck in the environment. The other thing is range enemies. Their projectiles can go through solid surfaces and it was annoying. The third things is the level design. Building after building after building. There are some places like vulcano and small harbor town. Although their design is somewhat diverse, in the end I find it boring and not very inspired.
Enemies are not very creative. Small imp-like creatures, orc without armor, orcs with armor and shield, big ogres, spell casting enemy and so on. But most disappointg are the bosses. I only saw two. They also have uninspired design and they are boring to fight.
Sound design is meh. Noting to remember. Music feels like typical for fantasy game, sound fx are okay and the voice acting is average. Don't expect something groundbreaking or something to remember here.
I'm somewhere in the middle about this game. Although old, there is something to see, something to enjoy. Melee characters are worth playing in my opinion. Everything else is like sound and level design, some of the classes, the AI are average and story – completely forgetable. I couldn't bring my self the finish the whole game. I almost reach half of the journey and got bored, so take my opinion with a pinch of salt. Nothing exciting happened during my time with the game. There is enough here that pushed me away, but it still have my cautious recommendation. Get it on sale. Why I recommend it? Because I can see something that others might enjoy, but not me. Melee classes have more interesting play style, than the others. The game is not garbage, I had some fun, but there is nothing here that could hold my attention for a long period of time. Maybe someday I will revist it to see if I can enjoy it more and finish it.

I've played many, many point-and-click mystery games, and many games based on Sherlock Holmes. This is, by far, one of the best I've ever encountered. It's seamlessly designed, beautifully crafted, amusing, intriguing, and unique. So, full and absolute recommendation.
The true moment where this game shines above all other Sherlock-ian homages is in the final moments of each case. Once you've collected all the evidence and pieced together the puzzle, you're presented with multiple "conclusions," that is, multiple theories of the crime that can fit the facts and evidence. While collecting all the evidence isn't too difficult, figuring out which theory is correct relies entirely on the player interpreting the facts, leaving you, and you alone, to make that final decision.
What's more, even once you've made your decision, you're given yet another choice: how will you close the case? And here, there's no correct, or incorrect, answer, leaving the ending of each story entirely up to the player, dependent on what you believe is the appropriate moral choice.
The combination of strict deductive methods and a very true-to-the-source portrayal of Holmes with this moral ambiguity actually got me to care about what I was doing in the game, to pay attention to the dialogue and plots moreso than just to solve the case. That, to me, is the best win a mystery series could accomplish.
However - PARTIAL SPOILER ALERT BELOW -
- NO REALLY THIS MAY RUIN A REVEAL FOR YOU -
- LAST CHANCE -
I have one caveat, concerning one, single scene, which happens to be the penultimate scene of the game and not actually associated with any of the individual cases.
There's ... some attempt at an overarching plot thread that lurks in the background of the cases and cumulates in a final confrontation after the last case is solved. You end up sitting through a cutscene that involves a militant revolutionary group explaining their motivations, which is very anti-aristocracy. If you lean left, you might call it a group of Victorian-era "99%" protesters. If you lean right, you might call them communist terrorists.
Either way it comes across as more than a little preachy, especially since, no matter what option you pick, you can't actually arrest them. (I could be wrong, because I haven't replayed the game with every alternate moral choice path to see if being a hard case could change that last scene, but I highly doubt it would. If you can arrest them, it's still weird, though, see below.) It's not because the game forces you to sympathize with them: it's stated, if you decide against the group, that Holmes lets them go because he's irritated at the person who needs to deal with them. Still, the fact that you sit through the leader's heated defense of his cause and then can't have them all arrested, and the wording choice in the final scene, indicates a very strong political preference on the part of the game designers.
Normally I would shrug and move on. It's their game; if I had fun playing it, and was engaged by the story, then a political or philosophical message is just an interesting element of the experience. The problem here is that the rest of the game is SO very wonderful by comparison, and so very well crafted to give the player that control over moral choice. Being given this ultimate choice that doesn't really represent a moral choice undermined the entire system.
Morover, Holmes is a very anti-political character. Anyone who's read the original stories will tell you that Holmes is the kind of man who has memorized the law and lives by it, and doesn't give a damn about politics. Much as modern interpretations might give him depth of feelings or awarenesses, the classic Holmes, which this game was trying very much to emulate, would never allow a group of people who admitted to planning and organizing a large-scale violent act to flee in order to potentially commit more violent crimes.
FINAL VERDICT -

text:
As puzzle games go, Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments is fairly tame. As tedious as the achievement for reaching all conclusions is (if that matters), the game is worth the experience - well thought-out characters, realistic motivations and a chance to play at being the world's greatest detective.
There are six individual cases, or chapters if you will, each with a unique crime for you to solve. Gameplay involves first gathering the evidence in the form of point-and-click / exploration. Suspects and other people are interviewed. During the course of doing this, sometimes additional information about clues you find can only be discovered by researching Holmes' archive, or by conducting an experiment, or even by chemical analysis. All of these actions combine to give you deductions, which take the form of facts floating around inside Holmes' brain, visualised by neurons firing between each other.
The next part is what I find to be the most fun though. Just having these facts floating around inside your head isn't enough. You have to put them together. For example: a person needs a certain
to wield a harpoon properly, also you know the victim was
. Put them together, and you conclude the murderer must be physically strong. Put enough of the facts together and you'll be able to conclude who the guilty party is.
It comes as no surprise that there are various conclusions for each chapter. Each of them makes its own kind of logical sense, and is fun to experiment with. There is even a 'correct' answer to each of the cases - and the opportunity to check whether you have the right one or not is entirely optional, meaning nothing is given away without your wanting it. The only problem I find with replaying for different endings is the necessity of starting the case over again from scratch - there is no option to simply replay your deductions from near the end of the case. This unfortunately makes for a bit of a grind as some cases have numerous location changes - many of which are for as little as a single item - meaning you will grow bored of seeing the interior of Holmes's carriage very quickly. One case has as many as six different endings.
More on the gameplay. I've already mentioned finding objects, interrogation, drawing deductions. In addition, there is lockpicking (an interesting take on a concept rife in so many games today), imagination (a little-used idea that works well to break up other gameplay elements), and there are also conversation events whereby Sherlock catches people out in lies. Leaving people gaping like fish and floundering for words is very enjoyable.
The cast for voice-acting is excellent, although I think it is soured by Robinson's aussie accent. There are two aussies in this game - while Lady Brackenstall sounds more genuine, Robinson sounds exaggerated, a bit too much like Steve Irwin for my liking. Perhaps for the time-period (1890s) this is accurate, and perhaps it adds to his character, but I just found it too over-the-top.
The visuals are mildly impressive. While nothing stands out as particularly fantastic, the landscapes and rooms depicted are done well enough that you feel transported to late 19th Century England. Typewriters and the general hubbub of Scotland Yard offices is one of the better sounds.
In closing, I should point out that the game is inspired by Arthur Conan Doyle's stories, and that
is a reference to Fyodor Dostoyevsky's novel of the same title - giving the gamer the opportunity to find the right culprit, and to make the moral choice of condemning or absolving their actions.

Interesting take on Sherlock Holmes and what choices he makes in cases. What is the aftermath? How does it affect his career, or more importantly, his conscience? Most games portray Sherlock as an unfeeling super-sleuth. Nice to see some humanity.
Also, he doesn't treat Watson like absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥as in
.

Depressing, but not quite as depressing as FTL.
This is actually a far better game than Oregon Trail, or most zombie games for that matter, because the bad luck can be remedied with good performance in the arcade sequences. There are several, and they aren't afterthoughts. They're actually fun minigames. Unlike the old action interludes they parody, they're designed to frighten and challenge while still giving you a fair shake at success. Despite its appearance, this is a new videogame first and a retro homage last. Its underlying design is sophisticated and graceful.
Much has been said about the awkward aiming controls, but they are like some ancient forgotten system unearthed by gaming archaeologists. I got used to them quickly, without ever becoming too comfortable. They add a manageable awkwardness to the combat encounters that I enjoyed.
My one objection was the jarring experience of losing outright when my main character died, something I did not expect after finding myself in a groove of what seemed like a classic party adventure. This game feels more like a successor to Might & Magic, Starflight, and indeed FTL than it feels like like a one-joke riff on a piece of pop nostalgia, and I was a little bummed to just have the story end with four of my party still alive. Then again, there's something to be said for never finding out what happened to those guys. It's a little haunting, a bit more of what we fear about death than usually makes it into a game.
Two bonus stars for an appropriate and pretty chiptune soundtrack, good production values, modern resolution options, and for somehow being much easier on the eyes than screenshots might lead you to believe.

tl;dr version first:
+ Solid graphics that aged pretty well
+ Serviceable music
+ Okay level design
(Yes, the only positives are still just "OK" and not great...)
- Literally everything else:
- Terrible clunky controls
- Overly simplistic and boring combat
- Generic medieval fantasy setting
- Even more generic story
- Voice acting ranges between mediocre to comically bad
Detailed version:
Someone gifted me a free key, so I went in with an open mind and low standards, and... it's still pretty terrible. I absolutely don't mind older games, and still play games from several generations ago and still enjoy them, but this is beyond janky. The controls are atrocious, even for the time. Older games like Soul Reaver and Ocarina of Time still manage to have fluid and serviceable melee combat and character movement and they aren't even necessarily purely combat-driven; this  is a hack-and-slash with little else than combat, yet it moves horribly stiffly, the hack and slash combat is repetitive and boring, and the hitboxes are a total joke. Ranged combat is even worse, aiming is clunky and painful. I didn't even get far enough to try any kind of magic, though I unlocked a druidess (who honestly looked more like a stripper than any kind of priestess or adventurer) but I was too bored to bother continuing.
I don't know why this is tagged as an RPG, this is a hack-and-slash action/adventure game (which isn't necessarily a bad thing, I love those too, but don't go in expecting an RPG); there are no RPG elements such as stats, character progression, looting, story choices, etc. Missions are linear; you buy the best loadout you can afford, and go in (again I don't have a problem with that kind of structure, but don't expect tons of exploration or non-linear progression or anything like that), and levels are short, with okay level design I guess. The only gameplay element are killing boring monsters, sometimes jumping, and picking up gold and keys or flipping switches. Oh yeah, the second mission is an escort mission, and gods help you if the NPC AI decides to walk in straight into the monsters and get himself killed. Because yep, that can happen. Oh, you activated a checkpoint, and died? Cool, you lose a bit of gold, but respawn with everything else exactly as is, which in theory would be fine except... meanwhile monsters are attacking your NPC escort and you've failed the mission before getting back to where you were.  Oops?
Don't waste your time on this mediocrity. Even if you're really really starving for an old-school hack-and-slash game, there are tons of better options out there. Like, say, any of the Ys games, or Dark Souls, Dragon's Dogma, Salt and Sanctuary, hell even the otherwise mediocre Bound By Flame and Lord of the Fallen are still much better than this.

One of the best geometric puzzle games I've ever played. I like games that throw you into gameplay with no explanation, but allow you to figure out the "rules" by trial and error. Klocki is a very pleasant game to play, with beautiful smooth graphics in soothing colours. There are a variety of mechanisms that get introduced as you progress through the levels: rotation, swapping, etc. and it's fun to figure them out. After a new mechanism is introduced, it starts you off easy, and then begins to combine them into quite complex puzzles that are challenging but not frustrating. It's not entirely clear whether there is only one solution for each puzzle, or if you simply have to find a solution that meets the criteria, but it's fun to think about different ways you could solve it. I could play this game for hours, and was just thinking "I hope this game never ends" when it brought me back to the beginning. Aww. This game is similar to Zenge, which was equally calming and entirely too short for my liking. As with that game, I would love to see some Achievements to make the game even more replayable. For example, complete a puzzle in under X number of moves, or complete a puzzle without triggering the error buzzer, etc. Overall, this is an absolute bargain, and either a good way to kill a few hours, or a nice way to infuse your day with a few rounds of brain teasers. More! More! More!

You could spend a dollar toward a good cause, like a food drive, or spend it on this game and have 60 minutes of  some of the smoothest-slick puzzle gameplay you've had in ages. You could also do both, but I'm not assuming you have that kind of money.

This is not a city builder game. It's a city builder simulation. The gameplay is very minimal - most of the time it's fiddeling with traffic. Which is great! It's your own self-inflicted puzzel. Traffic quickly becomes a nightmare if you don't know what you're doing (I still don't), but its still a ton of fun to build a city and watch it grow.
If you're someone who doesn't like mods, or "cheats," I can't recommend this game. By defualt, you start in an empty map with absolutly nothing. You're supposed to start small and branch out, getting access to more tools as your population grows. But those tools they hide away are vital to run a functioning city, and you'll eventually have to bulldoze your entire starting zone because it is so inefficent compared to everything you can build at high pop levels. Theres a really simple fix to all this: pop on the infanite money "mod" built into the game and download a mod off the workshop to have everything unlocked from the start so you can get straight to building a city. When you feel confident about your layout, you can always turn off infanite money, but by that point  you'll be swimming in cash.
I still love it. I think you will too - but that really depends on what you want out of your city builder. Skylines pushes you hard into one type of city - one of clean energy, tight motropolises, and a service economy. Industry is there, sure, but it really discourages you from using those. What it does do, it does well.

I started playing this game back in PSP, and I must say, I don't regret re-buying it on Steam in the slightest. Nevertheless, my review shall cover things for those who haven't played the game yet.
First, the story. If you don't mind slow-paced story in exchange for
world-building, then this game is for you. Why? Trails in the Sky takes it sweet time not only to develop its rich world and main characters, but also its truckload of NPCs. Each of them has their own story as well, making the game feels lively and vibrant.
(Oh, and if you want stories with well-written female characters? Yes, this game is for you!)
Second, the visual presentation. Falcom clearly put A LOT of love into the game's world and characters; see how detailed the character models are? The buildings? Those airships? The little road signs that you see along the way? One of the reasons why I don't regret replaying Trails in the Sky in PC is because of those small details, which help me to appreciate its world more.
Next, the gameplay. The traditional turn-based/strategy mix fits the game's overall flow well; not too fast-paced, but also not to the point of being slow and boring. Also, despite its apparent simplicity, this game can easily kill you if you're tactless enough...which is something I learnt in REALLY hard way in a few of the boss fights. In addition, the sheer number of missable stuffs in this game gives good replay value.
As for the soundtrack, I don't think there's anything to be said. It's Falcom, so it's bound to be awesome. ;)

Given the paucity of JRPGs available for the PC, I really wanted to like this game, but I am unable to reccommend it. TLDR the game is too steeped in JRPG tropes, and ultimately the story is a bit too by the numbers to my liking. It's possible that the coming Second Chapter will be a much better experience...I will wait and see.
For reference, I enjoyed a lot of the SNES era JPRGS, as well as many of the PS1 era games. Some I played for the first time decades after thier release, so arguably nostalgia plays a lesser role in my enjoyment of the older JPRG games.
pros:
-massive amounts of interactive text: NPCs say lots of unique stuff, which changes before and after events. you can buy newpapers, read books. it's a pretty extensively realized world.
-interesting battle/magic system: timing when and where spells and actions play out gives the game a nice layer of strategy to it. the orbment magic system lets you mix and match spells, which is slightly different for each character based on thier orbment grid.
-reasonable difficulty/leveling progression: the enemies were never really too easy or too hard when I played through, which I thought was impressive.
cons:
-boring characters: all of the charaters adhered to anime tropes, with minimal depth to them. Estelle is the tomboy and determined genki girl. Joshua is the love interest with a dark past. Schera is the  MILF-y character who drinks and likes sadomasochism. and so on. Even the plot twists and backstory that's revealed were common anime trope twists and backstory.
-smoldering and sluggish story: most of the reveals do not surface until very near the end of the game.
-boring quests and sidequests: the gameplay in this regard boiled down too frequently to traditional MMORPG type quests, where you fetch me this item, and kill this one monster.
-uninteresting art design: the game leans heavily on common fantasy anime style, the game fails to stand out from its predecessors and peers.
-magic system progression is broken: for whatever reason, some (maybe most) high level magic spells would not scale sufficently to warrant thier use. I constantly relied on low level spells because they simply did more damage per MP use.

Another Sherlock Holmes adventure game, where as the famous detective , you have to solve 6 varied cases such as thefts, murders and missing persons.
+ Awesome presentation, best looking adventure game i have ever played, especially the character models are some of the best i have seen in gaming.
+ The cases you have to solve are varied and the atmosphere is dark, grim at times, the writing and dialogues are excellent.
+ Great soundtrack and voice acting.
+ Gameplay wise you use the famous skills of Sherlock : collect clues, examine them, use your tools at Baker's street, interrogate suspects at crime scenes or at the Scotland Yard, reconstruct crime scenes and use intuition skills to discover hidden clues, use your loyal dog , use disguises and much more to collect all the evidence and from your deductions name the guilty parties. Apart from discovering who is guilty you have to make moral decisions as to what their fate will be and at the end of each case you get to see the percentage of other people's choices. There is great freedom of choice, since after gathering some evidence you can choose who is guilty or continue playing , since most of the times you have to go beyond the obvious and collect more clues to find the truth.
+ Unless you do everything right in each case from the first time , there is some replayability, i had to replay 2 of the cases since i was biased the first time playing them .

This is one of the most polished adventure games i have ever played, definitely the best adventure game of the year (although my heart still prefers the dreamfall chapters) and one of the best of the last years. Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments Review
Yes Watson, it is elementary.... we have a very solid 3rd person Detective game here.
It is certainly an improvement on the previous instalment of the series with better gameplay, better graphics, better deduction system, but still some room for improvement.
I won't be doing a detailed review on this one as it will inevitably create spoilers. I will however note that each case has several possible conclusion (wrong and correct ones) and it is possible to get carried away by a wrong version or uncertainty. If however you are paying attention to all clues (which are not that hard to find) and apply common logic you would not have issues with this game, you will enjoy it.
Time wise, if you go slow and read through all the in-game materials you are looking at 15-17 hours of gameplay.
On the negative side I can say that once you get hold of it the game becomes easy, controls are a bit glitchy, and there is a lack of British humour (there is some, but could have been more).
All in all this is a solid detective game that flows in an interactive story of each individual case you work on. 7/10

A very pleasant surprise. This game surprised me by having a pretty sophisticated way that events can chain and collide to produce many different results. For fans of the stories, it's a great reimagining. I can't say for sure if it will impress those who aren't familiar with Doyle's books but simply like adventure games, but I think it ought to work for both kinds of players.
As with any adventure game, there are occasional snags where you think the elements are uncovered but the game requires one more tiny nudge to prove that you've understood. Those rare occasions can be a little frustrating, but aside from that it's a very polished indie game with a lot to recommend it. Some people have complained that they weren't entirely sure if they'd got the right man/woman at the end of each case - if that happens to you, you probably haven't solved the crime correctly. I think it's good that the game allows you to get it wrong without telling you plainly, and only shows you that you were right if you were right, but not everyone will see that as a strength.

Any Sherlock fans must buy this game immediately.  I wish I didn't even buy it during the sale to encourage the publishers to continue their brilliant work.  It allows you to step into the mind of the great detective and solve the cases yourself.  My only complaint was that some of the case conclusions were a bit too easy, but otherwise the difficulty was perfect in that it wasn't too mind numbing but not a breeze either.  Thank you for taking the time to portray Sherlock and Watson faithfully to Arthur Conan Doyle's creation.

In my opinion, this Sherlock Holmes game is the best Frogwares has created to date. I found myself fully engaged and as a Sherlock Holmes' fan, utterly delighted.
Pros: -Shorter cases. I enjoyed the longer cases in previous games, but felt the shorter cases were easier to wrap my mind around and get a complete sense of the whole mystery. It was also easier then to sift through evidence and come to a sound conclusion.
-Getting to come to your own conclusion. In the previous games, Holmes guided you through. In these games, you ARE the detective. And you can get it wrong. It makes the game all that more intense since I know I can lose.
-The ease of assessing information. The file system makes it easy to look over all the information you have gathered. The deduction board was is an ingenious way to put the clues together. You make links between different information and evidence to form conclusions and there can be multiple conclusions.
-The mysteries are solvable. I do not like it when a mystery game's answer comes out of nowhere and you feel that you never had a chance to solve it. The mysteries in this game are all solvable. If you go over the clues, review evidence, reread dialogue and think about it, you can get the right answer. I got all but one of them correct. I had determined to go over all the evidence thoroughly before deciding on a final answer and that helped. But still, pressing the button to launch my conclusion always had me nervous! I looked back over all the evidence of the one mystery I solved incorrectly and realized what erroneous conclusions I had drawn.
-In my opinion, the best addition is the morality choices. In Conan Doyle's stories, Holmes often makes moral decisions concerning the fate of the culprits. He does not consider himself necessarily bound by conventional law. The morality choices were an added layer that made the game all the more real and like the Holmes stories.
-Two of the stories are Conan Doyle stories. They were modified a little, but not enough to take away Conan Doyle's original plots. I am a Conan Doyle fan and so enjoyed getting to play his own stories. One was an obscure enough story that I recognized it, but didn't remember much about it and so had to figure it out along with all the other mysteries. The other I knew very well and flew through the case, but it was still fun to be in the story.
-The variety of the cases. Nothing was redundant. Each case was unique and completely held my interest.
-Telescope easter egg. So funny.
Cons: -As someone who adores the Conan Doyle stories, I didn't like the characterization of Mycroft. It seems the thing these days in recreated Holmes stories and shows to make Sherlock and his brother antagonists. They just are not like this in Conan Doyle's stories. At one point, Sherlock tells Watson in one of the Conan Doyle stories that he has gone to Mycroft at times for help. And if Mycroft were to show up asking Sherlock for help, he would not be indifferent.
-The characterizations of Watson and Holmes also suffer a little. Watson is turned more towards the bumbling idiot Watson. Sherlock is made more aloof and cold than in previous games.
-In one of the mysteries, a clue is worded in such a way that it can lead the player to an incorrect conclusion. I decided to ignore the wording in light of other evidence and that led me to the right answer, but I was worried it would be incorrect because of the clue wording.
-There is less freedom to explore your environment than in previous games.  The game boxes you into an area and if you wander to the edge throws the map in your face. That was a little off putting and reminded me I was playing a game. I would have rather Holmes had said something like, "There is nothing interesting over there."
-Final screen. Once you've finished the whole game it seems like there is going to be a cut scene, but nothing happens.

I really enjoyed this game. The graphics are beautiful and the Victorian settings look and feel realistic without any noticeable anachronisms. Each episode has its own look and feel with a different theme: Roman baths, elaborate gardens, wealthy estates, etc. The dialogue and voice acting are excellent.
The puzzles aren't hard, so the game moves along at a pleasingly quick pace. I only had to consult a walkthrough once. This would be a really nice game to try out as a first foray into the adventure genre.
It's very fun to try and put the clues together at the end of the case to make the right decision. I actually decided incorrectly on one of the cases, so it's not always a completely obvious foregone conclusion. You do have to think.

Pony Island is the worst type of game to take itself seriously (and yes, it does). It practically mocks the player's intelligence and is one of the worst horror games ever made.
Creepypastas are made fun of in many corners of the internet, mostly for their absurd clichés and in general terrible writing. The average story is about a "relatable" teenager who gets a mysterious video game from a yard sale. After playing it, lo and behold, the game is incredibly corrupt and features hyper-realistic blood, satanic symbols, and a klefka laugh somewhere. Then the player's model starts begging for help as the narrator begins to vomit uncontrollably.
The criticism is fair. Horror should not derive from explicitly featuring gore and signs from the devil. It should derive from fear of the unknown, well written imagery, and a proper atmosphere. Because of this, most people can recognize and ridicule bad creepypastas for their terrible interpretations of what horror fiction is. Good horror games such as Amnesia know to stay away from the ideas utilized by Creepypastas, and instead use the human's inherent fear of the unknown to its advantage (obviously not all creepypastas are completely terrible, the vast majority are). Pony Island clearly does none of these things. The inability for people to see these issues in Pony Island is beyond me.
The game attempts to create horror by contrasting the kid-friendly original facade of the game with the real evil side of the game, filled with crying death ponies and messages by the devil. But this "horror" is incredibly immature for the same reasons that make creepypasta immature. The game again and again reminds the audience that "it was made by Satan himself", and it calls the player childish derogatory terms ala "mere mortal". It is also apparent that the game believes adding creepy looking binary (yes, literally 1s and 0s) everywhere will result in the audience weeping in fear. In other parts of the game, it unironically uses creepy looking ASCII to increase the horror value. Keep in mind, this game takes itself seriously.
The puzzle mechanics, or should I say mechanic, are all the same. You pretty much lead a key to a finish line by properly placing a bunch of obstacles to get through logic gates. At first, the idea was sort of neat, but after the 20th time I finished it, I could not help but grow impatient. The puzzles are practically the same thing over and over again. They are boring, repetitive, and dull, which is bad considering solving these puzzles is 90% of the game. Other parts of the game involved you moving your mouse sporadically across the screen in hopes you would find a button that would allow you to proceed to the next level. This is completely brainless design, but I don't think the creators of Pony Island cared for quality anyway.
You also have to proceed levels eventually by controlling a crying pony with devil wings that shoots binary death lasers to kill evil devil skulls that are trying to kill you. Again, this game is taking itself seriously.
There are many, many things wrong with Pony Island. It is a disgrace to the horror genre, and is a disgrace to the medium. Many flawed horror games I can still give credit for trying (Five Nights at Freddies) for doing some aspects right. I cannot usher any praise for Pony Island. It is a game stained with terrible design and mind bogglingly awful writing. Stay away at all costs.

This is not a city builder game. It's a city builder simulation. The gameplay is very minimal - most of the time it's fiddeling with traffic. Which is great! It's your own self-inflicted puzzel. Traffic quickly becomes a nightmare if you don't know what you're doing (I still don't), but its still a ton of fun to build a city and watch it grow.
If you're someone who doesn't like mods, or "cheats," I can't recommend this game. By defualt, you start in an empty map with absolutly nothing. You're supposed to start small and branch out, getting access to more tools as your population grows. But those tools they hide away are vital to run a functioning city, and you'll eventually have to bulldoze your entire starting zone because it is so inefficent compared to everything you can build at high pop levels. Theres a really simple fix to all this: pop on the infanite money "mod" built into the game and download a mod off the workshop to have everything unlocked from the start so you can get straight to building a city. When you feel confident about your layout, you can always turn off infanite money, but by that point  you'll be swimming in cash.
I still love it. I think you will too - but that really depends on what you want out of your city builder. Skylines pushes you hard into one type of city - one of clean energy, tight motropolises, and a service economy. Industry is there, sure, but it really discourages you from using those. What it does do, it does well.

"The Sad Story of Emmeline Burns" is what you expect. A tearjerking visual novel game that tells the story of a little girl. For a free game, this exceeded my expectations!
Graphics:
The drawings in this game were pretty unique! It was a combination of regular artwork with a little anime touch to them. It is bright, colorful, and cheery.
Story:
This is the story of Toma Andrews, who is a socially awkward girl. She feels her name has no meaning whatsoever and believes she is nothing. There is one weird thing that her and her mom have in common: they love to visit the graveyard and love talking about their ancestors. One day though, she skipped school and hung out at the graveyard again. This is where she comes across a peculiar girl named Emmeline Burns.
And...I stop there for spoiler purposes. All I can say about the story is OH MY GOD THE FEELS!!! I actually cried during the end of the game and for the characters of the story. The story is just...downright beautiful and tear-jerking.
Music:
I loved the piano pieces in this game. It fits perfectly with the story and the graphics. It was a combination of relaxing, bittersweet happiness, and sadness. I could get absorbed into this soundtrack.
Gameplay:
Visual Novel. You know the drill. Oh...it does have extras though! A music box, a gallery, and an extra scene when you complete the game!
Overall:
The Sad Story of Emmeline Burns pulls your heartstrings with tragedy, happiness, and bittersweetness. This is one of those games where everything comes together. The beautiful piano music, the bright and beautiful unique artwork, and the bittersweet tearjerking story.--Okay. Why is this game free to play? Seriously, if I known it would be this good, I'd fork over my money without waiting for a sale(yes I'm that cheap). Ahem...right. As I said before, this game exceeded my expectations. Normally, you see reviews "Eh...it's my money's worth." or "Another crappy free-to-play game." However, this is different. This is a visual novel gem that everyone should play through and proves, regardless of what happens, everything will turn out well in the end as long as you see it through.

I really enjoyed this puzzle game. It takes the "start on one block and run along all other blocks without reusing a block or getting trapped" and it adds a couple things. You're an adventurer collecting coins. And since you can't pass a level without standing on every block (including the coin ones) you'll never lose out on your growing fortune. On the flip side, I have no idea what those coins are for but.... they sure are fun to collect! Also, on each level, is a brown box which is your exit. So try to angle towards that last. If you run onto the brown block without stepping on all the others, there's a weird explosion noise and you begin at the start of the level.
There are 60 levels and most you'll probably whiz by. But I found quite a few a little challenging and I found all of them fun. This game won't win any graphic awards but the music was nice and catchy. If you enjoy puzzles and particularly if you enjoy 100%ing a steam game, I recommend this. If you're looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if you're looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

Even though Hook was and is still very successful and popular, it always felt monotonous and too easy; it simply bored me despite its elegant concept. Klocki, however, introduces two important changes to such an elegant puzzle concept – diversity and challenge.
There are various gameplay mechanics all going very well together. The general goal is to move tiles to achieve a closed circuit.
Moving the tiles is done by either swapping two tiles on a grid, rotating them, rotating several tiles at once or by sliding them to empty places. Given the available moving mechanics, you have to figure out how to correctly arrange the present tiles.
These tiles can be black squares who mustn't touch each other, red or yellow wires who have to be connected and red or green areas who have to be connected as well. All of those might also be immovable, which adds another great gameplay element.
Another important aspect to mention is that you can't just move all tiles where you wan't them to be. There are "grids" based on the perspective of the level which show you which tiles are interchangeable.
Klocki offers many levels and I needed about 45 minutes to complete all of them. These levels begin very simple and slowly introduce new concepts leading to more complex levels. The complexity is never too high, but high enough to maintain a small challenge (in contrast to Hook, where there was no challenge at all for me). This way, you will consistently enjoy it (provided that you don't always need brain-twisting puzzles) and have a relaxing experience.
All in All

As a fan of adventure games i am always looking for new and entertaining adventure games to play. I‘m very picky and not every adventure game will satisfy my needs. I have stumbled on Sherlock Holmes Crimes and Punishment a while ago and added it to my wishlist. I bought it on summer sale and i don‘t regret it. I love the game.
First thing what caughts  the eye is graphics. It is rare for an adventure game to have a really good graphics. Keep in mind that „technically good“ and „nice to the eye“ is different. A drawn 2D graphics can look much better than technically more advanced 3D graphics with poor 3D models. I remember when Broken Sword gone to 3D graphics, it looked awful, i was angry about that, i was disappointed that developers decided to go that way instead of just classical 2D graphics. It was a trend at that time and it was a bad trend. Sherlock Holmes Crimes and Punishment is one of those adventure games in full 3D where graphics looks really nice. Character face models are amazing. It lacks better animations like in Beyond two souls, Heavy rain or LA Noire, but i guess this game had much smaller budget, so it‘s really amazing what they had achieved in graphics department. Environments looks great too. You can take rally nice looking screenshots. The environments are different and pretty detailed. In short i don‘t have any complaints regarding graphics.
The game consists from 6 chapters which are 2,5-3 hours long each. The gameplay consists from exploring the crime scene, taking notice of every detail, gathering evidence and talking to the witnesses and victims. After all these things are done you can start a deduction process where you must make connections between collected statements and evidence and get a conclusion. There are few outcomes in every case, there‘re always few suspects and you can wrongly accuse a person of doing a crime and condemned him. But most fun is to find out who‘s the real culprit is. Even when you find him you can absolve him or make him guilty so that he would receive his punishment. It‘s your moral choice at the end of the chapter.
The game is not too hard but it‘s not easy either. You can be stuck at some point not knowing what to do. As always it‘s just some small thing you missed. There are some puzzles in the game. Each case has few of them. I like that puzzles are all different and are pretty logical and not too complicated except for lock hacking puzzles. They‘re in every case and sometimes you get more than one of it. But you can skip the puzzles, it doesn‘t have any impact to the story or outcome.
All in all i recommend this game to everyone who loves adventure games, you will not be disappointed. This is one of those hidden gems (*cough* The Book of Unwritten Tales 2 *cough*) made by a small company which probably didn‘t pay back.

This game reminds me of why I spent hours playing Nancy Drew games when I was younger. I love mystery type games where you have to search for clues but this game is a bit more than that. You get to make choices and moral decisions with different possible outcomes. There's not a set path that eventually leads you to one conclusion. It's possible to reach multiple conclusions and find different characters guilty. You have to choose whether you will condemn or absolve them and that has its own outcomes too. It is possible to reach a wrong conclusion! Also, you can reach the correct conclusion but mess up during a mini-game at the end and not receive your acheivement. (You can replay the endings though.)
The scenery is pretty awesome and I especially love the atmosphere in some of the places. The Blood Bath case is my favorite so far with all the different places to explore and clues to find. There are a few somewhat creepy-feeling places in this case too which I love. :)
My only complaint is that there are long loading screens and lots of them. There is a black loading screen before you get to the carriage loading scene. A loading screen for a loading screen is a little frustrating. But at least during the carriage loading screen you can open up your casebook or check deductions so it's not too bad.
Overall I would defintiely recommend Crimes and Punishments, especially if you are a Sherlock fan, and I'm definitely going to be checking out the other Sherlock games after I finish this one.

Just Hero is an old school platformer under the guise of being a "difficult" game; however, the issue is not that the game is difficult, but it seems to have been purposefully released with bugs that make it difficult.
The most prevalent issue you will encounter is a lack of response with your jump. As your character gets too close to an edge, your character will not jump, and instead fall down. This is echoed with several other negative reviews. Falling normally wouldn't anger me, but in this game, any fall that is from a height greater than your jump will damage you. If, while you are falling and get damaged, you fall again, you will continuously take damage as you hit descending blocks. It's definitely a difficult system, but it wouldn't be nearly as bad if your jump registered.
This game is all about jumping. It requires you to perfect your jump to long-jump across pits, and because of that, I'll end this review here. The gameplay is incredibly poor with the issue of jumping. You will not have fun. It turned a 5 minute game into a frustrating 20 minutes, and I didn't feel happy or accomplished when I beat this game. If you aren't good at this game, it's not because you're not good at this game, it's because the developer released a poor game that doesn't respond to controls that gamers have been accustomed to over the years.
